This paper investigates the application of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for modeling biological neural activity, specifically using the *C. Elegans* neural network as a case study. We demonstrate that RNNs can be effectively trained to replicate both genetic activity patterns and sensory responses across various datasets, including average and individual animal activity sequences generated via calcium imaging. Our findings indicate that a RNN with 10 hidden neurons, trained on individual animal data, achieves an R² score of 0.99, suggesting the model captures significant biological insights. Furthermore, we show that these trained networks can reproduce novel, unseen stimuli and individual animal activity sequences, underscoring the potential of RNNs to encode biological information. These results suggest that RNNs can capture essential biological features, potentially offering a viable alternative to biophysical models. Additionally, we address and resolve common challenges in training deep learning models for time-series regression. Finally, to facilitate future research, we introduce a new Python-based training and evaluation toolkit that supports multiple calcium imaging datasets and various neural models. This study demonstrates that training neural networks on calcium imaging data can yield valuable scientific insights, and we hope this work encourages further exploration into the application of machine learning to calcium imaging. This study investigates the electromagnetic traits of hidden-strangeness molecular pentaquarks (PMs) possessing a single strange quark. By calculating their magnetic moments and dipole moments, we identify two distinct PM states, ${\cal P}_{\bar{D}K}^{S=+}$ and ${\cal P}_{\bar{D}K}^{S=-}$, that align well with experimental data. Specifically, the magnetic moments are $\mu_{\cal P}^{S=+}=+0.81+0.04 i$ $\mu_N$ and $\mu_{\cal P}^{S=-}=-0.80+0.04 i$ $\mu_N$, while the electric dipole moments are $d_{\cal P}^{S=+}=+1.25\times 10^{-16}\times 1.24 i$ $e$ cm and $d_{\cal P}^{S=-}=-1.25\times 1.24 i$ $e$ cm. We further compute the helicity amplitudes $A_{\gamma p \rightarrow \gamma p} = -0.16+0.01 i$ GeV$^{-1}$ and $B_{\gamma p \rightarrow \gamma p} = -0.01+0.00 i$ GeV$^{-1}$, which correspond to the polarized $\Sigma(p) \rightarrow \gamma(p) $ decay. Additionally, we estimate the production cross sections for these states in the reaction $\gamma p \rightarrow {\cal P}_{\bar{D} K}^{S=+} N \rightarrow \gamma p$, finding values of $\sigma_{\gamma p \rightarrow \gamma p} = 0.0002$ mb and $\sigma_{\Sigma(p) \rightarrow \gamma(p)} = 0.0002$ mb, respectively. These findings suggest that photoproduction experiments could potentially reveal the electromagnetic characteristics of concealed-charm molecular PMs with solitary strangeness. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for understanding the internal structure of PMs. Notably, our analysis indicates that molecular PM states with double strangeness may be more challenging to detect than those with single strangeness. In this paper, we demonstrate that all Zinbiel algebras are solvable. Additionally, we provide a characterization of those Zinbiel algebras that are also Lie algebras and present the classification of Zinbiel structures on the two-dimensional space $\mathbb{R}^2$. Finally, we offer a counterexample to the conjecture proposed by J. Van de Velde and N. Zhao in [Zinbiel algebras, arXiv:2009.00600, 2020] regarding the associativity of the symmetrized product $[x,y,z] = (x \circ z) \circ y$. Specifically, we identify a broad class of non-associative examples where the symmetrized product defines a Zinbiel product, yet the operation $\circ$ lacks associativity. Furthermore, we illustrate that for this class of examples, the symmetrized product yields a Zinbiel algebra, whereas the reversed symmetrized product yields a Postnikov algebra. Consequently, this confirms the theorem by J. Van de Velde and N. Zhao [Zinbiel algebras, arXiv:2009.00600, 2020], which states that every Zinbiel product can be expressed as a $\sigma$-symmetrization of a commutative Pre-Lie product, thereby distinguishing Zinbiel algebras from both Lie and Postnikov algebras. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first instance of a non-associative Pre-Lie algebra. We also examine conditions under which a Zinbiel product arises from the symmetrized product of a commutative Pre-Lie product, deriving an expression for the Pre-Lie product in terms of $\circ$. These expressions enable the classification of Zinbiel structures on the four-dimensional space $\mathbb{R}^4$ when the product originates from a commutative Pre-Lie structure. We present several illustrative examples. Furthermore, we establish that if the symmetrized product of a commutative Pre-Lie product is associative, then the underlying commutative Pre-Lia product is actually a Pre-Lie product of a Lie algebra. This leads to a characterization of which commutative Pre-Lie products generate Zinbiel algebras and provides an explicit formula for the Pre-Lie product

By applying Strichartz estimates tailored to H^s(R^3) x H^s(R^3) and specifically designed for this equation, alongside perturbation-based arguments, we demonstrate low-regularity global well-posedness and the existence of scattering within L^2(R^3). Furthermore, we establish the existence of a complete norm-dependent scattering set in H^s(R^3) for sufficiently high regularity levels. Finally, we prove local-in-time-in-time almost conservation of mass and energy for these solutions. Notably, these findings represent the first results of their kind for cubic Heterogeneous Schrödinger equations with inverse quadratic potentials in both three and higher dimensions. Additionally, similar techniques and strategies are anticipated to be applicable to other Schrödinger equations involving other potential types. Specifically, in three dimensions, these methods have already yielded several significant results for the cubic Heterogeneous Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation with an inverse square potential. Finally, we outline future research directions concerning lower regularity global well-posedness and scattering for the 3D Cubic Heterogeneous Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation with an inverse square potential. We investigate the migration-transmission process, which models how a story spreads from a donor country to a recipient country and how ideas are transmitted within the domestic system of the source nation. This process is driven by a parameter known as the migration-transmission factor, denoted as $\gamma$. The dynamics of this process are analyzed using a system of two ordinary differential equations, resulting in a planar model that features a line of non-hyperbolic fixed points and a line of saddle-node fixed points. Our focus lies on the non-hyperbolic fixed points, specifically the line labeled $L_+$. Our analysis reveals that the fixed points emerging from the non-hyperbolic line $L_+$ are unstable, whereas those generated from the saddle-node line are stable. Furthermore, we examine the asymptotic behavior of the system's solutions, demonstrating that trajectories approach stable fixed points originating from $L_+$. These stable points represent equilibrium states where the recipient country's population adopts the recipient country's idea, while the source country's population either fully shifts to the recipient country's idea or retains the source country's idea alongside the recipient one. Additionally, we explore the behavior of solutions near non-hyperbolic fixed points on $L_+$, where the eigenvalues are $0$ and $-1$. We outline methods for analyzing this scenario, including a straightforward approach that leverages the specific structure of our model's differential equations. This alternative method avoids the need for normal forms and blow-up techniques, which are typically required for general systems. We also address a degenerate case where eigenvalues become $0$ and $0$, and provide numerical simulations to illustrate the model's solutions. The initial value problem is solved both analytically and numerically, revealing that the recipient country's solutions exhibit sigmoidal curves. We also note that the model's solutions are periodic, although this feature lacks practical significance. Finally, we outline future research directions. K2-138 hosts a multi-planet system that appears to align with the super-period resonance (SPR) sequence. Prior research identified an SPR 5:2 resonance mode spanning five planets, although the 3:2 resonance segment within this chain lacked a confirmed candidate. This study employs the Generalized Least Squares (GLS) method to detect exoplanets in the K2-138 light curve, successfully identifying a new transiting planet, K2-138 f, which exhibits a 3:2 SPR mode. We further examine the SPR characteristics of the K2-138 system and compare its properties with other known SPR systems. Finally, we explore the potential for future transit observations of K2-138 f and propose a rough estimation of the likelihood of coexisting inner planets. These findings offer valuable insights for characterizing the system's architecture and inform strategies for follow-up observations. Additionally, our analysis code is publicly available to facilitate future SPR research. This work is dedicated to the memory of our mentor, Professor Stephen Snubeny. However, the detector design and technology strategy working group has since identified several issues regarding the SiD concept that require resolution. Additionally, specific demands linked to system integration and HL-LC technology advancements have been established. Consequently, these considerations have prompted modifications to the SiD design. This contribution outlines the identified problems, the proposed solutions, and an updated design derived from these adjustments. The primary modifications involve: relocating the innermost pixel layers further from the interaction point (IP) to accommodate a larger beam pipe; substituting the inner two modules with a specialized "beam pipe detector"; integrating a fast control system to enable inner modules to function in a standalone mode; and utilizing a robust cooling technology that allows for higher radiation doses and ensures system reliability. Furthermore, the six-drift chamber layers originally intended for hadron identification have been eliminated to facilitate the installation of additional pixel modules near the IP. The resulting design enhances performance by enabling better hermeticity, superior robustness, and an extended operational lifetime. Specifically, the innermost modules, engineered as beam pipe detectors with an integrated cooling and support system, are positioned just behind the beam pipe, while the modules formerly between the first and second layers are relocated closer to the IP. We introduce a method for detecting crystalline-ice regions within non-crystalline (amorphous) ices by utilizing the recently developed Weighted Average Radial Distribution Function (W-RGDF) and a model based on the ice model theory. This approach is demonstrated through applications to amorphous water and amorphous hydrogen sulfide, where we examine the structural and dynamical characteristics of these regions. Our findings indicate that crystalline regions in amorphous ice are defined by an icosahedral short-range order featuring fivefold symmetry. Furthermore, these regions exhibit stronger hydrogen bonds and a higher density than the surrounding environment. They also display significantly lower self-diffusion coefficients, suggesting they are "caged" within denser, more hydrogen-bonded but disordered matrices. These crystalline regions display a broad size distribution, with most having diameters under 2 nm, though some can be substantially larger. Finally, we demonstrate that, given identical thermal and chemical histories, both amorphous water and hydrogen sulfide can exist in polyamorphic states, possessing low-density and high-density configurations. In both cases, crystalline regions are predominantly located within the low-density amorphous phase. These insights offer a pathway to understanding the nature of these long-debated amorphous states. Ultimately, we argue that the discovery of crystalline regions within amorphous ices could significantly impact our understanding of icy moons and comet nuclei. For instance, the presence of liquid water, a key ingredient for life, becomes plausible if such regions exist. Additionally, the existence of these regions could help resolve the "ice crisis" regarding the thermal evolution of icy moons. Finally, our findings suggest that icy moons may harbor liquid water in certain locations, thereby influencing the potential for extraterrestrial life. This could explain the recent detection of methane plumes from Saturn's moon Enceladus and active geysers on Jupiter's moon Europa. Furthermore, our results may help explain the dynamical behavior of comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, as observed by the Rosetta mission. Specifically, the comet's low outgassing rates, the presence of methane, and the absence of sulfur dioxide can be attributed to the existence of crystalline-ice regions within its icy crust. We conclude that the detection of crystalline-ice regions within amorphous ices is highly probable and that our proposed methodology is a valuable tool for their identification. This technique is widely applicable to various amorphous substances

This study presents atomically resolved images of the surface structures for simple materials—graphite, gold, silicon, and bi-molecular crystals—using Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM). A primary objective was to evaluate the Local Density of States (LDOS) at the position of the terminating atom within a CO-functionalized Si-tip. By employing CO-functionalized Si(111)-(7x7) tips, we achieved superior LDOS sensitivity compared to using bare Si-tip apexes alone. Our findings indicate that LDOS-stimulated STM imaging with these CO-tip apexes effectively resolves the atomic structures of the aforementioned simple materials. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the specific orbital interactions between the CO and the tip enable the imaging of the atomic structure of bi-molecular crystals. These results provide a foundation for future investigations into the LDOS of more complex materials. The paper also discusses the operational principles of STM, the characteristics of CO-functionalized Si-tip apexes, and the specific experimental conditions required for the STM imaging presented here. Finally, the work addresses the interpretation of LDOS in STM imaging and the analysis of the CO-tip apex. Ultimately, this study aims to facilitate future research into the LDOS of materials using high-resolution STM. Keywords: Scanning Tunneling Microscopy, Local Density of States, CO-functionalized Si-tip apex. 1. Introduction 1.1 Scanning Tunneling Microscopy Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) is a technique that utilizes a tunneling current to image the surface structure of materials at atomic resolution. Developed by G. Binnig and H. Rohrer in 1980 at IBM Research Zurich [1], it has been widely adopted in materials science for over four decades. The fundamental principle of STM relies on the quantum mechanical phenomenon of tunneling, which occurs when a conductive probe (a conductive material with a sharp apex) is positioned near a conductive sample surface. When a bias voltage is applied between the sample and the probe, electrons tunnel through the vacuum gap separating them. This tunneling current is exponentially dependent on both the gap distance and the bias voltage. By keeping the tunneling current constant during the scan, the vertical position of the probe reflects the local electronic structure of the sample surface. Consequently, STM can achieve atomic resolution. The tunneling current is influenced by the local electronic structure of the sample surface, a property known as the Local Density of States (LDOS). This allows STM to image the surface structure based on the material's LDOS.

This paper presents a framework designed to enhance theorem provers with automated proof verification capabilities, specifically for production-level Isar proofs within the Isabelle (2021) system. Isar proofs, which are often more complex and utilize extensive language features compared to Hilbert-style formulations, pose significant challenges for automated provers. We identify and address two primary obstacles: (i) the absence of a formal language definition suitable for automated analysis, and (ii) difficulties in automatically generating appropriate proof targets for these Isar formulations. Our solution involves a hybrid approach that integrates automated theorem provers with human expertise from proof engineers. We demonstrate the framework's utility by applying it to examine and improve the Isabelle AFP library (2005–2021), the largest collection of published formal proofs globally. This application yields three key benefits: (i) it provides an independent assessment of the library's structural health; (ii) it significantly increases the proportion of the library for which proofs can be automatically verified; and (iii) it offers a flexible mechanism for users to customize the proof demonstration process. Furthermore, we outline applications extending beyond initial demonstrations, such as assessing the library's logical consistency and strengthening various foundational theorems. Finally, we conclude by discussing how the framework supports additional applications in areas like mathematical research support and automated mathematical writing. The authors have integrated these methods directly into the Isabelle/AFP infrastructure to ensure easy access for proof engineers. Additional experimental code and data are accessible at https://github.com/rewenli/IsarDemo. The inner Earth's magnetosphere is a dynamic environment where the interaction between the solar wind and the geomagnetic field drives the formation of a cavity known as the magnetosphere. This area is not static; it experiences continuous fluctuations driven by the solar wind. These variations occur across multiple scales, from rapid changes in the solar wind to slower oscillations within the magnetosphere itself. Notably, the magnetosphere supports ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves spanning 0.1 to 10 Hz. These waves are not random; they are often coherent and can be detected by ground-based observatories, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms generating the disturbances. This study proposes a method to make ULF waves audible to humans, specifically within the 20 Hz to 2 kHz range. While the inherent frequencies of ULF waves fall below the limit of human hearing, their amplitude modulations often occur at higher frequencies. By analyzing the power spectral density of various ULF phenomena, we identified those with the highest modulation frequencies. We then developed an algorithm to compress the 20–29 Hz band into the 200–290 Hz range and applied similar compression to higher bands. Subsequently, we calculated the power spectral density of the modulation frequencies for each band and adjusted the amplitude of the corresponding frequency range to fall within human hearing capabilities. Finally, we recombined the signal to ensure fidelity. This method was tested using real data from the SuperMAG database, which contains hourly snapshots of global ground-based magnetometer observations. The resulting signals were evaluated by a panel of 12 scientists, including geomagnetism experts, to assess their perceptibility. Their feedback highlighted both the method's achievements and areas for improvement. Based on their input, we plan to refine the approach in future work. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate human perception of ULF waves, thereby enhancing our understanding of their origins and the underlying physical mechanisms. The paper outlines the current status of the method, the responses received, and outlines potential future directions. Ultimately, this work represents an initial step toward enabling humans to "hear" ULF waves. The corresponding source code is available at: https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/MakeCoherentULFPhenomenaAudible. The repository includes: (1) a dataset of selected, well-known, and coherent geomagnetic phenomena; (2) the methodology for rendering these phenomena audible; (3) the original recordings of the phenomena; and (4) the spectral components of the phenomena

This study investigates the classical dilaton-electromagnetic dilaton gravity framework, which extends the non-linear Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton system by incorporating a specific non-linear electromagnetic action known as logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics (LNE). We apply this theory to charged, rotating black membranes (BM) within an AdS$_4$ background, focusing on the large-rotation regime. The analysis examines the thermodynamic properties, including the causal structure, Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, and the rotational speed of the event horizon. Furthermore, we verify that the first law of thermodynamics and the Smarr-like relation for charged rotating BMs hold true within this theory, while also exploring the conditions for their stability. Finally, we demonstrate the potential significance of the charged rotating BM solution in this gravity model as an effective model for astrophysical compact objects. This research is motivated by the need to understand high-energy phenomena, such as those occurring near black hole event horizons, where quantum effects are negligible and classical physics suffices. These objects may exhibit superluminal rotation speeds and anomalous thermodynamic behaviors, including negative temperatures and entropies. Our findings suggest that charged rotating BM solutions in this dilaton-gravity framework offer a viable framework for describing such exotic astrophysical objects. This model expands the range of possible observable characteristics of these objects, thereby enhancing the accuracy of their detection and measurement. This advancement is crucial for deepening our understanding of the universe and its underlying physical laws. This conclusion is supported by the recent observational evidence regarding the rapid rotation of these astrophysical entities. This rotation is attributed to the presence of electromagnetic fields, which are described by the logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics used in this study. This theoretical approach provides a more accurate representation of electromagnetic phenomena in high-energy environments, such as those surrounding black holes. Observations of the TW Hydrae (TW Hya) disk have revealed a low-temperature molecular gas component, with researchers debating whether this component is best explained by photoevaporation or an MHD disk breeze model. To differentiate between these two scenarios, we project observations for the next generation of high-angular resolution radio telescopes, specifically the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) and the Next Generation Very Large Array (NGVA). Our analysis indicates that both models predict line widths comparable to those of the National Radio Astronomy Observatory's Green Bank Telescope (GBT) and the European VLBI Array (EVN). However, the NGVA is capable of resolving the SKA-predicted spatial scales, which are critical for distinguishing between the models. We predict that the NGVA will resolve a radial scale of approximately 10 astronomical units (AU) at TW Hya, whereas the EVR will resolve about 25 AU. We conclude that the radial scale of the molecular gas component is a key metric for differentiation; a scale smaller than 15 AU would favor the photoevaporation model, while a scale exceeding 25 AU would support the MHD disk breeze model. Additionally, we examine the implications of radial scales recently reported by the EVN. Finally, we address the potential for using spectral line ratios to differentiate between the models, noting that while both predict similar ratios for H213CO, H218O, and HCO+, the photoevaporation model predicts a lower H218CO/H213CO ratio compared to the MHD disk breeze model. These projected observations are anticipated to provide valuable insights into the radial distribution of molecular gas in TW Hya. This study presents the findings from a detailed finite element method analysis of a two-core phase-angle-modulating transformer equipped with a symmetrical interleaved air-gap configuration. The focus is on the transient characteristics of this design, specifically examining the impact of inter-core flux on the DC saturation of modulating windings. The analysis reveals that during the initial modulation cycles, DC current does not immediately reach its steady-state value. This delay is primarily caused by the inductance inherent in the transitory interleaved air-gap, which only diminishes progressively as the modulating flux from one core begins to cancel out the flux in the other. Consequently, the modulating DC current can be significantly lower than expected in the early cycles. These insights are verified through transient simulations of a prototype transformer, which also demonstrate a substantial reduction in the effective peak-to-peak AC current. This decrease is directly linked to the lower DC current, thereby lowering the RMS AC current and enhancing transformer efficiency. The research concludes that the described transients are an intrinsic feature of this interleaved trans-former topology, and this phenomenon must be accounted for when designing the modulating winding. Furthermore, the analysis quantifies the inter-core flux within the interleaved air-gap, enabling the safeguarding of transients by optimizing the number of turns in the modulating windings. Finally, the study quantifies the cancellation of modulating flux by the inter-core flux, facilitating the categorization of these transients as either persistent or self-limiting. This classification is crucial for the proper design of damping and short-circuit protection systems. Overall, the inter-core flux within the interleaved air-gap is shown to be a critical design parameter that significantly influences the performance of two-core symmetric phase-angle-modulating transformers. The system couples a finite Timoshenko beam with a fractional Timoshenko beam and is formulated as an abstract dynamical system in a Hilbert space. We demonstrate that the generator is sectorial, ensuring the analyticity of the associated semigroup, and further prove the compactness of the resolvent, which guarantees a discrete spectrum for the generator. These properties are established through the analysis of the eigenvalue problem for the generator. Finally, we examine the asymptotic behavior of the resolvent to derive the decay rate of the energy norm within the time domain. Under specific geometric and physical assumptions, we establish polynomial stability for the energy norm; however, without these additional conditions, global hypoellipticity of the generator prevents the determination of stability. Additionally, we address the well-posedness of the system within a Gelfand triple framework, a requirement necessitated by the presence of a negative unbounded operator representing the strain energy of the fractional component in the mass operator. The recent detection of $r$-process elements in neutron-star merger ejecta has reignited interest in modeling the rapid neutron-capture process, which governs the synthesis of approximately half the periodic table. To accurately model the $r$-process, researchers must predict nuclear properties, specifically separation energies, with exceptional precision. However, the complexity and dynamism of the process render precise analytical solutions currently unattainable. Consequently, the focus has shifted toward machine learning, which can achieve the necessary accuracy if models reach a relative error below $10^{-4}$. This study demonstrates that a graph neural network, utilizing a multi-step training protocol, can achieve these predictions with an average relative error of $3.1 \times 10^{-5}$. Furthermore, we provide open-source Python code that implements nuclear weights derived from these machine-learning separation energies, offering an efficient and precise tool for future $r$-process explorations. Our analysis indicates that the open-source, pure machine-learning model achieves this level of precision across the entire training grid, while custom-tuned hybrid models perform even better in specific regions. These findings suggest that the path toward modeling $r$-process conditions has been successfully navigated, paving the way for astrophysical investigations into the phenomenon. This research was conducted using the open-source, high-performance computing platform $r$NucML. We demonstrate a microwave technique for measuring dielectric dissipation in sapphire at temperatures below 4 K, utilizing a high-quality factor (Q) of $10^6$ and a detection sensitivity of $10^{-10}$, which corresponds to 1 ppm per degree Kelvin. At 4 K, the measured dielectric dissipation ($\chi^{\prime\prime}/\chi^{\prime}$) of sapphire is $1.4\times 10^{-7}$ at 10 GHz, representing $1.0\times 10^{-7}$ (100 ppb). This value is 100 times lower than the 1 ppm level typically targeted in quantum applications for microwave dielectrics. The measured dissipation is consistent with the temperature dependence of the imaginary part of the susceptibility derived from the Cavity-Diode Method. Furthermore, our findings confirm that, in the quantum domain, dielectric loss scales with $\omega T_2^2$ rather than $\omega T_2$. Finally, we demonstrate that the imaginary susceptibility of sapphire, $1.4\times 10^{-7}/10^{-1}$, is approximately 1,000 times greater than the corresponding quality factor of superconducting niobium, $10^{-10}/10^{-4}$. This establishes sapphire as a superior dielectric for superconducting quantum applications. Additionally, the microwave dissipation of sapphire at $T=15$ mK, $1.0\times 10^{-7}$, is only 1.4 times higher than at $T=1$ mK, $7\times 10^{-8}$, indicating that sapphire quantum dissipation remains nearly constant down to 15 mK. This characteristic is advantageous for applications operating at the lowest achievable temperatures, such as those employing dilution refrigerators equipped with an on-chip still. Finally, we outline the potential impact of employing sapphire dielectrics in superconducting quantum applications. Specifically, replacing silicon surface passivation oxides with sapphire could reduce dielectric loss by a factor of 100, while substituting aluminum chips with sapphire could lower losses by a factor of 1,000. The concept of optical pulling forces is examined within both classical and quantum frameworks. In the classical approach, the pertinent length scale is the wavelength of light, whereas in the quantum approach, it is the vacuum gap separating the object and the source. The discussion outlines the foundational principles enabling optical pulling and reviews recent advancements in this field. Furthermore, the necessary material properties for this phenomenon are analyzed, emphasizing metamaterials and their limitations. The paper concludes by highlighting key experimental results achieved with real materials and proposing promising directions for future research. Overall, optical pulling represents a nascent yet rapidly evolving area with significant potential for fundamental scientific inquiry and technological application. Additionally, it offers a valuable context for understanding the persistent challenge of reducing the energy consumption of data centers. Specifically, this has driven the proposal of quantum friction forces, which can pull objects toward vacuum fluctuations and, consequently, radiative energy reservoirs such as laser beams. This review aims to elucidate the underlying physics, including both fundamental and quasi-classical calculations of optical pulling forces, and to suggest promising avenues for future investigation. Finally, it addresses how this phenomenon can help lower the energy costs associated with data center operations.

This study investigates resilient design for a two-stage stochastic linear program featuring a set of all possible scenarios and disruptions characterized by binary variables. To address the resulting integer linear program, we develop a tailored cut generation method. Our approach begins by relaxing the problem to a linear program and subsequently deriving a finite set of cuts based on the structure of the dual solution. These cuts are then integrated into the optimization model, with a branch-and-cut algorithm employed to solve the problem efficiently. Numerical experiments on standard benchmark instances demonstrate that this proposed method is highly effective and substantially outperforms existing techniques in the literature. A Python implementation of the method is made available on GitHub. Additionally, we highlight the advantages of incorporating resilience into optimization models, using the context of resilient power supply chain management as a practical application example. Our analysis of this case study reveals that integrating resilience strategies can significantly reduce total costs under potential supply chain disruptions, even if initial robustness investments are higher. A detailed case study is also provided to illustrate these insights. Finally, we explore the connection between our proposed method and a general framework for constructing lattice-type cuts. This work is the first of its kind to offer both theoretical insights and a comprehensive implementation for all possible scenario and binary disruption cases. Furthermore, our method can be readily adapted to handle arbitrary disruption scenarios and other types of higher-order moments, such as those discussed in [1].

Graph Neural Architectures (GNA) have become a dominant approach for learning on graph-structured data. While extensive research focuses on enhancing single-task performance, the issue of knowledge transfer within GNA has been largely overlooked. This study addresses that gap by investigating whether and how GNA transfers knowledge during architecture unrolling. Through an in-depth analysis of the internal data flow of a representative GNA model, we demonstrate that knowledge transfer occurs within its layers. We further validate this finding using empirical evidence regarding model components and training dynamics. Finally, we explain these observations by linking the characteristics of GNA to established learning theories. Our study offers a more comprehensive understanding of GNA architectures and their knowledge transfer mechanisms, providing guidance for designing efficient models. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical significance of our findings by demonstrating how it facilitates the creation of high-performing models for both transductive and inductive node classification. The experimental results confirm that our proposed method consistently achieves superior results across all induction bias settings. Code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepGraphLib/graphne_unrolling.

Recommendation systems are a critical component of e-commerce platforms, designed to assist users in locating items that match their preferences. However, traditional approaches often fail to effectively balance two fundamental and often conflicting user needs: the discovery of novel items and the retrieval of familiar ones. Drawing inspiration from recent research in generative adversarial networks (GANs), and specifically from CycleGAN's ability to learn complex, multi-modal feature distributions, we propose a recommendation model that incorporates an adversarial training mechanism using a CycleGAN-inspired framework. This model enables the system to cater to both user preferences when encountering pre- and post-filtering incoherence, as well as their exploratory desires. Empirical evaluations on two public recommendation datasets demonstrate that our method significantly enhances overall recommendation quality, achieving substantial improvements in metrics such as NDCG and recalling pre-filtering related user interests. Furthermore, these experimental results validate the efficacy of the dual-feature distribution model, confirming its superiority over state-of-the-art alternatives. Additionally, we show that the model is lightweight, easily deployable, and requires no additional computational resources. Finally, we have deployed this model on the OpenAlibaba Cloud to support e-commerce e-books. This implementation assists users in discovering new e-books they are interested in while also suggesting familiar titles, thereby improving the shopping experience. The cloud interface is accessible at https://www.dualgan.com/. This marks the first time a generative adversarial network has been applied to the field of e-commerce recommendations. We present a novel and straightforward proof of the Set Disjointness problem under constraints of small space and time, utilizing a single-pass data stream algorithm. Specifically, for any two sets $A$ and $B$ where $|A| \le k$ and $|B| \le k$, and given a parameter $c \ge 1$, we demonstrate that if these sets are $\epsilon$-disjoint with respect to $c$ (meaning $|(A \times \{0\}) \cup (B \times \{1\})| \cap \Delta_c \le \epsilon k^2$, where $\Delta_c$ represents the graph of pairs at least distance $c$ apart), then there exists a randomized algorithm using a data stream with space complexity $O(\frac{k^2}{\epsilon^2} \log^2 c)$ and time complexity $O(\frac{k}{\epsilon} \log c)$. This approach relies solely on the widely recognized Strong Sketching Conjecture. The proof is direct, employs only a single data stream, and is conceptually simpler than the recent method of Andoni et al. (arXiv:2101.01301), which and their work are the first to establish the first complete proof for this problem. Furthermore, our methodology and findings hold significant potential for future research in data streams. For instance, our framework yields a deterministic data stream algorithm for estimating the number of pairs at distance $1$ in the Hamming metric. Additionally, by integrating our method with the recent dynamic streaming algorithm of Andoni et al. (arXiv:2101.01301) for the Set Disjointness problem, we achieve an algorithm with space complexity $O(\frac{k^2}{\epsilon^2} \log c \cdot \log^2(n/k))$, time complexity $O(\frac{k}{\epsilon} \log c)$, and one-sided error probability $\epsilon$. This represents the first data stream algorithm to resolve the $\{1,2\}$-set disjointness problem, surpassing the previous best solution by approximately a factor of $k$. The momentum-dependent spin response function for a classical Heisenberg ferromagnet in its paramagnetic phase is derived using the classical Ornstein-Zernike formalism, based on its Fourier transform, valid up to the second order. This response function is demonstrated to rely on fractional powers of momentum. The scale and exponent associated with the momentum-dependent component are fixed by two conditions: the first mandates that the function converges to the Ornstein-Zernike result at zero momentum, while the second requires a specific connection to the momentum response of the non-linear sigma model—a well-known quantum spin-ferromagnet in its paramagnetic stage—derived via the functional renormalization group method. The criticality of this second condition is highlighted because incorporating the momentum-dependent term into the classical spin-response function enables the recovery of the correct momentum scaling and the universal momentum-dependent exponent for a quantum spin-ferromagnet, as determined by renormalization group and functional renormalization group methods. Furthermore, this derived momentum-dependent spin-response function is shown to satisfy current experimental neutron scattering data for the high-temperature paramagnetic phase of the local moment antiferromagnet LaMnO$_3$. Finally, it is demonstrated that including the momentum-dependent term in the spin-response function allows for the renormalization group recovery of the momentum-independent critical exponent $\gamma$ for the specific case of the classical ferromagnetic Heisenberg (or Ising) phase transition. Consequently, the study elucidates a previously unidentified momentum-dependent component of the spin-response function in the high-temperature paramagnetic phase of a classical ferromagnet. Additionally, it addresses a longstanding issue regarding the determination of the critical exponent $\gamma$ in the classical ferromagnetic phase transition, a problem that has persisted for over half a century. This issue involves a conflict between the conventional two-scale-factor universality scenario, which predicts a non-universal $\gamma$ exponent, and the novel two-scale-factor universality scenario, which predicts a universal $\gamma$ exponent. The analysis reveals that the conventional scenario applies only to systems where the finite-$k$ response function is independent of momentum, whereas the two-scale-factor universality scenario governs systems possessing a momentum-dependent response function. Notably, the novel two-scale-factor universality scenario is the first to successfully resolve the uncertainty surrounding the critical exponent $\gamma$. These findings are of significant general importance, extending beyond the specific systems examined in this study. We introduce a novel single-atom experimental setup utilizing an optical multidiffraction architecture based on a space-time optical lattice combined with an atomic quantum simulator within a UCNephoscope integrated circuit. This approach facilitates individual atom trapping, state modulation, state preparation, and fluorescence detection. The proposed scheme demonstrates superior optical efficiency and simplicity compared to existing methodologies. Furthermore, we validate the feasibility of this scheme using numerical simulations that successfully model atom trapping, manipulation, and detection. This method holds significant promise for applications in quantum information science and quantum metrology using atomic systems. Additionally, our work establishes a foundation for integrated quantum systems and paves the path for large-scale single-atom arrays designed for quantum simulation. The experimental configuration is expected to greatly advance atomic quantum technologies. All experimental parameters can be readily optimized using the provided Python-based theoretical package. This study investigates the influence of electron-electron interactions on both linear and nonlinear Hall conductivities within a quantum chaotic system modeled as a $2N$-site antidot under a strong magnetic field. Interaction effects are incorporated using the large-$N$ expansion approach. Our findings indicate that interaction does not alter the quantized plateau values of the linear Hall conductivity; however, it produces a finite peak near zero magnetic field that vanishes in the large-$N$ limit. Regarding nonlinear Hall conductivity, we observe significant differences between conductivities derived from current eigenstates versus single-particle states without interactions. In the large-$N$ limit, the large-$N$ nonlinear Hall conductivity yields zero at low fields but exhibits two zero-crossing peaks at higher fields, contrasting with a function that consistently changes sign without reaching zero for the single-particle case. Additionally, we demonstrate that the nonlinearity-induced peak experiences a shift in the large-$N$ limit compared to the non-interacting scenario, attributing this phenomenon to interaction effects. Finally, these results highlight the critical role of electron-electron interactions in quantum chaotic systems, suggesting potential implications for quantum Hall devices. Future research will employ density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and time-dependent DMRG techniques to further explore interaction effects in both one- and two-dimensional quantum chaotic systems. \newline
Keywords: Quantum chaos, many-body quantum systems, non-linear Hall effect, electron-electron interaction. \newline

The COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, has resulted in over 100 million infections and more than 2 million deaths globally. As the virus spreads rapidly, healthcare workers face escalating risks of contracting the disease. This risk is particularly high for radiologists, who frequently diagnose potential patients without wearing masks. The lack of personal protective equipment (PPE) stems from severe shortages caused by the massive global demand for masks to contain the pandemic. Consequently, the absence of adequate PPE, combined with prolonged exposure, leaves radiologists with a high probability of infection.

To address this, we propose a solution that integrates language models with radiology. By utilizing large-scale speech-to-text models, we can enable radiologists to communicate with patients mask-free. The system listens to the radiologist's spoken words and immediately translates them into text, which is then projected onto an augmented reality device like Microsoft's HoloLens for the patient to read. This real-time transcription ensures that diabetologists can communicate safely without wearing masks.

To develop this system, we introduce a new public dataset comprising 1,000 audio clips of radiologist-patient conversations. Our analysis reveals that radiologists frequently discuss breathing issues, often using colloquialisms and non-standard medical terminology. We fine-tune a large-scale speech-to-text model on our dataset to improve the accuracy of automatic speech recognition. Additionally, we explore a few enhancements to the transcription system to ensure effective communication. We anticipate that our approach will facilitate safe communication between radiologists and patients, thereby reducing the risk of pathogen transmission. This work is released as open-source to foster further research and development. Our contributions include: (1) a new dataset of radiologist-patient conversations, (2) a framework for immediate audio-to-text conversion, and (3) a dialogue enhancement system for non-standard medical language. We also provide a user-friendly interface for the transcription system, demonstrating its efficacy through a case study on diologist-patient interaction. The code is available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/immediate-transcription. The dataset can be accessed here: https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/immediate-transcription/tree/main/data. The models are available at: https://huggingface.co/ashishkumar12345/immediate_transcription. The documentation can be found at: https://immediate-transcription.github.io/.

Let $P_{f}^{\infty}(d)$ represent the platform set associated with a bicritical rational map $f: \mathbb{C}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{d}$. This set, defined as the quotient of the Fatou set $F_{f}$ by the group generated by the return maps of the first return times, raises the question of its structure. We demonstrate that, with the exception of one specific case where $d=2$ and $f$ is anti-linear, $P_{f}^{\infty}(d)$ is connected. Furthermore, when $d=2$ and $f$ is holomorphic, we provide an alternative characterization of platform sets. Additionally, we establish that, again excluding a single exception, $P_{f}^{\infty}(d)$ functions as both a Julia set and a Fatou set for a specific bicritical rational map $g: \mathbb{C}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{d}$ whose graph contains $d$ copies of the graph of $f$. Finally, we examine the dynamics induced on $P_{f}^{\infty}(d)$ by the maps $f_{n}: \mathbb{C}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{d}$, where $f_{n}$ denotes the $n$-th iterate of $f$ restricted to a fundamental domain $U_{n}$ of $P_{f}^{\infty}(d)$. For $d=2$ and $f$ being holomorphic, we prove that the limit set of the sequence $\{f_{n}\}_{n \geq 0}$ is a single fixed point, whereas this property fails to hold when $f$ is anti-linear. To substantiate these findings, we present several illustrative examples. The findings in this study were presented at the 2021 Global Analysis Week. Keywords: Global Analysis, Bicritical Rational Maps, Platforms Sets, Fundamental Domains. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 37F10, 37F15, 37F20.

MoS2 and WS2 represent the leading examples of 2D semiconductors, yet their 3D bulk counterparts exhibit work functions (approximately 4.6 and 5.1 eV) that are significantly higher than those of top-tier 2D materials like phosphorene (~4.6 and 5.1 eV). This study utilizes a combined density functional theory (DFT) and GW approach to investigate the thickness-dependent work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity of bulk MoS2 and WS2. Our findings indicate that GW calculations are essential for achieving accuracy, as they reveal that the work functions of both materials decrease from their bulk values to roughly 3.3 and 3.7 eV for few-layer MoS2 and WS2, respectively. These results align with existing experimental data. Furthermore, GW calculations demonstrate that the ionization potentials and electron affinities of both bulk and few-layer MoS2 and WS2 are substantially lower than the corresponding values in phosphorene. These outcomes suggest that GW-calculated electronic properties of few-layer MoS2 and WS2 are comparable to or even superior to those of phosphorene. Consequently, GW calculations are deemed essential for accurately determining the electronic characteristics of bulk and few-layer transition metal dichalcogenides. This research provides a reliable theoretical basis for future applications involving these materials. Additionally, the employed GW methodology is expected to be highly effective for calculating the electronic properties of other bulk and few-layer materials. Universal supervised learning can be modeled as the transfer of modifications via $\delta$-lenses. In this process, a complex supervised learning problem is decomposed into simpler, specialized sub-tasks known as modification transmission. Each sub-task involves moving semantic modifications from a source object to a target object through an abstract representation, which is modeled as a $\delta$-lens. This framework encompasses multiple well-known machine learning and computer vision techniques, including standard and semi-supervised inductive and transductive transfer learning, as well as editing operations for neural networks and convolutional neural networks. The paper outlines various strategies for defining $\delta$-lenses and discusses how universal modification can be observed and modeled using program analysis and category theory. Furthermore, it demonstrates the potential for formalizing concepts and reasoning about modification transfer that are currently only informally addressed in existing literature. Finally, the study argues that universal modification serves as a general foundation for supervised learning, enabling the unification of diverse methods and the application of formal methods to analyze and reason about their properties. </s>

We demonstrate the well-posedness of the uniform constant phase approximation (UCPA) within mean curvature flow. This approach, introduced by Bronsard, Stinner, and Wang in 2019, is proven here for the first time in the literature. Our proof relies on establishing novel regularity properties for a specific type of varifold. Although UCPA is designed to handle mean curvature flows that remain close to a linear subspace, we demonstrate that the standard linear evolution of a plane constitutes a weak solution, even under minimal smoothness conditions. Specifically, we show that the initial data's varifold possesses a bounded m-dimensional Hausdorff measure and a countable, $\mathcal{H}^m$-finite set of branch points, with no additional regularity guaranteed for the associated density. We identify a significant gap in the original proof and address it by developing a linearized theory for UCPA. This solution involves imposing a smallness condition on the second fundamental form and utilizing a novel time-weighting technique. Furthermore, we establish the continuity of the solution with respect to initial data under a suitable metric. Finally, we demonstrate the stability of UCPA under uniform convergence of varifolds. These findings pave the way for future extensions of the method to scenarios where the flow remains close to a non-linear submanifold. Additionally, we examine a seemingly minor yet crucial aspect of UCPA: the selection of the approximating sequence of submanifolds. We demonstrate that, under the established smallness condition, this selection is not arbitrary but is uniquely determined by a novel variational principle, which we term the "minimal linearization." This discovery may hold independent significance. In the final section, we present a more general theory for constant phase approximations, showing that both the linear and submanifold cases are specific instances of this broader framework. We identify the appropriate constant phase approximation for any mean curvature flow and establish its stability under uniform convergence of varifolds. Notably, we show that the minimal linearization and minimal submanifold approximation are both instances of this generalized constant phase approximation. Overall, our findings suggest that the concept of constant phase approximation is more fundamental than previously recognized. Specifically, we propose that the underlying principle of minimizing the area of fluctuations around the submanifold is intrinsic to certain mean curvature flows and should be investigated independently of any specific approximation method. This study examines the computational efficiency of linearized Boltzmann equation (LBE) solvers for rarefied gas dynamics involving multiscale length and time scales. The research demonstrates that the D3Q19 lattice (a three-dimensional model with 19 velocity nodes) combined with the Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook (BGK) collision operator yields highly accurate solutions within approximately 30–40 physical time steps. These findings are supported by employing asymptotic-preserving (AP) algorithms on the unit cube, conducting outer-flow linearized Bhatnagar–Cambell–Sykes (CBC) calculations, and representing the multisphere atmosphere in the Earth's gravitational field. Furthermore, the analysis explores the link between the BGK relaxation time and the LBE algorithm's convergence velocity toward its steady state. Finally, the report investigates the relationship between the BGK collision model's Knudsen number and the asymptotic regime of rarefied gas flows. These insights could significantly speed up the computation of LBE-based numerical solutions for both internal and external rarefied gas problems. The multi-modal grouping (MMG) technique is a well-established method for analyzing multimodal signals, primarily used in seismology to study earthquake sequences. This method identifies multiple distinct clusters within a time series and calculates the average duration of the intervals separating them. We have applied MMG to analyze multimodal time series data recorded by the Horizon-10T and magnetic field instruments at the McMurdo Station in Antarctica. The McMurdo station, situated on the Ross Ice Shelf, features an ice thickness of approximately 4 km, making it ideal for investigating how magnetic fluctuations travel through the ice. The 10T device, equipped with six coils oriented along the X, Y, and Z axes, measures magnetic field variations in all three dimensions. The 10T signal consists of two components: a transduced field generated by the coils and the original geophysical field present at the sensor's location. The MMG algorithm was applied to this signal after subtracting the transduced component. We analyzed 10T data collected during two distinct periods at McMurdo: one during a geomagnetic storm and another under stable conditions. Results indicate that multimodal grouping can be identified across all three spatial axes (X, Y, Z) during geomagnetic storms, whereas no significant multimodal grouping was detected under stable geomagnetic conditions. These findings suggest that Axion Quark Particles (AQPs) are unlikely to be generated by geomagnetic storms when AQPs exhibit a strong correlation with solar activity. However, if AQPs are not correlated with solar activity, these results imply that AQPs are not associated with geomagnetic storms at McMurdo during such events. Furthermore, we examined MMG signals from a time period with stable geomagnetic conditions at McMurdo. Our analysis reveals that no multimodal grouping signals were detected during the entire observation period under stable conditions. We also observed that the autocorrelation function of the 10T signal under stable geomagnetic conditions lacks the periodicity characteristic of AQPs. Consequently, we conclude that AQPs are not present during geomagnetic storms under stable conditions at McMurdo as recorded by the 10T device. We propose that AQPs may instead be linked to other phenomena, such as solar activity or underground nuclear explosions. We anticipate that AQPs will be detected under stable geomagnetic conditions at McMurdo during solar activity or underground nuclear explosions. This structure underpins numerous algebraic and categorical constructions, including group representations, Clifford algebras, von Neumann algebras, tensor categories, and duality in quantum information theory. Our goal is to present a statistical physical interpretation of these structures. We interpret the elements of $\mathcal{X}$ as observables representing yes/no questions regarding a physical system. The function $f$ denotes the non-contextuality of these questions, defined as $f(x,x')=0$ if and only if questions $x$ and $x'$ can be jointly measured. Consequently, $f$ encodes the compatibility structure of the system. The function $g$ captures correlations between compatible questions; specifically, $g(x,x')=1$ indicates a negative correlation, whereas $g(x,x')=0$ signifies a positive correlation. We demonstrate that the algebraic structure of 2D Pauli graphs can be recovered solely from the statistics of pairwise joint distributions of compatible questions. Furthermore, we establish that any 2D Pauli structure arises from a classical configuration model. This finding offers an alternative conceptual framework for understanding these structures and their associated algebraic formalisms. Finally, we illustrate that any 2D Pauli structure can be interpreted as a classical system with global correlations. This interpretation provides a novel perspective on constructions that extend beyond classical systems, such as the Pauli, Clifford, and Gauss graphs. These models serve as the foundation for numerous applications in quantum information theory, including quantum error-correcting codes, entanglement verification, and the verification of quantum devices. Our findings suggest that these applications may possess interpretations that are, to some degree, classically simulatable. We explore several such examples. Additionally, we examine applications within the realm of contextual hidden variable models. We demonstrate that any 2D Pauli structure can be viewed as a contextual hidden variable model, where correlations are encoded within a contextual function. This result enables us to construct noiseless contextual hidden variable models for various structures, such as the Pauli and Clifford graphs. Precise classification of images is essential for numerous computer vision applications. For instance, in autonomous driving, the brain processes visual data from the real world to generate commands for the body. The development of novel x-ray optical components is currently driving advancements in both laboratory experiments and astrophysical observations. However, as the x-ray wavelength range utilized by these devices shifts from meters to nanometers, significant challenges arise in achieving broad-field use with high sensitivity and resolution. This review examines current methods for boosting the optical performance of wide-field x-ray devices, addressing three primary categories of imperfections: intensity variations, spatial distortion, and blurring. We specifically focus on x-ray grazing incidence technologies, which are essential for both astrophysical missions like Chandra, XMM-Newton, and future successors such as Athena, as well as for ground-based research. Ultimately, we analyze the most effective strategies for enhancing the optical specifications of these devices. Given the growing interest from commercial entities in producing x-ray optics, we also provide an overview of the underlying physical principles and the mathematical tools required for characterization. Furthermore, we explore methods for simulating the performance of these devices. A key finding is that while Monte Carlo simulations offer the highest accuracy, they are computationally intensive and often impractical for characterizing complex devices; consequently, we advocate for a hybrid approach combining Monte Carlo methods with ray tracing to balance precision with computational efficiency. Finally, we outline an open-source Python-based ray-tracing package that facilitates characterizing and optimizing grazing incidence devices. This tool is freely available to assist researchers in advancing x-ray technologies. By integrating this software with Monte Carlo simulations, users can achieve the highest level of detail possible. Additionally, we present a dedicated website dedicated to x-ray device characterization, which serves as a valuable resource for those interested in the field. This platform provides access to the software, along with extensive information on device performance, imperfections, and improvement techniques. We believe this comprehensive online resource will be highly beneficial to the x-ray community. A full version of this review is available as a white paper. Recent studies on the Kitaev compound $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO}_3$ have suggested the presence of Kitaev interactions. However, this claim faces controversy due to conflicting experimental findings regarding magnetic order, long-range entanglement, and the presence of Majorana modes. In this work, we demonstrate that applying stress to single crystals of $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO}_3$ triggers a dimerization transition that eliminates antiferromagnetism. This evolution was examined using neutron diffraction and specific heat measurements. While hydrostatic pressure was previously noted to shift specific heat features linked to Kitaev interactions, we show that these shifts actually correspond to magnon excitations within a pre-existing ordered state. Furthermore, the stress-induced destruction of magnetic order contradicts recent proposals of long-range entanglement and Majorana modes in this material. Finally, we analyze how structural distortions influence Kitaev interactions, offering insight into why various experimental techniques have yielded divergent results. Our findings underscore the necessity of conducting stress-free experiments to accurately address the ongoing debate surrounding $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO}_3$. This mechanism drives an ultra-relativistic electron beam from a localized region within a bubble formed by the ultra-intense field and a linearly polarized drive laser, subsequently amplifying the beam's transverse polarization anisotropy. This enhanced polarization anisotropy stems from two factors: (i) electrons extracted from the bubble's lower-intensity side experiencing greater average laser field amplitudes than those from the upper side due to self-focusing in the lower quadrant; and (ii) electrons from the lower side acquiring higher longitudinal momenta than those from the upper side, a result of the laser's spectral self-steepening. We anticipate that this newly discovered injection and amplification method will significantly boost the performance of high-quality electron beams essential for applications such as free-electron lasers, gamma-ray sources, and particle-in-cell simulations. Double beta decay serves as a sensitive mechanism for investigating fundamental properties of established nuclei and discovering new particles. This study reports a novel, improved lower limit on the half-life of $^{204}\mathrm{Pt}$ double beta decay, achieving $T_{1/2}^{0\nu} > 1.8 \times 10^{20}$ years, which represents 100 times greater sensitivity than previous measurements. These findings mark the first detection of $^{204}\mathrm{Pt}$ and the most sensitive limits to date for neutron dark matter scattering. While colorization has recently gained significant research interest, most colorization networks (CCNs) are limited to specific datasets and struggle to generalize to unseen datasets due to their overfitting tendencies. To address this, we introduce Cross-Camera Profound Colorization (CCPC), a general CCN designed for multi-dataset colorization. CCPC utilizes two novel components: the Profound Convolutional Neural Network (ProNN) and Cross-Camera Profound (CCP) Convolutional Layers. The ProNN is a lightweight, robust feature extractor capable of capturing high-level features from large-scale multi-modal datasets, including ImageNet, YouTube8m, Kinetics400, and WebVideo. The CCP Convolutional Layer adapts these ProNN features for CCN convolution operations. By leveraging large-scale multi-modal data, our approach enables the network to learn robust features that significantly enhance performance on datasets it has not encountered during training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CCPC outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multiple datasets it has never seen before, achieving colorization results that are both visually appealing and realistic. We demonstrate that in any local, continuous, and non-reversible symmetry within a many-body quantum system, there must exist a low-energy excitation, representing a direct analogue of the Nielsen-Ninomiya fermion doubling theorem. Drawing from recent developments in both classical and quantum field theory regarding continuous non-reversible symmetries, we establish a novel local quantum field theory model featuring a non-reversible symmetry and calculate its low-lying spectrum. Our findings indicate that this model exhibits an infinite set of symmetries, with each symmetry corresponding to a specific excitation. Furthermore, each excitation can be isometrically mapped to a classical free particle moving on a torus, where the classical motion remains invariant under the symmetry transformations. We also present a many-body quantum system, analogous to the field theory model, which displays a non-reversible symmetry and possesses a single excitation at a specific energy level. This excitation exhibits Nielsen-Ninomiya doubling, resulting in two distinct ground states that cannot be mapped to one another via any local unitary operator. We propose an alternative proof for an entanglement-quantified version of this fermion doubling phenomenon. Our results suggest that every system possessing a non-reversible symmetry must have at least one low-energy excitation, thereby demonstrating that non-reversible continuous symmetries are prohibited in such quantum many-body systems. This finding extends the Mermin-Wagner theorem to cases where dimensionality $d$ exceeds 2. Additionally, we show that our findings align with recent studies on non-reversible continuous symmetries in both classical and quantum systems. We demonstrate that these prior works exhibit infinitely many symmetries, implying the Nielsen-Ninomiar fermion doubling does not occur in them. We introduce a novel method for investigating intermodal forward Brillouin scattering (IBS) within solid-core photonic crystal threads. This technique enables the simultaneous detection of multiple acoustic modes supported by the thread. By employing this approach, we successfully observed and analyzed IBS I-curves linked to both the first and second order optical modes, as well as the first acoustic mode. This work not only broadens the application scope of photonic crystal threads but also lays a foundation for developing high-performance sensing devices utilizing IBS. The integration of robotics and cybersecurity is becoming increasingly critical, particularly for autonomous vehicles where motion planning must account for cyber threats. Conventional cybersecurity measures, which rely on detection and response, often fail to address threats emerging in real-time. This paper introduces a novel, resilient cybersecurity framework capable of addressing and mitigating threats as they materialize. By utilizing Control Barrier Functions (CBF), the proposed approach ensures that robotic motion planning remains free from cyber attacks, specifically targeting communication links and manipulating received sensor data. Furthermore, this method guarantees that the robot's trajectory adheres to its physical constraints. The study provides a rigorous proof of the existence and uniqueness of solutions for motion planning under attack conditions, alongside numerical validations. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a case study involving an unmanned aerial vehicle navigating a dynamic environment while facing cyber threats. Simulation results confirm that the method successfully generates attack-resilient trajectories that comply with the vehicle's physical limitations. Additionally, the cybersecurity resilience is quantitatively assessed by comparing the system's performance before and after the implementation of the proposed approach. The findings indicate that Control Barrier Functions can effectively prevent cyber attacks on motion planning systems. Furthermore, an analysis of computational complexity reveals that the approach is highly efficient, as an attack-safe trajectory can be planned with minimal additional processing time. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. **Keywords:** Cybersecurity, Motion Planning, Control Barrier Functions, Dynamic Robotics, Cyber-Physical Systems.

Specifically, for surfaces with one end, two saddle links represent distinct homotopy classes if and only if they are Morse-Smale with respect to every possible dilation. We apply this result to construct affine structures on certain one-ended surfaces and demonstrate that any Sullivan vortex can be transformed into any other via an appropriate dilation. Furthermore, we offer a partial characterization of dilation surfaces where saddle links are nonequivalent precisely when they are mapping class nonequivalent. In the case of mapping class nonequivalent saddle links—nonequivalent under any mapping class—the associated dilation structures cannot be related by any mapping class. Additionally, we introduce a novel class of mapping class nonequivalent dilation surfaces where saddle links are nonequivalent precisely when they are mapping class nonequivalent. Finally, we offer a partial answer to an open question posed in *Inventiones mathematicae* 227 (2017), confirming that mapping class equivalence does not necessarily imply equivalence under any dilation. This study proposes a method for generating random networks based on network properties. The analysis examines how randomly selected networks evolve correlation and functional connectivity. A primary finding indicates that networks evolve functional connectivity even under minimal correlation. Additionally, we have applied this algorithm to reconstruct a human brain using all available structural connectivity data. While the resulting network exhibits high degree functional connectivity across most regions, it also demonstrates strong correlations between rest-fMRI network properties and those of other primate brains. We conclude that an algorithm producing networks with complete correlation is essentially equivalent to functional connectivity maximization via fMRI data averaging. Consequently, a more robust definition of brain networks should be derived from resting-state fMRI data rather than structural connectivity. Furthermore, we have introduced a novel method for identifying brain networks that integrates multiple complementary approaches. This methodology is also applicable to human brains derived from algorithms based on structural connectivity. We present an explicit unitary transformation linking two unitary representations of the Heisenberg group: one defined on $G_1=\mathbb{R}^m\otimes SU(2)$ and the other on $G_2=\mathbb{R}^{m+2}$. Utilizing this isomorphism, we develop a Taylor expansion for operators acting within the unitary representation of $SU(2)$. This expansion decomposes such operators into a series of Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann transformations. A specific instance of this formula is examined, and the text concludes by highlighting the connections of this approach to the geometry of $S^3$ and $S^5$. Additionally, we demonstrate how to derive geometrical quantities from the transformation and outline its utility in constructing geometrically invariant differential operators. Finally, we indicate its relevance to non-Abelian gauge theories. The work begins with essential background on the Heisenberg group, the unitary representations of $SU(2)$, and the tensor product of unitary representations. Subsequently, in Section 2, we establish and prove a theorem regarding a Taylor expansion for operators in the unitary representation of $SU(2)$, followed by an explicit construction of this series and an analysis of its properties. Section 3 details an application of these findings to the geometry of $S^3$ and $S^5$. In Section 4, we examine geometrically invariant differential operators on $S^5$ and illustrate how they can be constructed as images under a specific term in the Taylor expansion of geometrically invariant differential operators on $SU(2)$. The final section explores an application of these results to non-Abelian gauge theories. Additionally, Section 0 provides necessary preliminary information regarding the Heisenberg group and $SU(2)$.

Given a Gaussian process $f \sim GP(\mu, C)$ and a future path-conditioning event $f(t+\tau) = y$, we derive a closed-form expression for the conditional distribution $f(t) | f(t+\tau) = y$. By applying this formula, we demonstrate that while the conditional covariance structure transforms non-trivially, the conditional mean is essentially a linear adjustment of the original mean. Furthermore, we establish that the conditional distribution of $f$ remains a Gaussian field, albeit with a shifted mean and modified covariance. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of this conditional distribution when the conditioning time $\tau \to \infty$. This paper outlines the design and primary performance metrics of a wireless connection between ground-based and sky-based sensor networks. The ground network is proposed to support a space-based sensor system designed to monitor Earth's atmosphere and weather systems. By using a wireless link between ground and space sensors, data collection becomes cost-effective and highly efficient. Additionally, the space sensors can self-diagnose and adjust sampling rates to maximize the utility of acquired data. Although ground and sky sensor networks are typically connected via wired or wireless links, the specific configuration proposed in this work has not yet been studied. Consequently, this study proposes ground-repeater and space-sensor architectures for the wireless ground-to-space connection and employs a Monte-Carlo simulation to evaluate the impact of various parameters on network performance. The results indicate that increasing the number of ground repeaters or the transmission power of ground and space sensors can enhance data collection rates. Furthermore, the optimal number of ground repeaters is found to be between 15 and 25. These findings can be extended to other ground and sky sensor networks.

While these significant achievements are now complete, significant challenges remain. This review examines future neutrino experiments designed to measure oscillation parameters with high precision and to explore physics beyond the Standard Model. We concentrate on the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), which leverages its extensive interaction volume and the profound underground depth of the Sanford Underground Research Facility to achieve unprecedented precision in probing the rich interaction dynamics of GeV-energy neutrinos. By analyzing the full range of DUNE's capabilities, we demonstrate its potential to significantly advance the study of neutrino interactions and the subsequent development of the accuracy era in neutrino physics. Furthermore, we highlight DUNE's ability to precisely determine the mixing angle $\theta_{13}$, a critical parameter for measuring the oscillation amplitude involving neutrino mass states. Additionally, the review explores DUNE's sensitivity to flavor-dependent new physics, such as non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI), and to dark matter phenomena, including dark matter production and dark radiation. We illustrate DUNE's high-precision potential through specific examples, such as refining the measurement of the neutrino magnetic moment and investigating baryon number violation. Ultimately, DUNE will usher in a new era of precise neutrino physics, driving a wave of innovative research that will significantly expand our understanding of the fundamental properties of matter. This report is intended to guide future experimental and theoretical initiatives in the coming decades, ensuring that the era of neutrino accuracy continues to yield remarkable scientific achievements. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive summary of DUNE's contributions to Earth science and geophysics. Overall, this review illustrates DUNE's versatility and underscores its essential role in advancing our knowledge of the fundamental interaction properties of matter. Finally, we address the social and societal implications of DUNE, emphasizing its relevance to global society. In conclusion, this review serves as a comprehensive overview of the DUNE experiment and its profound impact on future neutrino physics. We strongly recommend that the international community fully support DUNE to ensure its realization and the tremendous scientific progress it will enable.
