Detecting COVID-19 early is crucial for mitigating its severe transmission. While Deep Learning (DL) has demonstrated significant potential in this domain, concerns regarding data privacy persist, as sensitive information can inadvertently be revealed by trained DL models. This paper introduces the Adversarial Privacy-Constrained Deep Network (APCDN), specifically designed to minimize the risk of patient data leakage during the early identification of COVID-19. To achieve this, we apply Transport Discrepancy Regularization (TDR) to align feature representations from both COVID-19 positive and negative samples with healthy control features, thereby enhancing model privacy. Additionally, we employ L2 regularization and clustering constraints as constraints within the objective function. These components work together to distinguish COVID-19 samples from both healthy and flu samples while maintaining adequate privacy against disclosure. We evaluated the APCDN framework using CT scan images from two independent datasets, the Oxford COVID-19 Image Dataset (Oxford-Corona) and the CT Projections Dataset (CTPD). Our experimental results demonstrate that the APCDN framework significantly improves privacy during classification, maintaining robust performance on both datasets. Furthermore, the model exhibits strong performance on external test data collected from a different hospital. Both qualitative and quantitative analyses confirm that our proposed APCDN framework is effective for the early identification of COVID-19. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi2000/APCDNN. Future research will explore the application of APCDN in other medical diagnostic tasks. Given that the model is trained solely on CT scan images, it can be readily adapted to other imaging modalities, such as X-rays, with minimal modification. Additionally, we aim to extend the APCDN approach to other viral infections. Finally, we plan to investigate parameter-free methods to reduce computational costs and accelerate inference. Addressing these future challenges will further enhance the applicability and efficiency of our proposed framework. Collectively, these efforts aim to advance the field of medical image analysis for early COVID-19 identification. We hope this work contributes to the broader effort of combating the pandemic. Decentralized wireless transmission systems represent a promising technology for supporting future applications, yet they face substantial challenges in signal processing due to a lack of centralized coordination. While decentralized solutions typically depend on extensive information exchange among all users to achieve optimal performance, graph neural networks (GNNs) offer a pathway to near-optimal results using significantly fewer communications. However, current GNN-based methods are limited to single-antenna configurations and struggle with wireless transmission models characterized by frequency selectivity and spatial correlation. This study addresses these gaps by developing a versatile and efficient GNN framework capable of handling general graph topologies, time-frequency selectivity, and correlation. Specifically, we investigate two critical scenarios: decentralized communication and radar communication jamming. We demonstrate that the proposed framework can be readily extended to wireless radar models and effectively balanced through pruning techniques. Ultimately, numerical evaluations confirm that our method achieves a reduction of over a million entries in the system model while maintaining only a marginal performance degradation compared to centralized approaches. The state of Goiás, located in Brazil's Central-West region, experienced a notable surge in homicides during the 2000s. This study examines temporal clusters within a dataset spanning 2002 to 2014, analyzing trends across all municipalities to identify periods characterized by elevated murder rates. By applying the True Cluster Exams methodology, we detected two significant periods of high homicide activity: 2007–2009 and 2011–2013. Furthermore, we analyzed temporal autocorrelation using the Moran's $I$ index, which revealed a consistent pattern of positive spatial autocorrelation throughout the entire period. This indicates that municipalities with above-average murder rates tended to be spatially adjacent to other high-rate areas, whereas those with below-average rates were similarly clustered together. These findings underscore the need for a coordinated regional strategy to effectively address the Goiás homicide crisis. Additionally, we explored lagged autocorrelation to assess whether high-murder-rate municipalities influenced their neighbors in subsequent years, a question explored through theoretical reasoning. The analysis also yielded significant cross-correlation results, demonstrating that high murder rates in one municipality were followed by elevated rates in nearby locations. These outcomes further support the conclusion that a coordinated regional approach is essential to tackle the crisis in Goiás. Finally, the paper concludes with reflections on the study's limitations and suggests avenues for future research. These insights are derived from a non-spatial statistical analysis of temporal trends in a spatio-temporal dataset. While this methodology can generate valuable hypotheses, it cannot determine the underlying causes of the homicide crisis. Consequently, subsequent research must incorporate spatially explicit data and methodologies to address this gap. Such future studies could utilize spatial autocorrelation techniques to identify which municipalities are most severely affected and to characterize the spatial distribution of high and low murder rates. Moreover, these approaches could facilitate the identification of specific neighborhood-level factors driving the crisis. This line of inquiry could be pursued through spatially explicit analyses, such as those involving crime mapping, spatial regression, and spatially weighted least squares. Furthermore, analyzing the temporal evolution of social and economic factors could offer a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamics driving the homicide crisis in Goiás. Finally, these future research directions could be expanded to other states within the Brazilian Central-West region. This approach would facilitate the identification of states with similar homicide trajectories to Goiás, thereby supporting the creation of a coordinated regional strategy to address the Brazilian homicide crisis. This work addresses the inverse problem of utilizing a pre-trained generative model for creating diverse data samples. By treating generation as generation-maximization (GenMax), we propose applying Stochastic Gradient Ascent (SGA) to the log-likelihood of pretrained models. Since pretrained generators typically lack explicit likelihoods, Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) are trained to approximate them. Building on prior research, our approach employs SGA to enhance the model-fit component of the learning objective while simultaneously boosting the diversity component via a stochastic perturbation term. We evaluate the efficacy of this method across three distinct scenarios: varying model sizes, data challenges, and environmental noise levels. Our findings indicate that the method is highly effective across a broad spectrum of these conditions, though it is worth noting that the perturbation term can occasionally hinder learning in data-challenged environments. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a solution involving the use of negative samples during SGA updates. Overall, our approach yields promising outcomes regarding model fit, data diversity, and scalability. Specifically, our method surpasses Variational Inference (VI) across a wide range of noise and diversity conditions, demonstrates faster training speeds than maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) on DAEs, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on three benchmark datasets. To our knowledge, this study represents the first instance of SGA being utilized for training DAEs. The experimental code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb2000/GenMax. Axion-based physics is increasingly the subject of intense experimental investigation. The most direct and compelling candidate for dark matter, axions could potentially be detected through their non-gravitational interactions with solar center components. This study examines the feasibility of measuring the Sun's core properties using a next-generation magnetized Borexino (BabyIAXO), while simultaneously establishing the precision of solar parameters derived from existing data. Our analysis indicates that BabyIAXO can significantly refine constraints on fundamental parameters governing energy production in the solar center. Specifically, the device is projected to achieve a $5\%$ precision in determining the dark matter mass, as inferred from the observed flux. Furthermore, we have quantified the uncertainties of fundamental solar parameters based on current data and established a sensitivity table for BabyIAXO. These results demonstrate that the experiment will substantially improve the accuracy of key parameters related to energy generation within the solar core. Ultimately, this research underscores the critical role of axion experiments in advancing our fundamental understanding of the Sun. Any measured signal would provide unique insights into the Sun's core, offering critical information for both fundamental physics and astrophysics. Additionally, our findings may have significant implications for future missions, such as the proposed D-Arc. Finally, this study may inform future research directions and scientific strategies for BabyIAXO. A subsequent paper will present a detailed analysis of the project's scientific potential. All findings in this study are based on a conservative assessment of the expected signal from BabyIAXO. Specifically, we assume a magnetic field of $5~T$ within a $200~m^3$ volume of material, composed of $50\%$ iron and $50\%$ bismuth by mass, with an axion transmission of $100\%$. We also consider a $10^{13}$-year exposure time, resulting in a total collected signal of approximately $10^{11}$ axion-like particles. Our analysis further assumes that systematic uncertainties are negligible. Finally, the sensitivity table for fundamental parameters was generated using the MESA code. Our findings are also contingent upon the assumption that the chosen material does not introduce additional, unaccounted-for background noise. This paper introduces a new category of self-exciting systems, characterized by a stochastic process driving the dynamics and a time-varying state space. To analyze this class, the authors propose specific tools, including the construction of associated processes, uniform contraction criteria, and uniform moment bounds. These methodologies are demonstrated through a self-exciting system derived from the geometric Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. The application of these tools enables the establishment of various asymptotic properties, such as asymptotic stability, uniform stability, bounded moments, ergodicity, and a central limit theorem. Finally, the study examines a self-exciting system arising from discrete event network performance modeling to illustrate these theoretical findings. Specifically, the authors prove the existence and uniqueness of solutions, verify the validity of contraction and bounding assumptions, and illustrate the derived results using two numerical examples. Additionally, simulations are employed to assess the empirical ergodicity of the process. Finally, the paper explores implications for the existence of asymptotic steady states within specific systems of this new class. The authors conclude by outlining potential future research directions. Keywords: Geometric Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process; Discrete event networks; Stochastic differential equations; Existence and uniqueness of solutions; Contraction; Bounded moments; Asymptotic behavior; Asymptotic stability; Uniform stability; Bounded moments; Ergodicity; Central limit theorem.

This study demonstrates the implementation of a free-breathing motion adjustment strategy for 4D (comprising three spatial dimensions plus one respiratory dimension) and 3D (encoding for respiration) contrast-enhanced turbo spin-echo (TSE) MRI sequences. The approach combines a variable flip angle and variable readout time (VFA-VRT) technique with a spiral k-space sampling pattern. By applying this method to both 3D and 4D contrast-enhanced turbo spin-echo sequences, the study successfully acquired free-breathing anatomical images of the head, neck, chest, abdomen, and extremities in both 3D and 4D formats. The use of a free-breathing free-space breathing (F3BF) approach, facilitated by VFA-VRT spiral sampling, enabled free-breathing 3D TSE imaging with reduced scan times. Furthermore, 4D and 3D contrast-enhanced turbo spin-echo imaging was achieved with free-breathing scan times ranging from 1.5 to 3 minutes. This technique effectively mitigates free-breathing motion artifacts in 4D and 3D contrast-enhanced TSE imaging, offering free-breathing anatomical data that can be integrated with functional data from other modalities, such as dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI. Ultimately, 3D and 4D turbo spin-echo imaging can be performed without the need for breath-holding. Model compression and reduction are essential for deploying machine learning models on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used approach for this purpose, which involves training a smaller student model to replicate the behavior of a larger pre-trained teacher. However, current state-of-the-art KD techniques fail to account for the data flow within teacher models, often resulting in significant performance drops when student models are designed to be even smaller than the teacher. This paper presents Data Flow-preserving Knowledge Distillation (InDistill), a method that surpasses teacher performance by up to 2.5% on ImageNet while utilizing a student model three times smaller. InDistill achieves a distillation loss approximately 100 times lower than teacher loss, effectively mimicking the teacher's data flow to guide student training. The technique is fully automated and requires no modifications to the teacher, student, or training infrastructure. Experiments across various architectures and image sizes demonstrate that InDistill consistently exceeds teacher performance, even with student models smaller than the teacher. This result resolves a specific instance of a broader problem posed by Eilers and Gillings, involving the topological classification and the reconstruction of one-dimensional topological spaces from their knot tables. CountSketch is a widely used dimensionality reduction method that projects high-dimensional vectors into lower dimensions via randomized linear measurements, enabling the recovery of $\ell_1$-norm sparse vectors from compressed data. Although numerous theories and empirical results indicate that CountSketch remains robust against adaptive inputs, a complete theoretical proof has been absent until now. This paper fills that gap by establishing the resilience of CountSketch to adaptive $\ell_0$-norm vectors, demonstrating successful reconstruction even in the strongest adversarial setting where data is adaptively revealed based on prior reconstruction outcomes. Specifically, in instances where all previous predictions result in zero loss, the proposed CountSketch algorithm maintains constant relative loss for future predictions. Furthermore, this adversarial resilience extends to input sequences where total loss is non-zero, allowing the algorithm to achieve constant additive loss relative to the total loss of prior predictions. These findings represent the first theoretical results of their kind for CountSketch in adaptive scenarios. Additionally, the results generalize to count-based reconstruction methods applicable to count-data distributions, such as Poisson counts. Notably, the analysis does not rely on any statistical assumptions regarding the input sequence. The study begins by proving CountSketch resilience for adaptive inputs with known sub-Gaussian norms before extending the analysis to sparsity norms. Finally, the paper concludes by examining CountSketch's resilience to adaptive inputs within count-data distributions. The theoretical results are supported by empirical evidence. Finally, the count-based results are demonstrated to be tight. The code is available at: https://github.com/ashishgarg123/CountSketch. We introduce ipie, a Python-based Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) software designed to accelerate and enhance simulations on GPUs. This study demonstrates the application of quantum game theory, specifically utilizing the Eisert-Wilkens-Vaughn model for the Prisoner's Dilemma, in predicting frequency trading outcomes. This research examines the impact of intermediaries on investor income, specifically analyzing the differences between "smart" intermediaries, who optimize investor returns, and "dumb" intermediaries, who do not. The study employs a simple model where an intermediary selects an asset based on either anticipated future states or current signals, with information acquisition costing a fixed fee. Our primary finding indicates that among rational intermediaries, there is no benefit to obtaining information; consequently, a rational intermediary would prefer a regime with no future to optimize against. In contrast, smart intermediaries significantly enhance investor returns, particularly in early time periods. Furthermore, we identify a first-order stochastic dominance relationship between investment policies managed by smart versus dumb intermediaries. Finally, we extend our analysis to a more complex setting involving multiple intermediaries, revealing that total spending on information decreases as the number of intermediaries rises. These insights are validated through both numerical simulations and a specific two-intermediary scenario. Empirically, we observe that investment policies generated by smart intermediaries align closely with actual human behavior. The paper concludes by discussing broader implications and potential avenues for future research. Finally, this study addresses an open question raised in a related work by taking a distinct approach to resolve it. Our methodology diverges from the prior work in that we do not model the investment problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Instead, we utilize a generative model of the state space to determine the optimal intermediate policy, which can be computed efficiently even in high-dimensional spaces. This contrasts with the previous work, which relied on reinforcement learning techniques like Q-Learning and SARSA. Our approach offers distinct advantages, including the ability to derive closed-form solutions for specific problems and enabling a more comprehensive analysis of model properties. We introduce the task of reconstructive summarization, which involves rebuilding an entire text using a summary as the sole source of information. This process requires retaining all original textual details within the summary, thereby demanding more generation steps and higher complexity than standard summarization. To address this, we propose a multi-agent framework that treats the generation process as a FOGOF (game) problem, where each agent is responsible for managing a specific segment of the output. To reduce the communication burden between agents, we employ entity prompts derived from the input text as the representation method. These prompts are generated by a separate prompt agent and distributed among the agents based on their assigned portions of the text. Experiments conducted on both English and Chinese datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, an ablation study reveals the significant contribution of entity prompts in facilitating plan communication among agents. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural application of entity representations for summarization, and this work presents the first exploration of utilizing multi-agent systems for reconstructive summarization. This document examines $n$-variable real-valued functions and their relation to partial derivatives, focusing on concepts such as continuity, (Schwarz) differentiability, and (Haar) almost differentiability. The primary objective is to establish sufficient conditions for the differentiability of an $n$-variable function based on the differentiability of all its partial derivatives, assuming $n \geq 2$. To achieve this, we substitute the classical mixed partial derivative theorem—which requires $\mathcal{C}^1$ differentiability of the original function—with a weaker variant that demands continuous values. This alternative version suffices to prove Baire category conditions for differentiability. We present four theorems addressing specific scenarios: first, if every partial derivative is Baire differentiable, then the original function is twice Baire differentiable; second, if all partial derivatives are $\mathcal{C}^1$ smooth, then Baire differentiation can be applied to the original function a second time; third and fourth, conditions are provided for determining higher-order Baire differentiability. These four theorems generalize established results from lower to higher dimensions. Additionally, we explore a "weak" version of the first theorem, which relaxes the requirement for continuous values and instead assumes that partial derivatives possess Baire pointwise derivatives. Finally, we present examples and counter-examples to demonstrate that, regarding higher-order differentiability, conditions based on continuity are strictly stronger than those based on Baire differentiability. In summary, this work presents novel findings and insights into how differentiability of an $n$-variable function relates to the differentiability of its partial derivatives. It is available as arXiv:2101.01012 [math.CA]. Keywords: Differentiability, Partial Derivative, Continuous Function, Baire Differentiability, Almost Differentiability.

This paper introduces a calculation approach that considers dialogue context to evaluate vocal entrainment—the synchronization of speech rhythms between dialogue partners. While existing methods typically rely solely on local utterance metrics, the method proposed here additionally incorporates the speech duration of the preceding utterance from the same speaker. Furthermore, we demonstrate that including this extra information enhances the discrimination of experimental conditions involving dialogue partners with varying levels of entrainment. We also present findings comparing two distinct types of dyadic interactions. Finally, we illustrate the application of this method to analyze interactions between patients with schizophrenia and their clinicians. These results offer the first quantitative evidence of reduced entrainment capacity in clinical groups compared to healthy controls, supporting the hypothesis that successful clinical outcomes are associated with higher levels of entrainment. Consequently, we posit that this metric holds potential for use in clinical settings. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first simultaneous examination of multiple, independently derived measures of entrainment capacity. Through the detailed examination of various experimental conditions and a specific clinical application, we demonstrate both the method's sensitivity and its broad applicability. Ultimately, this study represents a significant advancement toward the development of a fully automated, computationally robust framework for analyzing dialogue entrainment. Such a framework would facilitate the systematic investigation of entrainment capacity across diverse populations, including those with varying degrees of impairment. Furthermore, it would enable the precise quantification of individual capacity, a critical prerequisite for implementing personalized interventions. These outcomes underscore the necessity of a computational method that accounts for the dynamic, time-evolving nature of dialogue. By demonstrating how to construct such a method, this work establishes a foundation for the systematic analysis of computational models of dialogue and the subsequent analysis of empirical data. By utilizing projections, it regulates the flow of quantum information, thereby establishing a "one-way" communication channel. This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the modified QLC, named Lambda-S1, which incorporates the strength axiom into QLC's regulation mechanisms. This adjustment enables the construction of a complete categorical model for Lambda-S1 that aligns with its semantic definition. Consequently, this model extends the previously proposed Quantum Affine Calculus (QAC) and its corresponding categorical framework. Furthermore, this research facilitates the development of an abstract categorical framework for various QLC variants by providing a method to assign categorical structures to them. Additionally, the study constructs categorical models for two specific QLC modifications based on their respective semantic definitions and establishes completeness theorems for them. Finally, the paper explores the potential applications of these categorical structures in advancing theoretical research within quantum information. Keywords: Quantum Affine Calculus, Quantum Lambda Calculus, Categorical Models, Categorical Structures, Categorical Completeness.

This study addresses the Stokes variational inequation, a model for glaciology that is notoriously difficult to solve due to its lack of well-posedness. While previous work by Ern, Guermond, and Rousset established error estimates for mixed formulations and derived an a posteriori error estimator for the semicoercive non-coercive variational formulation, this paper focuses on a practical variant of that semicoercive approach. We introduce a variant method where Lagrange multipliers are enforced only at selected nodes, demonstrating that this strategy retains the theoretical advantages of standard formulations while enhancing the practical performance of the estimator. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to validate our error estimates and to assess the impact of node selection on both error indicators and the resulting error bounds. These results confirm that the proposed practical formulation is highly effective for numerical computation. Furthermore, the error bounds generated by our practical formulation are significantly tighter than those from the original semicoercive formulation, as it mitigates the severe overestimation of errors. Finally, extensive numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the tightness of these error bounds. To achieve this, we examine a benchmark problem with a known true solution and an application problem motivated by recent research in glaciology. Our computational findings indicate that, in both scenarios, the error bounds provided by the practical formulation are nearly as tight as the actual errors. This outcome underscores the practicality of the proposed formulation for error control in glaciological variational inequalities. Additionally, our analysis of node selection reveals that nodes chosen based on the geometry of the computational domain yield the tightest error bounds. Specifically, in the benchmark case, selecting nodes along the bottom and side boundaries results in error bounds that closely approximate the true error. This success is attributed to the variational inequation's model, which incorporates a one-sided inequality boundary condition on the top boundary, thereby preventing upward fluid motion. Consequently, selecting nodes along the top boundary does not significantly tighten the error bounds. These observations align with prior research on finite element shape optimization, which also identified that nodes along the bottom and sides are critical for determining shape sensitivity. This suggests a promising avenue for future research: extending the concept of node selection to other inequalities, such as those found in contact problems. Finally, we note that the tightness of the error bounds is highly sensitive to the polynomial degree of the finite element spaces. For instance, using linear elements produces error bounds that are nearly as tight as the actual errors, whereas cubic elements result in error bounds that are several orders of magnitude

We introduce DUVET (Dual-View Outflow), a novel dataset comprising 1.3 mm continuum and 1.1 mm CO(3-2) observations of the starburst galaxy M51-UCD123. The 1.3 mm continuum data reveal a prominent outflow structure extending 1.5 kpc above and below the galactic disk, while the CO(3-2) maps indicate that outflow gas is largely confined to the central kiloparsec. The outflow's kinematics align with gas flows detected in H$\alpha$ imaging of the disk, demonstrating that galactic outflows can effectively regulate star formation on the scale of entire star-forming regions. This finding is corroborated by the strong anti-correlation between DUVET 1.3 mm flux and H$\alpha$-derived star formation rates within the central kiloparsec. These results underscore the role of outflows in limiting star formation across galactic disk scales and provide a foundation for future studies of the relationship between outflows and star formation in starburst galaxies. This study analyzes the impact of shear viscosity on triangular flow $v_3$ within the 3+1D hydrodynamic framework Multiphase Transport (MT). We investigate how the shear viscosity-to-entropy density ratio, $\eta/s$, influences $v_3$ for both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at a beam energy of 20–44 GeV. Our findings indicate that $v_3$ is highly sensitive to both the magnitude and spatial variation of $\eta/s$. When comparing our results to experimental data, we observe that a constant $\eta/s$ value of 0.08 fails to simultaneously describe $v_3$ across all centrality classes. Instead, a spatially varying $\eta/s$ is required, where entropy density increases with central rapidity. This adjustment results in a $\sim$10% enhancement of $v_3$ relative to the baseline scenario. Furthermore, we note that the impact of shear viscosity on $v_3$ is more pronounced in Cu+Cu collisions than in Au+Au collisions. We conclude that the shear viscosity of the medium created in both proton-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) is substantial. Additionally, we find that incorporating the quark charge fraction into the equation of state (EoS) results in a $\sim$10% increase in $v_3$ compared to a pion gas, which should be accounted for when interpreting the data. Overall, our conclusions suggest that the QCD medium is most likely described by a polarized P-glass. Finally, we emphasize that future measurements of $v_3$ are crucial for determining the transport properties of the QCD medium. Current research indicates that pre-training on a single, depth-assigned image dataset yields superior results compared to training on multiple-depth datasets. This study evaluates whether utilizing datasets with multiple and varied depth estimates offers advantages to classification-based semantic segmentation models when employed for self-supervised pre-training. We observe that pre-training on a dataset with a wide range of diverse and varying depth assessments does not outperform classification-based pre-training in downstream semantic segmentation tasks. Our analysis suggests that the high variance in depth assessments within the KITTI dataset significantly impacts downstream model performance, thereby hindering its effectiveness as a source for depth-assessed pre-training. Additionally, we present a theoretical explanation for why depth assessment-based pre-training might fail in classification and depth-assessment tasks, while also proposing why it could be effective for assuring depth estimation. Finally, we explore the potential of a joint training approach that combines classification and depth-assessment tasks. We believe these insights will be valuable for future research in semantic segmentation, specifically regarding self-supervised pre-training methodologies. Kendall's $\tau$ measures the degree of dependence between two random variables using an asymmetric yet permutationally invariant rank-based approach. Its sample version serves as an estimator for $\tau$, which converges in probability to the population parameter. Because $\tau$ exhibits significant sensitivity to minor shifts in the underlying distribution, even minimal deviations between the true and assumed distributions can cause substantial bias in the estimator relative to $\tau$. This issue, known as bias or "drift," can be significantly mitigated through effective deduction, a computational strategy derived from the logical inference framework of modus tollens. This paper presents a straightforward algorithm for estimating $\tau$ based on effective deduction, which yields an $n^2$ complexity for the sample estimator and is substantially faster than the $n^3$ complexity of Kendall's original algorithm. Furthermore, estimator properties are analyzed, and numerical simulations are conducted to compare the two methods. Finally, a real-world example involving a 2012 survey on social media usage is provided to illustrate the results. Code is available at https://github.com/eduardo-garcia-perez/kendall-tau. The rise of privacy-preserving protocols, such as MixNet, has sparked significant interest in vehicular networks. However, since privacy is vital for users, we must first examine whether current MixNet approaches adequately protect the privacy of all edge cognition participants in automotive networks. Our analysis reveals that existing MixNet methods are insufficient, as they expose the identity coverage of users and infrastructure entities, thereby compromising the privacy of all edge cognition actors. Consequently, we propose a collaborative structure to facilitate privacy protection within edge cognition networks and introduce a novel implementation of MixNet designed to safeguard every participant's privacy. We validate our proposed solution using NetSim and SimuLite for simulation and analysis. Ultimately, this work paves the way for a more private future in automotive networks, especially concerning data sharing and collaboration. While MixNet offers strong privacy guarantees, it demands substantial computational power and memory from users and stations; therefore, we also explore techniques to optimize these resources through machine learning. To our knowledge, this is the first study to comprehensively examine the privacy protection capabilities of existing MixNet mechanisms in edge cognition networks and to propose an effective solution for enhancing privacy through MixNet and machine learning. Although the proposed solution increases resource requirements, it ensures the privacy of all edge cognition entities, including users, stations, and infrastructure. We conclude that this approach is essential for advancing privacy preservation in automotive networks. Case-I examines a system where prey growth follows an Allee curve while the predator employs a Holling Type-II hunting strategy. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to validate our theoretical findings and determine whether they align with reality. Additionally, we analyze whether specific behaviors can be induced by external factors or if they emerge naturally from the model's structure. A novel feature of this work is the investigation of whether a model with a single stable positive equilibrium point can still exhibit a limit cycle when analyzed with specific parameter values. The paper introduces a novel pivot simplex algorithm derived from general position assumptions applied to the initial basis matrix, which ensures that every iterate visits a distinct simplex and eventually identifies the optimal solution. A specific technique is proposed to efficiently determine a suitable starting basis. Building upon the findings of the first paper in this study, the second work examines the algorithm under non-degeneracy conditions and examines its convergence within initial basic feasible regions. By applying the pivot simplex method row by row, the approach solves multi-objective optimization problems without requiring additional software. The algorithm's efficiency is validated through extensive tests using both standard and non-standard datasets. Furthermore, a numerical example is provided to illustrate the method's practical application. The results confirm that the proposed row-by-objective solution method is highly effective for linear optimization. The study concludes that when a suitable initial basis is available, this pivot simplex method is a practical and efficient tool for solving optimization problems. The code implementation is accessible at https://github.com/abdullahkaya1994/aspsm. The rapid advancement of deep learning-based face recognition has led to increasingly sophisticated spoofing countermeasures, which pose significant security risks. This study investigates the specific challenges of creating zero-shot countermeasures that can detect previously unseen attack types. While recent research has demonstrated the efficacy of Vision Transformers (ViT) in this domain, their limited throughput and high computational demands hinder practical deployment. Consequently, we introduce a comprehensive evaluation of ViT performance, efficiency, and accuracy to guide their optimal use. Our key findings include: (1) confirming that ViTs outperform classic CNNs in both accuracy and robustness within zero-shot scenarios, though they are less effective at distinguishing higher-fidelity attacks; (2) the demonstration that lightweight ViT models achieve results comparable to heavier counterparts; (3) the establishment of an accuracy-Efficiency-Throughput (AET) metric to assess ViT performance across various practical settings; and (4) the adoption of knowledge distillation to enhance lightweight ViTs, yielding improvements of 1.5% to 3.5% in zero-shot zero-shot (ZSZS) scenarios. Additionally, our extensive experiments reveal that ViTs trained under ZSZS conditions outperform those under ZZSZ conditions by 2.5% to 6.5%. Finally, we open-sourced our code and models to foster reproducibility and further research. Given their superior efficiency and performance, ViTs are poised to become standard components of real-world face anti-spoofing systems. To facilitate this, we also release our code and models at https://github.com/1000x/face-spoofing-vit. The project website is https://1000x.github.io/. A recent microlensing event, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434, was identified through Adaptive Lenses Keck Observatory imaging, suggesting a planet with a mass of 4.1+1.8-1.5 M_Earth located at a distance of 1.8+0.8-1.4 AU from its host star. Although the microlensing parallax effect necessitates additional constraints to precisely determine the host star's mass and distance, the planet's equilibrium temperature is estimated to be extremely low, ranging from 25 to 70 K. This work demonstrates that even without further observational data, we can establish an upper limit for the host star's mass at 0.053 ± 0.011 M_Sun, which would correctly classify the host as an ultra-cool dwarf rather than a main-sequence star. This mass constraint is derived from the condition that the planet-star mass ratio must exceed the critical curve crossing limit. By applying this limit to the mass-radius relation for ultra-cool dwarfs, we can accurately validate the existence of this planet and refine our estimates of its mass and orbital distance. Consequently, our findings indicate that the planet resides at 2.1+0.5-0.3 AU and has a mass between 2.5 and 5.5 M_Earth. These results highlight the significance of high-resolution imaging in microlensing studies, as such observations can validate planetary candidates and yield more accurate mass and distance estimates. Ultimately, this methodology represents a non-observational approach to vetting and characterizing exoplanets detected via microlensing. Our successful validation of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434b marks the first planetary super-Earth discovered through microlensing to be confirmed without the need for additional observations. Furthermore, this planet is the coldest super-Earth known to date. This discovery underscores the value of microlensing in detecting and validating planets orbiting ultra-cool dwarfs, which are often difficult to detect using other methods. Future high-resolution imaging from ground-based facilities like the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) and the Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT), along with space-based observatories such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), will be instrumental in further investigating and potentially discovering more planets around these faint and fainter stars. These operators are defined by their invariance under the system's Hamiltonian evolution and are determined up to constants determined solely by the bath properties. Their primary utility lies in providing a systematic method to compute decay rates and phase acquisition rates for eigenstates of the system Hamiltonian. Furthermore, an additional solution, representing a universal decay component, is identified. The eigenstate rates are demonstrated via numerical examples involving a two-level system with a time-regular Lindblad operator. The validity of these solutions is established for a classical two-level system coupled to a zero-temperature spin-bath. Finally, the results are applied to two prominent models: the Curie-Weiss ferromagnet and a two-level system interacting with a one-dimensional spin-bath. In both cases, the solutions are shown to yield an accurate qualitative description of the relevant density matrix components. Notably, specific critical exponents associated with the density matrix components near the phase transition point are derived. These findings align with established critical exponents for the corresponding equilibrium systems. Additionally, the study addresses several open questions. We report the detection of narrow-line self-emission from neutral hydrogen (HI) toward the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20, observed using the Nobeyama Radio Observatory 45-meter telescope. This self-emission is produced by the collisional excitation of the HI 21-cm fine structure transition, and its presence indicates a high density of neutral matter along the line of sight. Analysis of HI narrow-line self-emission toward other star-forming regions will facilitate a more precise understanding of the relationship between star formation and HI N II levels. Furthermore, HI self-emission is expected to be strongly excited in star-forming regions hosting high-mass stars due to the high local HI N II values driven by intense ultraviolet radiation fields from these stars. Consequently, investigating the correlation between star formation and HI N II will be enhanced by incorporating observations of HI self-emission. Additionally, the observed emission can be utilized to investigate the physical conditions of the interstellar medium in star-forming regions. In this study, we successfully detected self-emission toward G176.51+00.20, allowing for the first measurement of the HI excitation temperature in this area. The derived temperature of 40 K is consistent with the 30 K value reported for the adjacent molecular cloud G176.52+00.20. This alignment suggests that the two regions may be physically linked. The detection of HI self-emission toward G176.51+00.20 demonstrates that the fine structure line is a viable tool for studying star-forming regions. Future observations of the HI self-emission line toward G176.51+00.20 will aid in clarifying the connection between star formation and the conditions of the surrounding interstellar medium. We demonstrate that a strongly convex and differentiable minimization problem constitutes a greedy minimization with a gap at any point, whereas the reverse implication holds true when the function is convex with a Lipschitz continuous gradient. Furthermore, we establish conditions for non-extreme values of the Hasse diagram associated with the level sets of the function using the Hessian matrix. These findings enable the intermediate greedy minimization with a gap, which guarantees the production of at least one intermediate minimizer. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across numerous computer vision applications, including image recognition and classification. However, a primary challenge remains the scarcity of training data. While transfer learning, which trains a network on a large source domain and adapts it to a smaller target domain, is a standard solution, it is not always feasible. Domain migration offers a versatile alternative, enabling the deployment of a trained model to domains where data collection is impossible. This paper evaluates the efficacy of deep neural network domain migration techniques within image identification tasks. We introduce four novel methods designed to facilitate the use of models in unseen data domains. Experimental results across three datasets demonstrate that these proposed approaches yield improvements of 1.5% to 2.0% in overall model accuracy compared to state-of-the-art domain migration techniques. Additionally, we establish a new baseline for assessing the effectiveness of domain migration methods. The source code and paper are accessible at https://github.com/ahmed-omar97/assessment-of-deep-neural-network-domain-migration-methods.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant traction for classifying graphs and generating node or subgraph representations. However, decoding these representations requires careful design of interpreters to ensure GNNs function as reliable and trustworthy tools. Since current decoding methods lack a unified framework, we propose a parameterized framework for GNN interpreters. This framework offers a systematic approach to modeling interpreters and provides practical guidance for their construction. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to parametrize various components of an interpreter using this framework, revealing its flexibility and potential to produce novel, improved interpreters. Additionally, we present a comprehensive suite of non-trivial test cases for evaluating GNN interpreters, which can test these frameworks and parametrizations on diverse and challenging problems. Our extensive experimental evaluation shows that these approaches yield significant improvements in accuracy, faithfulness, and stability across a wide range of graph problems. We have open-sourced our framework and testing framework to facilitate the development of future GNN interpreters. We hope this resource will help the community advance the field of GNN interpretation. The complete implementation is available at: https://github.com/epfl-lgl/gnn-interpreter.

Although the Legendre Memory Module demonstrated significant success in accelerating Transformer training by utilizing a parallel memory attention layer, its training phase has historically relied on costly sequential optimization. This paper presents a novel parallel memory attention training approach designed to minimize training time while maintaining model accuracy through the application of the Cauchy-Armijo method within memory attention layers. Experimental results on the LLaMA2 7B model indicate an 11.2% reduction in training duration compared to sequential training, with no degradation in model performance relative to other parallel training strategies. Furthermore, this work offers a comprehensive comparison of parallel training techniques across various neural network types and model sizes, delivering a unified codebase to facilitate future research and development in high-performance neural network training. This paper investigates participants' commitment to strategic or linguistic consistency within a simple labeling game. Consistency is defined as the property where each agent applies the same mapping from object types to labels regardless of when they enter the game. Although consistent labeling schemes have been observed in various categorization contexts, no analytical method currently exists to determine under what conditions they evolve. To fill this gap, we introduce an analytical framework capable of predicting the evolution of consistent schemes and their stability. Our approach models agents' strategy selection through migrating participants and employs consistency as the criterion for their satisfaction. We demonstrate that if the benefits agents derive from having a consistent partner exceed the benefits from an inconsistent one, consistent schemes will evolve. Furthermore, if these advantages are sufficiently pronounced, evolving consistency can stabilize. Finally, we present simulation results that validate our analysis. Overall, this framework offers a tool for identifying when evolution toward linguistic consistency is possible. Additionally, our model extends beyond simple labeling games, offering a method to understand how social selection mechanisms influence the evolution of agent types. For instance, we apply this mechanism to the learning process of agents acquiring behavioral skills required for successful team play. In this context, agent types correspond to skill levels, consistency represents the ability to predict a teammate's skill, and the selection mechanism reflects the principle that agents prefer partners of known ability over unknown. Our findings indicate that this evolution also leads to stability. By clarifying the dynamics of evolution driven by the preference for known over unknown partners, this research provides a foundation for developing effective training programs for sports teams. Specifically, it suggests that training should be structured so that high-skill agents consistently pair with other high-skill agents, as this promotes stability. These results hold significant implications for sports training, as stability is a crucial factor in achieving success. Sports teams are widely recognized as successful when their members share consistent behaviors and beliefs. Consequently, understanding how to cultivate consistency is essential for achieving team objectives. Our results provide insights into how to foster consistency in teams and explain how this process contributes to success. Specifically, the findings suggest that training high-skill agents to behave consistently is more effective than training low-skill agents to do so. This conclusion is based on the observation that when high-skill agents become consistent, low-skill agents are compelled to do so as well, whereas the reverse dynamic does not occur. Thus, this research provides a foundation for training programs designed to develop consistent teams. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are widely used to solve partial differential equations, yet their training via the least squares residual often suffers from slow convergence due to spectral bias. While spectral bias can be mitigated through the use of higher-order Adams methods, these introduce numerical instability. In this study, we demonstrate that adding a second-order Adam optimizer effectively addresses spectral bias without compromising numerical stability. We validate this finding across various high-dimensional partial differential equations. Furthermore, we analyze the underlying reasons for this improvement and establish a link between progressive training via Adam and spectral bias utilizing the singular value decomposition matrix of the linearized training process. These findings offer valuable insights for training PINNs on complex problems. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/kevinhcheung/Momentum-Spectral-Bias. Additionally, a supplementary video is available at https://youtu.be/4211111111. Finally, our results indicate that momentum-based optimization enhances both the training and generalization performance of PINNs. Code: https://github.com/kevinhcheung/momentum-pinn. arXiv preprint at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.03098. This study investigates a coupled system featuring two damped wave equations and one undamped wave equation, where the undamped component is linked to the coupled subsystems via integral boundaries. Specifically, the coupled undamped waves are dissipated through a pointwise undamped Kelvin-Voigt term that becomes locally disrupted. We demonstrate that solutions to the coupled damped waves decay exponentially in the $H^1 \times H^1$ norm, while the system is uniformly stable if and only if it is exact observable using observation data taken within the undamped, undriven wave equation, observed through both a pointwise undamped wave and a locally undamped, undriven coupled wave. Furthermore, we establish that the coupled waves decay polynomially in the $H^1 \times H^1$ norm, with the polynomial decay rate determined by the order of the discontinuity. Finally, we derive an observability inequality for the undamped coupled wave system with locally disrupted damping, where the constant depends on the order of the discontinuity and appears in the exponent of the stability estimate for the coupled system. This dependency is explicit, and we demonstrate that it can be removed. Additionally, the proof techniques employed are applicable to systems with moving point sources. Notably, the proof utilizes techniques from [10] alongside a novel approach to handle the local discontinuity in the damping term. This novel approach involves constructing a specific cutoff function to manage the local behavior of the coupled wave, followed by applying weighted energy estimates to derive an observability inequality for the system. This methodology is also effective in addressing coupled problems with time delays. In safety-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) contexts, the need for human-learnable models is critical. However, current approaches face two significant challenges: they are limited to simple, well-defined environments, and their learned models suffer from high complexity, making them prone to overfitting. To address these issues, we introduce a novel hierarchical RL framework that utilizes logical rules to direct the search process and generate explanations for the agent's behavior. By employing Inductive Logic Programming, our approach simultaneously inferts a set of logical rules from observed states and actions. Experiments conducted in both tabular and sparse reward settings demonstrate that, despite operating with far fewer samples than existing methods, our approach produces simpler, more generalizable models that remain safe. Furthermore, it reliably identifies underlying rules within the Markov Decision Process, enabling the acquisition of policies in environments that standard model-based RL struggles to solve. Finally, the system can effectively communicate its actions to humans by providing partial observability information. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchulz2000/EMLRL.

Initially, we demonstrate that this asymmetry manifests in the optical response of a mechanical oscillator when driven by compressed quadratures. Additionally, we analyze the impact of QCIOA on the optical cooling of mechanical oscillators. Our findings indicate that QCIOA can achieve the fundamental cooling limit and surpass the critical strain threshold required to observe a phonon blockade in a quantum transducer. These results offer a novel approach to controlling mechanical oscillators and hold potential applications for quantum information processing. Furthermore, our analysis provides a pathway to observe nonclassical effects in quantum transducers that convert mechanical excitations into optical sidebands within quantum networks. Finally, we examine the quantum resources needed to achieve QCIOA, highlighting its significance for quantum information processing. In this context, we propose a quantum transducer scheme utilizing a phonon-based interface to generate QCIOA, which can be implemented in existing experimental setups. This study addresses the Fenton minimax problem concerning the function $f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_{j}e^{2\pi i\xi_{j}x}$ by determining the optimal constants $|c_{j}|$ and frequencies $\xi_{j}$. Initially presented as an alternative to classical minimax problems, the issue was formulated by J.C. Fenton in 1953 within the context of amplitude modulation. Furthermore, we resolve a longstanding query posed by J. Beckus in 1993 regarding constants $c_{j}=1$. Our findings indicate that the optimization problem adheres to a convex-convex structure, enabling the development of a straightforward direct method based on the Weierstrass theorem and the Cauchy-Schwarz equality condition. This approach is particularly effective for small values of $j$ and $m$. Additionally, we propose a novel iteration scheme derived from the developed theory, which is well-suited to the problem's specific characteristics. Numerical results generated via this scheme are provided for all $m \leq 5$ and $j \leq 10$. We also demonstrate that our results improve upon those of S.J. Li and A. Kaniuth in specific cases. Finally, we suggest that an end-point issue noted by Beckus is likely a misinterpretation, and we offer a proof of this claim. We also conjecture that $m+1$ local minimizers exist for the optimization problem, with the direct method identifying the one characterized by smoothness. We further propose an extension of the problem to a vector context and outline the numerical results for this generalized scenario. Our analysis indicates that Beckus's conjecture is valid for $m \leq 10$ but fails for $m=11$. We offer an explanation for Beckus's conjecture and suggest a potential resolution for the case $m=5$. Ultimately, we conclude that Beckus's conjecture is not optimal for general $m$. Throughout this work, we also examine analogous problems in their concave-convex structure, providing numerical results for these variations. To facilitate broader application, we have established a webpage and established an open problem for the community. We anticipate that these resources will serve as a valuable tool for the field. Finally, we acknowledge the support of Dr. K. Kwon for the numerical computations. We are confident that our work will contribute to solving other open problems and advancing research in this area

We introduce a direct detection experiment for sub-GeV/nucleon spin-dependent dark matter ($\chi$) interactions, utilizing a 100 g $^6$Li target at the Max Planck Institute for Physics in Munich. This setup leverages the fact that $^6$Li is predominantly composed of protons bound in a deuterium-like configuration, making it highly effective for identifying nuclear recoil events. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed experiment can achieve sensitivity to spin-dependent cross-sections of approximately $\sigma_{sd} \sim 10^{-41}$ cm$^2$ for dark matter masses around 1 GeV, which is three orders of magnitude more sensitive than current bounds. Furthermore, we find that this experiment will constrain or rule out a broad range of spin-dependent interactions predicted by recent models. Blind image restoration (BUR) addresses the challenge of recovering high-quality images from low-quality sources by simultaneously estimating the image and the degradation model. This paper introduces a novel approach for single image restoration that treats the image as a superposition of multiple patches, where each patch is modeled as a linear combination of basis images. The basis images are iteratively updated using a conjugate gradient algorithm, while the mixture weights and degradation model parameters are inferred through a variational Bayesian (VB) framework. The proposed VB algorithm is applied to image restoration, demonstrating effective recovery of images corrupted by various models. Experimental results indicate that the method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhenghaochen1992/BlindImageRestoration. Furthermore, additional results and videos can be found at https://github.com/zhenghaochen1992/BlindImageRestoration-Results. The accompanying video, titled "Blind Image Restoration based on Kernel mixture," is available at https://github.com/zhenghaochen1992/BlindImageRestoration-Results/tree/master/videos. Nonuniform associative algebras constitute a noncommutative generalization of graded associative algebras, offering a noncommutative framework essential for studying dynamical quantum groups and their associated quantum spaces. These algebras serve as a key instrument in the study of quantum integrable systems, specifically regarding the construction of noncommutative, nonabelian $R$-matrices and the analysis of quantum Yang-Baxter equations. Within this context, associative Yang-Baxter equations have been formulated and analyzed. Recently, the authors have developed the concept of braided nonuniform associative algebras, which generalize braided associative algebras, and have derived the corresponding braided associative Yang-Baxter equation. This paper presents a further extension by introducing and examining nonuniform super-Yan-Baxter equations within the framework of braided nonuniform associative algebras. Within this framework, we establish the notion of an $R$-matrix and derive the associated braided quantum Yang-Baxter equation. Subsequently, we define $R$-matrices on braided nonuniform Hopf algebras, demonstrating their existence under specific conditions. This paper presents a formal framework for validating the logical structures of statements used to describe the behavior of imperative programs. While Hoare logic has been extensively studied and developed, recent advancements have enabled the formal validation of Hoare quadruples through proof theory and category theory. Building on these advancements, this work extends the validatation framework to accommodate richer logical forms—such as predicated types, modal operators, and higher-order order-sorted functions—and more fundamental statement types, including pre- and post-condition specifications. Consequently, this creates a bridge between natural language and formal semantics, facilitating the semantic analysis of pre- and post-condition specifications and enhancing the formal validation of programs specified with these statements. To demonstrate the practical utility of this approach, the paper includes examples drawn from the specifications of both synthetic and real-world Java programs. All definitions, proofs, and program analyses presented in this work have been implemented using the Coq proof assistant.

Canopus is a Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) replica state machine (RSM) designed for distributed systems. It features a streamlined protocol that reduces network communication overhead by leveraging asynchronous broadcast channels and minimizing the frequency of synchronous interactions. Furthermore, its replica implementation is optimized to enhance scalability. Canopus has been successfully deployed in various cloud environments, including AWS, Azure, and GCP, where it manages the serving of application data. However, current Canopus deployments are constrained by storage and computation bottlenecks. Canopus stores all received application messages in memory on every replica to maintain consistent ordering for the construction of deterministic state. Consequently, applications generating many small messages face significant computational overhead due to the sequential processing required for these messages in Canopus. This paper demonstrates how these Canopus-specific characteristics can be exploited to scale Canopus replicas, thereby addressing both computation and storage constraints. We introduce several techniques to scale Canopus based on these opportunities. Our evaluation results indicate that these techniques can reduce storage and computation bottlenecks by up to 4x and 2x, respectively. Furthermore, bottlenecks related to slow application functions can also be mitigated. Overall, Canopus can achieve 2x to 4x higher throughput compared to other BFT systems. To investigate the impact of cholesterol on membrane deformation and mechanical properties, we employed the coarse-grained MARTINI lipid model. Our simulations utilized an ensemble of laterally heterogeneous membranes containing varying concentrations of cholate as a model for cholesterol. We calculated the spring constant for various planar and spherically symmetric geometries, accounting for both lipid tilt and curvature. Our findings indicate that including cholesterol does not alter the MARTINI model's bending modulus; this result holds true regardless of whether cholesterol is distributed uniformly or unevenly. Furthermore, our computational approach enables the simultaneous analysis of multiple membranes, facilitating a statistical assessment of membrane properties under varying conditions. These results align with several experimental measurements regarding the effect of cholesterol on bending modulus, while contradicting others. Our analysis of the conflicting experimental data reveals that the observed discrepancies may stem from: (i) the coarse nature of certain experimental methodologies, (ii) potential artifacts arising from the purification process used to isolate pure lipid types, and (iii) the inherent laterally heterogeneous nature of lipid distributions in membranes. These conclusions are consistent with prior experimental findings. Additionally, our statistical analysis of the effects of cholesterol concentration on membrane deformation supports earlier experimental data, although it contradicts some other later studies. This model is derived using a specific operator ordering and employs a holonomy basis. The energy spectrum of high-energy cosmic rays is governed by energy-dependent sources and propagation mechanisms. To investigate this interval, physicists rely on data from extensive air showers generated by ultra-high-energy cosmic rays. This study presents, for the initial time, a comprehensive catalog of the most energetic showers recorded during the operation of the Pierre Auger Observatory under Phase I. This paper outlines the methods employed to locate and confirm these extreme events. The selected catalog comprises 22 showers, with energies surpassing 57 EeV, as derived from the Auger "simple" energy estimator. These events, which are crucial for constraining theoretical models, are also analyzed using an improved energy estimator. This analysis identifies a systematic energy bias inherent to the primary estimator. After applying a correction to the energy estimates for these 22 showers, the resulting energy distribution aligns closely with other available estimates from competing experiments. The authors propose that this catalog will facilitate future research utilizing Auger data. Furthermore, they offer an assessment of the capability to detect and observe the theoretically predicted "knee" in the energy spectrum using the full dataset accumulated by the detector. The observed events within the 50–100 EeV energy range are predominantly attributed to hadronic interactions, whereas those exceeding this threshold may originate from both hadronic and leptonic processes. Consequently, the catalog includes events from both regimes: 10 Auger events with energies between 50 and 100 EeV, and 13 events exceeding 100 EeV. Finally, the study examines the characteristics of these events regarding their energies, arrival directions, and arrival times. The observed data do not indicate any anisotropies in the sky distribution of these ultra-high-energy cosmic rays. The showers with energies above 100 EeV display a dipole-like distribution, though the statistical significance remains insufficient to confirm an anisotropic arrival direction. The observed excess in the Northern sky is attributed to the known Galactic plane. The energy estimates for these 22 highest-energy showers are accessible via the Auger Web Interface. Additionally, the shower directions and arrival times for these events are available through the same interface. This work was conducted by an international collaboration. A core component of realizability semantics involves modeling higher-dimensional coherence, where operations that are only equal up to a higher degree must be explicitly represented rather than merely assumed. We demonstrate that revised Gray categories, equipped with implementations, possess a compact structure that captures this aspect of semantics coherently. Specifically, there exists a strict 2-functor that maps full, realizability-compatible primitive tension-based rewriting semantics to them, serving as the categorical foundation for the type checking process. Furthermore, we establish that this semantics is free by proving that the 2-functor has a left adjoint. The construction of this universal right-adjoint is performed inductively, with each step providing a meaningful interpretation of the syntax. Ultimately, our construction yields a context-free grammar that generates the syntax responsible for coherence type checking. To demonstrate its utility, we apply this grammar to generate coherence terms within a specific subset of the programming language MultiPar. Additionally, we show how to extend the grammar to automatically name coherence type and proof variables based on the structure of the coherence terms being constructed. To support empirical validation, we have implemented this entire approach in Agda. Our implementation serves as the foundation for the coherence management tool Coherence, which handles coherence management tasks. We conclude by presenting several use cases that illustrate the utility of this semantics. These examples include coherence proofs for subtyping between processes in the programming language MultiPar, the management of coherence terms within a subset of Nominal Logic, and both human- and computer-aided approaches to managing coherence terms. Finally, we wrap up by discussing potential future research directions. This paper extends the work presented in [10]. Co-author J. K. We examine the "pigeonhole" scenario demonstrated by Ralph *et al.* (arXiv:1003.2534) from the perspective of quantum information, treating the parties as qubits. By computing entanglement measures for this system, we investigate the evolution of its entanglement structure. Our findings indicate that when all modes are considered, the phenomenon resembles genuine multipartite entanglement. Conversely, if the polarization degree of freedom is isolated, the system exhibits bipartite entanglement, causing the pigeonhole effect to vanish. These results offer a novel perspective on the pigeonhole phenomenon and deepen our understanding of its underlying quantum features. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the phenomenon can be observed within the transversal mode degree of freedom at near-infrared wavelengths, suggesting potential experimental verification. Finally, our examinated phenomenon is significantly more robust against noise than the one previously demonstrated by Ralph *et al.* (Phys. Rev. Lett. **104**, 230506 (2010)). This increased robustness stems from the non-orthogonality of the transversal modes, which renders the phenomenon less susceptible to decoherence. These discoveries may facilitate the design of new quantum information protocols. For instance, they could be applied to quantum key distribution, where a reduced key rate is acceptable in exchange for enhanced robustness. Additionally, our work challenges the traditional view that pigeonhole phenomena are merely nonlocal correlations, indicating a broader class of nonlocal effects. This insight may inspire researchers to explore additional resources, such as entanglement, in quantum nonlocality. Ultimately, our study advances our comprehension of the pigeonhole phenomenon and paves the way for further investigation into its various attributes. The most critical component of the Cosmic Ray Anti-Neutron Detector (CRAND) is the time projection chamber (TPC), which is engineered to identify the proton fragment of the 1-10 GeV/c cosmic ray anti-neutron (CRAN) following its capture at approximately 400 km low Earth orbit (LEO). This study presents a Monte Carlo analysis of the dominant cosmic ray proton component of CRAND captures within the TPC at this altitude. The analysis utilized a three-dimensional model of the TPC, derived from the 2018 design, to simulate proton interactions within the detector material. At 400 km LEO, the differential flux of protons across the model's momentum range of 1 GeV/c to 10 GeV/c ranges from 1.0 to 1.5 x 10^-8 cm^-2 s^-1 (sr^-1 (GeV/c)^-1), with the peak differential flux occurring near 1 GeV/c. A total of 10^6 proton tracks were generated and tracked through the TPC model, with 99.9% of the simulated protons producing at least one charged particle track within the detector. The resulting track length distribution in the TPC gas was analyzed to determine the maximum track length, which was found to be 1.95 meters. The calculated average track length was 0.52 meters, while the root mean square deviation was 0.22 meters. The primary factor influencing the track length distribution is the angle of the proton's path relative to the TPC's central axis. Additionally, the probability distribution for the number of tracks generated per proton was analyzed, revealing an average of 1.02 tracks per proton and a standard deviation of 0.42 tracks. The mean track multiplicity was determined to be 2. The frequency distribution of the angle between the central axis and the incoming proton's path was also examined. Finally, the probability distribution for the number of primary cosmic ray protons required to generate a single track in the TPC gas was analyzed, with an average of 4.6 primary protons needed to produce one track. These findings are expected to significantly enhance the understanding of the cosmic ray proton component interacting with the TPC, thereby improving the overall comprehension of CRAN capture events at 400 km LEO. Ultimately, this research will aid in optimizing the TPC design to maximize the detection efficiency of CRAN captures

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently become essential tools for various artificial intelligence applications, yet current research often lacks a unified, profound, and universal design principle for creating effective GNN frameworks. This paper addresses the critical issue of how to construct a general framework from which all meaningful GNN models can be derived. We propose a universal pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton as the fundamental structural blueprint for GNN frameworks. This skeleton is designed to be adaptable, allowing any specific meaningful GNN to be derived by reconfiguring the graph skeleton within local modules. In essence, any meaningful GNN framework is constructed by reorganizing local structure through link rewiring. We demonstrate the universal applicability of this framework across diverse real-world applications, including node classification, image classification, recommendation, and community detection. Furthermore, specific instances of GNN frameworks derived from this design are provided for the MNIST and IMDB node classification tasks, as well as the standard iGraphComm task for community detection. The experimental results confirm the framework's high effectiveness and scalability. This study offers a universal and profound perspective for creating general GNN frameworks, significantly advancing the theoretical understanding of the field. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhongtao1214/pyramid_gnn.

Recent years have seen growing interest in private low-rank matrix completion, a task that involves inferring a matrix known to be of low rank from a few partially observed noisy entries. This paper presents the Huber framework, a general framework for private matrix completion that leverages low-rank constraints to reduce noise in partial observations. We provide a theoretical analysis of the error trade-off between the reconstruction and approximation errors under both $\ell_2$ and Huber loss functions, as well as noise sample count, to identify the optimal parameters for the differentially private Huber framework. Furthermore, we introduce a distributed, differentially private algorithm for low-rank matrix completion founded on this framework, demonstrating through numerical experiments that it outperforms various existing methods. Our implementation of the distributed Huber framework achieves a $1.5\times$ significant improvement over a leading prior method. Finally, we illustrate the framework's utility in two real-world scenarios: private gene expression matrix completion and private commute time estimation. In both cases, our proposed methods surpass current approaches, delivering substantial improvements of $2\times$ and $4\times$, respectively. We report the discovery of a prominent gap in the protoplanetary disk of CIDA 1, an extremely low-mass star with a mass of 0.009 solar masses and an age of 11 million years. This gap, identified through ALMA observations, is situated between 100 and 200 au from the star and possesses a width of 50 au. The gap's position relative to the star aligns closely with the orbit of a massive planet detected in a direct imaging campaign by the same team. Our analysis of the gap's morphology and location, along with observations of the planet, supports an in situ formation scenario for this massive planet. We demonstrate that the planet's mass is approximately 10 Jupiter masses and that its migration rate is significantly slower than the gap's migration age. This study represents the first instance of both a massive planet and its corresponding gap being identified simultaneously, providing robust evidence that massive planets can form via in situ gravitational instability and remain stationary even at vast distances from their host stars. Additionally, we show that the gap in CIDA 1 is more pronounced than those observed in other T Tauri and very low-mass star systems, yet its shape and position are consistent with those around brown dwarfs and massive and very low-mass stars. This suggests that the formation of massive planets via in situ gravitational instability is more common around objects with higher masses than previously believed. The presence of this gap may also influence the chemical and physical properties of the disk material within and outside the gap, potentially affecting the formation of low-mass planets and the migration of massive planets. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for understanding the initial mass function of planets and the migration and formation of massive planets.
