The intense absorption of intergalactic Lyman-$\alpha$ photons by neutral hydrogen prevents Lyman limit photons from reaching Earth, creating a Lyman-$\alpha$ "wall" in the intergalactic medium (IGM) beyond the mean Lyman-$\alpha$ density fluctuation scale. This phenomenon generates a "screen" of ionized bubbles surrounding the observer. We introduce the concept of a "Lyman-$\alpha$ screen" to describe this ionized layer and have developed a prototype instrument to conduct astronomical photometry through it. Utilizing Lyman-$\alpha$ photons scattered from the screen, the prototype aims to achieve approximately 100 times greater sensitivity than Lyman-limit photons passing through. This device consists of a large-area (100 cm$^2$) single LYSO:Ce scintillator coupled to a three-channel microchannel plate (MCP) detector. The spectrally selected MCP outputs are converted into digital signals by three silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), which are subsequently processed by a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). This paper investigates the distributed detection of set-isometric graphs within symmetric networks, a challenge referred to as Set-ISoNet. Leveraging the structural symmetry of these networks, we introduce graph devices, which function similarly to coset devices in conventional symmetric networks but operate on graph isomorphism classes instead of individual vertices. We establish sufficient conditions ensuring the existence of a Gaussian distribution defined on graph isomorphism classes that function as valid graph devices. Furthermore, we reduce the original problem to a scenario involving binary set-isometric networks, where we propose coset devices for this simplified context. Finally, we demonstrate the existence of a Gaussian distribution over isomorphism classes of single-vertex sets that align with these coset devices. Collectively, these components constitute a solution utilizing graph devices to address the Set-ISoNet problem. This methodology mirrors the conventional approach using coset devices and Gaussian distributions on single-vertex sets in standard symmetric networks, specifically for set-invariant decision-making. Additionally, we examine multiple testing and hypothesis testing as initial stages of set-isometric and single-vertex-set-isometric decision processes, respectively. The paper concludes by detailing several examples of set-isometric networks. Notably, one example indicates that Set-ISoNet cannot be reliably solved, even when utilizing graph devices constructed from either Gaussian distributions on single-vertex-set isomorphism classes or those on single-vertex isomorphism classes. This finding underscores the necessity of formulating and resolving Set-ISoNet problems based on isomorphism classes of set vertices rather than single-vertex isomorphism classes. The proposed framework is also applicable to symmetric networks with set-invariant decision-making requirements. To achieve this, sets of graphs representing single-vertex isomorphism classes are treated as single-vertex sets, and single-vertex isomorphism classes are managed as single-vertex set isomorphism classes. In this scenario, graph devices are defined over single-vertex set isomorphism classes instead of set vertex isomorphism classes. Crucially, this approach does not rely on Gaussian distributions over set vertex isomorphism classes, thereby avoiding the need to address the existence of such distributions on set vertices. The paper presents multiple instances where graphs on single-vertex isomorphism classes yield single-vertex set isomorphism classes, yet these classes do not correspond to set-isometric networks. Image Cataloging (IC) represents a novel and promising domain within image search and retrieval, aiming to dynamically maintain and update the content of images that are not directly searchable. This process involves learning and applying transformations to convert images into a new form that is both visually comparable and searchable. Currently, research in this field is in its nascent stages. Existing methods rely on manual annotation of image sets and the creation of catalogs by experts, which is labor-intensive and restricts current studies to static catalogs with fixed sets of visual elements and their transformations. In contrast, this paper introduces a dynamic approach to image cataloging that enables users to interact with and annotate images, thereby generating catalogs on demand. We propose a new deep learning architecture designed to jointly model visual transformations and their inverse operations. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model significantly outperforms strong baselines. Furthermore, we present a web-based application built around this model to facilitate user interaction with image catalogs and showcase its versatility through various use cases. The source code for our models and application is publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/DynamicImageCataloging. The paper itself is also available as a video on the same platform. The image search functionality utilized in our demonstration is provided by Google. Finally, we invite the community to explore the potential of image cataloging and its applications in real-world scenarios. Our goal is to foster collaboration between researchers and practitioners to develop this emerging field and enhance its practical utility. We believe that adopting a dynamic approach to image cataloging is essential for the domain's success, as it ensures the model remains relevant to the specific image cataloging tasks required by users. By enabling users to define catalogs rather than relying on pre-annotated datasets, the community can better understand which transformations and visual models are most effective for cataloging real images. Furthermore, this dynamic approach facilitates rapid prototyping and iteration, which are critical for developing practical solutions. We look forward to collaborating with both researchers and practitioners to advance the image cataloging field and realize its potential in practical applications. Our vision is that image cataloging will become a fundamental capability for users and systems interacting with images, serving as a powerful tool for visual communication and collaboration. We believe that a dynamic approach is the most effective way to achieve this vision and enable image cataloging to make a real impact on how people work with images. We are committed to supporting research and development in this area and providing resources and support to the community to help advance image cataloging as a practice. The keyless communication framework eliminates the necessity for a shared key between transmitter and receiver by utilizing the statistical characteristics of the channel. This process relies heavily on channel hardening, which refers to the phenomenon where channel realizations converge to a constant as the number of antennas grows. In contrast to channel-dependent keyless schemes, this work investigates channel-independent keyless communication over i.i.d. block fading channels and evaluates their performance using sum rate as the metric. Specifically, we analyze keyless verification over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels, observing that achieving a non-vanishing sum rate is impossible in this environment due to the absence of channel hardening. Consequently, we analyze the performance of keyless verification over independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) block fading channels, deriving the asymptotic sum rate as the number of antennas increases. Our findings are validated through numerical results, and we also examine the impact of channel covariance matrix structure on performance. Ultimately, we demonstrate the efficacy of this keyless framework by comparing it against the classical channel-independent keyless framework. Finally, we evaluate the performance across different network topologies, including star and partial mesh networks. The problem of a particle rolling without slipping on a horizontally moving rough surface, resulting in washboard potentials, is re-examined within a Lagrangian framework to account for rolling effects. By applying the Euler-Lagrange formalism to derive the equation of motion for the generalized coordinate representing the particle's relative phase with the potential peaks, an exact solution is obtained in the weak-coupling limit. This approach reveals a "new" dispersion-free coherent state that resonantly bounces between two effective Landau-Zener barriers, a phenomenon termed the Schl\"appkoefizient. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that rolling without slipping fundamentally alters the dynamical phase, thereby eliminating the standard interference pattern and replacing it with one governed by the complementary Schl\"appkoefizient in the weak-coupling regime. Finally, the theoretical framework is validated by analyzing a recently observed experimental realization of this washboard potential, specifically the optically trapped and manipulated ground state of a doped ion in a crystal. The calculation of the coherent state's lifetime indicates that, in the context of ion qubits, rolling without slipping must be incorporated into physical models. These findings underscore the necessity of including rolling effects in research concerning artificial quantum systems, including those based on superconducting circuits. Additionally, the study sheds light on the connection between coherent and coherent-like quantum states. Notably, the theoretical framework developed here is broadly applicable to research involving driven two-level systems. In conclusion, this work highlights the significant role of rolling effects in systems featuring dispersion-free movement within washboard potentials. Specifically, it establishes the existence of a universal phenomenon where rolling effects cause coherent states to transform into "coherent-like" states during evolution. This insight may offer a valuable perspective for interpreting recent experimental findings regarding "coherent-like" states and the "quantum-to-classical" transition. Moreover, it may enable the design of new quantum devices capable of generating "coherent-like" states on demand. Overall, this research provides a significant foundation for advancing our understanding of quantum mechanics and developing future quantum technologies. Specifically, it establishes a new paradigm for coherent quantum computing and communication by enabling the manipulation of quantum states and gates based on "coherent-like" states. This could lead to more efficient and robust quantum computing and communication systems, as "coherent-like" states offer certain advantages over conventional coherent states, such as increased robustness against decoherence and error correction. We present a new framework for estimating impulse response functions (IRFs) through local projections, designed to mitigate numerical errors inherent in directly computed responses. This noise correction is achieved by inferring structural parameters from historical data, ensuring that past impulse responses align with past residuals. We examine various estimation techniques within this framework and demonstrate, via simulations, that these methods effectively handle small sample size challenges and yield substantial gains in mean square error compared to standard local projection estimates. Furthermore, an application to impulse response data derived from estimated DSGE models highlights the substantial benefits of the proposed approach. Finally, we define a novel criterion for selecting significant IRFs, which depends on the magnitude of historical responses relative to the estimated model's own residuals. Our results indicate that applying this criterion to impulse responses generated by local projections successfully filters out spurious and unstable results. The paper concludes by discussing how this significance criterion can be utilized in structural macroeconomic analyses. Supplementary materials, including a user-friendly R package and replication data, are available at https://www.politico.org/localprojections. The package also implements a significance test for impulse responses from Dynamic Factor Models (DFM), which was subsequently extended to allow for the selection of significant IRFs within a DFM framework. This functionality is accessible at https://www.politico.org/dfmselect. Additionally, we detail modifications to ensure that selected IRFs possess structural parameters consistent with historical impulses. Finally, we explore the application of these algorithms in macro-fiscal analysis, where they have proven highly effective. Specifically, we show that when fiscal shocks are derived from estimated IRFs, the resulting changes in macroeconomic variables remain stable and robust. To ensure reproducibility, all relevant data and code are provided in a public repository at https://www.politico.org/fiscalanalysis. The paper also includes a section on the application of these algorithms to analyze the impact of fiscal policy during the COVID-19 pandemic. This section features an extensive sensitivity analysis of large fiscal stimulus packages, revealing substantial differences in outcomes based on the specific shock used. However, when multiple shocks are aggregated, the results become more robust, and the outcomes of large fiscal packages remain stable and reproducible. Notably, the long-term effects of fiscal policy appear minimal, while short-term effects are amplified. These findings underscore the critical importance of accurately identifying and quantifying fiscal shocks. Finally, we address the challenges associated with communicating these results to a broader audience. We calculate the angular part of the Casimir angular momentum for a point charge in an empty, rotating frame within the Rindler wedge of Minkowski spacetime, defined by a finite temperature and acceleration. Our findings demonstrate that the angular Casimir momentum is finite, in contrast to the uniform Casimir momentum of a point charge in this wedge, which is known to be infinite. Furthermore, we show that the sign of the Casimir angular momentum is opposite to that of the angular momentum of a real point charge in the wedge, indicating that it does not simply compensate for the angular momentum of real electrons. This result aligns with expectations, as the symmetry of electron spin around the Rindler trajectory differs from the symmetry of thermal momentum within it. Finally, we examine the physical significance of our results in the context of test particle orbits in rotating frames, specifically addressing whether rotating electrons emit radiation. We argue that if rotating electrons do emit radiation, it would be Rindler radiation rather than Larmor radiation, thereby preserving the validity of the equivalence principle. Consequently, we contend that the quantum vacuum in a rotating frame exhibits non-zero angular momentum, a concept previously explored in the context of angular acceleration. This conclusion also resolves the issue of angular charge neutrality in a rotating universe. We anticipate that these findings will inspire further research into frame-dragging effects in quantum field theory, their connection to frame-dragging in general relativity, and the associated energy costs in terms of the Hamiltonian. Additionally, we propose that our findings may help explain the origin of dark matter. Specifically, we suggest that the significant mass density of dark matter in the universe can be attributed to the finite density of Landau charge density in an accelerating frame, a result derived in our earlier study. In this paper, we extend this analysis to the angular momentum of electrons, showing that it is also finite. This suggests that rotating electrons, rather than bulk matter, may be the source of dark matter. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this conclusion is consistent with the existence of a dark disk of matter around the center of galaxies, thereby supporting the hypothesis that dark matter originates from the angular Casimir momentum of electrons in an accelerating frame, as previously established. Finally, we note that our conclusions regarding dark matter are compatible with recent observations of galactic rotation curves, which have been widely used as evidence for the existence of dark matter. Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that involves identifying entities within sentences and categorizing them accordingly. This paper introduces a method for enhancing NER performance by leveraging the hyperbolic space inherent in language semantics. We propose a hyperbolic embedding space designed to offer superior context representation, which, when integrated with an entity labeling network, forms the foundation of the Detailed NER Enhancement via Hyperbolic Space (DEHS) model. Furthermore, we develop a novel hyperbolic space induction model, the Hyperbolic Progressive Self-training Entity Recognition (HPSE-RH), which iteratively and self-supervisedly generates high-quality training data from unlabeled data to further boost entity recognition precision. Experimental outcomes on the English Wikiann and Universal Dependencies (UD) datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach. The code is accessible at https://github.com/123456789gh/DEHS.

The widespread adoption of cloud computing has significantly influenced various scientific and technical fields. Virtual machines (VMs) serve as the foundational element of cloud technology, enabling users to rapidly deploy and scale resources as needed. However, load imbalance caused by the heterogeneous nature of VMs often results in performance degradation. To address this issue, we have created Prepartition, a new load distribution approach designed to enhance resource utilization within VM environments. Our primary objective is to assign work items to VMs in a way that prevents overload and eliminates the need for pre-partitioning data. Prepartition operates by distributing each work item across all VMs in a round-robin fashion, dynamically adjusting the workload based on real-time performance metrics. We conducted extensive experiments to evaluate our method's performance. These results demonstrate that Prepartition outperforms both the random allocation method and state-of-the-art techniques, such as DynamicLoadBalancing, while incurring only a slight increase in computational overhead. Consequently, Prepartition is well-suited for cloud data hubs handling big data processing and other parallel tasks. We have open-sourced the method to facilitate its use in diverse cloud environments. A preliminary version of this work was presented at CIKM 2019. The dynamic nature of modern systems makes forecasting essential, yet prediction remains a challenging task. While equilibrium forecasting aims to determine long-term system states, existing methods often suffer from the curse of dimensionality and lack the capacity to learn dynamic representations. To address these issues, we introduce the FENet framework, which utilizes the fixed-point property of mappings to identify a low-dimensional dynamic representation. Our central hypothesis is that equilibrium can be more effectively learned through the fixed-point mechanism of a mapping than other equilibrium definitions. We validate FENet's superior performance in both prediction and dimensionality reduction across various datasets, including Lorenz90, El Niño, and El-Salvador. Additionally, we demonstrate that FENet can be extended to predict continuous trajectories. Finally, we show that the features generated by FENet yield state-of-the-art results in representation learning. Our source code is available at https://github.com/ashishgarg12345g/ashishgarg12345g.github.io/EquilibriumLearning. Furthermore, our findings have been featured in the cover story of Communications of the ACM. This study examines the research of Bareinboim and colleagues (2016, 2018, 2020), which establishes identification conditions for inferring causal relationships from observational data using observational graphs augmented with front-door and backdoor variables. These conditions guarantee that a specific causal model can account for certain observed joint probability distributions. The current work derives analogous limits regarding the causal capabilities of systems designed to intervene on target variables based on available observational data. Furthermore, the analysis explores extensions to high-dimensional settings involving vectors of random variables, with additional findings on constraints within these environments. Finally, a empirical simulation study is conducted to assess the impact of structural causal model (SCM) specifications on the precision of discovering these cause-limited capabilities within SCMs. Specifically, it evaluates the performance of algorithms designed to identify such models when parameters are estimated through various observation-based learning methods, including those that rely on causal assumptions to enhance performance. This approach extends existing structural equation learning techniques to their inverse problem and is applicable to high-dimensional scenarios. The proposed algorithms demonstrate robust performance across a variety of scenarios, including those featuring high-dimensional confounding. Additionally, these algorithms can be enhanced by incorporating domain knowledge via causal graphs. The cause-limited capabilities identified by these methods hold significant potential for diverse applications, such as determining whether causal models can be identified and utilized for prediction, control, or policy learning. They also facilitate decisions on whether to deploy existing systems or invest in developing new ones to address specific problems. The ability to quantify these limits provides a metric for evaluating the utility of available data and existing systems in achieving desired objectives. This framework supports cost-benefit analyses for making informed deployment decisions and aids in designing effective interventions for both existing and future systems. Furthermore, understanding these causal boundaries allows for the identification of necessary additional data collection efforts required to achieve specific goals. This approach fosters a more systematic method for learning, deploying, and upgrading causal models, ultimately leading to improved interventions. This represents a significant step toward achieving the ultimate objective of causal modeling: effective intervention. The results also have important implications for high-dimensional causal modeling, an area that has seen limited development compared to non-parametric and parametric statistical methods. This study introduces a method for maintaining secure predictive surveillance in linear time-invariant systems against covert attacks. While prior research has focused on the robustness of convex cost-based predictive surveillance against observable attacks, it has been established that these predictive filters can be vulnerable to system failures undetectable by outputs, a problem known as covert attack. Although alternative approaches employing prediction-based residual analysis have demonstrated resilience to such failures, they often suffer from low sensitivity. To address this, we propose an effective solution by integrating prediction-based residual analysis with predictive surveillance based on convex costs. We demonstrate that this proposed approach simultaneously achieves high sensitivity and robustness when detecting covert failures. Furthermore, we establish that predictive surveillance using convex costs remains effective in detecting a broad range of covert failures, even when those failures remain invisible to the predictive residual analysis we employ. Finally, the efficacy of our approach is validated through a simulation study. Notably, we also examine how the selection of the prediction-based residual analysis component influences the performance of the resulting predictive surveillance filter. The simulation results confirm that our proposed method outperforms existing existing approaches and that all theoretical findings are consistent with these outcomes. Notably, we observe that while our proposed approach is robust against most covert attacks, it remains susceptible to a specific subset of covert failures that are effectively detected by predictive surveillance using convex costs but are undetectable by the included prediction-based residual analysis. This highlights a significant trade-off inherent in our proposed solution. Ultimately, we demonstrate that predictive surveillance utilizing convex costs is inherently robust against observable attacks, a fact that our proposed approach leverages to detect covert failures that would otherwise go undetected. However, it is important to note that predictive surveillance based on convex costs is not robust against all types of attacks, including certain covert failures, a limitation that our proposed approach also inherits. To overcome this limitation, we propose incorporating prediction-based residual analysis into predictive surveillance filters. Crucially, we show that this enhancement does not compromise the sensitivity of the predictive surveillance filter. Our approach offers two significant advantages: first, it enables the detection of failures that are undetectable by prediction-based residual analysis when used independently; and second, it ensures robustness against all types of attacks, including various forms of covert attacks, which is not guaranteed by predictive surveillance based on convex costs alone. We refer to predictive surveillance with convex costs combined with prediction-based residual analysis as predictive surveillance using predictive Cost-Residual Analysis (PCRA). Document summarization for Indian languages remains a largely unexplored domain. While machine learning methods have successfully transformed document summarization across various languages, no significant research has yet focused on summarizing texts in Indian tongues. This study introduces an unsupervised, language-agnostic approach utilizing graph representations to generate summaries. The text is modeled as a graph where an attention-based neural network identifies the most critical nodes. These key nodes facilitate information exchange between the encoder and decoder within the encoding-decoding framework. Experiments conducted on multiple Indian languages demonstrate that the Graph-Assembled Encoder-Decoder (GAE-ISumm) significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ashwin-krishnan/GAE-ISumm.

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are a type of generative model that produce data by learning a latent space. To ensure the quality of generated samples, the code within this latent space must maintain a strong geometric structure. In contrast, the latent spaces of most existing VAEs lack this organization, resulting in poor sample quality. To address this, we introduce the Constrained Minimum Square VAE (CMS-VAE), a novel architecture designed to learn well-organized latent spaces and substantially improve the quality of its outputs. Our experiments demonstrate that the CMS-VAE outperforms state-of-the-art VAEs based on the Intrinsic Dimensionality Estimator (IDE) metric, indicating more organized latent spaces, and also achieves superior sample quality, as evidenced by higher Inception Scores (IS). These results highlight the CMS-VAE's significant potential for generating high-quality data. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-chen/CMS-VAE. The proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) has sparked significant interest in developing smart environments, particularly within home automation. However, a primary challenge remains: ensuring that data transmitted between devices is authentic and trustworthy. This difficulty is compounded by the rising demand for private, secure, and sustainable solutions. To address these issues, we propose an innovative system for tracking household appliances using a hybrid positioning algorithm that integrates Visible Light Communication (VLC) and LoRaWAN. Furthermore, we utilize blockchain technology to securely store and manage all relevant information. Our findings indicate that this system can accurately monitor appliance locations with an error margin under 10 centimeters. This survey examines the current state of research in parameterized algorithmics and complexity regarding the upward planarity testing problem. Upward planarity determines whether a digraph can be represented as a straight-line drawing on two parallel lines such that all edges align with the vertical direction. This graph-theoretic challenge is addressed through various parameterizations. We focus on the parameters vertex degree, feedback vertex set size, and vertex feedback length. We present comprehensive algorithms and a detailed analysis for each parameter, covering both algorithmic strategies and complexity aspects. Finally, we outline open problems for future investigation. We anticipate that these insights will assist researchers in developing new parameterized approaches to upward planarity. Additionally, our proposed algorithms for vertex feedback length and feedback vertex set can be adapted to serve as effective heuristics for upward planarity testing. We believe these techniques will advance the field of upward planar drawings, particularly for drawings of dense graphs. All discussed concepts are implemented in the open-source software package UpwardPlanarity (http://www.upwardplanarity.org). This implementation includes not only upward planarity testing but also several useful extensions, such as upward planarity testing with user-defined constraints and the generation of optimal upward planar embeddings. We hope this free access to these tools will enable users to explore various graph classes and their upward planar properties. We trust that providing a software implementation will foster greater interest in upward planarity and encourage the community to contribute further extensions and improvements. Finally, we acknowledge that many of the results presented were derived in collaboration with members of the Combinatorial Graph Drawing Group at TU Dresden. We are deeply grateful to them for their support, collaboration, and friendship. We also express our sincere appreciation to all collaborators for their invaluable contributions. Thank you.

Ensemble methods have proven highly effective in machine learning by combining multiple models to surpass the performance of individual ones. This paper introduces a method for creating robust, generalizable, and accurate probabilistic models from large-scale, noisy, crowdsourced data regarding disease risk factors. By integrating ensemble modeling with a novel approach to human uncertainty, we define a human softmax distribution that accommodates both stochastic and epistemic uncertainty. We hypothesize that training ensembles on such noisy data will yield more reliable and generalizable predictions regarding health risk factors. We further posit that measuring uncertainty through the lens of human softmax distributions will enhance the practicality and utility of these models for end-users. Finally, we demonstrate that utilizing ensemble modeling alongside human softmax uncertainty metrics outperforms traditional approaches like maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and deterministic models in generating accurate, high-confidence human risk factor profiles. This methodology is particularly advantageous for identifying risk factors in populations with limited biological data. Our methodology is publicly accessible via GitHub (https://github.com/brandonr123/Ensemble-Human-Softmax). Additionally, the model is available for download from the Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/45q92/. Our analysis employed 1,000 synthetic data points derived from 100 participants across ten human risk factors. We evaluated four probabilistic modeling techniques: MLE, deterministic, human softmax (single model), and human softmax ensembles (100 models). To assess and compare the uncertainty distributions of these models, we applied standard entropic metrics including Shannon entropy, Theil's uncertainty, and minimum probability. Results indicate that human softmax ensembles produce the most accurate models with the highest confidence intervals for risk factors in this synthetic population. Specifically, ensemble models outperformed deterministic models by 100% in accuracy and achieved 30% higher confidence for risk factors. Furthermore, ensemble models surpassed both deterministic and single-softmax models in generating accurate, high-confidence profiles for ten specific risk factors. These findings suggest that ensembles offer the most reliable and confident characterization of specific risk factors within a population, even when individual models struggle with high noise levels. Overall, our analysis demonstrates that ensembles generate superior models for characterizing risk factors in this synthetic population, surpassing the performance of maximum likelihood estimation and deterministic approaches. This is especially beneficial for populations with scarce biological data, such as those in low- and middle-income countries. We examine the stability of equilibrium outcomes in a one-dimensional nonlocal contest governed by Bayes' rule, involving $N$ players with private values drawn independently and identically from any distribution. Players' strategies involve reporting a quantity that may differ from their private value, with payoffs determined by the chosen outcome function and their true value minus the reported quantity. Resolvability refers to the existence of a Bayesian Nash equilibrium in strictly monotone strategies. Under an almost monotone distribution assumption, Gross and Nalebuff (1999) demonstrated that resolvable thresholds are established at the density's support endpoints, whereas Jensen and Ritzberger (2001) showed that resolvable distributions with finite first moments must be monotone. This study removes the almost monotone density assumption and proves that for any distribution with a finite first moment, a Bayesian Nash equilibrium in strictly increasing strategies exists. Furthermore, within the class of quantum nonlocal games, we show that any maximally correlated quantum strategy profile is resolvable. This finding contrasts with a recent result by Pycia and Yang (2020), which indicates that in certain correlated quantum games, no Bayesian Nash equilibrium exists among strictly increasing strategies when players possess strictly concave strictly increasing utility functions. Our findings suggest that the absence of such an equilibrium in those specific games stems from the players' strict utility properties rather than non-monotone density support or other distribution characteristics. Additionally, we explore the link between resolvable and monotone equilibria. Finally, we generalize our main findings to $N$-dimensional settings. These contributions advance the understanding of the existence of Bayesian Nash equilibria and contribute to the broader field of quantum game theory. The vortex lattice represents the dominant zero-field state of a superconductor in its ordered regime. Recent theoretical findings suggest that vortex-vortex interactions can reverse sign, implying the existence of distinct vortex-lattice phases connected by a grid vortex-crystal-to-enclosed-vortex-glass transition. To date, experimental confirmation of this transition has been absent. In this study, we present microwave reflectometry data from a high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate that demonstrates a clear transition between these two vortex states. This observation marks the first direct proof of the vortex grid transition and indicates that the vortex-crystal phase possesses greater robustness than previously believed. Furthermore, our results establish that a single superconductor can exhibit both the vortex-crystal and vortex-glass phases. Finally, the observed maximum in in-plane conductivity aligns with percolation models. These findings are essential for developing new technologies for manipulating and confining vortices in superconducting devices. Additionally, they offer a pathway to investigate the relationship between vortex lattice structure and the dynamics of quasiparticle excitations. To achieve this, we developed a novel method to manipulate vortices using microwaves under a magnetic field. This technique enables the study of vortex dynamics and the verification of theoretical predictions regarding the relationship between vortex position and quasiparticle excitation dynamics. By combining microwave spectroscopy with magnetic-field manipulation, we can test the link between quasiparticle excitations and vortex grid transitions, thereby advancing our understanding of superconductivity in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates. This approach is expected to significantly enhance the study of vortex dynamics in these materials. Directional flow in heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and the LHC is a critical signature for understanding the strong interaction quark-gluon plasma (QGP). Recent studies indicate that thermal photons emitted during the pre-equilibrium stage carry significant flow anisotropy, which can enhance experimental observations of thermal photon directional flow. This work advances upon earlier findings by calculating thermal photon directional flow under conditions where the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) exhibits strong viscosity anisotropy. Our results demonstrate that the vector and triangular flow modes of thermal photons are robust observables capable of precisely constraining viscous anisotropic coefficients of strongly interacting QGP at heavy-ion colliders. Specifically, the thermal photon transverse momentum differential multiplicity, directional flow velocity, and elliptic flow parameter ($v_1$) at an average transverse momentum of $\langle p_T \rangle = 1.5$ GeV/$c$ are identified as optimal observables for extracting the shear viscosity coefficient $\eta/s$ at the QGP initial stage. Furthermore, the high transverse momentum directional flow spectral asymmetry, defined as $A_{\eta_{\perp}/\eta_{\parallel}} = (v_2^{\eta_{\perp}} - v_2^{\eta_{\parallel}})/(v_1^{\eta_{\perp}} - v_1^{\eta_{\parallel}})$, serves as an excellent observable for determining the bulk viscosity coefficient $\eta_{\parallel}/\eta_{\perp}$ at the QGP initial stage. These findings underscore the unique utility of thermal photons as an essential tool for investigating QGP viscosity at the start of heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, we predict that a future measurement of thermal photon directional flow at a future circular collider (FCC) could significantly enhance the precision of viscosity constraints for the QGP created in RHIC and LHC collisions. Consequently, this research establishes a foundation for developing viscosity meters using thermal photons. Finally, we advocate for a dedicated experimental search for thermal photons in heavy-ion collisions to enable the precise study of QGP viscosity at colliders. This investigation is crucial for a comprehensive understanding of the QGP, which is expected to be strongly anisotropic at the initial stages of heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, our results suggest that future measurements of thermal photons will be essential for a thorough understanding of the QGP. We anticipate that upcoming experimental efforts to detect thermal photons will yield valuable insights into the properties of the QGP.

We present an analytical method for determining the free energy of two distinct magnetic phases in triangular and kagome lattices, which emerge below two specific temperatures. This approach is applicable to both the ferromagnetic (FM) phase, valid for all spin magnitudes on triangular lattices, and the 12-sub-kagome (12k) spin-1/ liquid on kagome lattices. This technique complements prior studies by S. Ye and X.-G. Wen (Phys. Rev. B 66, 045101) regarding the kagome lattice and the findings of S. Ye and X.-G. Wen (Phys. Rev. B 67, 015114) on the presence of a phase on triangular lattices for spin values $s < 1/2$. Our findings confirm that the order parameter of the ferromagnetic transition equals the Sussman order parameter, aligning with numerical data from S. Ye and X.-G. Wen (Phys. Rev. B 67, 015114). Furthermore, we demonstrate that the order parameter on kagome lattices is a composite of the Sussman and N\'eel order parameters, thereby establishing that the N\'eel order parameter vanishes in the ferromagnetic phase. Finally, we show that the critical exponents associated with the ferromagnetic transition on both lattices are not universal; they depend on the relative strengths of exchange couplings and the temperature at which the spin value was fixed. Consequently, we predict that the zero-temperature ground state on kagome lattices is not the 12k spin-1/ liquid but rather a ferromagnetic state. This outcome resolves a longstanding debate concerning the ground state of the $s=1/2$ kagome lattice, which originated from conflicting exact and numerical results. Ultimately, the ferromagnetic phase is characterized by a finite probability of finding the system in the 12k state, indicating that the two phases coexist in the thermodynamic limit. This coexistence implies that the finite-temperature phase diagram on kagome lattices features a line rather than a point, a prediction supported by recent DMRG calculations (J. Liu, Y. This paper addresses the statistical analysis of such experiments within a material informatics context, focusing on identifying which intervention effects are active in underlying mechanisms. We introduce a framework utilizing model-based feature regulations to establish an "identifiable" subset of effects, leveraging the dependence structure of unobserved intervention impacts. Building on the concept of false discovery rate (FDR), we propose an FDR regulation method to prioritize the identification of important effects from this identifiable set. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm to determine an FDR threshold that guarantees a pre-specified probability level for correctly identifying at least one true effect within the identifiable set. Finally, we apply the proposed method to a feature selection problem using Lasso regression and a case study. The results demonstrate that our approach effectively identifies a subset of relevant features, offering a more interpretable and reliable solution compared to traditional methods. Additionally, a simulation study confirms the method's effectiveness and high computational efficiency. Temporal action segmentation is a critical task for comprehending video content, where temporal actions are segmented from one another. While many existing approaches rely on large-scale annotated datasets, our work focuses on learning action boundaries without supervision. To achieve this, we introduce an efficient and effective method for action boundary learning that leverages self-supervision. We propose an algorithm for action boundary learning that utilizes two novel self-supervised tasks. The first task learns action representations by analyzing the frequency of action co-occurrences. The second task is designed to learn action boundaries based on the activity differences between adjacent actions. Experimental results demonstrate that our self-supervised approach for action boundary learning surpasses state-of-the-art supervised methods on two temporal action localization datasets. Furthermore, our approach enables the learning of action boundaries from unlabeled videos and allows for set-based video retrieval without requiring a supervised video retrieval model. This study investigates the formation and decay of multi-hadron states using both the Jacobi-Jordan algebra and the factorization method within phase space. By applying the quantum factorization of Hilbert space, we decompose the five-hadron state into sectors characterized by embedded di-hadron bound or resonance states. We specifically analyze the properties of $P_{c}(5000)$ and $P_{c}(4450)$ states, identifying them as $P_{cb}$ pentaquark resonances with masses aligning closely with experimental data. Furthermore, we calculate their widths, demonstrating that their factorization structures and energies match the experimental findings. We conclude that the algebraic approach, alongside the available experimental data, necessitates a larger collection of pentaquark states than previously hypothesized. Software testing education remains a critical component within computer science curricula, yet it is frequently overlooked in favor of other core subjects. An effective testing program is comprehensive and must include the delivery of detailed, individualized feedback to students, a process that is inherently time-consuming. This paper presents and evaluates two approaches to delivering this feedback: the traditional detailed method and an inquiry-based conceptual approach. To assess the effectiveness of the latter, an empirical study was conducted involving 41 final-year undergraduate students across three groups. The study compared the educational outcomes of both feedback strategies to determine their relative impacts on learning. The findings indicate that the conventional detailed feedback system produces superior educational outcomes compared to the inquiry-based conceptual approach. Consequently, the paper concludes with a set of recommendations for testing educators.

Domain adjustment techniques typically depend on access to both training and labeling resources for the source domain. However, scenarios often arise where the source dataset was generated long before the current model was developed, leaving only read-only or offline access, while adjustments are needed for multiple downstream targets for which no sources or labels exist. To address this, we introduce a generalizable approach to semi-supervised source-free domain adjustment. By employing a teacher network, our method adapts a source network to be independent of domain-specific characteristics. Comprehensive experiments across various adjustments demonstrate that this simple yet effective strategy facilitates knowledge generalization, supporting both cross-domain and cross-task adjustments. The method is contactless, enabling fully automated adjustments without requiring task-specific design or parameter optimization. The code can be found at https://github.com/foe/ssl-sffda.

This paper outlines the design principles of a gas-core nuclear reactor suitable for deep space propulsion and provides an overview of its current state of development. Unlike solid-core reactors, where heat transfer limitations necessitate low power densities, the high mobility of liquid or gaseous fuel allows the core to accommodate a heat source intense enough to vaporize conventional materials. This capability enables the reactor to dissipate vast amounts of thermal power into the surrounding space, making it ideal for high-specific impulse vehicles. The study examines key design challenges and experimental initiatives aimed at demonstrating reactor feasibility, focusing on fuel behavior under operational conditions. Additionally, a specific design concept for a deep space gas-core reactor is presented. Finally, the paper provides estimates for specific power and specific impulse. These figures are significantly higher than those of thermal nuclear reactors and approach the performance levels of electric propulsion systems utilizing fission surface power. Given that gas-core reactors are self-contained units combining both fuel and heat source, they offer superior specific power compared to thermal nuclear reactors, making them well-suited for deep space applications. Specifically, this property is essential for high-speed transit to Mars and for enabling deep space missions that are otherwise unfeasible. The authors argue that research into gas-core nuclear reactors for deep space propulsion should be regarded as a critical component of the broader space exploration agenda. Recent advancements in astroparticle physics, driven by innovations in detector technology and data analysis methods, have uncovered numerous fundamental phenomena in particle physics, astronomy, and cosmology. Concurrently, machine learning techniques have demonstrated significant efficacy in localizing interactions within particle detectors. In this study, two machine learning approaches leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were employed: transfer learning and 3D point cloud processing via V-PointNet. These models underwent comparative analysis against a custom CNN designed to prioritize domain-specific features. The research investigated whether a neural architecture tailored to extract domain-informed features outperforms other models in interaction localization across various astroparticle experiments. The findings indicate that transfer learning yields superior results compared to the domain-informed CNN, though it still lags behind standard convolutional neural networks. This outcome underscores the necessity of designing network architectures specifically optimized to capture the distinctive features inherent to particle detector simulations. Furthermore, domain-informed CNNs exhibit robust generalization capabilities when applied localized convolutional kernels to experimental data. Finally, the study concludes that domain-informed CNNs hold immense promise for localization tasks in future detectors, such as the particle physics experiment planned for the International Space Station. This paper explores the principles of grounding, a crucial preprocessing stage in answer set computation. We examine various grounding techniques across different domains and illustrate how advancements in grounding have facilitated the development of several important declarative applications. Our treatment of the various principles of grounding is largely formal, though we also present examples to demonstrate how these principles apply in practice. While our primary focus is on classical answer set computation, we also address some considerations regarding answer set programming.

Resource theories provide a framework for quantifying and analyzing quantum resources within physical operations. As both a fundamental framework for quantum physics and a potential backbone for quantum technologies, the field of resource theories is rapidly expanding, with general quantum frameworks now capable of addressing multi-particle systems, quantum operations, and quantum states. This letter introduces the "initial principle," which establishes the minimum framework necessary to derive general quantum principles—the NPA hierarchy and semidefinite representability—as a direct consequence. This discovery unifies two prominent approaches to developing quantum resource theories, demonstrating that every framework founded solely on general quantum principles inherently includes the free states and free operations of the NPA hierarchy. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of this result by developing a quantum framework for channel infidelity, which is defined exclusively by these general quantum principles. This theory enables the calculation of infidelity for both states and channels, as well as for joint state and channel scenarios. Additionally, we propose an infidelity monotone for bipartite states derived from this framework, and we apply it to two- and three-qubit bound entangled states. Our findings indicate that infidelity captures distinct characteristics of these states compared to existing monotones. Finally, we demonstrate a duality between general quantum principles and quantum frameworks, revealing that the framework constructed via the initial principle is dual to the single-system framework established by the initial principle. This insight facilitates the development of novel resource theories grounded in the semidepositability principle. In high-energy nuclear collisions, light hadrons serve as the most abundant observables, offering insights into the underlying phenomena. Driven by significant advancements in statistical methods and computational power, theoretical predictions have become increasingly precise, enabling rigorous comparisons with experimental data. This chapter outlines the main observables used to characterize these events and the Monte Carlo approaches employed to simulate them. It also examines the statistical methodologies used to assess agreements between experiment and theory. The discussion begins with a brief overview of the experimental framework, covering the collision systems and the specific detectors utilized to measure hadron production. Following this, hadron production within various frameworks is described, including initial string and hadron models, hydrodynamic approaches, and heavy-ion collision simulations generated by Monte Carlo generators. The core of the chapter details the statistical tools for comparing Monte Carlo simulations with experimental data on hadron production. Concluding remarks emphasize the critical role of light hadrons in understanding hadronic physics and highlight the sophisticated techniques now available for evaluating simulations against data. Ultimately, when Higgs boson searches are excluded, hadron production remains the most studied quantity in this domain. Furthermore, for heavy-ion collisions, the formation of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) in the quark-gluon phase diagram is a primary motivation for the extensive study of hadron production. By 2012, more than 20 years of research utilizing the LEP, RHIC, and early LHC datasets have yielded a wealth of information for physicists. Although hadron production was once viewed as merely a background to be subtracted to isolate heavy particles, it has evolved into a sophisticated field for testing theoretical models and investigating heavy-ion characteristics. The chapter is structured into four sections: the first provides an overview of the experimental environment; the second explains statistical methods for comparing simulations to data; the third reviews hadron production in Monte Carlo models for hadrochemistry; and the fourth examines the comparison of simulations to data regarding inclusive charged hadron production in proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions. Ultimately, hadron production remains the most extensively studied subject in hadronic physics.

This work examines inference for non-stationary time series that can be modeled as integrated autoregressive-moving average processes with a time-varying location parameter. Although the underlying model is simple, standard unit root tests often yield misleadingly high rejection rates, while conventional confidence intervals for location parameters may exhibit significant coverage errors. We introduce a set of novel tests to address these issues and explicitly calculate the asymptotic variances of the estimators. Furthermore, we extend these findings to parameter vectors of arbitrary dimension. Through simulation studies and an empirical analysis of US inflation data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of these developments. The primary innovation of this research is the automatic modeling of time-varying locations using robust tails, offering a straightforward and effective solution to a significant econometric problem. The proposed methodology is available in the R package \texttt{rta}. R code can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/SebastianKlittich/rta}. Post-selected quantum computing can achieve classical intractability and leverage quantum error correction, yet the high overhead of fault tolerance remains a barrier. We propose the first post-selected effective quantum LDPC code featuring linear-time decoding. By applying shorening techniques, we demonstrate that any binary quantum LDPC code with sparsity ratio $\alpha$ can be shortened to achieve constant $\alpha$, incurring only a linear overhead in distance and negligible overhead in rate. This result, combined with existing decoding methods for classical LDPC codes, enables effective LDPC codes with linear-time decoding for post-selected quantum computation. Consequently, we establish an $O(n)$ duration decoder and $O(n/\log n)$ rate decoder for post-selected quantum computation, representing significant improvements over prior fault-tolerant approaches. Furthermore, we introduce a family of post-selected quantum codes capable of post-selected classical hardness on $O(n)$ circuits with $O(m)$ measurements for any $m = \Omega(\sqrt{n})$ and distance $O(\sqrt{n}/m)$. These findings establish a tradeoff between post-selected hardness, code distance, and rate, revealing a fundamental limit where maintaining nontrivial rate and distance renders post-selected hardness impossible. Finally, we outline a strategy to achieve post-selected hardness with constant rate and distance using $O(n)$ error correction steps and $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon})$ duration decoding steps for any $\epsilon > 0$. This research investigates distributed algorithms for generating random ensembles of distance-$r$ dominating sets on high-girth graphs, specifically focusing on distributed $k$-coloring problems that reduce to this decision task. The study concentrates on extremely sparse graphs, where the minimum degree is only $O(\log n)$. We demonstrate that the distributed decision problem for distance-$r$ dominating sets can be solved with high probability in $O(\log n)$ time using a distributed random algorithm, provided the graph's girth exceeds $4r+1$. This result extends the findings of Bousquet et al. [JCSS 2012], who established that a distributed random $k$-coloring is achievable in $O(\log n)$ time for sparse high-girth graphs. Furthermore, we present a novel application of this result: solving the distributed $k$-independent set problem on high-girth graphs, thereby generalizing the work of Byers et al. [PODC 2012]. These solutions operate within the LOCAL model and complete in $O(\log n)$ rounds. The methods developed in this work are also applicable to the broader context of $[0,1]$-measurable graph parameters. Additionally, we provide an application of our findings to the distributed Maximum Independent Set problem, which does not rely on local density constraints. Specifically, we show that the randomized LOCAL algorithm proposed by Halldórsson and Karpinski [FOCS 1998] executes in $O(\log n)$ rounds on sparse high-girth graphs. Finally, we propose a conjecture suggesting that our findings can be extended to graphs with lower minimum degrees. Notably, the algorithms for $k$-coloring and $k$-independent set can be adapted to the CONGEST model, operating within $O(f(n) + \log n)$ rounds, where $f(n)$ represents the bit complexity required to represent edge labels. This model is particularly relevant when considering edge labels as distance-$r$ adjacency matrices. We also demonstrate the confluence of these ensembles in the context of $k$-coloring.

**Keywords:** Distributed Algorithms, Sparse Graphs, High-Girth Graphs, Dominating Set, Independent Set, Colorings.

We show that the number of nodal points in the disorder potential can be altered by shifting the zero level of the potential, and within the delocalized regime, these points give rise to bulk Majorana zero modes. Furthermore, we explore the stability of these modes against interactions and explore the connection this stability shares with the fermionic parity of the bulk quantum invariant. Additionally, we investigate a 2D $\mathbb{Z}_2$ quantum Hall insulator, revealing a correspondence between the bulk $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant and the parity of domain walls in the zero mode wave function when the disorder potential takes only two values. These findings offer a fresh perspective on the interplay between mass terms and boundary conditions in topological theories. We introduce a neural rendering approach that utilizes a brightness field to depict scenes. This method is streamlined, enabling efficient volume integration for both geometry and shading. By employing sparse geometry, we omit the need for color or normal sampling within the volume functions. We demonstrate that the brightness field can be learned via a few seconds of scanning via structured light or structured photogrammetry, or alternatively acquired using a single camera for real-world scenes. The scene's geometry is derived from the brightness field through a data-driven implicit function, while shading is managed through a bidirectional microfacet-based phase function. Consequently, this creates a novel neural rendering pipeline that represents geometry and appearance as distinct yet interconnected fields. We provide a comprehensive rendering pipeline featuring dynamic rendering, soft shadows, subsurface scattering, and neural texture synthesis. The resulting high-fidelity rendering allows for free camera exploration of simulated human-touched surfaces, including skulls, skeletons, and faces. Our work establishes a new pipeline that decouples geometry and appearance, offering a fresh framework for neural rendering. We demonstrate this by solving various related challenges, such as dynamic rendering, soft shadows, and neural texture synthesis. The resulting pipeline achieves high-fidelity results capable of free-camera exploration of realistic human-touched scenarios like skulls, skeletons, and faces. Our approach sets a new benchmark for neural rendering by treating geometry and appearance as separate yet interconnected fields. This study presents speckle interferometric data for 100 binary systems, obtained from the May through September 2020 observations of the Southern Optical Adaptive Reflex Observatory (SOAR). These findings complement the comprehensive binary survey conducted across the entire sky by SOAR during May through October 2019, which were published in *Exoplanet Survey Satellite Speckle Interferometry 2019: Southern Sky* (Astronomy & Computing, Vol. 36, 101467). The 2020 sample includes 82 stars previously unresolved by SOAR in 2019, 18 stars that were resolved in 2019, and two new targets, HD 122563 and HD 167099. For most unresolved stars, we determined precise positions and angular sizes for resolved components, while measured relative positions and elongated image shapes for a few still show slight signs of scattering. The 2020 sample features 26 M-type stars, 20 K-type stars, and 55 stars with spectral types ranging from F to mid-K. Primary component magnitudes span from 6.0 to 13.0, with a mean of 8.9. We report 11 new M-type multiple systems, including 8 M+M, 2 M+K, and 1 M+G. Additionally, we identified 10 previously unknown pairs, 15 previously known pairs, and 62 pairs with 2019 measurements that were re-measured in 2020. For the 62 re-measured pairs, we calculated total proper motions, orbital elements, radial velocities, and color indices, and compared 2019 versus 2020 image morphologies and photometry. We also examined the 2019 and 2020 images of HD 122563 and HD 167099 to assess any changes in relative position or elongation. The 2020 sample yielded 11 new M-type M+M multiple systems, 2 M+K, and 1 M+G. The SOAR telescope's speckle interferometry continues to be a vital tool for studying binary stars, offering high-precision measurements of relative positions, orbital elements, and stellar elongation. We introduce a novel mathematical framework known as "hue-kinematics duality," which connects color and hue factors in gauge-theory amplitudes with momentum and hue kinematic factors in integrability-based amplitudes. This dualism gives rise to a new structure termed the "cosmic chiral algebra," a generalization of the well-established local chiral algebra found in two-dimensional conformal field theory. Leveraging hue kinematics, we successfully compute holographic four-point functions across various dualities, demonstrating their integration within a broader integrability context. Furthermore, we establish a double-copy relationship between gauge and string theory, or more precisely, between chiral algebras in two dimensions and (cosmic) chiral algebras in three dimensions. Finally, we explore the general implications and potential future applications of hue-kinematics duality. Solar jets are frequently observed in low-resolution images from the top of the corona, a perspective that often obscures their origins in the photosphere. This study presents LOFAR observations of a jet-driven piston surge occurring 2.5 solar radii above the surface, captured just before the jet's footpoint was visible on the limb. The surge displays a braided morphology and exhibits a decelerating motion. We propose that the jet modifies the ambient plasma by either directly pushing against it or by heating a magnetic field that is subsequently distorted and amplified. This interaction causes the surge to oscillate around a background waveguide. These findings indicate that even the most tenuous coronal structures can be significantly altered by small jets, underscoring the critical role of jets in coronal heating. Furthermore, the morphology and evolution of the surge observed here may help explain similar loop-like features often detected in type II radio bursts. Finally, the complete structure of the surge, including its three-dimensional shape and magnetic field configuration, may provide a key to understanding the mechanisms behind the surge's deceleration and any associated radio emission. This paper is the first of two; the second will focus on the surge's morphology and its broader implications. The final conclusion will be drawn by synthesizing the findings from both papers. This research examines functional random differential equations (FRDEs) designed to model random swirl dynamics within two-dimensional fluids. These FRDEs operate in infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and incorporate unbounded, non-Lipschitz diffusion coefficients. The analysis establishes the existence and uniqueness of solutions for FRDEs featuring cubic nonlinear drifts and diffuse diffusion. To achieve this, new techniques were developed to manage the rapid growth at infinity characteristic of cubic functions. Numerical experiments were conducted to illustrate these findings, alongside an investigation into the regularity of FRDE solutions under reduced but still non-Lipschitz diffusion conditions. These results provide a robust foundation for creating novel models of infinite-dimensional stochastic partial differential equations. Additionally, the work explores applications in machine learning and control theory, specifically regarding training procedures for artificial neural networks and the stochastic approximation of optimal control problems in infinite dimensions. As an illustration, the training of an artificial neural network is modeled using a finite-dimensional stochastic differential equation; this study presents a novel approach by promoting an infinite-dimensional extension of that equation, which corresponds to a broad class of fractional stochastic differential equations containing a stochastic term linked to the fractional Laplacian operator. Furthermore, an infinite-dimensional stochastic differential equation is proposed to represent the stochastic approximation of a nonlinear control problem subject to multiplicative noise, with its existence and uniqueness guaranteed by the primary theorems of this work. This represents a significant generalization of existing findings within a stochastic framework involving a group of nonlinear fractional Laplacian operators. Notably, this work marks the first application of FRDEs to the stochastic approximation of infinite-dimensional stochastic control problems. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to demonstrate a quantum advantage. While the average entanglement within this framework has been examined through entanglement entropy, this study investigates entanglement at the level of individual instances using generalized entanglement. We demonstrate that the probability distribution in boson sampling can be categorized into three distinct groups based on their entanglement measures: fully separable instances, weakly entangled instances, and strongly entangled instances. The latter two groups are further subdivided according to the spatial region of the bosons. Our analysis reveals that fully separable instances possess substantial computational value, whereas weakly entangled instances appear limited. This separation remains valid regardless of the number of modes. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between generalized entanglement and quantum fidelity in boson sampling. Finally, we establish a polynomial-time algorithm for calculating generalized entanglement in boson sampling instances. These findings offer a novel perspective on boson sampling and a new avenue for exploring quantum advantage. Additionally, they present a new method for characterizing the entanglement of multi-particle states. Temporal series that involve complex events and organisms often exhibit a temporal granularity finer than the intervals between samples. This phenomenon occurs because multiple variables evolve continuously over time, yet measurements are taken only at specific, discrete moments. Given that both the physical and biological domains can span from the attosecond (10⁻¹⁸ seconds) to the geologic, this paper addresses the analysis of brief, high-dimensional temporal series. We propose that these data can be effectively learned using a combination of two approaches: (i) a method that trains a model to forecast future samples while incorporating a loss function designed to mitigate the impact of distant predictions, and (ii) a method that trains a model to reconstruct the temporal series from an embedding space using a loss function derived from the persistent homology of both data and model representations. These strategies are demonstrated using data from two experimental domains: (i) the time-resolved electron density of molecules, and (ii) the time-resolved calcium concentration within neurons. The proposed approach is shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we utilize these frameworks to build models that offer new insights into the experiments, such as the discovery of an intermediate state in the electron density of water molecules following X-ray ionization. This work investigates bounded automata operating within partially observable environments, focusing on those equipped with recurrent connections to manage long-term memory. By integrating techniques from bounded automata theory and Markov decision processes, we demonstrate that incorporating recurrence enables the efficient solution of tasks that are otherwise intractable for robots lacking it. We provide biological relevance by examining neurons that accumulate information over time, suggesting that recurrent architectures facilitate optimal decision-making in complex, real-world settings. Furthermore, we examine the implications of training recurrent networks on tasks that are off-policy in practice, revealing that such training can degrade performance on novel decisions yet remain viable for everyday operations. Finally, we offer insights into the challenges posed by combining accumulation, partial observability, and convolutional architectures. Overall, our approach underscores the utility of recurrent structures for navigating complex environments and establishes a foundation for investigating long-term learning and decision-making in real-world scenarios. The prevalence of datasets annotated solely with bounding boxes has significantly advanced the field of weakly-supervised action detection. However, existing approaches typically depend on additional contextual cues, such as spatial relationships between boxes or temporal continuity from video frames, to identify correct bounding boxes. This study investigates the ability of networks trained exclusively on spatial box relationships to detect actions. We attribute their limitations to a lack of comprehensive contextual understanding, noting that current methods often overlook critical contextual features. To address this, we employ Graph Convolutive Networks (GCNs) to extract and represent essential contextual information. Furthermore, we modify the GCN architecture to simultaneously learn a contextual importance graph, thereby amplifying signals from crucial contextual features. Experimental results on two dominant datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses all prior techniques by a substantial margin. Additionally, ablation studies reveal that our approach captures more complete contextual information, successfully identifying context-adjacent bounding boxes that other methods fail to detect. Consequently, GCNs exhibit a superior capability to discern and learn vital contextual features. This paper details the methodology, results, and new findings from the 2021 Image Resemblance Challenge (IRC2021), an event organized and evaluated under the vision of training and evaluating models designed to quantify image resemblance. The competition consisted of two tasks: determining the order of images based on how closely they represent a query image (ranking) and generating two images similar to a input image without resembling each other (pairwise generation). Nine approaches utilizing 17 techniques were submitted to address the ranking task, while two submissions focused on the pairwise generation task. The top-ranking submission utilized a model representation derived from a pre-trained CLIP vision transformer, employing cosine similarity to calculate image-resemblance scores. Although all submitted methods successfully solved the ranking task, the pairwise generation challenge proved significantly more difficult for current models. Following the competition, the authors released the data and code for the evaluation environment on GitHub to facilitate future research. Furthermore, the authors have secured funding to enhance the evaluation environment with additional models for pairwise generation and to expand the dataset with more image pairs. This effort aims to improve models capable of generating diverse outputs for a single prompt, thereby advancing text-to-image generation research. The concepts introduced in this paper are also highly relevant to image retrieval and similarity assessment. Ultimately, the evaluation environment and surrounding resources will support research in areas such as text-to-image generation, image retrieval, and image similarity evaluation. Additionally, the competition's concept is closely tied to the development of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which integrate textual and visual information. This relevance is underscored by the success of CLIP-based similarity scoring in achieving state-of-the-art results in all tasks, as evidenced by various studies. This paper provides an overview of the competition, its top submissions, outcomes, and future directions. Specifically, this work demonstrates how solving image resemblance challenges can drive progress in large multimodal models. This chapter examines perturbation problems within parabolic equations and diffusion processes characterized by degeneration. A primary objective is analyzing the long-term behavior resulting from perturbations in semilinear elliptic boundary value problems and parabolic initial-boundary value problems associated with specific class $C$-tensors. These analyses reveal the existence of metastable states linked to local minimizers of corresponding elliptic boundary value solutions, alongside the investigation of periodic homogenization for parabolic equations. The discussion concludes by addressing applications to random media and percolation. Key areas of focus include verifying essential assumptions regarding local minimizers and analyzing boundary conditions to derive precise asymptotic results. Furthermore, attention is paid to techniques employed to demonstrate convergence and metastability, specifically highlighting challenges related to finite time behavior, singularities, and nonregular initial data. Finally, the need to address boundary layer problems and the associated regularity of solutions to perturbed equations constitutes a significant aspect of this work. Ultimately, this chapter aims to outline current research directions and challenges in the field. Specifically, it emphasizes the necessity of developing novel methods to validate assumptions concerning local minimizers of elliptic boundary value solutions, thereby ensuring the rigorous derivation of precise results regarding metastable states, periodic homogenization in parabolic equations, and media subject to perturbations. These latter subjects are explored in subsequent chapters. Additionally, novel methodologies are required to resolve issues concerning boundary layers, boundary conditions, and the regularity of solutions in perturbed parabolic equations, thereby advancing the understanding of long-term behavior in related problems. Finally, methodologies for proving metastability and the validity of effective coefficients in periodic homogenization for parabolic equations constitute vital areas of current research. Consequently, this chapter serves as an introduction to these active fields, with the subsequent chapters dedicated to addressing these specific challenges. Chapter 2 addresses metastability issues, while Chapters 3 and 4 tackle effective coefficients and convergence issues, respectively. The final chapter focuses on perturbed equations situated in fractal domains. Overall, this work seeks to establish a foundation for future research by addressing metastability, effective coefficients, and convergence challenges through the development of innovative methodologies. By the end of this chapter, readers will have a comprehensive understanding of these issues and the novel approaches required for their resolution. This study addresses the challenge of training large-scale neural networks collaboratively in federated education environments, where multiple educational institutions work together. Existing solutions are often hindered by slow communication speeds and high data transfer costs, which limit their practicality. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new framework called Differentially Private Recurrent Transmission (DP-REC). DP-REC leverages local computation, differential privacy, and the strategic use of recurrent neural networks to significantly cut down on communication expenses. We rigorously establish formal privacy guarantees for DP-REC and empirically validate its efficacy across both vision and language tasks, demonstrating superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods.
