This study examines the sensitivity of the precision electroweak oblique parameters $S$, $T$, and $U$ to the $Z_2$-breaking soft-mass term $m_{12}^2$ within a two-Higgs-doublet model, where all other parameters are held fixed. The analysis demonstrates the existence of narrow bands in the $m_{12}^2$ vs. $\mu_{2H}$ plot along which the $S$, $T$, and $U$ oblique parameters remain insensitive to $m_{12}$. These bands, which shift depending on the specific oblique parameter, align with regions previously identified as the vacuum-insensitive zone. Additionally, the analysis confirms that the $m_{12}^2$ band corresponding to the $U$ parameter is notably narrower than those for the $S$ and $T$ parameters. Furthermore, while a general analytical expression for the relative sensitivity $\frac{\delta U}{U}$ is derived, it is also validated through extensive Monte-Carlo simulations. Finally, the study addresses the constraint that the $Z_2$ parameter $m_{12}$ must not be treated as completely arbitrary; specifically, if $m_{12}^2$ is unbounded, the $U$ parameter becomes highly sensitive to $m_{12}^2$, rendering it impractical to constrain $U$ without introducing further assumptions. This limitation is also illustrated via Monte-Carlo analysis. A similar sensitivity of $U$ is observed in other multi-Higgs models. The implications of these findings for the $Z_2$ symmetry of the 2HDM are also explored. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive sensitivity analysis of the $S$, $T$, and $U$ oblique parameters with respect to $m_{12}^2$, while also discussing the limitations associated with the $U$ parameter. These insights are also relevant to other extensions of the Standard Model. The code used in this analysis is available at [1]. Additionally, the findings regarding the vacuum-insensitive band were previously presented in [2]. Finally, the sensitivity analysis of $m_{12}^2$ was also featured in a presentation at the 12th International Conference on the Study of the Strong Interactions of Hadrons (Hadron 2021), which can be viewed here [3].

This paper examines a use case involving information transfer from ConceptGraphs, which utilize GraphQL's Shape Expressions (SE) to model related data objects, to RDF using Apache Jena's Resource Oriented Design (RO) principles. To evaluate this scenario, we analyzed three real-world ConceptGraphs: two knowledge graphs built with the Apache Tuscany Stack (representing I18N and Ontology Language descriptions) and one additional graph for organization structures. The paper outlines the technical challenges encountered during this transfer and introduces the Jena Transfer Framework (J-TRF), a tool designed to execute this process automatically. We demonstrate J-TRF's functionality by presenting two specific transformations: one converting ConceptGraphs to RDF and another transforming RDF back to ConceptGraphs. Finally, the study evaluates the generated data's quality through three lenses—RDF characteristics, data integrity, and data completeness. We conclude by discussing potential improvements for both the transfer process and the resulting data quality. Given the growing trend of exposing related data as connected objects, the J-TRF tool offers a practical solution for bridging modern object-oriented and resource-based architectures. Furthermore, the framework's design supports future extensions to handle additional semantic considerations, such as links, properties, and cardinality. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first work to address related real-world concept graph transformation problems. Our findings are also the first to demonstrate the benefits of automatically transforming object graphs to RDF while preserving semantic information. This is achieved through a three-step process: (1) annotating the Java code base with Javadoc comments, (2) generating ConceptGraphs from the code base, and (3) transforming those ConceptGraphs to RDF using the proposed J-TRF tool. This three-step approach marks a novel contribution to graph transformation research. Additionally, the paper contributes to data quality research by introducing a data quality assessment tool that evaluates the J-TRF's transformation process across three dimensions: (1) Jena's RDF characteristics, (2) the preservation of semantic information, and (3) validation of data integrity and completeness. The study concludes by suggesting a future extension to address the challenge of identifying equivalent classes and properties when mapping ConceptGraphs to RDF. This proposal addresses a significant issue in graph transformation research, as it highlights a lack of methods for preserving semantic equivalence between graphs and graphschemas. Recurrent tasks in econometrics and operations research include analyzing production and cost functions, modeling efficiency and losses within the non-essential housing sector, and backtesting financial strategies. These challenges are frequently addressed by estimating a convex function that approximates data from below. This paper introduces pyStoNED, a free, open-source Python library that unifies these applications and simplifies estimation, hypothesis testing, and robustness analysis. pyStoNED streamlines data preparation and presents estimations in clear visual formats. The library is distributed under the 3-Clause BSD license and can be installed via pip. The accompanying application code is available at https://github.com/BigDataEconomics/PyDNE. Furthermore, the examples in this paper can be reproduced using only Python and pyStoNED, requiring no additional software. This document serves as an introduction to the library's capabilities. Additional details, including our publication record and usage examples, can be found on our website at https://bigdata-economics.com/. pyStoNED is maintained by the researchers behind the Nonparametric Convex Regression lab (http://www.dneuro.org), a group dedicated to advancing data-driven methodologies in economics and business. Their work focuses on developing new tools for inference and estimation in nonparametric convex models, with applications spanning production economics, operational efficiency, and financial markets. For instance, pyStoNED supports inferring production set characteristics, including production functions, factor demands, and cost functions. It utilizes nonparametric convex regression to estimate a convex function from data that convexly separates the origin. Beyond estimation, pyStoNED calculates standard errors via bootstrapping and performs extensive hypothesis tests, such as testing convexity, monotonicity, and input/output disposability. Beyond economics, pyStoNED also addresses optimization problems by approximating convex data from below to derive optimal solutions. The pyStoNED team welcomes contributions from researchers interested in nonparametric convex estimation and has established a forum at https://bigdata-economics.com/forum/ to discuss applications and collaborations. We invite you to explore the potential of pyStoNED for your own research. To get started, install the library using pip: pip install pyStoNED. This study examines the detection of a light scalar ($m_\phi \lesssim 50$ GeV) through the $t \bar t \phi$ process at the LHC. Building on recent work that derived the effective $t \bar t \phi$ interaction from a well-defined scalar sector within the Standard Model, we investigate the sensitivity of a simultaneous search for Higgs bosons produced via both gluon fusion and this specific channel. We analyze potential conflicts between constraints established by LHC scalar physics measurements and LHCb tetraquark decay observations. Furthermore, we establish lower limits on the scalar width at 16 TeV, evaluating how various selection criteria influence this exclusion range. Finally, we project the future reach of the scalar mass search for Higgs-like resonances in this final state using both current data and projected LHC luminosity. These findings are supported by a detailed numerical study incorporating full next-to-leading order QCD corrections for the production cross section and a thorough treatment of all relevant backgrounds. Notably, we observe that Higgs bosons with a lifetime shorter than approximately $10^{-25}$ seconds are more readily identified in the $t \bar t \phi}$ channel. This conclusion is reinforced by an additional search conducted at lower luminosity and a narrower transverse momentum window. Additionally, we explore strategies to mitigate the substantial QCD background inherent to this search. Specifically, we demonstrate that the $t \bar t \phi}$ cross section can be significantly reduced by selecting events with at least one b-tagged jet, whereas this method has a comparatively minor impact on the signal. Consequently, we emphasize the critical role of incorporating QCD corrections in both signal and background calculations. We further illustrate that incorporating NLO QCD corrections in scalar signal modeling can result in up to a 50% increase in the transverse momentum distribution of the Higgs candidate, thereby substantially lowering the background level. This enhancement arises from the inclusion of real radiation, which is essential for accurate QCD modeling. Our findings suggest that achieving a transverse momentum of approximately 100 GeV for the Higgs candidate is crucial for the successful identification of light scalars in the $t \bar t \phi}$ channel. This requirement is particularly pertinent for Higgs bosons with a lifetime shorter than $10^{-25}$ seconds. Current state-of-the-art language models are trained in a supervised setting, requiring annotated data for monitoring. In contrast, our models are unmonitored, being trained in an unsupervised manner with no annotated resources. This study demonstrates that analyzing language models is feasible without supervision and can even surpass monitored state-ofthe-art models in certain NLP tasks, particularly those involving distribution shifts. We provide a comprehensive overview of the capabilities of unmonitored foundation models by introducing novel, small-scale, few-shot (2 examples per class) classification benchmarks. These benchmarks are designed to require no training data, distributional knowledge, or human supervision, focusing on detecting distribution shifts in text across various languages, scripts, and domains. Our results highlight the models' proficiency in few-shot text classification, code classification, and sentiment analysis, with performance varying by language. Finally, we discuss the models' limitations, such as their inability to handle certain scripts and their failure to detect distribution shifts in other NLP tasks. Overall, this work shows that analyzing pretrained language models can exceed state-of-the-art performance in specific scenarios, offering valuable insights for the responsible development of language models. The benchmarks are available at https://github.com/robert-os/unmonitored-few-shot-capabilities. We analyzed high-resolution spectra of 12 Be-stars from the Be30DOR3 catalog within the 30 Doradus Starburst Region to determine their atmospheric parameters. Our findings indicate that these stars exhibit a broad range of effective temperatures, primarily concentrated between 14,000 and 17,000 K. Furthermore, our results suggest that surface gravity is not a reliable indicator for distinguishing between nonrotating and rotating stars. Finally, our study identified and confirmed the binary nature of HD 212931 and 30 DOR V1-1. Our analysis of Be30DOR3 stars reveals a broad distribution of V sin i values, with the majority falling between 100 and 200 km s$^{-1}$. Additionally, the detected binary fraction is notably high, at 25%. This paper is the first in a series dedicated to analyzing the properties of Be30DOR3 stars in the 30 Doradus region. Future papers in this series will focus on the mass distribution, luminosity, and evolutionary status of these stars. Our subsequent study, III, will examine the binary nature of Be30DOR3 stars, while paper IV will address their atmospheric parameters. Finally, paper V will explore the impact of stellar rotation on the line profiles of these objects. All spectral data utilized in this study are available in our repository. This study investigates inverse text standardization, the process of normalizing orthographically variant characters within a specific language to a standard form using NLP techniques. While recent neural inverse standardization models demonstrate high accuracy, they depend on extensive, high-quality training data. We explore a method to generate additional training text for English by leveraging text generation models. Our results show that a data augmentation strategy combining synthetic text from various generation models significantly enhances performance on the standard English benchmark. This finding is robust across different models, architectures, and synthesis quantities. Additionally, we evaluate two text generation approaches: a non-neural model based on Kneser and Ney's algorithm and a neural model built on the GPT-2 architecture. Our experiments indicate that the non-neural algorithm is more effective for expanding training data in inverse standardization tasks. We also examine a technique for creating high-quality synthetic text for inverse standardization by fine-tuning a pre-trained multilingual model on a limited corpus. Furthermore, we introduce a novel data-driven, unsupervised, cross-language approach for English-Spanish inverse standardization that achieves state-of-the-art results without requiring parallel training data. Finally, we assess various text generation models and algorithms across multiple synthetic text volumes, demonstrating that even a small number of generated examples can improve performance. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/abhi-1999/Inverse-Text-Standardization. Our findings are expected to be of interest to researchers in both inverse text standardization and text generation domains. This work establishes a shape optimization result for a spectral problem involving the Hermite operator under a Robin type boundary condition. By employing techniques from mollification, compactly raised gradient flows, and semi-classical analysis, we prove a Faber-Krahn type inequality. Furthermore, we provide an explicit computation of the first eigenvalue corresponding to a ball and demonstrate that it serves as an asymptotically sharp constant. Finally, we examine the spectral characteristics of a ball as a limit case. A detailed report on the spectral geometry of this problem is forthcoming. Finally, we present numerical computations designed to identify a minimizer within the class of radial functions. We introduce NFT-K, a memory-efficient kernel approximation method for Non-Exchangeable Tangent Kernels (Bostan et al., 2021). By leveraging the inherent block-diagonal structure of NTK matrices, we develop a tangent core that enables linear-time matrix-vector operations and low-cost storage. Compared to the original NTK method, which requires $O(n^2)$ memory, NFT-K reduces memory usage to $O(kn)$ and cuts matrix-vector multiplication time from $O(n^2)$ to $O(kn)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of NFT-K within deep learning, specifically for training convolutional neural networks. Experimental results indicate that NFT-K enhances both training and inference performance. Additionally, we release an open-source implementation of NFT-K. Achieving multiple social attributes in synthetic speech remains a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce a straightforward and effective framework for integrating various social traits, including femininity, age, emotion, and music, into specific speech samples. Our method leverages social feature discriminative neural networks (SFDNNs) to analyze both input samples and training data, enabling the creation of speech with desired traits. Evaluation results demonstrate that our approach successfully generates speech with targeted characteristics. Furthermore, quantitative analysis reveals that features enriched with multiple traits retain interpretability more effectively than those enhanced by a single trait. This development holds significant potential for applications such as virtual assistants, conversational agents, and personalized communication tools. By achieving multi-trait integration, this research deepens our comprehension of social signals within speech and paves the way for more sophisticated and adaptable AI-driven communication solutions. We propose a dark sector characterized by the $U(1)_{B-L}\times St(1)$ symmetry, where $St(1)$ denotes the maximal modular $A_4$ subgroup. This sector posits that modular $A_4$ serves as the symmetry of the dark sector, while $U(1)_{B-L}$ acts as a gauge symmetry linking the dark sector to the visible sector, thereby establishing a unified framework between majoron and trinification theories. We demonstrate that the dark sector can simultaneously account for dark radiation, matter anti-matter asymmetry, and dark matter luminosity. Notably, dark matter luminosity arises from a small fraction of stable dark matter alongside a stable relic dominated by decays occurring after matter-anti-matter oscillation. Furthermore, we establish a lower limit on the mass of stable dark matter and investigate the potential detection of dark matter through small scale structure formation. Finally, we outline experimental constraints and future prospects for our proposed dark sector. These findings suggest that the dark sector, defined by the $U(1)_{B-L}\times St(1)$ symmetry, is highly robust and offers a comprehensive explanation for a broad array of experimental observables. Consequently, it is strongly recommended to rigorously test the dark sector in future experimental and observational endeavors. Specifically, we advocate for precise measurements of the effective number of neutrinos ($N_{eff}$) and the matter/anti-matter asymmetry, alongside astrophysical observations of the dark matter power spectrum. Additionally, we suggest that future collider experiments should search for small dark matter masses ($\lesssim 10^{9}$ GeV) within the parameter range $0.01 \lesssim \theta \lesssim 1$, as well as investigate the stability of small scale structures. These efforts could potentially uncover a dark sector composed of majorons, which we propose should be prioritized for detailed investigation. Finally, we note that our proposed dark sector could be realized within both string theory and the standard field theory framework. Specifically, our proposal is compatible with the well-motivated $E_8\times E_8$ string vacuum, which is recognized as a viable candidate for string phenomenology. Moreover, the proposal is consistent with the well-motivated trinification symmetry, which is expected to be realized in super-weak coupling regions of the trinification gauge group parameter space. In triaxial nuclei, the minimal distance between adjacent protons and neutrons exhibits an oscillatory dependence on the three spatial coordinates. The collective wave function of a core is constructed using the average envelope of this minimal distance. The two-body relative energy, derived from the self-energy of a particle-hole excitation, is obtained by calculating the expectation value of the energy eigenstate relative to the core. By optimizing the envelope function through the minimization of the energy eigenstate's total energy, the energy spectrum relative to the core is determined. For the ${}^{111}$Cd nucleus, the calculated spectrum aligns well with the experimental transition energies. Furthermore, the calculated energy spectrum aligns with experimental data, exhibiting the same sequence of energy levels and transition strengths. The symmetry of the collective wave function with respect to the y and z directions of the three-dimensional coordinate system arises from the symmetry of the average envelope of the minimal distance. This symmetry is maintained throughout the collective excitations of the wave function relative to the core. Consequently, the minimal distance concept demonstrates its validity as a collective variable for the collective motion of triaxial nuclei. Additionally, the derived energy spectrum for triaxial nuclei serves as an input for investigating other multi-nucleon excitations. In this study, we specifically examined one- and two-particle excitations, while one- and two-hole excitations will be addressed in future work. The broader concept of collective excitations in triaxial nuclei, extending beyond single-particle excitations, remains an open question. Future research will also explore whether the symmetry of collective excitations relative to the core persists for multi-particle excitations. Ultimately, the symmetry of the collective wave function of the minimal distance acts as a constraint on the wave function, influencing the symmetry of the energy spectrum. This study further demonstrates that the optimal envelope of the minimal distance is nearly identical to the optimal mean-field potential used to generate the collective wave function. The symmetry of the collective excitations of the wave function relative to the core is attributed to the symmetry of the collective excitations of the optimal envelope of the minimal distance. In both one- and two-particle excitations, the symmetry of the collective excitations of the wave function relative to the core arises from the symmetry of the collective excitations of the optimal envelope of the minimal distance. Future work will investigate whether the symmetry of the collective excitations of the wave function relative to the core is retained for multi-particle excitations. We introduce the concept of polyphase Golay complementary structures (pGCS) and establish both constructive and existence conditions for them. Utilizing phasors in the frequency domain, we prove that polyphase pGCS cannot exist for any degree $L$ when the length $N$ satisfies $N \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that polyphase Golay complementary sequences (pGCS) of length $N$ and degree $L$ exist if $N$ is a perfect power and the degree $L$ adheres to a condition dependent on the prime factorization of $L$. Additionally, we provide several design methods for pGCS when $\mathsf{deg}(L) \leq 3$. Finally, we illustrate the application of polyphase pGCS in radar pulse compression. The constructed examples can be accessed at https://github.com/zhongtao1992/pGCS. Our results indicate that polyphase pGCS are more practical for signal processing than current polyphase PS-PC complementary sequences, as they require fewer levels and exhibit a constant peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR). Specifically, for a degree $k$, polyphase pGCS achieve $\mathsf{phasel}(k)=k$ with phases confined to $\{0, 2\pi/k, \dots, 2\pi(k-1)/k\}$, whereas polyphase PS-PC complementary sequences of length $N$ and degree $k$ cannot exist when $N$ is a perfect power. In terms of performance, the mean squared side lobe level of a random pGCS of length $N$ and degree $k$ is approximately $1/N^2$, which is superior to the best known result of $O(1/N^2+\log^2(N)/N)$ for polyphase PS-PC complementary sequences. Our findings also extend the nonexistence of polyphase PCS to all degrees $k$ for lengths $N$ where $N$ is a perfect power, improving upon the previous bound of $k \leq 3$. These results also generalize the existence and nonexistence of polyphase PCS regarding the degree $k$ and length $N$ established by the authors in [1]. This study addresses the challenge of unsupervised alteration recognition in multispectral images by integrating features derived from both spatial and spectral dimensions. To achieve this, a deep convolutional autoencoder architecture is employed, modified to incorporate a separate autoencoder component responsible for processing spatial features. Change detection within the integrated framework is executed through the computation of the mean absolute difference between the input and output images. The approach is evaluated across three datasets—WHIGHS, Pavia University, and Pavia Center—using three distinct alteration types: post-fire scenarios, post-landslide scenarios, and post-war scenarios. The proposed integrated method is benchmarked against several integrated and non-integrated algorithms designed for alteration change detection. Experimental results demonstrate that the integration of feature-rich deep autoencoders within the proposed architecture yields superior accuracy in alteration change detection. Furthermore, the integration of deep spatial and spectral feature autoencoders enhances the robustness of the proposed deep autoencoder-based framework for detecting alterations in hyperspectral imagery. Finally, the high accuracy achieved by the proposed algorithm in unsupervised alteration change detection underscores its potential utility for various real-world applications. This study examines the link between entropy and viscosity using molecular simulations. The viscosity of both molecular fluids (dimers and linear argon-like molecules) and atoms (spherically symmetric Lennard-Jones and soft-sphere fluids) varies with entropy ($S$) in a similar manner. When viscosity is plotted against $S$, the correlations between distinct fluids are notably tighter than those observed with entropy, defined as $S_{\rm cor} = S - S_{\rm dis}$, where $S_{\rm dis}$ represents the entropy of a reference hard-sphere system with a contact value matching that of the target fluid. The value of $S_{\rm cor}$ is largely determined by the specific correlation between viscosity and density. The research also investigates the relationship between $S_{\rm cor}$ and the Enskog number ($X$), which measures the ratio of actual to hard-sphere entropy. A strong correlation exists between $S_{\rm cor}$ and $X$ for all simulated fluids, including both spherical and molecular systems. Finally, the entropy-viscosity relationship is analyzed using the thermodynamic residual entropy proposed by Ladd and Evans. This analysis reveals a strong correlation between the thermodynamic residual entropy and $S_{\rm cor}$ for both molecular and atomic fluids. The convergence of these findings suggests that the thermodynamic residual entropy serves as a more effective state variable for describing the viscosity of molecular fluids than total entropy. This conclusion is supported by a new, highly accurate equation describing the thermodynamic residual entropy of a Lennard-Jones fluid as a function of density and temperature. Collectively, these results indicate that the thermodynamic residual entropy of a fluid is a more universal quantity than the standard residual entropy. Furthermore, the paper proposes a novel thermodynamic residual entropy, termed "dynamic residual entropy," which exhibits an even stronger correlation with viscosity than the thermodynamic residual entropy does. Finally, the work explores the connection between the thermodynamic residual entropy and the excess free energy. A strong correlation is found between these two quantities for systems with soft potentials, whereas the correlation weakens when interactions are dominated by hard-core repulsion. These insights are illustrated using viscosity and thermodynamic residual entropy data for hard- and soft-sphere fluids. The study concludes that dynamic residual entropy offers a more universal and accurate description of fluid viscosity than thermodynamic residual entropy. This work outlines a cyclical cosmmodel grounded in standard $\Lambda CDM$ theory, utilizing a scalar field to manage the Big Crunch and subsequent Big Bang phases. Although the model adheres to conventional $\Lambda CDM$ dynamics during the expansion epoch, it diverges from the standard paradigm at late times by predicting a transition to a contracting universe rather than continued expansion. This scenario avoids a true singularity, maintaining a finite entropy at the turnaround point, thereby enabling a smooth and reversible universe reversal. The model demonstrates agreement with observational data, including the Hubble constant ($H_0 = 67.8 \pm 1.3$ km/s/Mpc), angular scale of acoustic peaks ($\theta_{\rm{S}} = 1.0408 \pm 0.0003$ rad), and the effective number of relativistic species ($N_{\rm{eff}} = 3.04$). Furthermore, we establish that this cyclical framework can successfully resolve the Hubble tension. Finally, we examine the implications of our findings for the nature of dark energy and emphasize the necessity of incorporating a universe reversal mechanism into $\Lambda CDM$ cosmology. This study investigates the concept of conflated spacetime within a concealed-variable model, where superdeterminism is interpreted as an infinite, one-to-one mapping between points in distinct spacetimes. We examine a variation of the Bell inequality specifically adapted for conflated spacetime and address the challenge of addressing locality in such frameworks. Furthermore, we explore how a concealed-variable theory based on conflated spacetime could be experimentally validated by analyzing the specific properties of the sinusoidal variable proposed by the Invariant-set hypothesis. Finally, we evaluate whether a sine-wave concealed-variable model can be formulated in a way that is compatible with established empirical data. Additionally, we demonstrate the possibility of constructing such a model that is inherently testable by suggesting a modification to the Alice and Bob correlation functions involving an extra term reliant on a variable with a known distribution. We emphasize that this novel approach to concealed variables is significant because it adheres to standard relativistic locality conditions and enables experimental verification. Finally, we detail the mechanics of this testable sine-wave model and outline the steps required to verify its predictions. The work concludes by discussing how these findings relate to other testable and experimentally verified sine-wave-based theories, including those of 't Hooft and Wigner. Specifically, the paper shows that the sine-wave model can be derived from 't Hooft's concept of a quantum lattice and that it is compatible with Wigner's sine-wave model, which serves as a classical analogue of quantum mechanics. We also address how the sine-wave model can be extended to a relativistic framework and outline the necessary modifications to the conformal symmetry algebra to accommodate an additional variable with a known distribution. Finally, we establish that the sine-wave model is compatible with an anisotropic universe and propose that it may provide a more accurate description of the early universe. We argue that the conflation of spacetimes in our classical, pre-Big Bang sine-wave model is essential for explaining the current observational data regarding the universe's expansion. We also note that our work supports the superdeterministic hypothesis, which posits that a classical, pre-Big Bang sine-wave theory could be compatible with the Bell inequality data. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for our understanding of the universe's origins and the nature of quantum mechanics. In summary, we show that a classical, pre-Big Bang sine-wave theory is compatible with the Bell inequality data and that it can be tested experimentally. We also argue that the sine-wave model provides a more accurate description of the early universe

This work examines FMG-class gauge backfields for the critical dimer model, defined by the vanishing of the characteristic polynomial's constant term. It demonstrates that fermion sectors within the Dirac sea can significantly influence the dimer fluid's ground state. The analysis begins by reviewing the equivalence between the Majorana fermion model and the dimers-on-a-lattice model, followed by an investigation of fermion sectors in the presence of a gauge background. Key findings include the identification of gauge-invariant quantities, such as flux and fermion number, and the revelation that gauge-invariant states need not possess a defined particle number. These insights into gauge fields interacting with fermions offer a framework for analyzing the dimer model's ground state. Finally, the study examines the spectrum of a generic two-dimensional Dirac fermion sector over an arbitrary gauge background, revealing a fermion gap that can be interpreted as an effective mass generated by the discrete gauge background. These results are utilized to investigate the dimer model's ground state within an FMG gauge background. Specifically, when the gauge field is periodic with a period matching the lattice spacing, the system exhibits a massive spectrum with a dimer gap. In this regime, the model is equivalent to a system of dimers coupled to a periodic potential. By calculating the single-dimer ground state, it is shown that the energy is periodic with respect to the zeroth component of the gauge field. Furthermore, it is established that the energy of a single dimer in this periodic gauge field can be expressed in terms of the energy of a single dimer within a uniform gauge field. Additionally, the study addresses dimers in a constant gauge field, deriving the necessary conditions for the model to remain in a dimer phase. Finally, the issue of dimer condensation is addressed by showing that the energy of a single dimer increases as the gauge field's frequency rises. These results are used to delineate the phase diagram for a specific class of gauge fields. The analysis concludes by examining the relationship between the dimer gauge-invariant state and the fermion gauge-invariant state, revealing a complex relationship that is only straightforward in a gauge field that is both constant and periodic. Specifically, for a gauge field that is both constant and periodic, the dimer ground state can be derived from the Dirac fermion ground state by summing over gauge-invariant fermion states. Embedded real-time systems utilizing heterogeneous hardware and software are increasingly common, yet their development remains challenging due to the high cost and complexity of ensuring robust real-time performance. To address this, we present T-Visor, a hypervisor that enables mixed importance scheduling across virtual machines. T-Visor leverages hardware virtualization assistance to execute critical tasks on a real-time, hard partition while managing less time-sensitive workloads on a best-effort soft partition. We have developed a comprehensive set of mechanisms and utilized hardware features to manage context switches and task migrations between these partitions, alongside a co-scheduler for handling migrations. Our implementation was tested across a wide range of workloads and system configurations, demonstrating consistent and predictable scheduling for hard real-time tasks across diverse workloads. Furthermore, the soft partition achieves near-optimal utilization across a broad spectrum of workload combinations. To our knowledge, this represents the first mechanism and implementation capable of managing mixed importance workloads on partitions with varying real-time guarantees. Additionally, we have released a detailed design document, source code, a task generator, and an integrator for external evaluation. We anticipate that T-Visor will assist developers in partitioning workloads and reduce the complexity of integrating mixed importance systems. A key benefit is the ability to isolate real-time tasks from non-real-time workloads, allowing developers to focus on optimizing task execution without worrying about interference from other tasks. The soft partition's ability to adapt to varying workloads also offers opportunities for energy savings. We expect that external evaluations will further enhance the tool's capabilities. Our goal is to make T-Visor accessible to the broader community to foster its evolution. We acknowledge that this work addresses a specific problem within the broader field of hypervisor research. We have also identified several research opportunities that extend beyond the scope of this paper, such as the trade-offs between runtime performance and security guarantees. We hope these opportunities will inspire further research in areas like security, energy efficiency, and multi-domain management. We believe that open-source development will facilitate these explorations. Finally, we recognize that the significance of hardware and software contributions in virtualization research is often underappreciated. We hope that providing a detailed design document, source code, a task generator, and an integrator will enable other researchers to evaluate the work on various systems and validate the proposed mechanisms. We also acknowledge that our evaluation did not cover all possible workload combinations, and we hope that more extensive testing will be conducted in the future. In summary, we have made significant contributions to the hypervisor research community

We introduce a minimal method for stitching panoramic images, building on an energy-based framework that leverages the gravity preference of physical cameras. This method derives pixel correspondences and camera parameters from multi-view geometry, while optimizing blending weights through regularized L1-norm gravity energy. The resulting technique offers both stitching quality and interpretability, as it attributes the final output to observable camera postures and directions. We provide comprehensive experimental results and the implementation for reference. Additionally, we outline several applications and future research avenues, including quality assessment, interactive stitching, and learning-based approaches. This study examines two coupled populations of type-I oscillators, where synchronization transitions are mediated by quiescent states. We introduce a novel abstract model that integrates an oscillators-populations framework with a Cournot duopoly economic model. This reduced system demonstrates complex dynamical behaviors, including chimera states characterized by coexisting synchronized and desynchronized groups, as well as a "coexistence of monopoly and duopoly" where one economic firm exits the market while the other maintains a monopoly. We establish a sufficient condition for the emergence of chimera states and analyze the system's dynamics, such as periodic and chaotic patterns, across various parameter values. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between monopoly and duopoly and the group synchronization and desynchronization (chimera) states. Finally, we explore the potential of these intricate dynamics to enhance economic efficiency within the model. To achieve this, we propose an algorithm that automatically identifies parameter values leading to efficient economic operation, accompanied by an illustrative example. Notably, this methodology is also applicable to other complex systems. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations. This work is the first of its kind to investigate chimeras in systems comprising coupled oscillators and populations, and it is the first to establish a link between chimeras and economic efficiency. These results hold significant implications for both physics and economics. The associated MATLAB code is available at [1]. Keywords: Cournot duopoly, economic efficiency, chimera state, complex systems, oscillators-populations system.

Resiliency is a critical factor when controllers operate under uncertainties like parameter variations and external disturbances. A primary approach to enhancing controller resilience involves incorporating evolutionary algorithms (EAs) to guide policy search. Previous research has utilized EAs to maximize the mean performance of Markov Decision Process (MDP) policies. This study extends that work by directing EAs to maximize policy robustness, defined as the area under the curve (AUC) of performance versus disturbance probability. We introduce two new robustness metrics: AUC-based robustness (AAR) and worst-case robustness (WCR). Using a mobile robot navigation task as an example, we compare EA-based optimization for mean performance, AAR, and WCR. Results indicate that maximizing AAR yields better average performance, while maximizing WCR produces the most resilient policies. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that AAR and WCR outperform standard evaluation metrics like MAE and MIC in guiding the policy search. Finally, we applied robustly optimized controllers to a real-world scenario involving a robot navigating an outdoor campus, validating the effectiveness of our approach in practical applications. This paper is the expanded version of [1].

This work introduces the theory of multi-layer graphs by utilizing an elevated slice algebra to define graph products. We introduce two fundamental operations, the cut and crush, which generate the class of DB-graphs, mirroring the reduction mechanism of classical slice algebras. By employing multi-layer graphs as representations for vector spaces, we construct a series of linear operators on these spaces that correspond to the algebra elements. This framework provides an abstract representation theory for multi-layer graphs, analogous to how sandwich representations offer representation theory for classical slice algebras. Specifically, we derive various matrix operators on vector spaces, including an elevated adjacency matrix, as reductions of the crush operator, along with their associated trace and cycle theorems. Furthermore, we derive the dimension formula for DB-graphs as a reduction of the crush operator and derive the dimension formula for multi-layer graphs from it. Finally, we derive the Euler formula for planar multi-layer graphs from the latter. The paper concludes by presenting several open problems. Notably, the proof of the Euler formula relies on an extended definition of the outer region, drawing parallels to the application of sandwich representations in classical slice algebra. This approach offers a promising avenue for developing the theory's applications, particularly in solving counting problems. Additionally, the theory's potential extends to graph theory, machine learning, and linear algebra. For instance, we demonstrate that the matrix of eigenvectors for a planar multi-layer graph, derived from the adapted adjacency matrix, can be interpreted as the sandwich representation of an abstract multi-layer graph. This interpretation could yield valuable insights for graph theory, drawing comparisons to the role of sandwich representations in classical slice algebras. The concepts of multi-layer graphs, layers, and their interconnections are also relevant to machine learning, as layered neural networks serve as a prominent example. Consequently, the theory holds the potential to contribute to the field of artificial intelligence. Finally, the theory of multi-layer graphs may also benefit the field of linear algebra. In summary, the theory of multi-layer graphs is intrinsically linked to the theory of slice algebras, and we anticipate that the former will reciprocally benefit the latter. We establish a low-energy effective theory for the pion-nucleon system that maintains explicit SU(2) isospin symmetry, adhering to chiral symmetry at a quantitative level through low-momentum modes. By employing a single low-energy constant, we achieve high-precision quantitative predictions for both electromagnetic low-energy charge densities and $\pi^+$-nucleon scattering data. Furthermore, our results indicate that the low-momentum pion-nucleon interaction is nearly charge independent. These findings offer direct empirical evidence that the low-momentum pion-nucleon interaction is quantitatively described by a single low-energy constant, which is determined by the value of the mass difference between the pseudoscalar and vector $\pi N$ states. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that the pionic contribution to electromagnetic form factors is negligible. Finally, we determine that the low-energy pion-nucleon scattering length is approximately $-1.43 \pm 0.05$ fermi. This value is significantly more accurate than the one derived from CUSP analysis and aligns closely with the prediction from chiral effective theory based on Weinberg's low-energy theorem. Furthermore, it falls within the estimated two-standard-deviation range of the most precise direct measurement of $a^{(+)}_{0S}$ obtained from the $S$-wave phase shift extraction by the PRC collaboration. Our analysis also reveals that the pionic contribution to the nucleon charge radius is minimal, consistent with the observation that the pion cloud constitutes only a small fraction of the nucleon's total charge. Consequently, the charge distribution of the quark core must account for nearly the entire charge of the proton. This study employs HyperZ, a machine learning-based galaxy redshift estimation method, to determine the morphologies of active galactic nucleus (AGN) host galaxies at redshifts $z<1$ within the 8,000 square degree Hyper Suprime-Cam Extensive Survey. We analyzed 1,018 SDSS DR7 identified AGN candidates from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Legacy Survey, cross-referencing them against SDSS $z\sim0.5$ photometric redshift catalogs. By comparing these sources, we derived morphological classifications for the AGN candidates. Our results indicate that 57% of the sample consists of disk galaxies, 30% are elliptical, and 12% are classified as uncertain. Additionally, we found that AGN candidates possess a higher fraction of disk galaxies compared to control samples of star-forming and passive galaxies at matching redshifts and luminosities. This finding is consistent with the established understanding that AGN activity is more prevalent in disk galaxies. Furthermore, we observed that AGN candidates exhibit a greater proportion of passive galaxies relative to star-forming galaxies than control AGN at similar redshifts and luminosities. These trends are most pronounced in the $z\sim0.5-1$ range, where the fraction of disk-like AGN candidates is approximately 60% higher than that of control AGN. These outcomes align with the known positive correlation between AGN activity and star formation rates, which are themselves linked to galaxy morphologies. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the utility of large-scale imaging surveys in efficiently classifying AGN samples. This represents a significant advancement in understanding the relationship between AGN activity and host galaxy morphology. Future work will leverage the Hyper Suprime-Cam Legacy Survey to examine the redshift evolution of AGN host galaxy morphologies across the $z<2$ range. This model proves viable when the short-distance components exhibit angular dependence relative to the third particle. We apply this framework to analyze various deuterium three-body observables, showing that the short-distance contributions in the dielectron and diproton channels differ significantly due to their distinct angular dependencies. Additionally, we estimate the magnitude of the short-distance trineutron contribution, which is likely to be negligible. Our predictions for these three-body contributions align well with existing experimental data. Furthermore, we show that three-body short-distance correlations can be approximated by a model utilizing three Gaussian widths that vary depending on whether the contributing pair forms a dominant low-$L$ or high-$L$ projection. These findings are highly relevant for observables in multi-nucleon short-distance correlations across other systems, such as those involving $e^+e^-$, di-pion, and (anti)deuteron production. This paper addresses the issue that complex-valued activation functions offer superior properties for information representation compared to ReLU, yet their adoption in deep education networks has been hindered primarily by training challenges. To overcome this, we introduce Co-domain, a straightforward method that transforms a complex-valued network into an equivalent real-valued one. Specifically, for a complex-valued linear layer, we derive a corresponding equivalent real-valued layer by deriving complex parameters from real parameters and converting operations on complex states into equivalent operations on real parameters. For a complex-valued nonlinear layer, we obtain its equivalent real-valued counterpart by modeling the equivalent post-activation states using complex-valued activation functions applied to a super-vector constructed from the real activation outputs. Experimental results indicate that Co-domain enables deep education networks to converge effectively, achieving accuracy improvements of 3.2% and 2.4% on the MMLU and GLUE benchmarks, respectively, compared to network structures previously used in this domain. The most probable map derived from the $X$-parameterization consistently displays numerous spurious cold and hot spots centered on the Galactic plane, which originate from foreground residuals. This phenomenon arises because the $R$ component lacks angular resolution. While current mitigation strategies involve either subtracting a separate map for $R$ or broadening its beam, both existing approaches suffer from significant drawbacks. The proposed solution involves modifying the $Q$ and $P$ components by applying a broadening effect, thereby eliminating X-artifacts in the resulting map without compromising total intensity. Furthermore, the variance of the posterior distribution is significantly reduced when a broadened map is utilized. This technique is highly effective for both simulated and observed data. When applied to Planck HFI data, the findings indicate that the previously reported cold spot in the most probable map is largely diminished. Additionally, the variance of the polarization map is substantially lower when generated from the probability distribution compared to Gaussian map makers, with the majority of this improvement attributable to the use of a broadened component. The study concludes that the posterior distribution should serve as a primary tool for CMB map making. Additionally, a method for creating the most probable map from the $R+I+U+V$-parameterization is presented, which avoids the overfitting issues inherent in the standard maximum probability approach. This alternative map exhibits reduced variance in both temperature and polarization compared to Gaussian map makers. Finally, a novel technique for estimating the significance of features in the most probable map is introduced, which relies solely on the distribution of features within the posterior. This method is applied to assess the significance of the CMB cold spot and other anomalies. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the correlation between temperature and polarization in the most probable map is strongly influenced by foreground subtraction, and it establishes a procedure for quantifying the uncertainty in feature significance caused by this effect. Finally, the most probable map is shown to retain a distinct large-scale imprint of foreground residuals. These results have been implemented in Giapeto, a new open-source code for maximum probability map making that supports $R+I+Q+U+V$-parameterization and offers various options for feature analysis. We address a prevalent issue in language-guided reinforcement learning (LCGRL), where an agent grasping objects must identify a specific target in the scene when provided with scene-relative descriptions. This uncertainty, caused by semantic ambiguity in the language, often leads agents to ignore the intended target and pursue incorrect ones. To resolve this, we introduce a training framework that utilizes an attention-based goal conditioner to choose head parts for a transformer policy, thereby reducing uncertainty by selecting target objects that best match the provided language. Our approach demonstrates significant efficacy across two distinct domains: a 2D TurtleBot simulation and a 3D simulation featuring a PPO-based policy. Furthermore, this framework is easily adaptable to other LCGRL problems beyond object search, such as navigation and manipulation. This paper serves as an extended version of our work, which was previously published as an OpenReview Short Paper [1]. Additionally, our code is made available for general use in other settings, as this study represents an initial step toward language-guided decision-making. We invite readers to explore our code repository at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/TARGETS.

The density matrix provides a comprehensive description of quantum states, yet state preparation and tomography remain formidable experimental challenges. The shadow method recently emerged as a practical and efficient approach for characterizing quantum multistate ensembles. This study extends the shadow method to the domain of quantum channels. By applying a unitary representation of supermaps to both inputs and outputs within a quantum channel experiment, we demonstrate the reconstruction of shadow states that fully describe the channel. These shadow states exhibit stability across different measurement runs and offer insight into the channel's properties. Furthermore, we illustrate their utility in directly calculating the output of an input state without performing the reconstruction. Our findings are validated through numerical simulations of various qubit and qudit channels. These results demonstrate that our approach offers a resource-efficient method for quantum channel description, with applications extending to the characterization of quantum hardware necessary for quantum computing and communication. Additionally, this method facilitates experiments aimed at studying the fundamental properties of quantum information transfer. Specifically, we examine the erasure and loss channels to analyze their erasure rates and decoherence lengths. Finally, we explore the potential of shadow states for designing quantum initialization protocols. One such protocol involves applying a channel to a reference shadow state to prepare a target shadow state, which may find applications in quantum error correction. This work advances the understanding and application of shadow states for future quantum information research. Experimental investigations into the proposed methods and applications are currently underway. This study investigates planar convex shapes from the perspective of geometric inequalities linking their Cheeger parameter to other geometric quantities. We present Keen's inequalities, which establish a relationship between the Cheeger parameter and the diameter, perimeter, and inradius. Additionally, we derive a set of complementary inequalities by connecting the Cheeger parameter to the outradius, width, and symmetry type number. Finally, we address the classification of sharp cases and develop techniques to construct nearly sharp examples. All numerical computations were performed using the Breadth function library. This work serves as a sequel to our coauthored paper, which established bounds for the Cheeger parameter and examined the sharpness of those estimates. Furthermore, the results obtained here can be utilized to derive various geometric inequalities regarding the symmetry type number, width, and outradius for convex sets. This study investigates the multi-body interactions among electrons in a uniform, infinite bilayer graphene system by employing an extension of the renormalization group method. The methodology involves constructing an effective Hamiltonian for bilayer graphene that includes a Coulomb interaction term alongside a uniform transverse electric field perpendicular to the layers. By applying the renormalization group procedure, the electric field is diagonalized within the basis of non-interacting states, followed by integrating out high-energy states to analyze the renormalization group flow. Results indicate that a transverse electric field exceeding a critical threshold decouples the layers, whereas fields below this critical value induce an many-body instability. This instability manifests as a finite energy gap across the bilayer bands at the Brillouin zone center and as a linear dispersion at the Brillouin zone boundaries. Furthermore, based on the renormalization group analysis, we demonstrate that these many-body instabilities persist even in the presence of a uniform magnetic field. Finally, the methodology is validated by comparing the derived renormalization group flow with the exact solution for non-interacting bilayer graphene. These findings offer a novel perspective on the electronic structure of bilayer graphene and may assist in guiding future experimental investigations. Additionally, this research offers a distinct alternative to the quantum Hall bilayer model, which has been the primary focus of recent studies exploring bilayer instability. Specifically, unlike the quantum Hall bilayer model which examines instability under uniform magnetic fields across all Landau levels, the current analysis considers electronic instabilities under magnetic fields without breaking time-reversal symmetry in every Landau level. The Ramsey series method stands as the most precise and widely utilized approach for analyzing Larmor precession frequencies. However, this technique is often executed in a fixed, non-adaptive format, which can result in suboptimal time allocations across individual experiments. To address this, we introduce a sequential Bayesian trial design to determine adaptive measurement times for each experiment within the series. By integrating this design with dynamic Bayesian analysis, we develop algorithms capable of real-time parameter estimation and uncertainty calculation. These dynamic methods are applied to a specific case study: determining the magnetic moment of the $^{171}$Yb$^+$ ion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that implementing adaptive trial designs is straightforward with current analysis algorithms and that these designs can enhance measurement precision. Specifically, a single experiment run sequentially yields results comparable to those from $10\%$ to $20\%$ fewer parallel experiments when using a fixed measurement time scheme. Additionally, we illustrate how these sequential measurements can be integrated into existing fixed-time experiments. Overall, the adaptive trial design and analysis methods presented here are applicable to any series measurement involving multiple sequential experiments. These tools facilitate parameter estimation, enable self-adaptive planning of measurement sequences, and support online decision-making. Consequently, they offer significant benefits for scientific research and technological advancements dependent on highly precise parameter measurements. Finally, a Python library is provided to facilitate the implementation of these sequential Bayesian trial designs and dynamic Bayesian analysis. This library is freely available to the community and can be utilized independently of any specific measurement scheme. By providing a flexible framework for adaptive measurement planning and parameter analysis, it promotes further research into adaptive measurement strategies. Additionally, it can serve as a starting point for developing new analysis methods, such as those for model selection or multi-parameter joint estimation. This study explores accuracy cosmology through the lens of primordial gravitational waves. We propose that the gravitational-wave (GW) spectrum observed today consists of two components: an advanced LIGO-band (ALB) spectrum amplified by cosmic acceleration and a wide-ranging "Hubble strain" (HS) spectrum rigidly determined by the Hubble constant, $H_0$. The $ALB+HS$ spectrum is derived from two distinct cosmological mechanisms: it is directly measured by current and upcoming GW detectors, including the Hubble Space Telescope and Pulsar Timing Arrays, and is also inferred from the observed discrepancy between distance and luminosity distance in an accelerating universe. We illustrate this framework using data from GW observations within the local universe and from cosmological surveys such as supernova surveys and cosmic microwave background experiments. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of this model for cosmology and gravity. This approach offers a promising new avenue for investigating cosmic acceleration, dark energy, and dark matter, while simultaneously enabling the measurement of the primordial gravitational-wave spectrum from inflation and testing various theories of early-universe cosmology and quantum gravity. Specifically, the $H_0$ component provides an independent, direct measurement of the Hubble constant, whereas Pulsator Timing Arrays will constrain stochastic GW spectra in the milliHertz range, potentially revealing signals from supermassive black hole binaries and gravitational waves generated by cosmic acceleration and inflation. Consequently, Pulsator Timing Arrays can serve as a new probe for cosmology, gravity, and early-universe physics. Ultimately, this model may provide the first direct detection of primordial gravitational waves and resolve fundamental cosmological problems, including the $H_0$ tension. Thus, this framework represents a paradigm shift in gravitational-wave astronomy, cosmology, and their intersections. This paper serves as a foundation for future research in accuracy cosmology, gravitational-wave spectroscopy, and the gravitational-wave backdrop. Notably, the $ALB+HS$ spectrum is expected to be observable in the near future by various GW detectors, including LIGO, Virgo, KAGRA, Advanced LISA, and Pulsator Timing Arrays. This model could transform gravitational-wave spectroscopy into a new tool for cosmology, with the first decade of GW observations already yielding significant results, such as the first direct detection of a binary black hole merger, the measurement of gravitational-wave polarization, and the first direct measurement of the Hubble constant. In this sense, accuracy cosmology and its associated GW spectrum provide a new perspective on the past, present, and future of cosmic evolution.

We introduce findings from observations of cometary gas emission centered on Comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) conducted on 2019 March 10 using the Atacama Compact Array (ACA). These observations represent the first detailed investigation into the spatial distribution of cometary gas, specifically targeting H2O, CN, CO, and CO2. The ACA's unique capability to observe cometary scattered light with exceptional sensitivity allows for the detection of gas distributions that deviate significantly from point-source expectations. Our results indicate that the emitting gas clouds are elongated along the comet's orbitally calculated velocity vector, with dimensions ranging from approximately 1000 km to 10,000 km. These clouds are situated roughly 10,000 km to 100,000 km from the nucleus, though they may extend much further. We propose that this structure results from the superposition of numerous point sources, potentially caused by a distributed source such as a comet nucleus possessing a highly porous, highly fractured, or spongy architecture. Furthermore, the CO emission is notably weaker than anticipated, suggesting that CO is not a primary product of photodissociation. Instead, CO is likely a direct outgassing species, which implies that cometary nuclei are more oxygen-rich than previously thought. Finally, the CO emission is observed to be more diffuse than H2O, CN, or CO2, indicating that CO2 is more readily converted into CO than CO is into CO+. Collectively, these observations suggest that cometary nuclei possess a distributed source of gas, a finding that may have significant implications for future cometary science. This study demonstrates that radio telescopes, such as those in the ACA, can significantly contribute to cometary research. We conclude by outlining the ACA's potential to advance this field and identifying key scientific questions that ACA observations could help address. Our observations of the cometary gas distribution align closely with emerging models of comet nuclei, which suggest that these bodies are more porous and fractured than previously believed. This supports the hypothesis that comets are "rubble piles" rather than monolithic objects. Additionally, our observations reveal that cometary gas clouds are not static but evolve over time, with their structure influenced by factors such as solar radiation, dust interactions, and orbital dynamics. To achieve this, we integrate the widely accepted NSGA-II evolutionary algorithm with a Branch and Bound strategy. The process begins by converting the continuous NSGA-II population into binary representations. Subsequently, the Branch and Bound algorithm operates on these binary strings to identify the most promising individuals, thereby reducing the search space. The procedure then executes Branch and Bound again on this narrowed population of elite solutions. We applied this proposed approach to two real-world problems: the single-source single-commodity fixed-charge network flow problem and the single-source single-commodity multi-commodity network flow problem. Finally, performance metrics were calculated to assess the effectiveness of the method. These metrics included the count of non-dominated solutions, the average distance to the ideal point, and the distance between the maximum and minimum values of each objective function. The analysis confirms that the approach is highly effective for solving the mentioned problems, demonstrating significant potential for future research. This paper provides a detailed examination of current challenges in biomedical data exchange and introduces a conceptual framework to address them. We explore interfaces that mediate data transfer between providers and users, with current efforts actively developing frameworks to securely and efficiently integrate resources across diverse cyberinfrastructure portals. Although numerous scientific disciplines have established successful data exchange systems, the biomedical field faces specific hurdles, including issues related to version management, metadata interoperability, and interoperability itself, which significantly increase the complexity and cost of exchange mechanisms. We identify three critical areas for improvement: (1) the necessity of a unified conceptual framework that harmonizes data access mechanisms, (2) the development of efficient and user-friendly data exchange and access tools, and (3) the implementation of a standardized, interoperable data exchange framework capable of supporting multiple data transfer methods. Additionally, we outline an agenda of research and development initiatives aimed at creating practical solutions to these problems. Our proposed approach involves developing interoperable extensions to existing cyberinfrastructure portals—common entry points for biomedical data access and exchange—thereby mitigating many current exchange issues. We illustrate this concept using a biomedical research use case involving clinical trial data exchange. Finally, we discuss key research and development challenges essential for enabling practical and effective biomedical data exchange. In many biological and medical contexts, sampling a subset of the exposure group is more practical than sampling the entire population. However, standard mediation analysis methods are invalid when applied to full-population samples derived from case-control data. This study introduces a stepwise framework to evaluate mediation effects using sampled data while accounting for sampling bias caused by this selection. The approach integrates weighted maximum likelihood estimation, model-based simulation, and the delta method. Applications to both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that this recognition and assessment strategy effectively mitigates sampling bias. Consequently, researchers analyzing sampled populations should apply these adjustments to ensure the validity of their mediation conclusions. Furthermore, this work aims to heighten awareness regarding the statistical pitfalls associated with performing mediation analysis on sampled populations. By analyzing executed actions and their outcomes, an agent can reconstruct a hypothetical "what would have happened if..." scenario, enabling it to address problems with greater insight. I propose that a comparable method applies to single-agent many-objective optimization, where sampling and renaming techniques can be viewed as assembled and executed plans. Finally, I establish that this method is mathematically equivalent to a recent strategy known as "hindsight summarization," which has already shown substantial performance gains in many-objective optimization. The interaction between the Sun and the interstellar medium shapes the global evolution of solar wind and magnetic field characteristics, a process that can be modeled using the "magnetic switchblow" concept. This framework explains the development of solar breeze flow patterns and the generation of characteristic field structures, such as coronal holes, stream interaction regions, and switchbacks. These patterns arise from the self-organization of the heliosphere into distinct regions of unidirectional and bidirectional field flow, driven by the specific boundary condition of a tangential field at the solar surface. We have examined over 100 in-situ measurements from the Parker Solar Probe to analyze the evolution of bidirectional field sectors and their correlation with the morphology of co-located plasma fields. Our analysis indicates that these datasets confirm the prevalence of Parker Solar Flow (PSF) patterns in the inner heliosphere, particularly during high-speed streams. Furthermore, our results align with recent findings by He et al. (2021) regarding the occurrence and generation of switchbacks. Additionally, we observed a strong inverse correlation between the energy flux of bidirectional sectors and the angle between the local magnetic field and the radial direction, supporting the tangential alignment hypothesis. Finally, the data corroborate the link between the energy flow of bidirectional sectors and the generation of switchbacks. Collectively, these results suggest that the Parker Solar Flow is a fundamental driver of solar wind evolution, especially within high-speed streams. This is further evidenced by the scarcity of radial bidirectional sectors in these regions, which likely results from the Sun's rotation sweeping out plasma as it accelerates to supersonic speeds. Consequently, the evolution of solar breeze flow patterns is intrinsically tied to the solar breeze velocity profile. Overall, our results strongly support the Parker Solar Flow hypothesis as a viable model for solar wind evolution in the inner heliosphere. This work was conducted within the PSP-PSW collaboration. This paper demonstrates that every countable noncommutative principal bundle can be represented as the fixed point algebra of a free countable group action on a unital C*-algebras. The term "countable" indicates that both the structure group and the gauge group within this framework are countable. Furthermore, we prove that the noncommutative countable principal bundle defined by a countable group action on a unital C*-algebra meets the conditions established by Lafforgue and Skandalos for their K-theory isomorphism formula, which serves as a generalization of the Serre formula. Additionally, we investigate the K-theory of these noncommutative principal bundles. Specifically, in the simplest scenario involving a rank one vector bundle over the circle, the relative K-theory of the associated group action on a unital commutative C*-algebra is shown to be isomorphic to the relative K-theory of a specific pair of free group algebras, thereby extending an earlier result by Higson and Roe. This finding provides a partial resolution to a question posed by Higson and Roe. Finally, this result represents a significant advancement toward addressing a question raised by Rennie regarding the Pimsner-Popa index pair relative to both K-theory and Ext groups. To achieve these advancements, we utilize techniques from both operator algebras and topology. Notably, our findings regarding Ext groups build upon the seminal work of Brown and Green concerning Ext groups for C*-algebras and their connections to topological K-theory. These insights are integrated with recent breakthroughs by Toms and Wu on extensions of C*-algebras and those by Higson and Rosenberg regarding the relationship between Ext groups and Ext groups for topological spaces. This synthesis of insights from operator algebras, topology, and noncommutative geometry enables us to establish a link between the Ext groups of a specific class of noncommutative principal bundles and the Ext groups of certain topological principal bundles. This link serves as a generalization of a prior result by Toms and Wu. To ensure the accessibility of this work to a broader audience, we have also included a detailed review of the foundational concepts from operator algebras and C*-algebraic K-theory that underpin these findings. In the R-parity even sector, R-parity conserving scissors modes are classified into local and global categories based on the signs of collective angular momenta $I_x$ and $I_y$ within left and right nuclear components. Conversely, R-parity violating scissors states arise from configurations where collective angular momenta in the left and right components differ. By utilizing the Double-Rotors Model, we introduce a novel class of R-parity violating scissors modes termed "adverse" r-modes. These states exhibit significant deformation amplitudes even at zero angular momentum, surpassing the characteristics of standard r-modes. Furthermore, these adverse r-modes can be incorporated into a systematic framework for interpreting experimental data. Specifically, for $^{196}$Hg, we predict the presence of adverse r-modes at excitation energies of 2.25 MeV and 3.0 MeV. This prediction aligns with recent experimental findings by K. Kowalski et al. (Phys. Rev. C 104, 041301(R) 2021), which identified a strong deformation amplitude of 0.85(10) at 2.25 MeV, nearly double that of the nearby local gamma-vibration at 1.95 MeV. We contend that the dominance of the adverse r-mode in $^{196}$Hg is essential to explain this observation. Additionally, we extend the analysis to other even-even nuclei, including $^{194}$Hg, $^{192}$Hg, $^{198}$Hg, $^{208}$Pb, $^{210}$Pb, $^{214}$Po, $^{218}$Po, $^{232}$U, and $^{238}$U. For each nucleus, we identify potential adverse r-modes and estimate their collective deformation amplitudes. Our findings indicate that these adverse modes are generally more deformed than the corresponding local gamma-vibrations. Finally, we propose that detecting and characterizing these adverse r-modes could serve as a valuable tool for investigating nuclear collective excitations. To facilitate this, we have developed a computer program capable of calculating the characteristics of adverse r-modes. This program is publicly accessible and can be utilized by the community to explore and understand the properties of these unique r-modes. This study introduces a cell-mean-based neural network (CN) model designed to solve both hyperbolic and elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs). Unlike traditional finite difference methods that discretize domains into grids, discretizing into cells, the proposed cell-mean CNN model utilizes both interior and boundary nodes of each cell. By applying Taylor expansions, the finite difference approximations at interior nodes are derived from values at surrounding boundary nodes; these approximate boundary values are then represented by neural network outputs. The model enforces the PDE's initial and boundary conditions through neural network inputs and incorporates the differential equation into its architecture. Consequently, solving the PDE reduces to a single forward pass of the trained network. Numerical experiments across one, two, and three dimensions demonstrate the method's efficacy for hyperbolic PDEs, while comparisons with the finite element method for elliptic PDEs reveal comparable accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed cell-mean CNN model exhibits superior performance compared to the vertex-based CNN model introduced in our earlier work. The results indicate that the cell-mean CNN model is highly effective for both hyperbolic and elliptic PDEs, is easily extendable to other types of differential equations, and offers computational advantages over the vertex model regarding memory usage and processing time. The cell-mean CNN model can be viewed as a finite element-based neural network approach. Future research will explore its application to systems of PDEs, integral and fractional PDEs, and integral equations. Additionally, the model's potential to address inverse problems, such as identifying unknown coefficients from observations, warrants further investigation. All computations were performed using MATLAB. Given the growing interest in PDE solutions via neural networks, this work offers valuable insights for researchers in computational mathematics, numerical analysis, and related fields. The accompanying appendix provides supplementary details, including detailed computational results, additional comparisons with the vertex model, and further discussion on computational aspects. These extensions are available in our cell-mean model repository, which also includes the original vertex model. While this paper focuses on forward problems, it is important to note that inverse problems present significant challenges; therefore, this work addresses only the forward PDE solution.
