The ALICE experiment has been meticulously redesigned to excel in data collection and utilization, featuring a novel upgrade of its inner tracking system and a substantial expansion of its external physics apparatus. This expansion incorporates advanced detectors capable of measuring particles with high precision across the full kinematic range. A key component is the upgraded Time-Projection Chamber (TPC), engineered to surpass data acquisition rates of LHC Run 3 by leveraging cutting-edge technologies. Additionally, the experiment will employ AI-driven algorithms to perform online event reconstruction and analysis. The objective of the upgraded ALICE is to deliver high-statistics measurements of heavy-ion collisions and proton-proton interactions alongside small systems. Furthermore, ALICE will continue to investigate quark-gluon plasma and its connection to its own creation. This paper outlines the ALICE upgrade and the anticipated physics results from the post-Run 3 era. Specifically, it addresses the advancements in heavy-ion physics, including the investigation of collective phenomena in small systems, the study of multi-meson correlations, and measurements of heavy quark energy loss and quarkonia suppression. The text also details upgrades to its exotic hadron program and the search for strongly interacting dark matter. Finally, the discussion covers the planned introduction of AI-based algorithms for online event reconstruction and analysis. The ALICE detector is expected to play a pivotal role in addressing fundamental questions regarding QCD and its high-energy phase. The paper concludes with a discussion of ALICE's future research and development program. The content is based on a presentation delivered at the International Conference on High Energy and High Field Physics (ICHEP) 2022 in Bologna, Italy. The conference was organized by CERN, CNRS/IN2P3, and the University of Bologna. ALICE is a member of the LHC experiments.

The non-local entanglement between future and past light cones in Rindler space-time generates, via geometric phase, a Berry phase within a spin-1/2 system situated at a fixed spatial location. This phenomenon demonstrates that fields embedded in accelerated frames possess correlations consistent with an "Unruh effect" from the perspective of a remote observer in the asymptotic frame, even at close proximity to the local observer. We demonstrate the detection of this remote Unruh effect through an interferometric setup involving a future-directed entangled photon and a spin-1/2 particle anchored far away, characterized by a phase shift in the polarization components of the photonic signal. The observed phase comprises the entangled light-cone structure and is analyzed using the entanglement spectrum of the field modes across different Rindler regions, which features a power-law decay indicative of entanglement between a Rindler wedge and the rest of the field space. This spectral characteristic offers a new approach to investigating the Unruh effect in quantum field theory. The proposed experiment is feasible given advancements in generating entangled photon pairs and stable acceleration technologies. We illustrate the entanglement spectrum using entangled photons generated at the source through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, a method compatible with current experimental capabilities. The resulting Unruh effect manifests as a phase shift in the polarization entanglement spectrum, which can be measured via quantum tomography. We provide a theoretical framework for these predictions, which can be tested in existing quantum optics laboratories employing ultralow-energy photon pairs. Furthermore, the entanglement spectrum exhibits characteristics of a conformal field theory, suggesting a link to the holographic principle. Consequently, our proposal offers a novel pathway to investigate quantum gravity. The remote detection of the Unruh effect serves as a fundamental test of quantum mechanics in curved spacetime, a critical component of the Quantum Space-Time initiative. Event planning for special occasions is often complex and time-consuming, particularly in non-English speaking regions where multilingual data is limited. This study introduces MEE, a dataset designed to facilitate Natural Language Processing (NLP) research for this domain. The dataset comprises 10,524 sentences in six languages—Bengali, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Korean, and Telugu—collected from social media sources such as Facebook, Twitter, and Reddit. It is manually annotated to identify various occasion types and their corresponding attributes, including date, time, number of guests, event type, location, budget, and budget constraints. The data was independently labeled by two annotators to ensure reliability, with a final set of resolved conflicts by a senior annotator. We conducted thorough evaluations of annotation quality, consistency, and inter-annotator agreement. Furthermore, we performed cross-lingual experiments using BERT-based models to demonstrate the dataset's utility in occasion planning. The source code and the MEE dataset are publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepNLP/MEExplainable. The dataset is licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Our findings indicate that the MEE dataset is highly valuable for advancing NLP research across multiple languages. Additionally, we have made the annotation guidelines available in the six original languages to enhance accessibility. This work is anticipated to inspire further research in NLP and low-resource settings. We welcome contributions from the community to expand the dataset with more languages and larger volumes of annotated text. This study examines the positivity of characteristic structures linked to characteristic classes via the Chern-Weyl map. By employing a novel technique involving the integration of differential forms on global vector bundles, the authors prove that these structures possess positive symbols. The technique's mechanism involves solving specific partial differential equations through a defined transformation and leveraging the flatness of a specific connection. As a result, this methodology offers a fresh perspective on establishing the positivity of these structures. A key innovation is the use of "characteristic forms derived from global vector bundles," which serve as an effective instrument for managing global characteristic classes within vector bundles through the application of standard differential operations. The paper concludes by detailing the construction of these forms. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that their approach yields a streamlined proof of a fundamental result by Borel and Serre regarding the relationship between characteristic classes and characteristic structures. Additional applications of this methodology are also presented. Finally, the paper includes an appendix detailing the historical development of the study of positivity regarding these characteristics. A translation of the work by J. Borel and D. The hard spectral states of black hole X-ray binaries (XRBs) are characterized by a multi-component spectrum comprising an optically thin power-law, a Comptonized disk component, and a thermal component from the companion star. This study investigates whether fluctuations in the secondary star's input (the "stellar breeze") can account for long-term changes in the XRB's thermal state. We conducted a long-duration, multi-wavelength observation of Cyg X-1 during its hard state using NuSTAR, XMM-Newton, and Swift. Spectral analysis revealed a thermal component consistent with the secondary star's photosphere, exhibiting a temperature of approximately 30,000 K and a luminosity of roughly 10^36 erg/s. Timing analysis identified a low-frequency quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) at approximately 1.5 Hz in both hard X-rays (3–10 keV) and UV light (250–400 Å), with the UV signal showing a higher fractional rms amplitude. These UV variability data align with fluctuations in the secondary star's thermal radiation. Our findings suggest that energy release from the secondary star's photosphere, driven by stellar breeze variability, can be accreted by the black hole to sustain a low-frequency, high-amplitude QPO in the hard state. Consequently, this work demonstrates for the first time a correlation between the secondary star's thermal component and the inner accretion flow in the hard state of Cyg X-1. Furthermore, our results provide a novel explanation for the origin of low-frequency, high-amplitude QPOs in the hard state of Cyg X-1. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings regarding the physical processes driving accretion in XRBs. This paper introduces a novel, collaborative framework for universal syntactic and semantic analysis. Its primary objective is to develop a shared analytical infrastructure capable of processing all human languages. The initiative has made substantial progress, including the Universal Dependencies Tree Bank, an interlinear annotation format for coherently analyzing multiple languages simultaneously, and the Universal Dependency Parser, which operates on this format. The paper examines the motivation behind this approach, which has become increasingly vital due to advancements in computational power and data availability. It also addresses the ethical implications of such tools and provides an overview of the formation process of the Tree Bank. Finally, the work outlines current progress and future directions regarding the Tree Bank and the associated parsing software. Through this collaborative approach to universal analysis, we aim to provide a unified infrastructure for linguistic research. This solution fosters international collaboration, thereby generating substantial linguistic insights and knowledge. Additionally, it contributes to society by delivering language processing services that are unified, consistent, and economically viable. This paper serves as a foundational introduction to universal analysis, offering a comprehensive overview of the field and its future prospects. It is particularly valuable for researchers and students new to the domain. Keywords: Universal Analysis, Universal Dependencies, Tree Bank, Parsing, Computational Linguistics.

Magnetized neutron star mergers are anticipated to generate neutrino-cooled accretion disks, from which the resulting outflows may leave the disk via jets, winds, or non-axisymmetric instabilities. While the impact of non-axisymmetric instabilities on unmagnetized disks is well-established, their role in magnetized scenarios remains uncertain. This study employs two-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamical simulations incorporating a dynamical magnetic field to investigate outflows escaping accretion disks around rotating neutron stars. Our findings indicate that the development of non-axisymmetric instabilities in magnetized disks is contingent upon local magnetic field strength, helicity, and the radial distance from the neutron star. Specifically, for initial conditions with a logarithmic magnetic field strength of $\log(B/{\rm G})=5.5$ at $r=100$ km, we observe helical outflows escaping the disk at radii $r\gtrsim 100$ km. In contrast, simulations with $\log(B/{\rm G})=5$ at $r=100$ km exhibit no helical outflows. Furthermore, we demonstrate that magnetic reconnection in these helical flows can significantly influence the thermal and dynamical evolution of the accretion disk. Our results suggest that magnetized neutrino-cooled accretion disks around neutron stars may be more likely to produce non-axisical outflows than previously assumed, thereby potentially altering the characteristics of outflows from neutron star mergers. Future research should employ three-dimensional simulations to further explore this phenomenon. Additionally, we provide updated estimates for the mass and energy of escaped outflows, finding them to be approximately 0.01 and 0.005 $M_{\odot}$, and 0.005 and 0.0025 B.E., respectively. These values align closely with earlier estimates derived from unmagnetized simulations. Consequently, the inclusion of magnetization in neutrino-cooled accretion disks around neutron stars does not appear to significantly affect the mass and energy of outflows escaping the disk. However, our work underscores the necessity of including magnetization in simulations of accretion disks surrounding black holes. Finally, we highlight the potential for helical outflows from magnetized accretion disks to serve as a mechanism for non-axisical exorcism. We investigate the tidal properties and merger rates of massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) by utilizing the ratio of central flux to maximum flux ($F/F_{\rm max}$) derived from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). A sample of 1,100 ETGs with masses between $10^{11}$ and $10^{12} \odot \odot$ was selected from deep imaging data, spanning redshifts $0.03 \lesssim z \lesssim 0.35$. We compared this data against a large set of $N$-body simulations to analyze how $F/F_{\rm max}$ varies with redshift, mass, and stellar velocity dispersion ($\sigma$). The simulations reveal that $F/F_{\rm max}$ is primarily determined by the velocity dispersion ratio ($\lambda$) at the time of a galaxy's last major merger, which is also strongly correlated with $\sigma$. Based on these findings, we established a universal relation between $F/F_{\rm max}$ and $\sigma$ for ETGs. This relation shows a clear redshift dependence, decreasing from $F/F_{\rm max} \sim 0.4$ at $z=0$ to $F/F_{\rm max} \sim 0.2$ at $z=2$. By applying this universal relation to the observed $F/F_{\rm max}$ values, we estimated the merger history for each galaxy. For the studied sample, we determined that approximately 10% of galaxies experienced their last major merger within the last 1 Gyr, while 80% underwent such an event within the last 5 Gyr. Additionally, the fraction of galaxies with merger rates exceeding 0.5 at $z=0$ rises from 10% to 50% between $z=0$ and $z=2$. These results are consistent with established evolutionary theories for early-type galaxies. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the tidal structures observed in ETGs are significantly influenced by recent mergers. Finally, we conclude that the universal relation between $F/F_{\rm max}$ and $\sigma$ serves as a valuable tool for understanding the flux-dominated structures of early-type galaxies. The nature of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) remains enigmatic, and various theories have been proposed to explain their origins. Certain well-reproduced, repetitive FRBs (wrFRBs) exhibit a distinct morphology characterized by a rapid rise followed by an exponential decay. The lack of optical detection in the GHz wrFRB source repeating at 16.38 Hz suggests that wrFRBs may not possess optical components. However, theoretical models indicate that optical emission could be postponed by up to approximately 100 seconds. This study aims to constrain any concurrent optical emission from wrFRBs. We conducted a systematic search for optical counterparts across 10 epochs spanning 1.5 years for the most stable 16.38 Hz FRB. No optical counterpart was detected in any epoch, with 90% confidence upper limits ranging from 21.4 to 24.4 mag. These findings rule out any simultaneous optical emission from wrFRBs with bolometric luminosities exceeding 10^38 erg/s at any moment. This dissertation centers on the conceptual design, performance optimization, and fabrication techniques aimed at achieving record-breaking laser parameters. High-power lasers are essential to numerous scientific and technological domains, including ultrafast diagnostics, high-energy density physics, particle acceleration, laser fusion, and industrial applications. The primary objective of this work is to push the limits of laser performance, specifically targeting peak power, pulse energy, and wavelength. To achieve this, we employ high-temperature solid-state lasers, frequency conversion methods, and the (4,0)20 whispering gallery mode (WGM) fiber laser. A (4,0)20 WGM fiber laser was designed, built, and integrated with a frequency conversion module to generate 1064 nm and 2020 nm (quad-rapler) high-power solid-state laser systems capable of multi-picosecond pulses. Additionally, we propose a new approach to record-breaking laser performance: utilizing high-temperature whispering gallery mode (WGM) microstructured polymer fibers as resonators. This method leverages the high thermal conductivity of polymers and the optical confinement inherent to WGM resonators. We have designed, designed, and fabricated a complex network of high-temperature polymer fibers, developed a multi-stage pumping architecture, and demonstrated the first high-power laser based on a ring of these fibers. We achieved 1.5 W of continuous wave (CW) power at 1064 nm with a Q-factor exceeding 10^6, delivering energy to an external load. Furthermore, we demonstrated the first step toward breaking the record for CW laser power in the infrared spectrum by incorporating frequency conversion. This research paves the way for high-temperature polymer fiber ring lasers to achieve record-breaking CW power, potentially reaching hundreds of kilowatts. Finally, we demonstrate the first multi-picosecond laser based on a high-temperature polymer fiber ring, capable of multi-picosecond pulses at high power levels. This system utilizes a (4,0)20 quad-rapler, which offers advantages such as large mode volume, high damage threshold, and high thermal conductivity. We have designed, enhanced, and built a laser system achieving 1.5 W CW power at 2020 nm with pulse durations between 10 and 20 ps. Text creation with large language models (LLMs) typically involves users inputting prompts and receiving responses, with customizations made via text-based instructions. However, the linear nature of LLM contexts often limits the model's ability to fully interpret complex instructions, resulting in outputs that fail to match user expectations. Drawing inspiration from human-collaborative creation, we introduce a new interaction paradigm that incorporates visual controls to enhance the collaboration between users and LLMs. This approach comprises a new API, a context design, and a model. Extensive user studies on tasks ranging from natural language generation to program synthesis demonstrate that our visual control interface enables more fine-grained collaboration, improving the task completion capabilities of existing LLMs. Furthermore, our secondary experiments on visual instruction following and the construction of a new benchmark reveal that pre-training with visual controls is highly effective for improving the generalization of LLMs. These results highlight the potential of our visual control interface and API to create more intuitive and expressive user experiences. To foster open research and community contributions, we have released the complete code, including the API, visual controls, training code, models, and benchmarks, at https://github.com/nyu-dl/observing-lm. Our paper and code can also be accessed at our project website: https://vision.fas.harvard.edu/observing-lm. Finally, our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/nyu-dl/observing-lm. Our project website is located at https://vision.fas.harvard.edu/observing-lm. Our paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01420. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/nyu-dl/observing-lm.

Collaborating with large language models (LLMs) to produce text typically involves users entering prompts and receiving outputs, with modifications directed through text-based instructions. These inputs are processed within a linear context, which can confuse LLMs regarding the relative importance of different context elements, leading to outputs that do not align with user expectations. Drawing inspiration from human-collaborative creation, we propose a new approach to text creation with LLMs that integrates visual controls to better align user expectations with model outputs. This new creation interface consists of three components: (1) a new API, (2) a context design, and (3) a model. Our paper, code, and model are available at https://github.com/

This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a ring currency protocol incorporating zero-knowledge proofs. Our approach achieves performance superior to both current ring currency systems and traditional zk-SNARKs, executing faster than the former and consuming less power than the latter. We evaluate this method against two benchmarks: delegated proving versus provoking zk-SNARKs, and Delegated RingCT versus Bitcoin, demonstrating that our solution outperforms all comparison groups. Furthermore, we implemented this proposal within the NULS blockchain framework, which serves as our testbed. NULS supports multiple application-specific blockchains (ASBCs), allowing for the demonstration of multiple use cases. We have already developed a specific instance where Delegated RingCT surpasses Bitcoin's proof-of-work mechanism in speed and energy efficiency. Additionally, we present a comparison of gas fees between Bitcoin and NULS, highlighting the superior cost-effectiveness of our proposal. Finally, we illustrate how to optimize block space utilization through a proposed method for selecting ring members. Our findings indicate that choosing ring members with similar transaction values maximizes space efficiency. We also provide a formula to determine the optimal number of ring members based on available block space. Ultimately, our analysis confirms that Delegated RingCT is both feasible and effective. We have successfully deployed this scheme on the NULS testbed, and our results validate the advantages of ring currency protocols over Bitcoin, specifically regarding transaction volume, cost, and speed. Given these benefits, ring currency offers a promising avenue for future research. Our goal is to enable faster, cheaper, and more efficient anonymous transactions through improved ring member selection strategies and the adoption of value-approximate ring currency. Additionally, we aim to extend ring currency to other use cases beyond payment systems, such as anonymous voting and anonymous job applications. We have already implemented a payment-specific ASBC as a use case, and we plan to develop ASBCs for anonymous voting and job applications in the future. To support these initiatives, we intend to create a tool that streamlines the deployment of ring currency into ASBCs, thereby simplifying the development process. By providing this tool, we aim to encourage more researchers to explore the potential of ring currency. We hope that Delegated RingCT will facilitate further research and accelerate the widespread adoption of ring currency protocols. Our vision is that ring currency will become the standard for anonymous transactions in the near future. We believe that by choosing speed, cost, and convenience as the primary metrics for anonymous transactions, we can achieve a more secure and efficient digital economy.

The BrABe system is designed to measure the transverse profile of intense electron beams. It operates by scanning a probe beam from a low-energy linac across the probe beam's transplane at a specific interaction point; the beam brightness at this point is characterized by its phase space volume. During the interaction, part of the probe beam is scattered into an unpopulated region of the transverse phase space, known as the "brightened" probe beam. By analyzing the evolution of this "brightened" state as it travels to the beamline spectrometer, the transverse phase space volume of the interaction point can be determined. This process is simulated using the code BrightnessScans. The simulation is validated by comparing its results to FLUKA simulations of the same interaction point, which accurately models both the interaction and the transport of "brightened" particles to the spectrometer. Furthermore, a series of simulations was conducted to examine the impact of particle loss in the transport line on the reconstruction of the interaction point's phase space volume. Finally, a set of simulations was performed to investigate how the size of the detected population of "brightened" particles influences phase space volume measurements. These simulations indicate that for beams with overlapping phase spaces, detecting 10% of the "brightened" particles yields more accurate results than detecting 20%, despite the longer path required to achieve the higher detection rate. This finding is attributed to the greater separation between the "brightened" and unscattered probe beam populations at the later detection time. Overall, the simulations demonstrate that the phase space volume of the interaction point can be reconstructed with approximately 10% accuracy. This level of precision is sufficient to identify topological changes in the phase space volume caused by nonlinear beam-beam effects. The findings regarding particle loss and detection rates are expected to be applicable to other beam-analysis techniques that scan the beam profile. Finally, a demonstration of the system's utility is provided by simulating the phase space volume of the first interaction point along the CLIC test facility. To achieve this, the simulation required knowledge of the beamline's linear optics and an initial estimate of the phase space volume at the start of the beamline. With this information, the phase space volume of the final interaction point was reconstructed with an accuracy of roughly 10%. This accuracy is sufficient to detect changes in phase space volume resulting from both linear and nonlinear beam-beam effects. The nonlinear changes were attributed to head-tail instability, while the linear changes were caused by beamstrahlung

Data-informed modeling (DIM) represents a hybrid approach integrating data-driven and physics-informed machine learning, blending mathematical rigor with interpretability. This survey introduces the concept of collaborative learning within DIM. Traditional machine learning seeks to learn objective functions from data; in DIM, however, the goal shifts to finding an optimal combination of physics-based models and learned components. We examine collaborative learning through the lens of optimization, where the objective function merges an empirical term from machine learning with analytical terms from physics-informed learning. Furthermore, we address scalability challenges in collaborative learning within deep learning frameworks by applying operator learning and model reduction techniques. Finally, we outline outstanding challenges and future research directions. Our aim is to inspire further investigation into collaborative learning within data-informed modeling. Key concepts include machine learning, physics-informed learning, data-informed modeling, operator learning, model reduction, and model reduction learning.

We introduce AskewSGD, an algorithm designed to adapt neural network architectures and weights for quantization. Unlike most prior methods that merely minimize quantization error, AskewSGD employs a novel constraint-based optimization approach. This method begins by annealing a range-constraint that forces quantized network parameters to deviate from a specific direction, allowing the network to self-adjust its random initialization to satisfy this constraint. By integrating this constraint with a sign-constraint, AskewSGGD achieves superior quantization performance compared to existing techniques. Additionally, because the range-constraint is eliminated during the back-propagation phase, the algorithm maintains computational efficiency. AskewSGD supports the training of networks with either fixed or variable architectures. When applied to fixed architectures, it produces networks with at-typical weight distributions that deviate from the usual "mean-centered" pattern. Furthermore, the sign-constraint is specifically tailored for quantization and can be substituted with other constraints to optimize networks for alternative applications. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet demonstrate AskewSGD's superiority over previous methods. Specifically, utilizing an architecture with 1M parameters, AskewSGD achieves 90.0% and 86.2% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, respectively, after quantization. On CIFAR-100, it also attains 92.0% accuracy using an architecture with only 284k parameters. For CIFAR-10, it reaches 93.4% accuracy with 284k parameters and 94.2% with 1M parameters. On ImageNet-1k, it achieves 76.7% accuracy with 1M parameters and 78.0% with 284k parameters. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/AskewSGD. Controling soft robots presents a significant challenge due to their complex, nonlinear dynamics and the difficulty of integrating sensors throughout the robot. The model-driven control (MDC) approach offers a potential solution by utilizing dynamic models to compute actuation signals. This paper provides a comprehensive review of MDC for soft robots, covering the underlying concepts, current state of the field, and unresolved challenges. We examine the various types of soft robots, the diverse modeling and control techniques employed across different applications, and identify key gaps in the literature. Furthermore, we propose several open issues and potential future research avenues, aiming to serve as a foundational reference for the community and to stimulate further investigation into this promising domain. Finally, the paper explores the potential of MDC in enabling robot learning. Given the rapid advancements in machine learning and deep learning, we contend that these methods will play a crucial role in advancing soft robotics in the coming years. Consequently, we argue that model-driven control is poised to be central to the future of this field. To substantiate this perspective, we present a case study on a pneumatic artificial muscle (PAM) demonstrating the integration of MDC with learning strategies. This work represents the first attempt to apply deep learning to soft robot control, and the accompanying code is made publicly available. Overall, our objective is to underscore the pivotal role of MDC in shaping the future trajectory of soft robotics. The $\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$-invariant authentic Jacobi form associated with the $\mathbb{R}^2 \simeq \mathbb{R} \oplus \mathbb{R}^*$ anti-symmetric space is investigated. We demonstrate that the Fourier expansion of this Jacobi function aligns with the Dirichlet series representation of the rank 2 zeta function originally proposed by Kubota and Langlands. Furthermore, we provide an alternative derivation of this relationship, thereby offering a comprehensive characterization of the authentic Jacobi function. Specifically, we establish a correspondence between Jacobi series and generalized Eisenstein series. Additionally, we exhibit another connection to Dubois-Violette's zeta function. Our proof of this third relationship relies on the analytic continuation of the Jacobi function across the complex plane, which is derived from its connection to Dubois-Violette's function. Consequently, our work yields novel results that complement earlier findings by J. Kubert and A. Lubotzky. Finally, our findings contribute to the development of J. Kubert's theory of "dual" zeta functions. In an appendix, we also present a proof of the Duality Principle for authentic Jacobi forms. This proof utilizes an approach analogous to I. R. Shifman's "proof by analogy," drawing parallels between J. Kubert's results on zeta functions and our findings regarding authentic Jacobi forms. The principle itself represents a generalization of the functional equation of an authentic Jacobi form. To demonstrate this, we employ an operator that maps authentic Jacobi forms to other authentic Jacobi forms while sending constant functions to constant functions. The proof of the Duality Principle also provides an alternative derivation of the analytic continuation of the constant function linked to Dubois-Violette's zeta function. Table-oriented fact verification demands table diserialization, information extraction, and composition to facilitate verification against natural language queries. This process involves identifying and versioning the specific tables utilized to support asserted facts. We propose a new challenge where verification must be performed on individual tables diserialized one at a time, rather than requiring access to the entire dataset. We empirically evaluate various composition strategies to guide efficient verification during incremental diserialization. Our findings indicate that, despite needing to verify far fewer tables, the model still requires access to a significantly larger number of tables to ensure performance. We further demonstrate that while local table composition is essential for performance, it is insufficient on its own. Ultimately, we show that optimizing for performance during diserialization can substantially improve the overall efficiency of table-oriented fact verification. We make our dataset, based on the TABFact dataset, and our evaluation code accessible to the public. This work seeks to inspire future research into table-oriented fact validation during the diserialization phase. Confrontational Networks (CN) are a type of generative adversarial network designed to learn a disentangled representation of a conditionally injected latent vector. While most existing research focuses on projecting this latent code into a fixed-direction axis within a latent "bottle-neck" space, we explore an alternative approach: embedding the latent information into an arbitrary direction guided by a projection field defined over the latent space. This method enables more natural and controlled text-image generation. Furthermore, our work introduces novel techniques for managing a higher number of words in the input sequence. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art performance on the CUB-200, FGVC Aircraft, and CIFAR-10 datasets. Additionally, we introduce the VQA dataset as a new, effective benchmark for controlling image generation. To improve subdivision efficiency, we employ nested nested intervals methods, which necessitate the comparison of subdivision factors across various samplers. This analysis reveals that existing samplers often lack efficiency, particularly in terms of varying subdivision factors for consecutive samples. We present a resilient algorithm capable of calculating distance tags for all edges in a weighted graph, where the tag for each edge corresponds to the weight of the shortest path connecting its endpoints. These tags must satisfy the triangle inequality when treated as edge weights. Our focus is primarily on graphs with treewidth $w$, where the algorithm's runtime should scale efficiently with both the number of vertices $n$ and the treewidth. We introduce a straightforward yet effective resilient strategy that adapts a recently developed exact algorithm for distance tagging in treewidth-based tree decompositions. Both the preprocessing phase and the execution phase of our method run in $O(npoly(w))$ time, with the polynomial's degree determined by the specific resilient distance tagging problem instance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for every resilient distance tagging instance targeting planar graphs, there exists a specific instance suitable for general graphs that requires at least quadratic time to resolve. This approach builds upon and draws inspiration from the treewidth-based exact algorithm by Chan et al. (2019). Finally, we extend this technique to address resilient shortest path problems within planar graphs. Our framework yields the most efficient known algorithms for resilient shortest paths in this context, achieving $O(n^{1+\epsilon})$ runtime for any $\epsilon > 0$, provided the number of fault pairs is bounded by $O(n^{2-2\epsilon})$. This represents a substantial improvement over the prior best runtime of $O(n^2)$ for the trivial $(1,1)$ resilient shortest path problem. Additionally, we show that any $(k,d)$ resilient shortest path problem on planar graphs can be solved in $O(n^{2-\frac{1}{k+\sqrt{1+4kd}/2}})$ time, which is provably optimal for the $(1,d)$ scenario. These findings rely on a recently introduced two-dimensional range searching data structure by Chan et al. (2018). We also propose a two-dimensional range searching problem with a quadratic lower bound, which is provably optimal for the $(1,d)$ resilient shortest path problem. This problem involves processing a set of points in a 2D plane and answering queries for the minimum value associated with points within a right triangle anchored at a query point, rooted specifically on one or both of the triangle's vertical or horizontal boundaries. To the best of our knowledge, this work marks the first application of two-dimensional range queries to the study of resilient shortest paths. This paper introduces a framework for out-of-domain detection within Gaussian process (GP) models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework for anomaly detection using an illustrative example. We establish a unified result integrating solutions to the complex Monge–Ampère equation with a constrained right-hand side, encompassing both Pluripotential Theory and Complex Geometry contexts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Alexandrov estimate holds with an optimal exponent $\min\{1,\alpha/2\}$, provided the right-hand side exhibits $C^{0,\alpha}$ smoothness. Additionally, we show that the Alexandrov estimate with the optimal exponent $1$ remains valid when the right-hand side is bounded. Our proof synthesizes the Alexandrov–Beckmann–Auer method, techniques from the Choi–Siu solution to the complex Monge–Ampère equation, and the Evans–Krzyżak–Mazowiecka approach to the real Monge–Ampère equation. This enhanced Alexandrov maximum principle holds significance beyond Pluripotential Theory. For instance, applying it to the Ricci flow on manifolds with lower curvature bounds yields a more robust estimate for monotone functions of the Ricci tensor than what ArXiv:2105.00221 achieves.

This study investigates time-domain metrics for a novel class of non-repetitive optical clocks. In such clocks, a local oscillator signal is compared against a reference signal derived from atoms, where transitions in the optical frequency band are governed by a four-level ladder system. We establish analytical formulas for the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the spectral line and the time-domain linewidth (TW), incorporating the impact of Rabi oscillations during laser excitation. Regarding comparative metrics, Rabi oscillations are demonstrated to cause both the TW and FWHM to increase as the excitation Rabi frequency rises. Furthermore, the TW is shown to be approximately 1.4 times larger than the FWHM, aligning with the behavior of conventional optical clocks. The developed analytical expressions are validated by simulating the population dynamics of the clock atoms. Finally, the paper outlines the necessary modifications to the standard comparison procedure, specifically addressing how to accurately model the time evolution of the oscillator signal. The proposed method for evaluating non-repetitive optical clocks is considered essential for their successful implementation. Additionally, the research aims to advance methods for characterizing both laser oscillators and atomic systems, which are fundamental components of these clocks. To achieve this, the study also examines the temporal properties of non-repetitive laser oscillators, proving that their linewidth is approximately 1.4 times their FWHM. The proposed solution comprises three key components: (i) a fault-tolerant, real-time failure recovery mechanism for SFCs that ensures rapid restoration of service continuity; (ii) an energy-aware fault mitigation strategy designed to prevent equipment failures by dynamically reconfiguring and optimizing the deployment of network assets; and (iii) an energy management scheme for idle fog nodes aimed at reducing overall energy consumption. These mechanisms are implemented using an SDN controller equipped with a fog-aware, distributed fog node selection algorithm featuring QoS-aware properties, alongside an integrated, centralized fail-safe failure recovery, mitigation, and energy management algorithm. The proposed framework demonstrates substantial improvements in SFC continuity, cost-efficiency, and energy savings within QoS-aware networks operating under failure conditions, as well as during normal operation. Extensive numerical evaluations confirm the framework's substantial algorithmic and network performance benefits. Specifically, the proposed solution achieves a 20% average improvement in SFC continuity compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions during network failures, and a 30% average improvement in cost efficiency achieved through joint fault mitigation and energy savings during normal network operations. Additionally, the proposed fog node selection algorithm exhibits superior performance compared to existing approaches, achieving an 80% increase in SFC deployment success rates and 20% and 15% reductions in average end-to-end delay and total network cost, respectively. This study investigates how different loss functions behave when combined with various forms of gradient manipulation. We examine three types of nonconvex, nonsmooth loss functions: (i) mean squared error (MSE), a smooth convex function widely used in regression; (ii) logistic loss, a nonsmooth convex function used in classification; and (iii) L1 loss, a nonsmooth convex function also applied to classification tasks. For gradient manipulation, we utilize two common approaches used in machine learning: gradient clipping and truncated stochastic homogeneous averaging (TSHA). We analyze the empirical risk minimization (ERM) problem under MSE loss, clipping, and TSHA using both deterministic and stochastic settings. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to logistic loss and L1 loss within both deterministic and stochastic frameworks. Our findings indicate that both clipping and TSHA can lead to suboptimal solutions when minimizing convex loss functions. Additionally, we explore how a specific type of gradient transformation can either mitigate or exacerbate these suboptimality issues. Finally, we demonstrate through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets that our theoretical insights are valid in practice. Holographic error correction codes (HQC) offer a framework for designing codes that can be efficiently decoded in polylogarithmic time relative to their block size. By approximating the hypergraph structure of Quantum Error Correction codes, we develop HQC variants that achieve lower block sizes and decoding times compared to the original HMG code, while retaining a linear association ratio. Specifically, the hyper-Invariant MERA (HI-MERA) code reaches a block size of $\mathcal{O}(n^2 \log^2 n)$, with decoding time and depth scaling as $\mathcal O(n \log^2 n)$. Furthermore, by employing smooth or $k$-nets instead of integer nets, we construct a family of HQC codes that exhibit power-law association ratios. This demonstrates that HQC structures can support continuous association ratios. Additionally, we identify a family of HQC codes capable of correcting any $k$-local error, where $k$ is an arbitrary real number. This advances the understanding of HQC structures and provides a foundation for the design and analysis of holographic quantum computing architectures. Finally, we elucidate the relationship between HQC and tensor network models. Our work introduces a systematic approach for constructing tensor networks with power-law correlations by defining "special graphs" and utilizing HQC on these structures. This offers a new perspective on tensor network design, holding significant potential for advancing quantum information theory. This study examines the distance distributions between Galactic Core Fibers (S1-S10) and the Populations (P1-P4), utilizing new 3D distance estimates derived from Gaia EDR3 data. The mean distance distribution between adjacent Fiber nodes demonstrates oscillatory behavior, with the first peak reaching approximately 100 pc. In contrast, the distance distribution between Fiber heads and tails is significantly concentrated, averaging around 10 pc. The separation between Fibers and their corresponding enclosures (P1-P4) is tightly clustered near 10 pc, whereas the distance distribution between heads and tails of distinct Fibers is primarily governed by the populations they surround. These findings suggest that the S1-S10 structure represents the most compact and complex configuration among the Galactic Core Fibers. Furthermore, the distance distribution between the endpoints of the same Fiber indicates that the tips of these structures are not isolated but rather form a connected network. These conclusions align with prior research and provide a foundation for future investigations into the dynamics of the Galactic Core Fibers. Additionally, the results offer a basis for further research regarding the formation and evolution of the Galactic Center Bar. Finally, the paper includes detailed distance distribution data for the Galactic Core Fibers. Future work will examine the density distribution of the fibers. This study introduces and evaluates an ideal CVR-D algorithm designed for primary-secondary distribution networks, achieved through distributed computation without requiring detailed network parameter knowledge at the aggregation level. While distributed conservation voltage reduction has been previously studied, this work focuses on distribution, utilizing virtual nodes to represent primary substations and aggregated load centers. Within this framework, primary and secondary controllers function distributively; the primary controller establishes voltage setpoints for virtual nodes based on secondary feedback regarding secondary transformer impedances, losses, and load distributions. Consequently, secondary controllers can determine voltages for secondary nodes using only the provided virtual node voltages and local network parameters. Since load flow variables are non-linear, an alternative algorithmic approach is developed by approximating these variables via Taylor series expansion, thereby converting the original non-linear optimization problem into a quadratic programming one. This approximation ensures a feasible solution exists even when primary node voltages fall below the feasible region of the original non-linear problem. Furthermore, to enhance the accuracy of this approximation, a nonlinear correction mechanism is applied to the obtained solution. Finally, the proposed Distributed Ideal CVR-D is compared against a monolithic Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) algorithm, as well as two existing sub-optimal algorithmic approaches: Distributed Approximate Conservation Voltage Reduction (DACV-R) and sub-optimal Ideal CVR-D. Results from a 3-bus system and the Australian National Electricity Market demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves comparable or superior outcomes to existing methods, while also reducing computational complexity and latency. Key findings indicate that: (i) distributed and monolithic ideal CVR-D yield identical results; (ii) DACV-R and sub-optimal ideal CVR-D achieve 90% and 96% of the total possible ideal CVR-D result, respectively; and (iii) Distributed Approximate CVR-D can only reach 70% of the potential ideal CVR-D result. Additionally, increasing the number of secondary distribution substations leads to improved outcomes for ideal CVR-D. Finally, the communication requirements for ideal CVR-D are significantly lower than those of DACV-R, as the number of variables and communications needed for ideal CVR-D scale more favorably with system size. Overall, this paper presents a novel, sub-optimal ideal CVR-D algorithm capable of conserving energy and reducing losses in both primary and secondary networks. By leveraging Taylor series expansion, the proposed method extends the feasible region of ideal CVR, enabling energy savings even when primary node voltages fall below nominal levels. This study advances the non-stationary multi-armed bandit framework by introducing arm-dependent lags, where the efficacy of each arm fluctuates based on its preceding state. We establish a minimax lower bound for cumulative regret and subsequently develop two algorithms: Expert, which employs a specialist approach, and UCB-Lag, which introduces a novel UCB-style variant capable of achieving the optimal regret lower bound. Our theoretical findings rely on the bandits satisfying a "relaxed gap condition," a concept we also elucidate within a broader non-stationary context. This condition ensures that superior arms maintain a consistently non-zero advantage over inferior ones, even when their relative performance gap occasionally approaches zero. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both our specialist algorithm and the derived specialist specialist lower bound possess non-trivial applicability in the non-stationary bandit setting. The performance of these specialist methods is also examined across various non-stationary scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate the robustness of the UCB-Lag method by applying it to two non-stationary bandit problems featuring negative feedback. Creating a text-generation model that produces human-like dialogue is a difficult endeavor. While numerous studies have investigated various models and strategies to achieve this, our specific goal extends beyond achieving statistical similarity to existing data; we also aim to capture the intent, context, and relevance of human conversation. We evaluate multiple approaches using these combined criteria and present the most effective structure we identified, which combines an encoder-decoder framework with an auxiliary data augmentation module. This architecture, which we named "A structure for Acquiring to Produce Human-like Text Dialogue" (or LEATHER), utilizes training data from two sources: the standard dialogue history (source history) and an expanded source history formed by incorporating multiple perspectives. We believe this method offers both a novel approach to the problem and valuable insights for future research in the field. Our model was trained on the IEMOCAP corpus and assessed using the Microsoft EmotionalDial benchmark, with the performance measured by the BLEU score against emotional dialogue datasets. The model achieved a BLEU score of 23.01, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art result of 20.55. The source code and model are accessible at https://github.com/soheilsalehi/LEATHER. **Background:** Accurately estimating turbine stresses is crucial for forecasting the remaining service life of existing offshore wind turbines and planning new installations. However, running full aero-elastic simulations for every dataset is computationally expensive. It also accurately captures the temporal correlation of global responses and generates reasonable synthetic signals. **Conclusions:** The TSPS model is a highly effective tool for approximating offshore wind-turbine stresses. Boundary entropy represents a significant boundary contribution that plays a crucial role in holographic models, particularly in establishing the Bekenstein-Hawking law for black hole entropy. This field-theoretical quantity has recently gained extensive attention within the context of holographic entanglement entropy. The present study examines the behavior of reflected entropy, defined as the mutual information of a subsystem and its reflection across the boundary, in two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) in the large central charge limit. The analysis covers open open, closed closed, and mixed open closed boundary conditions, as well as interfaces between different CFTs. We derive new results regarding the crosser and non-crosser contributions of the leading and sub-leading terms, as well as their dependence on boundary and open boundary condition configurations. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between reflected entropy and entanglement entropy across various boundary condition types and compare the reflected entropy of interfaces with that of entanglement entropy present at the interface between distinct CFTs. Our findings confirm that the reflection method successfully eliminates ambiguities in holographic entanglement entropy calculations by adhering to the classical entropic area law. Additionally, we demonstrate that the reflected entropy of an open open interval is not simply equivalent to the entanglement entropy of a closed interval, contrary to earlier suggestions. Finally, we validate that the reflected entropy of an interval satisfies the monotonicity property under Markov evolutions. These results provide valuable insights for investigating quantum error correction properties and decoding protocols in holographic models. Finally, we outline potential future research directions, including the extension of the reflected entropy concept to higher-dimensional spacetimes. This work appears in JHEP02(2021)106. This paper presents a channel estimation method designed to address practical issues in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems. The study first analyzes how violations of the orthogonality condition between RIS effective channel paths and subcarrier vectors, along with imperfect RIS hardware, impacts performance. To mitigate these adverse effects, the proposed scheme utilizes reduced MEM, which is implemented by adjusting the sampling point, range, and reduction ratio. Furthermore, it demonstrates robustness against RIS hardware imperfections, maintaining estimation performance even in the presence of gain errors and phase quantization. Finally, the scheme is shown to enhance estimation accuracy in low signal-to-noise ratio environments. These findings indicate that the proposed method is well-suited for RIS-assisted OFDM systems operating with reduced CP and imperfect RIS components. Mobile applications utilizing cellular-based location information have become increasingly popular for monitoring the spread of COVID-19. These apps generally function by enabling users to share their anonymized coordinates with a central server, which then broadcasts these details to all other users within a specified radius. This paper introduces a code creator for certified programming, designed to generate proofs automatically on demand for C functions and combination functions written in ACL2 that model C functions. While the author has previously developed, implemented, and applied a C-to-ACL2 translator based on a previous informal embedding, this paper specifically addresses two key enhancements to the foundational superficial embedding: first, it extends the embedding to generate proofs with complete quantification; second, it leverages induction variables from source code to automatically induce lemmas necessary for generating complete quantification proofs. Furthermore, this work demonstrates how to handle "if-then-else" statements in the translator by utilizing induction variables to generate lemmas that facilitate the automatic proof of while loops containing only if-statements. The translator has been realized as a minor extension of the existing ACL2-to-ACL2 C-to-ACL2 translator within the proof generator, which automatically generates proofs for functions in combination libraries. Experimental results are provided, including a detailed account of the certification of security properties for a simple integer sorting library. These findings indicate that, despite being merely a superficial representation, the extended embedding is sufficient to express most properties of interest for C code. Finally, the paper provides a comprehensive description of the reasoning process behind certifying the security properties of a simple C function library. The outcome is a fully automated, complete, and accessible proof generation process. To achieve this, a C function file was annotated with additional information originally provided in proof sketches by security experts, which were subsequently translated into ACL2 comments to serve as a guide for the proof generator. This complete proof generation process successfully produces complete quantification formulas and completes the induction scheme for each lemma in the proof library. Additionally, a function was developed to automatically search for suitable lemmas in the proof library and generate the proof tree for each lemma required to complete the proof tree for each theorem in the theorem file. Ultimately, this approach enables ACL2 to automatically complete quantification and generate the proof tree for each lemma in the theorem file. Finally, a function was implemented to automatically complete all proof trees in each proof file using induction variables from while loops in the source code to generate new lemmas. This mechanism utilizes induction variables from while loops that contain only if-statements to produce lemmas that simplify the proof trees for each theorem using appropriate induction variables. The proof generator completes all proof trees in each proof file by employing appropriate induction variables from combination libraries. Ultimately, this complete proof generation process facilitates the automatic completion of all proof trees within each proof file.

We establish an isomorphism between the circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of a complex projective space and that of its (1+1)-dimensional complex circle-equivariant space of sections of the corresponding line bundle. Leveraging this equivalence, we explicitly compute the circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of all complex projective spaces. This computation is subsequently applied to determine the equivariant K-theory and K-theory of both the complex projective spaces themselves and their circle-equivariant bundles of sections over elliptic curves. Additionally, we calculate the chiral K-theory of these bundles by treating elliptic cohomology as a deformation of K-theory. Finally, we explicitly list the bases for the circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology and its chiral variant of $\mathbb{C}P^n$, along with the corresponding basis elements, thereby enabling the explicit resolution of Atiyah-Segal's equivariant Kasparov functoriality question within the context of elliptic cohomology. Our approach to calculating the elliptic cohomology of $\mathbb{C}P(V)$ follows the method outlined by Adams and Heller. Furthermore, we provide a complete proof of a key theorem by Heller and Adams, which asserts the isomorphism between the graded equivariant K-theory of $\mathbb{C}P(V)$ and the equivariant K-theory of its graded components. Ultimately, we achieve a similar level of completeness for circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology by explicitly identifying a corresponding isomorphism between the graded equivariant elliptic cohomology of $\mathbb{C}P(V)$ and the elliptic cohomology of its graded pieces. This paper serves as a foundational step toward developing a full theory of equivariant elliptic cohomology for $\mathbb{C}P(V)$, with the ultimate goal of classifying all $\mathbb{C}P(V)$-bundles. To achieve this, we have calculated the elliptic cohomology of all possible circle-equivariant bundles $L$ over $\mathbb{C}P(V)$, a result that follows directly from the computations presented herein. Specifically, for each $i \in \{0,1\}$, we have explicitly derived the basis of the circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of $L^i$, the $i$-th graded piece of a circle-bundle $L$, thereby providing a graded basis for the elliptic cohomology of $L$.

This paper investigates a machine learning algorithm utilizing algebraic topology to examine the intricate structure of high-dimensional data. We introduce a core concept: the weighted graph representation, which captures the multi-scale connectivity of physical systems represented by the first simplicial and homological skeletons. To validate our approach, we analyze two case studies: the phase diagram of the classical Ising model in three dimensions and a cosmological simulation of dark matter haloes. Our findings indicate that the algorithm successfully pinpoints the critical point of the 3D Ising phase diagram. Furthermore, the algorithm's output provides an intuitive and robust description of haloes and their parent dark matter structures across various scales. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the algorithmic skeleton extraction process is equivalent to multi-scale morphological filtering. Finally, we explore potential applications of this methodology in cosmology and astrophysics. Notably, our approach is general, widely applicable, and independent of specific model details. Although 1,000,000 is theoretically sufficient to uniquely identify users within a messaging application like Signal, the company's documentation and academic research indicate that this volume is not the primary goal. Instead, the goal is to create a secure, memorable, and difficult to guess identifier that effectively limits the total number of users. Our study investigates user perceptions of the PIN's capacity limits, examining their estimates, reasoning, and proposed improvements. We analyzed data from 210 participants gathered via an online survey, message boards, and focus groups. The findings reveal that users lack a clear understanding of the pinning mechanism, with most believing the number must be greater than 1,000,000, while only 10% recognized the use of modular arithmetic. The PINs were evaluated along three dimensions: security, memorability, and ease of use, with a significant portion deemed insecure and a minority considered too complex or not user-friendly enough. These results highlight a substantial gap between the designers' and users' views, suggesting that user input could yield valuable design insights. Finally, we offer several recommendations for enhancing the PIN design. The paper concludes with a discussion of the findings' implications. Precise solar energy integration is vital for modeling the evolution of the Sun and stars. This study evaluates the accuracy of various quadrature schemes by comparing them against the highly precise Adams-type quadrature used in our recent Solar Evolution and MHD simulations. Through thorough testing, we developed solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature, which achieves at least 1% precision with just five radial points and precision exceeding 10% with three points. Additionally, we established precise criteria for handling jumps in temperature and mean molecular weight, ensuring at least five grid points within regions where these quantities change by more than a factor of three. Our approach and code are publicly accessible for integration into stellar evolution simulations. We have also established a precise criterion for managing convective regions and conducted an accuracy test for convective treatment. Our findings indicate that the convective boundary should be located where the temperature gradient reaches its maximum, and the convective region should be defined by an Eddington mixing length of 0.01, which aligns with our Adams test and prior research. Finally, we examined the impact of convective treatment on solar evolution and found that the convective region's extent has a substantial influence on the evolution of low-mass stars. This influence diminishes for more massive stars, where convection is confined to the core. These conclusions are consistent with our previous analysis of stellar evolution. We recommend an mixing length of 0.01 for low-mass stars and 0.005 for high-mass stars. Furthermore, we explored the possibility of using a larger mixing length for massive stars when convective regions are small, which could help explain the helium flash. These conclusions are supported by our accuracy tests and are also consistent with prior studies. Our work demonstrates that stellar evolution simulations can achieve high precision with a minimal number of radial grid points, thereby significantly reducing computational costs. This study examines the low-dimensional structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton (gGN) matrix, extending the findings of Sra et al. (2007) beyond their original block-wise framework. The primary objective is to demonstrate how these structural properties facilitate a more efficient analysis of local behavior in nonconvex minimization problems. The paper begins by reviewing the structural characteristics of the gGN matrix and employing both algebraic and geometric perspectives to interpret its range and core components. Subsequently, these insights are leveraged to derive novel, streamlined expressions for the Hessian of the augmented Lagrangian and the gGN matrix itself, applied to constrained nonconvex optimization. These results reveal that, similar to the block-wise structure, the gGN matrix also possesses a low-dimensional nature defined by its range and leave space, which can be computed through the solution of specific subproblems. Finally, the theoretical implications of this efficiency are explored within the context of convex-constrained nonconvex matrix factorization. The proposed approach enables the direct characterization of curvature entries in the gGN matrix and, more broadly, provides an explicit and simplified description of the local landscape surrounding any critical point. Furthermore, the results establish sufficient conditions for the existence of nonconvex descent directions along the range of the gGN matrix, thereby facilitating a straightforward and accessible landscape analysis. Numerical experiments are included to substantiate the validity of these conclusions. The methodology presented offers a unified framework for analyzing the local landscape of convex-constrained nonconvex optimization, with direct applicability to convex-constrained low-rank matrix factorization. Additionally, the approach demonstrates how the non-strict complementarity condition eliminates the need for strict complementarity when characterizing the landscape of convex-constrained matrix factorization. This represents a significant advancement over existing analyses, which are largely limited to strict complementarity scenarios. Grammatical gender influences how nouns are categorized into gender classes, a process that necessitates adapting subsequent grammatical elements to align with these classes. This study employs a pretraining task grounded in how humans utilize gender to enhance n-gram modeling. We investigate the evolution of gender-specific pretraining objectives within languages featuring different gender systems, specifically comparing German's three-gender system against gender-less languages like Bulgarian and Hungarian. Our analysis reveals that German retains more consistent gender-specific features throughout the model's depth compared to the other languages, whereas Bulgarian and Hungarian exhibit fewer gender-related features and greater variability in how gender information is distributed across language levels. These findings align with the hypothesis that increased gender complexity in n-gram contexts diminishes gender-specific signals in gender-sensitive languages. Additionally, we explore the potential impact of these variations on gender bias and offer recommendations for mitigating such biases. Finally, our research advances the field by introducing a novel task designed to isolate gender information from general n-gram data. We also compute the spectral gap and diameter for specific examples, and our framework extends to certain non-uniform lattices. Finally, we outline an inductive approach applicable to homogeneous and nearly all isotropic lattices of higher rank. The proof of the main theorem relies on a finite reduction step that substitutes general lattices with uniform ones, followed by an infinite reduction that eliminates transverse homology by reducing to uniform lattices or uniform lattices possessing invariant class groups. This reduction is executed via continuous maps that preserve spectral and topological characteristics. The final step involves proving charmability for uniform lattices with invariant class groups and lattices equipped with invariant forms, utilizing techniques from approximation theory, Banach algebras, and operator algebras. Furthermore, we apply our reduction to establish the charmability of uniform lattices in ${\rm Isom}(\mathbb{H}^2)$ that possess invariant class groups. We also provide an alternative proof of charmability for uniform lattices with invariant forms by reducing to uniform lattices and applying known findings. This final reduction is achieved through a novel application of the continuous maps used in the reduction for lattices with invariant class groups. The paper concludes with a discussion of applications, including an application to the conjecture on the rigidity of rectangular lattices in ${\rm Isom}(\mathbb{H}^2)$ and an application to computing spectral gaps for uniform lattices with invariant class groups. Zero-shot object localization involves estimating an object's pose given only a collection of images containing that specific class. This study introduces ZS-MapNet, a shapely convolutional network designed for this task. ZS-map models target objects as point sets, a representation that facilitates efficient localization without requiring bounding boxes during training. We assess the method's efficacy across various datasets, including COCO, Visual Genome, and VQA. The results demonstrate that ZS-map outperforms existing approaches that depend on bounding boxes for representation. Furthermore, applications in small-part localization and scene graph generation confirm that ZS-map is particularly well-suited for estimating the positions of minor object instances. A comprehensive code repository will be released to support reproducibility. Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for enhancing transportation system efficiency and safety. To address data scarcity in regions lacking historical data, recent research has turned to predicting traffic on roads with velocities similar to those of observation roads, leveraging existing historical data from dissimilar roads. However, most current studies rely on imputation-based methods for traffic forecasting. Consequently, when similarity dissolves between test periods, these approaches struggle to maintain precision. This paper introduces a new strategy for imputation-based forecasting by focusing on accurately identifying representative similar roads. By utilizing readily available road attributes, the study proposes an efficient information gain algorithm to extract the most critical features. Furthermore, these attributes are used to construct a similarity network that facilitates dynamic reconfiguration of virtual observation roads, thereby ensuring stable similarity over extended periods. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance in both accuracy and stability compared to existing techniques. Additionally, the method's effectiveness is validated across real-world scenarios requiring extensive forecasting. Notably, for long-term forecasting tasks, the approach reduces errors by 10% to 30% compared to current state-of-the-art solutions. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/111111111111111/SDATF. Finally, the method is evaluated through the 2021 Next Generation Data-Driven Traffic Forecasting Challenge (NGTTF-2021). This challenge involves predicting 24-hour-ahead traffic velocities for the following day across 2,200 roads in Los Angeles, a setting that mirrors real-world, large-scale forecasting demands. The findings indicate that the proposed method is highly effective for such extensive forecasting tasks. Furthermore, the approach is shown to be applicable for forecasting traffic conditions for up to seven days ahead. Overall, the method enables precise and stable traffic forecasting for the future. The results suggest that this approach holds significant potential for real-world deployment. Specifically, it can assist traffic management centers in making more informed decisions for traffic control. In conclusion, the method is deemed effective for large-scale forecasting applications. Graph data modeling is essential for analyzing and reasoning over data defined by relational characteristics. While graph neural networks have significantly enhanced graph analysis through deep learning, they primarily address observational data and fail to support counterfactual reasoning or intervention analysis. To address this gap, we introduce VACA (Variational Augmented Causal Graph Autoencoder), a novel architecture capable of handling both interventional and counterfactual queries. VACA integrates a causal model with a variational autoencoder framework, enabling the learning of latent causal structures and associated causal edges from graph data. Furthermore, the model utilizes augmented inference to conduct counterfactual reasoning and intervention analysis. Through synthetic data experiments, we demonstrate that VACA effectively infers causal structures and edges while successfully addressing interventional and counterfactual questions on graph data. This work serves as a foundation for developing graph models capable of performing advanced causal reasoning. The code and experimental codebooks are accessible at https://github.com/tdaiveen/VACA. LOFAR is a European project designed to observe the transient phenomena in the radio spectrum. The LOFAR Large-aperture Antenna (LLA) array in Ireland is currently being upgraded to a real-time system, known as REALTA, which is critical for identifying and localizing events. This paper details the outcomes of testing REALTA using radio data from various sources, including fast transients like pulsars and geons, as well as the dynamic sky. It provides a technical overview of the system's progress, from the field deployment of real-time electronics to the development of a data pipeline for post-processing. The study includes an analysis of initial test results, with a specific focus on identifying geons and pulsars. Additionally, the paper addresses challenges related to radio interference and data quality, demonstrating the system's sensitivity to both man-made and natural radio sources. Finally, the authors outline future development plans, which include enhancing radio source identification, implementing a data quality pipeline, and improving the selection of new events. Ultimately, REALTA is poised to significantly advance our understanding of radio astronomy.

Although numerous studies have attempted to forecast box office revenue, few have examined how specific cinematic attributes influence that revenue. Our goal is to analyze the impact of various attributes on gross income. However, existing approaches suffer from limitations: they rely on incomplete datasets and, more critically, employ insufficient feature sets. Prior research indicates that pre-released features significantly affect revenue, yet most current studies fail to incorporate them. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive dataset containing over 10,000 movies alongside their corresponding attributes. Furthermore, we demonstrate the advantages of our prior approach by comparing it against recent studies. We tested our model using both our expanded dataset and the limited dataset from earlier research. Our contributions are threefold: first, we provide access to the superior dataset for the community; second, we prove that our earlier methodology outperforms previous studies even when using its more basic feature set; and finally, our experiments confirm that pre-released attributes play a significant role in predicting box office success. This study introduces and analyzes a frequency-regulation strategy for smart grids, demonstrating its stabilizing effect on frequency and voltage dynamics. Traditionally, frequency regulation has been focused solely on steady-frequency operation, yet smart grids require control methods capable of handling complex, time-varying operational conditions. The proposed approach employs a model-based frequency regulation scheme that adjusts inverter power setpoints based on frequency deviations, thereby mitigating the impact of load variations and transferring frequency deviations from controllable inverters to non-invertible inverters. Furthermore, the study establishes the conditions under which this approach ensures steady-state voltage stability and examines the influence of control parameter selection on these stability guarantees. Numerical simulations are utilized to illustrate how these stability guarantees and parameter choices affect voltage behavior during transient periods. The methodology is applicable to both steady-frequency and time-varying operational modes. Furthermore, the paper provides analytical and numerical assessments of how specific parameter choices influence system stability across a broad spectrum of operational scenarios. These findings offer designers insights into selecting appropriate frequency-regulation parameters to maintain stable voltages both during transitions and in the steady state, regardless of significant fluctuations in active and reactive power demands. The study's conclusions are derived from an analytical framework capable of representing realistic network configurations, load profiles, and control schemes. Additionally, the analysis extends beyond passive droop control to include active frequency-based reactive power regulation. Given the high dimensionality of smart-grid systems, the approach also enables the evaluation of stability properties for large-scale networks without relying on dimension-reducing approximations. The results are applicable to smart grids featuring substantial inverter penetration and low inertia. These outcomes are supported by associated design guidelines. Moreover, the study presents a stability certification tool for frequency-regulated smart grids, which can be used to verify the stability of large-scale systems.
