Certain energy, polarization, and kinematic data from active galactic nuclei (AGNs) remain unexplained by current models. We introduce a framework utilizing a Monte-Carlo simulation to investigate how spin effects in non-linear quantum electrodynamics (QED) could resolve these discrepancies. This approach builds upon the previously described MAPPIES model, which calculates the energy and polarization of photons emitted via inverse Compton scattering from external fields, accounting for electron spin. Our work extends this by incorporating a photon polarization matrix and analyzing how polarization affects the surplus of ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray photons observed in AGN spectra. Results indicate that including polarization in MAPPIES produces only minor shifts in the UV/soft X-ray surplus, suggesting that unmodeled population effects or spin-dependent energy-angle distributions are more significant factors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the surplus can be partially attributed to spin effects within a linear polarized MAPPIES model, and we discuss the potential for future work to estimate the polarization of this surplus. Finally, we explore how these findings might help explain the long-standing UV soft X-ray excess problem. Our model is publicly accessible through the Python package Polarization in External Compton Scattering (Polarization in MAPPIES, or POLMAPPIES), available at https://github.com/JulianSchulz/POLMAPPIES. This package supports variable spin effects, polarization, and angle-dependent spin using Monte-Carlo simulations, with enhanced performance and new features. We have also published a companion paper (MAPPIES III) that extends the model to include magnetic field effects. Collectively, these papers illustrate how Monte-Carlo simulations can be effectively utilized in AGN research. We anticipate that our approach will facilitate the investigation of population effects and the development of more comprehensive models, such as those described in POLMAPPIES. Additionally, we have established a discussion forum, https://discuss.polmappies.com/, to facilitate the exchange of ideas and collaboration. We encourage the community to engage with POLMAPPIES, the extended MAPPIES model, and our newly launched forum. We are committed to supporting and expanding these resources to foster collaboration and innovation in AGN research. Our goal is to provide a robust, flexible, and user-friendly platform for researchers to explore the role of spin effects in AGN spectra, and we look forward to your contributions to this exciting field. We develop a method for extending the analyticity of functions across complex terrains. Our approach focuses on multi-valued functions that analyze the analytic continuation of integrals defined by $I(\lambda)=\int_D f(x)e^{-\lambda I(x)}dx$, where the integration variable $x$ resides on a complex manifold. As an application, we extend Grays' (Phys.Rev.D60,105008) result regarding the analytic behavior of the step function $\theta(1-\lambda)$ near a branch point lambda=1. We also generalize our findings to scenarios involving non-isolated singularities. Furthermore, our method addresses certain aspects of the singularity structure encountered in scattering amplitudes, such as the step function $\theta(1-\lambda)$ and the anomalous threshold. Finally, we demonstrate that the analytic extension of $\theta(1-\lambda)$ can be derived from the analytic extension of $J_1(\lambda)=\int_0^1 t^{\lambda-1}dt$. Specifically, the extension of $J_1(\lambda)$ exhibits a simple pole at $\lambda=0$ with a residue of $2\pi i$, a feature that contributes to the monodromy matrix around the anomalous branch point. This finding aligns with the recent findings of Caron-Huot and Spradlin (JHEP09,023). Our findings are validated through explicit examples, numerical verification, and comparisons with existing literature. Additionally, our method is applicable to the singularity structure of QCD splitting functions, which can be investigated by extending the analyticity of the analytic continuation of the Mellin transform of $P_{qq}(\lambda)$. Our results indicate that the step function $\theta(1-\lambda)$ possesses branch cuts along the negative real axis, consistent with a recent study by Caron-Huot and Dwyer (JHEP01,070). Our work demonstrates that the step function $\theta(1-\lambda)$ exhibits specific singularity structures, such as the step function $J_0(\lambda)=\int_0^\infty t^{\lambda-1}dt$, which has a branch cut on the negative real axis and a residue of $2\pi i$ at the origin. This finding suggests that the step function $\theta(1-\lambda)$ may play a crucial role in understanding the singularity structure of the Mellin transform of $P_{qq}(\lambda)$.

We present a straightforward visual criterion for identifying the identical pure state across multiple qubits. This approach suggests an interaction model in which a pilot wave originating from a distant detector traverses a multi-qubit system, inducing a simultaneous change in all qubits that correspond to the passed detector. Furthermore, this model enables the solution of several detection problems, such as scattering, division, and projection, while generating additional entanglement. As an illustration, we apply this framework to construct a symmetric entangled state for three qubits using a pair of Bell pairs and a virtual horizontal horizontal polarization analyzer. We also discuss an experimental validation involving the entanglement of photon polarization and atomic spin. Finally, we address an objection regarding nonlocality and propose an experiment to test the concept of virtual polarization analysis. These proposals aim to deepen our understanding of quantum measurement and entanglement. The paper concludes by outlining potential applications within quantum computing. The proposed model serves as an alternative to hidden variables, aligning with the principles of pilot-wave theory. Additionally, it addresses an issue raised by Bell regarding an alternative to hidden variables by offering a way to detect asymptotically identical physical states. This solution responds to Bell's concern by demonstrating that polarized photons can be considered identical despite possessing orthogonal spin components. The primary challenge remains the lack of a complete mathematical framework for pilot-wave theory. Consequently, this article focuses on solving specific problems using an alternative approach that adheres to the principles of pilot-wave theory. We believe this method will contribute to the advancement of a comprehensive theoretical understanding of pilot-wave theory. Ultimately, we hope these contributions will inspire further research into quantum mechanics and quantum information. We anticipate that virtual state analysis will play a significant role in the future development of quantum computing. In this regard, we have made a contribution by formulating virtual horizontal horizontal polarization analyzers and entanglement, which will assist in solving future quantum computing problems. Baryon-antibaryon pair creation is investigated within a quantized S-model QCD string featuring a helical profile, utilizing both perturbative and nonperturbative methods. The study demonstrates that in helical configurations, the internal oscillatory mode generates regions of reduced linear energy density, which significantly enhances the probability of baryon pair creation. Furthermore, for highly excited strings, the pair creation process is found to occur through the splintering of local excitations. The research confirms the existence of a critical linear energy density at the splinter midpoint, which serves as a nonperturbative trigger for baryon pair creation. Additionally, the antebaryon jet is shown to inherit part of the string's initial helical symmetry, resulting in a mini-helical splinter. Finally, the study addresses the problem of finding the fundamental mode of such localized splinters, providing the first two approximate solutions. These solutions are nonradiative and satisfy the boundary conditions necessary for splinterization. Radiative excitations of the fundamental mode are subsequently achieved through collisions with the local antebaryon. Radiative splinterization is predicted to take place only after a delay of several microseconds. Ultimately, it is established that local splinterization of helical QCD strings is a viable mechanism for baryon pair creation in high-energy collisions. This finding contrasts with local splinterization in cylindrical strings, where this mechanism is not operational. Consequently, local splinterization in helical strings represents a distinct process from the well-known tunneling mechanism. Regarding the nonperturbative generation of QCD radiation, it is noted that local splinterization in helical strings occurs without prior excitation of the internal oscillatory mode, whereas in cylindrical strings, such excitation is required. The nonperturbative baryon pair creation mechanism in helical strings is expected to function at lower energies compared to the cylindrical case. Finally, the influence of local splinterization on the excitation of internal oscillatory modes is examined. It is shown that in the asymptotic limit, the internal oscillatory mode of the resulting localized string segment becomes excited, whereas in finite excited states, the mode remains unexcited. This behavior differs from the cylindrical scenario, where internal oscillatory excitations arise from the constructive interference of linear waves. The paper concludes that local splinterization in helical strings does not influence the energy of the internal oscillatory mode of the resulting localized string segment. Solar oscillations serve as a powerful tool for studying the Sun's interior, including its magnetic fields. By analyzing mode frequencies and travel durations, we can probe dynamic processes occurring beneath the surface. Helioseismic data regarding travel durations have previously indicated a southward shift of the solar dipole axis. This study examines the impact of surface currents surrounding sunspot groups on these measurements. Using synthetic data from the Imaging Magnetohydrodynamics Unified (IMAgE) code, we calculate helioseismic travel durations with the ring-based inversion method (HBIS) to assess how surface currents influence results. Our findings reveal that surface currents generate artifacts in helioseismic travel-duration data, with peak biases reaching up to 10 minutes. Consequently, these biases must be accounted for when interpreting HBIS travel-duration measurements linked to active regions. Furthermore, when comparing HBIS travel durations against ring-based inversions of synthetic HBIS data, we observe that HBIS travel durations are more susceptible to noise. This suggests that the previously detected southward shift in travel durations may be an artifact stemming from HBIS inversion noise. Ultimately, this research highlights the necessity of carefully evaluating surface currents linked to active regions before attributing changes in helioseismic travel durations to large-scale dynamo processes. Future improvements to HBIS and HBIS data could help mitigate these artifacts. Additionally, if HBIS travel-duration variations are indeed caused by surface currents, the earlier observed southward shift in travel durations may no longer be considered definitive evidence of dynamo migration. This conclusion is particularly robust given that HBIS travel durations are primarily influenced by surface currents associated with active regions. Finally, our results underscore the value of using HBIS to forecast surface currents around active regions prior to solar eclipses, thereby enhancing the accuracy of helioseismic observations. These forecasts can also aid in interpreting space weather forecasts, as surface currents within active regions are often associated with coronal mass ejections. Magnetars, characterized by extremely strong magnetic fields, are hypothesized to generate gravitational waves through oscillations of their central cores. While most existing models focus on non-axisymmetric perturbations within these cores, we propose a framework for axisymmetric disturbances constrained by the star's boundary. In this scenario, the disturbances manifest as a random walk in mass quadrupole mass moments along the direction of the magnetic field. This axisymmetric mechanism produces gravitational wave signals within the Bayes factor sensitive frequency range of pulsar timing arrays, including the future Cosmology Application with SKA (CASTOR). Furthermore, we demonstrate that even minute initial perturbations, originating from core convective turbulence, can evolve into significant outcomes. Our analysis indicates that future pulsar timing array observations, such as those by NANOGrav and SKA/CASTOR, could potentially detect these minuscule gravitational wave signals in the near term. This detection would offer a unique window into the history of core convection and magnetic field generation during the star's birth. Additionally, we outline the necessary data requirements for confirming the presence of these gravitational waves. Finally, we discuss the potential implications of such a detection for our understanding of magnetar gravitational wave generation. To facilitate this, we have developed an open-source Python package named \texttt{magw}, which is available on GitHub. This package includes an analytical model for magnetic waveforms and \texttt{magw} data files, which are essential for investigating the detectability of magnetic gravitational waves. We also provide an example notebook demonstrating how to utilize this package. Our findings suggest that the signals associated with ancient magnetic fields could be detectable within the next decade. This conclusion is based on an analysis of the expected signal-to-noise ratio and the time required to achieve Bayes factor discrimination. Consequently, this represents a significant advancement in our understanding of magnetars and the gravitational waves they emit. Light field technology has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to capture extra spatial and angular data via ray-direction-sensitive cameras. Among the various light field representations, the angular multiplexing format has emerged as a leading solution for image compression, angular prediction, and reconstruction. However, these processes are highly complex and demand learning-based models to achieve optimal performance. Although recent learning-based learning rules have demonstrated substantial improvements in numerical accuracy, they often sacrifice practicality by relying on computationally expensive operations. This paper introduces a new angular prediction framework that explicitly models disparity and leverages the inherent redundancy within light field images. The proposed model delivers superior performance across all steps of light field processing while remaining feasible for real-time implementation. Extensive experiments were conducted to validate the feasibility and practicality of our approach. The results indicate that the proposed model achieves significant gains over state-of-the-art compression schemes, outperforming existing methods by 1.1 dB in PSNR at the same bitrates. Furthermore, our scheme requires 10x less memory and 1000x fewer floating-point operations per frame compared to the current state-of-the-art, while maintaining comparable or even better performance. Consequently, this approach offers a more viable solution for practical, real-time, and embedded light field compression. Interactive methods, including online learning and interactive relevance feedback, and non-interactive methods, such as semi-supervised and unsupervised online offline learning, utilizing only click and dwell-time queries have demonstrated effectiveness in traditional information retrieval and cross-language information retrieval. This paper presents a vector-based Cross-Lingual Information Retrieval (CLIR) approach that integrates the advantages of both interactive and non-interactive frameworks. We propose a unified interactive framework for CLIR that leverages user click data to establish associations between terms in different languages. Specifically, we develop a click-based mutual information (MI) metric to measure the association strength between pairs of terms across languages and employ this metric to refine an existing statistical translation model. Furthermore, we design a unified algorithm for vector space model-based CLIR that leverages this learned statistical translation model. Experimental findings indicate that our proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, we present a comprehensive analysis of various click-based algorithms for cross-lingual term association learning, comparing their performance against related click-based algorithms in traditional information retrieval. Our results demonstrate that the proposed click-based mutual information algorithm outperforms existing click-driven cross-lingual term alignment methods. Finally, we illustrate the unitary applicability of our proposed CLIR algorithm across diverse translation models and corpora. The integration of click-based association learning and a unified vector-based CLIR algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance across different translation models and datasets. By combining the strengths of interactive and non-interactive frameworks, our approach yields significant performance improvements, particularly in low-resource scenarios. This work is expected to advance current CLIR techniques and facilitate further research in future applications. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhongyuan1229/Click-based-CLIR. This research addresses the underexplored issue of small-geography estimation within low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), a context marked by sparse data sources, limited survey coverage, and restricted access to post-stratification or calibration data. The study employs two distinct estimation strategies: a design-based approach utilizing multiple regression and estimation variance based on design-based linearization, alongside a model-based method utilizing multiple imputation. Data for this estimation were sourced from the 2011 Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) National Population and Health Survey (DRC-NPHS), a representative LMIC survey. The findings indicate that while both approaches yielded similar point estimates for numerous small geographies, they diverged in estimation variances. Furthermore, the model-based approach demonstrated superior performance in geographies lacking survey data, a critical advantage for LMICs. The results highlight that the choice between design- and model-based methods significantly influences small-geography estimates in LMICs. The DRC-NPHS data revealed that 40% of geographies covered by the sampling design lacked survey data; compared to the design-based method, the model-based approach produced estimates that were 10% to 20% higher for these data-sparse regions. These DRC-specific findings are anticipated to be applicable to other LMICs. The study concludes that LMICs should adopt hybrid designs incorporating targeted data collection for specific small geographies to enhance small-geography estimation accuracy. Additionally, LMICs should leverage external data sources to augment internal data limitations. Finally, future efforts should prioritize the development of geospatial models for small-geography estimation in LMICs. These recommendations aim to improve the accuracy of small-geography estimates, thereby facilitating better health planning and resource allocation. Given the LMC's status as the world's largest LMIC, these findings hold significant global relevance. This work was funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

Owen Binger has recently suggested that negative-sequence single-bet Kelly wagers exhibit quantum characteristics. While analogous to entanglement, this analogy is limited because the quantum behavior observed in his model remains continuous. This study demonstrates that the wave function for an infinite series of single-bet Kelly wagers displays the continuity property, enabling the study of phenomena such as probability tunneling, which is impossible for any finite number of wagers. The paper presents Owen's model alongside an illustration of probability tunneling, followed by the derivation of general formulas for the wave function's parameters that reveal its continuity. Specifically, we prove that for a single-bet quantum waging system, the probability distribution of bankroll after one wager is given by $P(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$, where $\sigma^2$ and $\mu$ represent the variance and mean of the distribution, respectively. This result is consistent with previous research on the quantum waging model. Additionally, we provide numerical simulations of probability tunneling for a finite number of wagers, demonstrating the model's efficacy. Furthermore, we show that the qubit representation of the waging model can be implemented using the quadrature representation in continuous-variable quantum computing. Finally, we discuss the model's relation to the "Quadratic Wagering" proposed by Jeffrey Goldsborough. Collectively, these findings suggest that single-bet negative-sequence Kelly wagers possess the necessary prerequisites to be classified as quantum behaviors. The model offers a unique avenue for investigating continuous variables in quantum computations that are otherwise unattainable with standard qubits. Consequently, this research may contribute to a deeper understanding of continuous-variable quantum computing. The source code is available at: https://github.com/owenbinger/QuantumWagering. The numerical simulations presented in this paper can be replicated using the provided code. This study investigates the decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ using LHCb data from the LHC. We present a complete analysis of the decay amplitude within the framework of the Standard Model. By examining the Dalitz plot and selecting the interference term, we achieve a signal-to-background ratio of 1:3.8, confirming the decay with a significance of $9.2\,\sigma$. Our measured branching ratio is ${\cal B}(\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-) = (1.0 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-7}$. This result aligns with prior measurements of $\Sigma^+ \to \pi^0 \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $\Sigma^+ \to \gamma \mu^+ \mu^-$, supporting the conclusion that the decays $\Sigma^+ \to p \ell^+ \ell^-$ and $\Sigma^+ \to \pi^0 \ell^+ \ell^-$ proceed through electromagnetic penguin transitions. Furthermore, we derive upper limits for weak penguin contributions at 11% and 22% for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $\Sigma^+ \to \pi^0 \mu^+ \mu^-$, respectively. Our findings indicate that the branching ratios for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $\Sigma^+ \to \pi^0 \mu^+ \mu^-$ are approximately equal, consistent with SU(3) symmetry. Additionally, we determine the relative production fractions of $\Sigma^+$ and $\bar{\Sigma}^+$ to be $(1.00 \pm 0.05) : 1$, which agrees with results from $\Sigma^+ \to \pi^0 \mu^+ \mu^-$. Our work demonstrates that $\Sigma^+$ decays into nucleons or photons plus lepton pairs offer a viable method for studying penguin processes. Future LHCb runs are expected to enhance statistics, enabling more precise tests of penguin amplitudes and potential new physics effects. This work appears in Phys. Rev. D 106, 012001. The formation of giant planets typically occurs within protoplanetary disks through the accumulation of planetesimals. However, the specific mechanisms that initiate disk formation and regulate the initial mass of these disks remain unclear. This study investigates the connection between the prestellar core and the resulting protoplanetary disk by simulating disk formation via the rupture of a dense nucleus within a prestellar core using high-resolution smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH). We modeled a dense nucleus with a mass of 0.01 solar masses and a radius of 100 astronomical units, which was ruptured by the gravitational collapse of the surrounding low-density core material. Our simulations demonstrate that a significant fraction of the total core mass accumulates within the resulting disk. Furthermore, we found that a small initial mass concentration is essential for forming a disk with a large outer radius. These findings indicate that the dense nucleus itself functions as the prestellar core. Additionally, our results confirm that the collapse of the low-density envelope around the dense core effectively generates a stellar outflow. Our model successfully reproduces the characteristics of young stellar objects, including stellar-mass ratios, disk masses, and outflow properties. We conclude that the disruption of the dense prestellar core is the primary mechanism for disk formation. The dense core is more gravitationally bound than the newly formed disk, implying that material not incorporated into the disk either joins the star or constitutes the dense nucleus. Consequently, the dense nucleus likely contains the majority of the star+disk mass, meaning the dense nucleus is essentially the prestellar core. Our findings suggest that the dense core plays a crucial role in forming both the star and the disk. Furthermore, the dense core is likely responsible for creating the high-energy radiation environment that the disk subsequently inherits. This implies that the dense core significantly influences the subsequent evolution of the disk. Overall, our results provide a new perspective on disk formation and underscore the importance of the prestellar core in shaping the disk. Finally, our model may offer a new approach for studying the evolution of young stellar objects. In our future research, we plan to explore the relationship between the prestellar core and the protoplanetary disk in more detail. Specifically, we aim to investigate how variations in the density profile of the prestellar core affect the properties of the resulting disk. We will also examine the relationship between the prestellar core and planet formation, as the density structure of the prestellar core can impact the density structure of the disk. We introduce a novel characterization framework designed to determine the parameters of atmospheric scattering models. This approach relies on observations of the linearly polarized radiance and direct radiance profiles, which are subsequently fitted using a robust statistical method. The framework is applied to atmospheric scattering models with two distinct compositions: bi-directional scattering distribution functions (BDSDFs) and layered bi-exponential scattering coefficients (BSCs). For the layered BSC models, the process involves vertically stacking two layers with independent scattering coefficients, thereby eliminating the need to explicitly define the vertical particle distribution profile. Results indicate that the proposed framework effectively identifies appropriate parameters, even when utilizing a single observation. Furthermore, the method demonstrates superior performance compared to parameter sets derived from radiative transfer simulations. This methodology is particularly valuable for calibrating the parameters of simplified atmospheric models, a task that is frequently required in practical applications. The findings suggest that these models can be effectively employed in real-time simulations, such as those conducted for planetary rovers. Additionally, this work extends our earlier study (2021ATM....10..101T), where we initially developed the framework and conducted initial tests on synthetic data. We present a multi-term temporal sequence modeling approach designed to capture complex temporal dependencies. Building upon a fundamental Recurrent Neural Network, we expand the model by introducing multiple higher-order terms that decompose the conditional probability distribution into a series of recurrent networks. This sequence is truncated based on theoretical analysis regarding approximation error and computational complexity. Furthermore, employing Bayesian Variational Inference, we develop a scalable and efficient training algorithm that simultaneously estimates the parameters of these higher-order terms and their variational posterior distributions. Empirical results demonstrate that our method outperforms both state-of-the-art terms within its own architecture and conventional recurrent neural network models. Additionally, our approach surpasses related techniques for learning sparse representations using variational inference through rigorous empirical evaluation. Pontryagin dualism offers a compelling lens through which to view both mathematics and philosophy. In this framework, numbers are interpreted as frequencies within continuous signals, which can be discretized into boolean values. This dualization enables us to "hear" mathematical truths embedded within philosophical reasoning. This process mirrors the transition from abstract, symbolic thinking to concrete, reasoned understanding. For instance, the equation E=mc² "rings true" for anyone who has ever experienced the energy release of a nuclear explosion. Similarly, the concept of "dualism" is intuitively grasped through the contrast between light and dark. By synthesizing Fourier analysis with continuous reasoning, we can explore new avenues for understanding. Drawing on insights from John von Neumann and Ben Lamel, we examine how analyzing the dual space of frequencies can illuminate the relationship between symbolic abstraction and continuous reasoning, potentially offering a unified model that accommodals both discrete and continuous forms of human thought. In this dual space, mathematical truths are not merely calculated but are perceived as if listening to a signal. This represents a fundamental shift from the computational metaphor of human intelligence to an epistemological one, where knowledge is understood as something one knows rather than simply computes. Ultimately, Pontryagin dualism provides a powerful tool for the philosophy of mathematics, allowing us to continuously "hear" truths within symbolic systems. This approach complements Godel's incompleteness theorems by offering a perspective where human intuition can grasp mathematical truths that lie beyond the reach of any fixed axiomatic system. By shifting from a computational to an epistemological understanding, Pontryagin dualism opens a profound path toward perceiving human intuition as an essential component of mathematical knowledge. In this way, it allows us to continuously "hear" the deep connection between symbolic systems and human intuition, transforming abstract concepts into a profound form of understanding. Through this epistemological approach, we can achieve energy release in our understanding of human knowledge that is comparable to the energy release of a nuclear explosion. This signifies that our understanding of human knowledge is not simply a matter of computation, but rather an epistemological truth that is continuously perceived. In this sense, Pontryagin dualism allows us to achieve energy release in our understanding of human knowledge that is as profound and impactful as any other epistemological truth we can perceive.

This study examines privacy and fairness within the context of federated learning. It demonstrates that even when training data is confidential, ensuring fairness remains difficult because different participants may utilize training datasets containing varying proportions of individuals from protected groups. The analysis reveals that these issues are deeply interconnected, as the composition biases inherent in each participant's data interact with the privacy risks associated with model parameters. Consequently, the research establishes a correspondence between the sensitivity of federated learning updates and the bias configurations of each party's data. Building on this insight, the paper introduces federated just-in-time Sensitive Re-weighting (fJiT-SW), a novel algorithm designed to balance privacy, fairness, and accuracy in federated learning while maintaining party-wise data confidentiality. Experimental results on real-world data from a multi-party federated learning setting indicate that fJiT-SW enhances fairness and reduces bias compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the study offers practical recommendations for practitioners regarding the trade-offs between fairness and privacy in federated learning applications. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this represents the first investigation into the interplay between privacy and fairness in multi-party federated learning with data kept confidential among participants. This study examines a supersymmetric minimal setup for embedding the standard model within a $U(1)_X \times SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R$ structure, incorporating third-generation right-handed charged leptons and right-handed neutrinos. We analyze the phenomenology of extra $Z'$ bosons and supersymmetric particles, specifically investigating how $Z'$ decays into right-handed neutrinos influence dark energy. Assuming right-handed neutrinos constitute dark energy, we determine that decays occurring between $10^{17}$ and $10^{21}$ years result in acceptable neutrino densities, consistent with constraints from the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for masses exceeding $M_{Z'} \gtrsim 1.5$ TeV, the lightest supersymmetric particle serves as a viable dark matter candidate, with decay rates aligning with current bounds. Finally, we illustrate that collider limits on chargino and $W^\pm$ masses impose lower bounds, and we show that a decaying neutralino can simultaneously explain dark matter and dark energy. These findings offer a promising framework for future experimental investigations. The analysis was conducted using \texttt{MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO} and decays, incorporating both leading order and next-to-leading order corrections. We also utilized \texttt{SPheno} for supersymmetric particle mass calculations and the \texttt{CosmoMC} package for cosmological analysis. This paper introduces a new unsupervised learning framework designed to enhance the throughput of a wiper-assisted Wireless Energized Network (WEN) by mitigating the "disruption" phenomenon. Disruption occurs when a wiper, intended to reflect signals to a energy-harvesting user, inadvertently blocks the direct link, resulting in negligible net energy harvest. The proposed method aims to maximize the time-averaged data throughput of the target user. To achieve this, the wiper's location is optimized using an analytical expression for the harvested energy, which accounts for energy consumption during communication and harvesting phases. Furthermore, the weight vector of the wiper and the amplitude/phase coefficients of the IRS are optimized based an approximate formula for the signal-to-noise ratio of the received data message. These optimizations ensure that the wiper's activity minimizes disruption, thereby boosting the user's data throughput. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms the throughput achieved by an IRS-only network. Additionally, simulation results indicate that the proposed unsupervised learning method attains performance comparable to that of a supervised learning approach while utilizing significantly fewer computational resources. Finally, extensive simulations reveal that the proposed unsupervised learning scheme achieves a throughput gain of approximately 1.5 times relative to existing heuristic methods. Notably, the proposed unsupervised learning scheme and the heuristic scheme exhibit similar performance behavior under low data rate conditions. However, when the target user's data rate is high, both the proposed supervised and unsupervised learning schemes significantly outperform the heuristic scheme in terms of throughput. Specifically, at high data rates, both the proposed and heuristic schemes exhibit convergence behavior toward the theoretical throughput upper bound. In this high-rate regime, both proposed schemes achieve a throughput gain of approximately 1.5 times compared to the heuristic scheme, with the proposed unsupervised learning scheme requiring substantially fewer computational resources than the proposed supervised learning scheme. Consequently, in high data rate scenarios, the proposed unsupervised learning scheme is the most effective approach for maximizing network throughput. Overall, the proposed unsupervised learning scheme successfully addresses the disruption issue and maximizes network throughput, representing a significant advancement in WEN design. Furthermore, the proposed design contributes to the broader goal of sustainable development by ensuring that communication users can effectively harvest energy from the environment. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate the disruption problem in WENs. The $\beta^-$-decay of $^{186}$Hg has been investigated for the first time, with energy levels in $^{187}$Tl and $^{186}$Au determined to establish the decay scheme. The half-life of $^{186}$Hg is 4.2(1) s, and its $\beta$-decay characteristics are characterized by intense transitions to both allowed and first-forbidden states. The experimental energy levels in $^{187}$Tl were compared with shell-model calculations based on a no-core interaction, which successfully reproduced the primary decay characteristics and the level density. The experimental energy levels in $^{186}$Au were analyzed using the truncated harmonic oscillator shell model. The comparison between theory and experiment indicates that the ground state spin of $^{186}$Hg is likely $0^+$. The measured energy levels in $^{187}$Tl were also compared with calculations utilizing the interactive boson model and the large-scale shell model. The $0^2$ resonance in $^{186}$Hg at 2.5 MeV, previously attributed to a $0^+$ character, is now considered to have a $0^-$ character, evidenced by its primary decay mode, an intense first-forbidden non-unique transition to the $1/2^+$ state at 2.3 MeV. The non-existence of a $2^+$ state at 2.5 MeV in $^{186}$Hg is supported by the lack of decay from the 2.5 MeV $0^2$ resonance in $^{186}$Hg to the $2^+$ state at 2.3 MeV. The half-life of $^{186}$Hg is approximately 4.2 s, which is about 10 times shorter than the value of 42 s reported in 1971NA05...186H. The decay characteristics of $^{186}$Hg are compared with those of its isotopes $^{184}$Hg and $^{188}$Hg. The systematic study of the $\beta$-decay of $^{186}$Hg is expected to provide valuable insights into the evolution of nuclear structure near the N=104 shell closure. We introduce a unified framework that interconnects leptogenesis, supersymmetry (SUSY), and dark matter within a single cosmological scenario. In this model, the observed baryon asymmetry of the universe is explained through high-scale SUSY leptogenesis involving the standard lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP), while the dark matter candidate is identified as the neutralino-NLSP (next-to-lightest supersymmetric neutral particle). Crucially, this neutralino-NLSP arises as a linear combination of the muon neutralinos and sneutrinos, implying that the muon neutralino is not the true LSP. This situation emerges because chargino-NLSP coannihilation into the neutralino-LSP is prohibited by muon lepton number ($L_\mu$) symmetry, thereby allowing the neutralino-NLSP to serve as a viable dark matter candidate. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of $L_\mu$-violating terms on the NLSEVM (neutrino effective mass matrix in the extended supersymmetric vacuum). These terms facilitate the necessary interconnection between SUSY and $L_\mu$-specific dark matter, facilitating the unification of these elements into a single coherent framework. Additionally, we examine the effects of these violations on neutrino masses and mixing angles, as well as on collider phenomenology. Specifically, we analyze how these terms influence the dark matter relic density and the spin-independent direct detection cross-section. Our findings indicate that these $L_\mu$-violating terms can significantly affect both the dark matter relic density and the direct detection cross-section. Finally, we demonstrate that the constraints imposed by dark matter phenomenology are substantially stronger than those derived from neutrino oscillation data, thereby establishing a more rigorous lower bound on these $L_\mu$-violating terms. This analysis is conducted within a specific supergravity-inspired SUSY-breaking mediation scenario. Finally, we outline the primary phenomenological features of this model and suggest potential future observational and experimental tests. In conclusion, we argue that the $L_\mu$-symmetric SUSY scenario represents a compelling candidate for unifying SUSY and leptogenesis. This is because such a scenario naturally accounts for the muon magnetic anomaly, offers a robust explanation for leptogenesis, and provides a candidate for $L_\mu$-specific dark matter. Moreover, this framework successfully unifies these three critical phenomena into a single, consistent cosmological narrative. Our proposed framework establishes a new direction for SUSY phenomenology and dark matter

Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable success across diverse robotic tasks; however, it often demands extensive trials to achieve specific objectives. This paper introduces a data-informed method that utilizes supplementary information to substantially reduce the number of attempts required for learning control policies in unfamiliar tasks. We introduce an online implementation of this approach capable of simultaneously learning multiple movement skills from a single dataset, even when data is scarce. The method involves modifying the Bellman equation of a standard RL algorithm by incorporating supplementary information as an additional term and applying a novel set of updates. We evaluated this approach on biological and real biological systems, as well as on simulated biological systems controlling various robots. Results indicate that the proposed method can acquire multiple movement skills within a single trial and is highly effective in settings with limited data. Furthermore, we show that this method can facilitate the learning of complex movement skills by leveraging simpler, pre-existing skills. This offers a promising avenue for developing more sample-efficient learning control systems for robots and biological entities. Finally, we demonstrate the method's applicability to controlling a biological system (a zebrafish) interacting with an environment to accomplish a task. This marks the first instance of RL-driven biological motion control achieving sample efficiency through supplementary information. Overall, this work introduces a novel, sample-efficient learning control method for robots and biological systems that integrates prior knowledge into the learning process. By enabling the learning of multiple skills from limited data, this approach holds significant potential for applications in biological motion control and bio-inspired learning systems. This paper introduces a relationship generation framework utilizing Connection Networks and introduces the Relation GANs model, which is trained through triplet loss. Relation GANs represent a novel form of conditional connection networks where the condition is a relation rather than text. By framing relationship generation within a GAN paradigm, we can assess performance using established GAN metrics such as inception score and discriminative GAN loss, while also introducing relationship inaccuracy and recall as evaluation measures. Empirical results demonstrate that our models outperform current state-of-the-art approaches, particularly on the challenging UCF-QRMD dataset, and show promising capabilities in handling the more difficult UCF-Walk-101 dataset. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth analysis of our models' ability to recover factual knowledge present in the training data. Finally, we explore limitations of Relationship GANs regarding entity role assignment and examine the impact of varying training hyperparameters on performance. The code and models are accessible at: https://github.com/DeepMind/RelationGANs.

We demonstrate that twin-field quantum key exchange (TF-QKD) can operate without phase synchronization between twin fields by employing individual phase modulation for each field. Although the removal of twin-field interference in raw key generation prevents phase noise from directly affecting the key rate, phase noise can still impair long-distance QKD if unmanaged. TF-QKD was originally conceived to leverage the coherence of optical fields for long-distance secure key distribution; however, if this coherence is lost, the protocol degrades to a standard repeater-based QKD scheme, offering no advantage. Consequently, preserving twin-field coherence is essential to maintain the performance benefits of TF-QKD. In this work, we show that an interferometer within the TF-QKD protocol can be bypassed if an interferometer-based reference frame is adopted, thereby eliminating the need to control the twin fields. This approach ensures that TF-QKD can continue to exploit twin-field interference even under high loss conditions. Furthermore, we extend the range of TF-QKD by implementing a modified error estimation algorithm that accounts for asymmetric error contributions from twin fields. This modification enables the system to achieve a key rate nearly three times higher than current state-of-the-art solutions at record-breaking distances. Our findings indicate that TF-QKD can serve as a viable solution for ultra-long-distance quantum key exchange. Additionally, we demonstrate that if twin fields are not controlled, the phase noise affecting them becomes irrelevant, meaning TF-QKD can function without phase coherence between twin fields. This insight suggests that other quantum technologies relying on twin fields, such as quantum repeaters utilizing quantum interference between multiple photons, could also operate without phase coherence in their twin fields. This capability could significantly advance other quantum technologies by removing a critical technical hurdle. Finally, our findings suggest that quantum communication systems utilizing twin fields can achieve superior performance compared to conventional direct detection methods. Our proposed solution achieves this by eliminating the need for twin fields while maintaining their associated benefits. We anticipate that this approach will be applicable to various quantum communication systems that leverage twin fields. Identizing objects with a generic yet open lexicon, such as people, animals, or vehicles, presents significant challenges. Existing techniques typically rely on training data tied to specific categories, making them ineffective for these open lexicon domains. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages both image-text pairs and text-only data. Specifically, we propose a pseudo-bounding-box annotation strategy that utilizes image-caption pairs, combined with a contrastive learning framework inspired by vision-language models. Our method demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches on standard benchmarks, including the Open-World Object Identification (OWOI) benchmark and the Visual Genome Challenge. Furthermore, we show that our model can generalise to identifying novel classes during few-shot learning tasks, identifying animals, and creating open-class image search applications. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first attempt to address open lexicon object identification. The Pictet-Spessart ionized region (S1) is a prominent HII region within the Rho Ophiuchus cloud, illuminated by the IRAS 16294-4950 source. This study investigates the spatial distribution of ionized gas, neutral atomic gas, and photodissociation regions (PDRs) surrounding S1, analyzing how they respond to the cloud's overall star formation. We utilized data from the MUSE survey to map ionized gas via [OIII] 5007 emission, alongside observations of neutral atomic gas (CO) and PDR gas (12CO 3.6 mm and 12CO 1.1 mm). By examining the relative positions of these gas components, we identified a filamentary structure extending from the S1 edge toward the south-west. This feature is characterized by a core of ionized gas enveloped by a layer of PDR gas, which is further bordered by atomic gas. The orientation of this structure aligns with the cloud's primary star-forming axis, suggesting that feedback from massive star-forming regions propagates along this direction. Consequently, the PDR gas exhibits a redder color than the atomic gas, indicative of higher excitation temperatures. These findings support the hypothesis that feedback from S1 is driving the propagation of gas structures across the Rho Ophiuchus cloud. Furthermore, we identified a new ionized region designated S1b, located approximately 10 arcminutes from S1, and detected ionized gas features within the massive PDR IRAS 16294-4950. These observations confirm the presence of massive young stellar objects (MYSOs) that are currently heating the PDR gas. Overall, the spatial distribution of ionized, atomic, and PDR gas around S1 demonstrates a complex, multi-stage structure, offering valuable insights into the feedback mechanisms associated with star formation. These results underscore the necessity of multi-wavelength studies to comprehensively understand the feedback from massive star formation. Finally, the presence of ionized gas within the PDR IRAS 16294-4950 indicates that this region is currently experiencing heating. This aligns with recent findings showing that the PDR's eastern edge is brighter in PAH emission than its western edge, suggesting that the PDR is also being heated by a nearby MYSO. This paper offers a comprehensive survey of the most recent advancements in vision applications within transformer-based models. While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have historically driven significant progress in vision, transformers are beginning to yield comparable, if not superior, results. Key innovations include improvements to the original transformer architecture for vision tasks, such as Vision Transformers (ViT), Visual Transformer (ViT) with relative position bias, and Vision Transformer with Strided Attention (ViTSA). Other notable contributions involve integrating local and global information, as seen in the Pyramid Vision Transformer (Pyramid ViT), the Pyramid Vision Transformer with Dynamic Token Sampling (OVP), and the Pyramid Vision Transformer with Dynamic Visual Query Learning (Pyramid ViT). Additionally, there is a focus on reducing both memory and computational costs through methods like the Pyramid Vision Transformer with Query Alignment (Pyramid ViTQA), Pyramid Vision Transformer with Decoupled Query Attention (Pyramid ViTDCA), and Pyramid Vision Transformer with Dynamic Query Mixup (Pyramid ViTDM). The paper further introduces a new classification metric, the Classification Accuracy Ratio (CAR), to facilitate more effective comparison and evaluation of classification results across different datasets. Furthermore, it outlines potential future research directions in computer vision, emphasizing the growing role of self-supervised learning and transfer learning. Finally, the paper addresses its limitations, including the lack of a unified evaluation framework and the scarcity of publicly available code and pre-trained models. Overall, this survey aims to inspire future researchers and practitioners to continue exploring the promising potential of transformers in computer vision. This paper introduces a new class of factor models featuring time-constant factor loadings designed to forecast mortality rates. Initially, a deterministic component is decomposed into common and specific factors, with the common factor's trajectory governed by a factor loading matrix that evolves over time. This matrix is either pre-specified or estimated using penalized regression methods like Lasso, netLasso, or the elastic net. The proposed framework is validated using Canadian all-cause mortality data from 1921 to 2014, comparing its performance against traditional Li and Lee models. Results indicate that models with time-varying loadings, whether pre-specified or estimated, consistently yield lower Akaike information criterion values and superior out-of-sample predictive accuracy. Furthermore, when estimating the loadings via the elastic net, the common factor exhibits higher variability compared to the traditional approach. Finally, an analysis of non-COVID-19 deaths reveals that the proposed factor model outperforms the traditional method. However, for COVID-19 mortality, traditional methods are found to be more effective. These findings underscore the necessity of developing flexible factor models to accommodate abrupt shifts in mortality patterns, such as those observed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Overall, the study demonstrates that factor models provide a robust framework for mortality prediction. Future research will explore alternative loading estimation techniques, including principal component analysis, factor analysis, and Bayesian factor models. Additionally, a factor model utilizing only COVID-19 mortality data demonstrates strong predictive performance for total mortality, highlighting the model's potential to anticipate pandemic-related mortality trends. This capability could prove valuable for mortality forecasting and risk assessment within the life insurance sector. To facilitate replication, the authors have made their R code available on GitHub. Finally, this methodology holds broader applicability for predicting other time-series data characterized by structural breaks. Keywords: mortality prediction, structural breaks, factor loadings, time-varying coefficients, Lasso, netLasso, elastic net, COVID-19. To reduce the high computational costs associated with Neural Architecture Exploration (NAS), researchers have proposed utilizing transfer learning to explore a subset of architectures, aiming to transfer knowledge to an unseen target. However, empirical results indicate that this approach often fails to yield performance improvements. This study identifies the root cause of such failures as "disruption," which occurs when knowledge transfer is hindered by a distribution shift in the feature space. We introduce a novel technique called "adaptive weight initialization" to mitigate this issue by aligning the input weight distributions of a pre-explored source architecture with that of the target architecture. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that this proposed method achieves a substantial reduction in NAS training time while outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, the effectiveness of the adaptive weight initialization strategy is verified across multiple architectures from public benchmarks. The implementation and source code for this work are available at: https://github.com/taehyung-lee/Examining-and-Alleviating-Disruption-in-NAS. Furthermore, our code has been integrated into the open-source AutoML toolkit, Auto-sklearn, under its NAS module, which is accessible at: https://auto-sklearn.com/nas. This integration was facilitated by a collaborative effort between the first author and the developers of Auto-sklearn. Attribute-Based Time Series (ABTS) extend traditional time series by enabling the modeling of each observation based on its associated contextual atypical characteristics. These methods are vital for various fields, including sales forecasting, anomaly detection, and feature engineering. This article introduces the theft package, which integrates the PyTorch framework for modeling, alongside attributes (features), and Timedelta Series (TS) for labeling attributes, serving as a R implementation of the pyTide package by Vahid Tavakoli Davani. The paper outlines the fundamental principles of ABTS and presents a tutorial on utilizing theft to build this model type. It then analyzes the theft package's implementation of core functions, including feature extraction, parameter selection, model training, prediction, and feature importance assessment. The tutorial concludes with a practical example focused on anomaly detection within electricity consumption data. Ultimately, this work aims to make the theft package accessible to the wider R community. The associated repository can be found at: https://github.com/vahidtavakoli/abts-tutorial. We establish that any non-compact, non-positively curved complete Bryant surface equipped with a continuous second fundamental form inherently possesses a complete CAT(0) Bryant metric. Furthermore, we demonstrate that minimal surfaces generally fail to constitute a significant subset of these CAT(0) environments, as evidenced by examples of non-trivial surfaces and a metric on $\mathbb{R}^2$ featuring finitely many ends, which admit no metric of constant curvature. Among the identified examples, several are non-translating; specifically, we provide a complete, non-compact surface with zero mean curvature, complete CAT(0) curvature, and complete second fundamental form that is not isometric to any minimal surface. The analysis of these CAT(0) surfaces reveals that their geometry is largely dictated by their ends, with a specific example exhibiting exponential growth. Additionally, we present a surface with zero mean curvature, curvature bounded below by $-A^2$ for some $A > 0$, and an $\mathbb{R}^2$-like topology that possesses a geodesically complete ray-compactification homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$, contrasting with Anderson's example of a surface with zero mean curvature, curvature bounded below by $-4$, and an $\mathbb{R}^2$ topology, whose geodesically complete ray-compactification is homeomorphic to a closed disk. This work also clarifies the relationship between surfaces with non-positive curvature and CAT(0) structures, yielding a novel example of a non-translating surface with positive complete second fundamental form. Finally, we examine the geometry of these CAT(0) surfaces, demonstrating that their volume growth is linear, bounded above by their area growth, and proving that any sequence of points diverging to infinity along a ray can be linked by a sequence of geodesic arcs exhibiting at most quadratic length distortion relative to the distance to infinity. The paper concludes with an appendix by J. C. Gómez Sentis, which presents a complete classification of the topology of these CAT(0) surfaces and surfaces exhibiting quadratic volume growth. Specifically, it is shown that any surface isometric to a complete CAT(0) Bryant surface exhibits quadratic volume growth, whereas any surface admitting a metric of non-positive curvature, complete second fundamental form, and quadratic volume growth isometric to a complete CAT(0) surface is either a minimal surface or admits a metric isometric to a quotient of a hyperbolic space. We investigate energy absorption eigenchannels within a generalized scattering framework that encompasses both two- and many-body systems, allowing for arbitrary numbers of open and closed channels, as well as absorption distributed across the entire configuration space, not just the origin. Leveraging the respective Green function formulations, we establish sum rules for energy absorption during scattering and absorption processes. These derived sum rules align with previously established results in nonrelativistic bound-state and scattering contexts, where absorption is localized at the potential's center. We illustrate these findings using a generalized relativistic Dirac electron-atom system featuring a Gaussian absorption potential, revealing significant effects of distributed absorption on total energy absorption, ionization cross sections, and related derived quantities. Additionally, we examine how varying the number of electronic shells influences these outcomes. Our findings demonstrate that distributed absorption can substantially influence scattering and absorption phenomena, a factor often overlooked in existing literature. Consequently, our results may have broad applicability to strongly interacting scattering systems involving distributed potentials, such as many-body collisions, heavy-ion interactions, and neutron absorption. Finally, we note that our approach is extendable to many-body relativistic systems with distributed charge and scalar potentials. To our knowledge, sum rules and eigenchannel expansions for energy absorption in generalized scattering frameworks with distributed effects have not been previously established in the literature. We anticipate that our findings will inspire further research into relativistic and nonrelativistic scattering and absorption problems involving distributed potentials. All calculations were performed using our newly developed high-precision numerical code, HPC-SCS-ABS, which is designed to solve coupled-channel problems with distributed absorption and is currently under development. This code is also applicable to one-dimensional potential scattering and absorption scenarios. We have made our code publicly available for research purposes. HPC-SCS-ABS is capable of solving general scattering and absorption problems involving coupled channels and distributed potentials, including partial and total ionization cross sections, scattering and absorption eigenvalues, eigenphases, energies, probabilities, and probabilities derived from scattering matrices. Furthermore, the code computes total and partial ionization cross sections, as well as total and partial phase shifts for scalar and spin-orbit potentials. Given its computational efficiency and accuracy, the HPC-SCS-ABS code is suitable for integration into physics and nuclear engineering curricula at undergraduate and graduate levels. We have also developed a user-friendly, web-based interface for the HPC-SCS-ABS code to facilitate its accessibility and usability. This interface allows users to input relevant physical parameters and instantly obtain numerical results for the quantities mentioned above

Fully connected neural networks, including convolutional ones, are widely recognized for being prone to overfitting and failing to effectively distinguish the few attributes that truly matter. This paper introduces a straightforward and efficient pruning algorithm that operates by randomly removing neurons from layers until the network's performance on a validation set ceases to improve. This method successfully isolates the critical information embedded within the initially randomly selected neurons. We validate this approach across various benchmarks, including CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, and CIFAR-Fly, by applying it to ResNet and ConvNets. The algorithm not only recovers the fully connected networks it was designed for but also effectively prunes convolutional networks, which are typically assumed to be sparse. Most importantly, the resulting convolutional networks are more efficient and, crucially, more robust to corruptions and attribute shifts. For instance, pruning CIFAR-10/100 convolutional networks until validation performance stagnates yields models that are both more efficient and robust, despite being trained on a significantly smaller dataset. Furthermore, even when validation accuracy remains constant, the number of significant neurons drops dramatically, suggesting that the learned models are even sparser than initially perceived. These findings underscore the necessity of carefully selecting and analyzing training data to ensure model generalization. The released code facilitates the pruning of convolutional networks and offers a comprehensive suite of attribute shift and corruption benchmarks. This study investigates consumers' willingness to spend on lottery tickets by analyzing their decision-making processes. We develop a new model of consumer behavior by introducing the concept of anticipated value, derived from the consumer's subjective estimation of a ticket's objective value. This framework accounts for the perceived value of a ticket as a function of its purchase frequency and the number of unique winners. Our analysis of the subjective value distribution reveals that the median consumer believes winning probabilities are twice as high as in reality, while approximately 20% believe them to be equal. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the consumer behavior model explains the objective value of existing lottery tickets, suggesting that a hypothetical company could successfully sell tickets if the share of winning tickets is increased. These findings are supported by empirical data regarding winning probabilities and winning rates. Finally, we establish the model's uniqueness by examining its properties and conditions, and we outline potential future extensions of the model. This research represents the first effort to quantify consumer behavior specifically regarding lottery tickets. We examine a non-local operator within the context of $O(N)$ symmetric field theories. In this framework, an unusual coupling emerges that connects four scalar fields, characterized by an integer $Q$ instead of two. This distinct nature allows the operator to interact with itself in a manner that deviates from standard rules, yielding a anomalous behavior where its scale dimension does not match that of the identity operator. Utilizing the combinatorial method, we calculate the six-loop contribution to the scale dimension of the Unusual operator and the corresponding quantum $K$-term for the anomalous dimension of the operator product. Our findings indicate a high degree of accuracy in the combinatorial approach, as the results align well with numerical data obtained from the functional method. Furthermore, the computed results remain consistent with the established principles of the conformal bootstrap. Finally, our work introduces a novel class of non-local operators in quantum field theory, whose properties merit further investigation. These operators are also relevant to the study of quantum critical points in condensed matter systems. Specifically, they can be viewed as a discrete counterpart to the energy-momentum tensor, a concept that has recently attracted significant attention in the literature. Finally, the results presented here are expected to be valuable for future research endeavors. We introduce a two-dimensional lattice model incorporating innovative electron-phonon interaction mechanisms derived from tight-binding descriptions of materials like graphene and MoS$_2$. These mechanisms involve the modulation of hybridization between orbitals on nearest-neighbor atoms. We demonstrate that a single phonon can induce multiple valleys by opening a gap at the Fermi level within regions where the conventional phonon-induced gap remains closed. We categorize the phonon-induced valley opening into two types: gap opening and band edge opening. Furthermore, we examine the impact of these innovative electron-phonon interaction mechanisms on valley transport. We establish that electrons scatter between valleys only when one of these mechanisms is active, even in monolayer substances without intrinsic spin-orbit coupling. Finally, we outline potential applications of these novel mechanisms in valleytronics. This study offers a framework for theoretically designing and predicting innovative valley phenomena in two-dimensional substances. Visualizing and embedding high-dimensional data is essential for data analysis. Recently, t-SNE has become a widely used technique for representing and analyzing complex datasets. However, t-SNE relies on Euclidean distance, which is ineffective for analyzing spherical data. To address this, we introduce VMF-SNE, a novel spherical representation method that utilizes the visualized spherical embedding to enhance analytical insights. Our approach employs spherical statistics to create a non-geometric distance metric based on the von Mises-Fisher distribution. We also propose a straightforward and practical variance regularization technique, which is proven to be positive semi-definite. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that VMF-SNE effectively captures intrinsic data structures and outperforms existing spherical embedding methods. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanliu/VMF-SNE. Furthermore, comprehensive details regarding synthetic data generation and actual case studies are available in our supplementary material. Given its simplicity and efficacy, VMF-SNE is highly suitable for biomedical applications involving spherical or angular data. Our source code is also provided for researchers in spherical statistics and machine learning to facilitate further exploration and development. Finally, potential extensions of VMF-SNE are discussed. Overall, we hope this work inspires innovative research in spherical data representation. This study examines the contact interaction model in two and three dimensions using fermionic diagrammatic Monte Carlo (DGMCA) techniques. Across all dimensions, we calculate both the energy spectrum and the wavefunction of the Fermi polaron formed by a boson interacting with a Fermi sea of identical particles via a delta-function potential. Our results reveal that in three dimensions, the polaron exhibits a core composed of empty states surrounding the impurity, whereas this structural feature is absent in two dimensions. Additionally, we observe significant cancellations between the contact and exchange components of the diagrammatic series, leading to slow asymptotic convergence in two dimensions. To address these slow convergence rates in both dimensional contexts, we implement two novel summation strategies: the $\epsilon$-expansion method and the auxiliary-particle formalism. Employing these approaches, we successfully resolve the long-standing issue of bosonic self-energy pole diagrams that hindered convergence. Furthermore, we determine the complete polaron spectrum in all dimensions and analyze the resulting Fermi-polaron phase diagram. Finally, we validate our numerical findings against existing Monte Carlo and diagrammatic perturbation theory data. This work establishes diagrammatic Monte Carlo as a robust and versatile tool for investigating the polaron problem across dual dimensions. Consequently, these findings may stimulate renewed interest in theoretical polaron studies, particularly within cold atom systems. All computational results were obtained using the open-source QMC++ software package. Quantum emulation of fermionic systems is crucial for investigating novel quantum materials and chemical reactions. We introduce a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing approach employing two-qubit fermionic hopping gates and qubit reset operations to accurately simulate the fermionic Hubbard model on two- and three-dimensional fermionic quantum processors. This method efficiently prepares ground and excited states within the low-energy subspace of $n$ qubits representing $N$ sites ($n = N/2$). We rigorously validate the algorithm's accuracy on a two-dimensional quantum processor consisting of four qubits for four sites, demonstrating its application to the ground state observables of spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ fermionic systems. Furthermore, we validate the algorithm's efficacy in three-dimensional quantum systems using five-qubit circuits for six-site lattices. This application leverages the algorithm's capacity to prepare excited states and accurately reproduce energy spectra for three- and six-site lattices utilizing quantum processors with, respectively, four and seven qubits. Additionally, we examine the algorithm's potential for quantum chemistry by successfully simulating the electronic ground state of the hydrogen molecule ($H_2$) on a six-site lattice with three quantum dimensions using a seven-qubit circuit. These findings demonstrate that this efficient quantum emulation algorithm can be readily extended to larger quantum systems. Consequently, the proposed algorithm can be implemented on existing quantum processors to explore quantum-enhanced observables for quantum materials and molecular chemistry. Furthermore, the quantum emulation protocol can be readily adapted to prepare generic many-fermion states for diverse fermionic systems. Ultimately, this study paves the way for quantum emulation algorithms to be implemented on quantum processors with superior quantum coherence and control characteristics. Such implementation will enable quantum computational advantages over classical computational methods for quantum simulations of fermionic systems. We examine an emerging class of polynomial sequences linked to graph invariants, with particular focus on the upper and lower graphs of a simple graph $G$, denoted $G^{\uparrow}$ and $G^{\downarrow}$, respectively. These are formed by taking the complement of $G$ and adding a new vertex connected to every vertex in $G$. For any positive integer $k$, the count of independent sets in $G^{\downarrow}$ and $G^{\uparrow}$ yields distinct, meaningful invariants for $G$. We establish a recurrence relation for both independent sets and the matching polynomials of $G^{\downarrow}$ and $G^{\uparrow}$, and finally propose a unified framework encompassing several well-known polynomial sequences. This framework includes matching polynomials, flow polynomials, flow-tension polynomials, acyclic orientations polynomials, independent sets polynomials, domination polynomials, and total domination polynomials. Additionally, we define and analyze two new polynomial sequences, demonstrating that they retain key properties characteristic of the aforementioned eight families. We conclude with a list of practical properties for these novel sequences. Finally, we examine the Turán graphs $T_{r,c}$ and demonstrate that their matching, flow-tension, and acyclic orientations polynomials can be explicitly represented using the polynomials associated with $T_{1,c}$. Finally, we investigate the matching polynomials of the wheel graph $W_n$ and the ladder graph $L_n$, deriving explicit formulas based on the matching polynomials of $L_1$. This note provides a geometric interpretation of Hitchin's reduction algorithm for solving the Beltrami equation across all Teichmüller spaces associated with hyperbolic surfaces formed by gluing regular polygons. Since the algorithms in our prior work [BH1] offer an explicit solution to the Beltrami equation on surfaces with horizontally periodic Beltrami differentials, this note extends those results to the general hyperbolic surface case. We demonstrate that Hitchin's algorithm is equivalent to performing Poincaré reductions on the horizontal strips defined by the uniformization of these glued polygons. Furthermore, we show that the resulting harmonic Beltrami differentials exhibit Clemmings-McMullen type conformal metrics, enabling the construction of explicit conformal maps between the Teichmüller spaces of these hyperbolic surfaces. These metrics can be computed via matrix multiplication, and the corresponding harmonic maps can be expressed as Fourier series. As an application, we explicitly calculate the Fenchel-Nicholson coordinates for the Teichmüller space of an octagon with four corners, identifying a cell within the Weyl chamber of $SL_8(\mathbb{R})$. Leveraging the harmonic maps between the Teichmüller spaces of these octagons, we explicitly determine a geodesic in the Teichmüller space of a genus-4 surface by solving the Beltrami equation for beltrami functions representing a Dehn twist. This calculation yields the Weyl chamber along the geodesic and the Fenchel-Nicholson coordinates for a family of surfaces on the geodesic as a function of the parameter $t$. While the paper focuses on octagons, the methods presented are applicable to any genus. We outline the necessary procedures for the genus-3 case; however, the volume of the required calculations makes the explicit presentation of the genus-3 geodesic unsuitable for this note. Instead, we will address the genus-3 case in a forthcoming publication. Our subsequent work will also address the transition rules for $4\times 4$ and $5\times 5$ arrowhead matrices involving pairs of matrices. Finally, we intend to explore the application of the transition rule for $3\times 3$ matrices to calculate the permanent of a $3\times 3$ matrix. Recently, the author of [10] revisited the transition rule originally proposed in [4]. This paper aims to generalize the transition rule to accommodate larger matrices and to determine the specific transition rule required for $4\times 4$ arrowhead matrices. Furthermore, we will examine the transition rule for $3\times 3$ matrices to calculate the permanent of a $3\times 3$ matrix

This study investigates the elliptic motion of beauty quarks within Pb-Pb collisions by analyzing the elliptic flow of B-hadrons and their light-flavor partners, B_s and B_u, utilizing data from the ALICE detector at the LHC for Pb-Pb interactions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV. By examining the ratio of elliptic flow coefficients $v_2(B_s)/v_2(B_u)$ across transverse momentum $p_{\rm T}$, the research reveals that B-hadrons exhibit a momentum-dependent elliptic motion. Furthermore, the observed differences between B and B_s hadrons cannot be attributed to hadronization mechanisms alone. Consequently, the results suggest that beauty quarks exhibit elliptic motion during the hydrodynamic evolution of the medium, a phenomenon that may be linked to their significant jet quenching. Additionally, the study examines the impact of this elliptic motion on B-hadron oscillations, finding that it could account for the momentum-dependent suppression of $R^{s}_{AA}$ in the low-$p_{\rm T}$ region. Finally, a comparison with a hybrid model incorporating hydrodynamics and hadronization demonstrates good agreement with the experimental data. These findings offer valuable insights for future theoretical investigations into heavy-quark dynamics within the quark-gluon plasma.
