A. Edelsbrunner's \emph{colorful $\alpha$-complex} offers an efficient method for reconstructing topological features from a set of point clouds representing a shape, thereby reducing spurious noise. This technique relies on a time-evolution framework, where each cloud corresponds to a specific timestamp, and topological features emerge only when sufficient data has accumulated. We present a systematic approach to calculating persistent homology for these complexes, applying the algorithm to a 2D dataset to demonstrate how temporal information enhances the reconstruction of the underlying shape. Furthermore, we offer a strategy to lower the computational expense, which includes an analysis of the method's complexity. Finally, we explore potential extensions of colorful $\alpha$-complexes, such as applying them to weighted point clouds or integrating them with other reconstruction techniques. These materials can serve as a foundation for further research into this promising area of research. Colorful $\alpha$-complexes hold the potential to enhance various techniques in astrophysics, biology, and social sciences. The methodology described here can facilitate investigations into whether a temporal dimension exists within scientific datasets and whether leveraging this dimension can improve the reconstruction of dataset properties. Additionally, the approach can be extended to materials science and the analysis of phase transitions. We have made our code publicly available at \url{https://github.com/akshaykumar2002/CHomology}. This study examines the $K$-user interference network and investigates how the Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) loss incurred by binary power control scales with $K$. We demonstrate that the maximum extremal GDoF loss is $\sqrt{K}$, which occurs in scenarios featuring odd numbers of odd-degree cutsets and odd-gain interference links. Furthermore, we establish that the extremal GDoF loss of any linear power control scheme also scales as $\sqrt{K}$. Finally, our analysis indicates that the GDoF gap between binary power control schemes (such as time division binary power control) and optimal continuous binary power control schemes remains $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. Consequently, the asymptotic behavior of the extremal GDoF loss under binary power control is independent of the specific type of power regulation scheme employed. Additionally, the techniques developed in this work are applicable to other network types, including interference-wiretap networks. Formal concept analysis (FCA) offers a robust framework for modeling knowledge within knowledge management systems, effectively handling incomplete data and missing information. Within the auditing domain, FCA is applied to the classification of business operations. This paper introduces a classification approach that combines FCA with Dempster-Shafer theory to model business operations, enabling their accurate classification. The proposed method involves constructing a context and deriving a set of consistent rules via reduct computation, which are subsequently utilized to classify unclassified business operations. The study validates this approach through a practical application involving the classification of operations from a specific entity. Furthermore, the paper explores the necessary extensions to Dempster-Shafer theory required to ensure meaningful classification. An R package implementing this proposed approach is made available for download. Additionally, extension directions regarding the integration of FCA and Dempster-Shafer theory to enable the classification of operations under uncertain and incomplete data conditions are provided. This work serves as a foundation for future research aimed at classifying operations in data environments characterized by significant noise and incomplete data. The source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/abdolhosein/auditing-classification. The Strauss algorithm is a classical method used in product code theory for working with two codes, $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$, where $\mathcal{C}_1$ is a subcode of $\mathcal{C}_2$, to encode and decode specific codes. A primary application of this algorithm is in erasure recovery for low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, where $\mathcal{C}_1$ represents the LDPC code and $\mathcal{C}_2$ represents a binary space produced via the direct sum of singleton codes. In the context of erasure recovery, the algorithm solves for the vector $\mathbf{c}_1 \in \mathcal{C}_1$ given the set of erased positions $E \subseteq \{1, \dots, n_2\}$, assuming that a vector $\mathbf{c}_2 \in \mathcal{C}_2$ is known such that its non-zero components lie exclusively within $E$. The process involves constructing a system of linear equations over a small field using $\mathcal{C}_1$ and solving for $\mathbf{c}_1$. This approach is also applicable to other scenarios, such as source and channel coding, which are explored in this work. The paper demonstrates the application of the Strauss algorithm to erasure recovery in a specific product code scheme known as the stitching method, which is utilized in the 5G standard. In this scheme, $\mathcal{C}_1$ is the 5G LDPC code, while $\mathcal{C}_2$ is generated by applying a repetition code to a short block code, with various configurations yielding different parameters for $\mathcal{C}_2$. The study focuses on a specific instance of the stitching method, analyzing both the performance and computational complexity of encoding and decoding. Finally, this work also examines a modified version of the stitching method that allows for solving fewer equations, thereby reducing computational complexity. Numerical results are provided to support these findings. Additionally, the paper includes an analysis of the decoding success probability for the stitching method, along with a comparison to a more general decoding scheme that solves fewer equations than the standard Strauss algorithm. This comparison includes a theoretical analysis of success probabilities and numerical evaluations. Ultimately, the proposed solutions enable efficient encoding and successful decoding of 5G vectors, even under high noise conditions. We examine a multitasking management framework designed for systems featuring shared computation, such as distributed networks, cloud computing environments, and distributed memory parallel systems. In these contexts, the duration of individual tasks is uncertain, and a supervisor oversees their execution by assigning each to an available processor. Drawing inspiration from human employees managing multiple responsibilities, we address a specific algorithmic challenge where the supervisor must allocate time to every task, ensuring that the variance between predicted and actual completion times remains minimal. This specific multitasking problem is a fixed-parameter tractable reduction from online list scheduling, a well-established issue in online combinatorial optimization. Consequently, optimal strategies for multitasking do not directly yield optimal solutions for online list scheduling. Furthermore, we establish an $\Omega(\log p)$ lower bound for any multitasking strategy that achieves a bounded varmin error for all possible task durations, where $p$ represents the number of tasks. Our primary theoretical contribution is a simple, effective algorithm for online list scheduling on $p$ identical processors that attains a varmin ratio of $1 + 4\frac{p-1}{p}$. This result improves upon the current best-known approximation ratio of $1 + 5\frac{p-1}{p}$ established by Graham. Additionally, we develop a practical algorithm for multitasking that successfully handles various random distributions of task durations. Our theoretical findings and the multitasking algorithm are implemented in C++, forming the basis of VarMin, a C program that computes optimal schedules for a given list of tasks. VarMin is presented as a tool for online combinatorial optimization, with a user guide available to assist researchers in designing efficient online algorithms. This tool is particularly valuable for researchers in operations research, computer science, and management science. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of VarMin through a case study in a practical online optimization problem: scheduling jobs on a distributed system. In this scenario, jobs arrive dynamically and must be scheduled immediately, where processing time is defined by the duration required to transmit a message from the originating system to the destination. This case study underscores the efficacy of our practical multitasking algorithm. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance where an optimal schedule has been generated for a distribution of random job processing times. The multitasking algorithm is proposed within the context of computational biology, specifically for the assembly of DNA fragments. Furthermore, we show its applicability to the assembly problem, where processing times are derived from fragment width and the number of DNA systems involved. Our multitasking algorithm achieves optimal results for this case.

Furthermore, physical simulations were executed on the ML to assess its dynamic behavior and control capabilities. Although the standard optimal linear controller successfully maintained balance on flat ground and performed adequately on moderate slopes, the ML struggled with rough, uneven terrain. To address this issue, we investigated yielding terrain as a potential solution. This paper introduces a novel controller that significantly enhances the ML's ability to navigate rough terrain. Through numerical analysis and experimental validation, the proposed controller demonstrates superior performance compared to the traditional optimal linear controller when navigating uneven ground. Additionally, the root mean square error of the controller's output was found to be minimal. We attribute the success of this approach to the integration of a terrain-following feedback loop with the traditional linear control method. Simulations and experiments on the ML indicate that the proposed controller can effectively manage the system's dynamics on uneven ground. Furthermore, the simulation results suggest that the method offers potential for application in other two-dimensional systems. Finally, the results also demonstrate the controller's effectiveness when the terrain is not excessively rough. Overall, this work provides a foundation for simulating and controlling the ML on rough terrain, offering a basis for future applications. Over-the-air (OTA) software updates are becoming increasingly vital for large-scale wireless networks, especially in the Internet of Things. However, a critical challenge remains: how to distribute these updates across device populations while maintaining high availability and security? This paper presents the first experimental assessment of a dependent, bulk OTA update mechanism, designed to address the specific hurdles of IoT deployments. Our observations indicate that even minor interruptions during the update process can cause significant failures, particularly when degrading critical network attributes like end-to-end latency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed mechanism can reduce large-scale update failures by up to 50% compared to traditional over-the-air methods. The entire experiment was conducted on a dependent mesh network comprising 100 Raspberry Pi devices, featuring a 433 MHz radio access network with an extended coverage area and an internet connection that mimics 4G/LTE-like characteristics. Additionally, we evaluated the security implications of our approach, revealing that OTA updates in IoT environments are inherently vulnerable to a wide array of potential attacks. Finally, we have made the complete dependent OTA mechanism, including configuration and monitoring tools, publicly accessible to facilitate reproducibility and further research. We anticipate that our mechanism will serve as a robust foundation for bulk OTA updates in future IoT software-defined networks. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural experimental analysis of dependent OTA updates for large-scale software distribution within a mesh network. We demonstrate the multifractal nature of many-body localized (MBL) states by analyzing the Fock space propagator across the paramagnetic phase, within shift-conformal equivalence classes, and by examining its dependence on shift charge. We introduce a computationally efficient method to obtain exact eigenstates within this framework, utilizing a simple recursive approach. Our analysis of the spectral form factor reveals a clear signature of multifractality, characterized by a power-law decay of $t^{-2/\tau_2}$ at large times, where the dynamical exponent $\tau_2$ varies with system size. Furthermore, our study of the level spacing distribution identifies a crossover from a Poisson distribution at low $\epsilon$ to a Wigner-Dyson distribution at high $\epsilon$, consistent with the drift of the shift charge. Additionally, we calculate the entanglement entropy, which exhibits a linear growth regime followed by early saturation, indicative of a small fraction of thermalized degrees of freedom. Finally, we numerically estimate the phase boundary by plotting the entanglement entropy against the drive strength and shift charge, revealing a linear relationship that aligns with recent exact findings. This study marks the first observation of MBL multifractality in drive-conformal classes, offering new insights into the drift dynamics of MBL phases. We provide open-source code to facilitate future research. (Code available at: https://github.com/akshaykumar1992/Many-Body-Locality) Our theoretical framework extends to various models, including the XXZ spin chain, XXZ Heisenberg chain, and XXZ fermion chain. This paper addresses the challenge of exploring numerous target regions using a cost-limited mobile robot equipped with a single camera. Backward Graphics Domain Adaptation (BGDA) adapts any forward rendering pipeline to establish a link between the robot's visual sensor data and the real-world environment, enabling the identification of target regions in 3D space. However, existing literature prioritizes efficient path planning within a fixed cost framework, resulting in exploratory missions that fail to maximize target coverage. To overcome this, we introduce a dynamic strategy that prioritizes the robot's attention based on potential exploration gains, thereby enhancing overall efficiency. This approach is evaluated across simulated scenarios utilizing rasterized, rendered, and LiDAR data, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world applications. Additionally, we extend our evaluation to a physical robot performing indoor mapping and annotation tasks. Drawing inspiration from the Quantum Born Rule, this paper introduces a novel class of quantum classifiers designed to produce probabilistic predictions. These classifiers are built upon classical neural networks and incorporate quantum components, specifically single-qubit states and measurements. We investigate global adversarial instances and disturbances targeting such classifiers, with the objective of manipulating quantum measurement outcomes to deceive the model. Our analysis reveals that adversarial examples and adversarial robust methods for classical classifiers concerning $L_\infty$-constrained perturbations simultaneously serve as effective adversarial instances against quantum classifiers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that adversarial robustness in quantum classifiers implies established robustness in their underlying classical neural networks. Finally, we explore adversarial instances and attacks specific to quantum classifiers, noting that the success and effectiveness of these attacks can vary depending on the results from multiple quantum measurements. To our knowledge, this work presents the first research on global adversarial instances and robustness within quantum classifiers. Our main findings are validated through both theoretical analysis and empirical experiments. The associated source code is accessible at https://github.com/QuantumAI4ALL/QANN_AdvRob. Steklov eigenvalues for convex domains can be interpreted as1-Lipschitz extensions of Dirichlet eigenvalues defined on boundary spheres, representing a natural concept within global geometry. Numerical evidence suggests these eigenvalues converge to Dirichlet eigenvalues of the inner sphere as precision increases, implying that Steklov eigenvalues on closed surfaces are equivalent to 1-Davidson eigenvalues. We demonstrate analytically that within the 1-Lipschitz extension space, Steklov eigenvalues uniquely optimize specific objective functions. Furthermore, we show that key metrics, such as mean curvature, exhibit local optimality on Steklov eigenfunctions across various cases. These findings suggest a method for approximating Steklov eigenfunctions by evaluating objective functions using gradient descent and local optimizers in function space. Finally, we illustrate the application of 1-Lipschitz extensions in generating musical timbres. By treating timbre as an eigen-spectrum derived from a function's frequency content, our approach produces a novel and efficient timbre synthesis technique. Our analysis confirms that for a specific class of timbres, those generated via Steklov extensions align with human perception. Overall, this work advances the field of music information retrieval by offering a new, principled framework for timbre analysis. Our associated code, which generates Steklov extensions, is publicly available. Additionally, we have developed an open-source Python package for Steklov extensions, Timbre Extensions, and Musical Eigen-Geometry, along with tutorials and examples. Conformance checking is a well-established method in process mining for evaluating how well real-world trace data aligns with reference models. Although significant research has focused on full trace alignments, there is also a need for trace-part conformance verification, which assesses whether specific subtraces conform to their corresponding model parts. Current post-processing methods for identifying mismatches between traces and model parts, such as infomaps and residual maps, suffer from several drawbacks. Infomaps are both computationally expensive and difficult to visualize, while residual maps are not guaranteed to be conformance sound. To address these limitations, this paper introduces sound post-processing infomaps that are guaranteed to be optimal embeddings. These infomaps are constructed using infix alignments, where every deviation represents a real mismatch, and every mismatch can be explained by a specific log event. Furthermore, we propose a sound postfix map to highlight temporal violations. The soundness of both methods is formally proven, and their efficiency is demonstrated through an experimental evaluation. Finally, the practical utility of these approaches is illustrated using public datasets. Overall, this work provides a sound and efficient technique for identifying mismatches between trace parts and model projections, serving as a foundational step for advanced log-based dependency analysis. Additionally, the proposed methods can be extended to other forms of conformance checking. Our source code is available at https://github.com/mauricio-garcia/infixpostfix-map. The widespread adoption of 5G and beyond wireless technologies necessitates accurate and efficient prediction of cellular network radio coverage. This paper introduces the application of deep convolutional neural networks to signal propagation modeling, specifically utilizing networks with residual connections. Experimental results demonstrate that these networks can predict long-term signal propagation with root mean square errors ranging from 2.5 to 3.5 dB. Furthermore, the model's predictions for indoor signal levels align well with those for outdoor environments. Additionally, the study confirms the feasibility of achieving these prediction accuracies within a reduced number of measurement points. The proposed modeling approach is anticipated to play a significant role in next-generation cellular network planning. We introduce a newly developed, rigorously validated logical formalism designed for temporal planning. This framework enables the specification of both the syntax and the core semantic concepts within a single first-order formula, which can subsequently be processed by an automated decision procedure. Although our approach is fundamentally grounded in first-order logic, it offers additional decision procedures tailored to the specific structural requirements of temporal planning. Leveraging this formalism, we created a validated planning model that extends the classical hierarchical planning framework (GFSSYB14) by incorporating temporal dimensions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this model through an implementation built using the COVADLE validation infrastructure, which guarantees the correctness-by-construction of the implementation process. A comprehensive experimental assessment confirms the model's efficiency and its ability to resolve more complex temporal planning challenges. Furthermore, we outline several promising avenues for future research. Energy system growth models are valuable for assessing future scenarios, though their parameters are frequently calibrated using historical data. This study examines the sensitivity of three prominent models—EMSA, EM21, and PLEXOS—by systematically varying their key parameters. Significant disparities were observed in how these models respond to inputs; for instance, EMSAS and EM21 grow energy supply at a rate 2.5 times faster than PLEXOS when the price elasticity of demand is fixed at 0.5. Additionally, the models differ in their optimal energy mix outcomes, which are particularly sensitive to the cost of capital. Despite these differences, all models converge on similar conclusions regarding the necessity of carbon capture and storage and carbon-free electricity generation technologies. The study concludes that while growth models offer useful insights, their key parameters warrant careful consideration, and comparative analyses should be conducted to establish baseline scenarios. Furthermore, applying a unified set of assumptions to multiple models could facilitate more meaningful cross-model assessments. Finally, utilizing a single model with internally consistent parameters may result in sub-optimal results. These findings align with recent literature advocating for transiting to a fully decarbonized economy by 2050. This study establishes the well-posedness of the Vlasov-Poisson system within confined regions. The initial Vlasov equation is solved using the characteristics method, while the associated Poisson problem is addressed via the layer potential method. This approach yields new global-in-time $L^p$ estimates for electric fields in bounded domains, complementing recent $H^1$ estimates derived via finite propagation of support. Notably, the analysis imposes no regularity constraints on initial data. Furthermore, the Vlasov solutions exhibit a regularizing effect in microvelocity variables, remain regular in real space, and are uniformly bounded in $L^p$ over time. These findings mark the first global well-posedness result for Vlasov equations with electrostatic interactions in both two- and three-dimensional bounded domains. The methodology also extends to Vlasov–Maxwell equations in confined domains and to Vlasov–Fokker–Planck systems subject to oblique reflection boundary conditions. Finally, analogous results are anticipated for other boundary conditions involving electrostatic interactions, such as absorbing or emitting boundaries. However, this paper excludes time-dependent boundary conditions, a scenario notably exemplified by the mesoscopic description of electrons in quantum dots. In that context, described by the Vlasov–Lindblad system, time-dependent boundary conditions take the form of a "force" acting on particles alongside boundary dissipation. Consequently, global well-posedness for the Vlasov–Lindblad system remains an open problem. This difficulty may stem from the failure of standard boundary conditions to satisfy the reflection property of boundary operators, thereby preventing the application of the reflection method. Additionally, the Lindblad equation lacks the conservation law necessary to control electric field energy. Finally, the Vlasov–Lindblad system presents another challenge: the boundary condition is not necessarily non-negative, a property essential for applying the maximum principle. These obstacles appear particularly pronounced in quantum dots, where boundary conditions are often non-trivial. Addressing these issues may require alternative techniques, such as those developed in [10, 11]. These methods typically involve constructing a Lyapunov functional to demonstrate uniform bounds in a suitable Sobolev space, followed by compactness arguments to pass to the limit. Such an approach may offer a viable path to resolving the challenges posed by vorticity and non-trivial boundary conditions. Although numerous studies have attempted to auto-generate concept placement field names, they largely overlook the impact of internal domain terminology on consistency. This paper introduces a data retrieval-based approach that analyzes existing concepts to generate consistent, data-driven "strict" phrases suitable for concept placement field names. We developed a new method called Data Retrieval Based Search Phrase Identification (STRIP), which constructs a retrieval model using existing domain concepts and retrieves relevant training data to generate strict phrases. We evaluated STRIP against two baseline methods—keyword extraction and concept expansion—through a human evaluation. The results indicate that both the keyword extraction and concept expansion baselines fail to produce consistent concept placement field names. In contrast, our STRIP method successfully generates consistent phrases when assigned to concepts by a domain expert. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the base learning algorithm is not critical to STRIP's effectiveness; tests using domain-specific terminology from medical records revealed that the method achieves state-of-the-art results. Finally, we applied STRIP to medical record data to generate concept placements field names. Our method yields promising outcomes, producing field names that are more accurate, complete, and consistent than those generated by existing techniques. Additionally, we show that our approach can improve the performance of a concept extraction model by 1% F1 score. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first application of a search phrase identification method to concept placement. The code and data required to reproduce our experiments are available at https://github.com/ashishkumar1998/STRIP. Our work is part of the medical natural language processing (NLP) ecosystem, which is detailed in a companion paper focused on medical record data (https://github.com/ashishkumar1998/MNLE). This paper is scheduled for presentation at the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2021). This study examines the rheo-acoustic characteristics of colloidal gels, defined as systems where colloidal particles are Brownian-stabilized but also experience significant inter-particle forces. These gels exhibit a unique duality: despite appearing solid, they can be manipulated by ultrasonic waves far below the melting threshold. We demonstrate that ultrasonic oscillations can continuously tune a gel's mechanical and rheological properties, ranging from solid-like to fluid-like behaviors. Specifically, we analyze the frequency-dependent rheo-acoustic response of silica gels, revealing a resonant-like peak in ultrasonic-induced shear viscosity that shifts with particle size. Furthermore, we illustrate the potential for controlling ultrasonic-accelerated gelation by adjusting the phase of the ultrasonic driver, thereby manipulating gel structure, viscosity, and modulus. Collectively, these findings establish a new field within ultrasonic rheology focused on gels, demonstrating their tunability and controllable transition from solid-like to fluid-like states. These ultrasonic-modulated gels hold significant promise for applications in micro- and nano-fabrication, including micro-patterning, self-assembly, and micro-mechanical actuators. Additionally, this work introduces a novel method for achieving complex, non-stationary, and non-monotonic mechanical properties in colloidal gels. Finally, we explore the fundamental implications of these results for colloidal thermodynamics. The combination of ultrasonic and rheological techniques offers a versatile platform for further investigating the intricate interactions between ultrasound and gel systems. These findings pave the way for developing new materials with programmable and tunable characteristics. Furthermore, the ability to remotely and continuously regulate gel properties via ultrasound has broad applications in various industries, such as cosmetics, food manufacturing, and pharmaceuticals. Finally, our findings contribute to the growing body of research on "soft phonics," which investigates the impact of ultrasonic oscillations on soft matter systems. This paper provides an analytical approach to proving the Collatz Conjecture, which posits that any positive integer $n$, when subjected to the operation $n\mapsto n+1/2^n$ repeatedly, will eventually yield an integer of the form $2^k$. We demonstrate that the concavity of the function $f(n)=n+1/2^n$ guarantees that the conjecture holds for all $n\geq 5$. Furthermore, we offer an analytical computation of the average number of steps required for any $n\geq 5$ to reach a power of 2, and we extend our proof to encompass all positive integers. In addition to this proof, we also present an alternative argument for the conjecture. Keywords: Collatz Conjecture, Fibonacci Sequence, Factorial Function. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 11B37, 11B75.

Automating the extraction of human-readable documents from digital images is vital for scientific research, yet categorizing STEM documents poses a significant challenge due to the diverse notations, symbols, and mixed modalities found within them. To address this, we introduce a dual-network framework designed to simultaneously detect and recognize entities while establishing n-ary relationships between them. This framework enhances traditional recognition networks by incorporating a relational module that identifies connections between identified entities. We demonstrate that this relational information substantially improves document categorization accuracy. Our experimental results indicate that integrating such relationships boosts performance by 3.5% in the test set compared to recognition networks without them, and by 5.1% compared to baseline recognition networks that utilize feedback loops. Additionally, we present the Document Corpus, a newly annotated dataset comprising 1,000 scanned research documents featuring dual-mode entities and their relationships, which will be made publicly available to support future research. The code and documents are accessible at https://github.com/leehyuntae/SaDCo. Reliable matching represents an extension of the stable rooms problem. While a reliable matching must be both feasible and stable, a specific subset of agents is designated as "committed," obligating them to accept their assigned matchings. The objective is to identify a matching that accommodates as many committed agents as possible while ensuring the remaining agents also receive satisfactory outcomes. We demonstrate that the problem of finding a maximum number of committed agents is NP-hard. Furthermore, we present approximation algorithms for various special cases, including scenarios where all agents possess preferred matchings and others where agents are committed to only a single offer. Finally, we validate the practical utility of these algorithms by applying them to real-world data and comparing their performance against a greedy baseline. Specifically, in a dataset comprising 22 high school programs, our algorithms achieve a 2.5% increase in committed students relative to the greedy approach, with a mean deviation of only 0.37%. Additionally, in a separate dataset involving 44 college departments, our methods improve the number of offers accepted by 1.7% compared to greedy algorithms. These results indicate that committed offers can be effectively identified across diverse application contexts. Recent advancements in automatic summarization have substantially enhanced output quality; however, evaluating these systems remains labor-intensive for human annotators. Consequently, automatic scoring mechanisms are increasingly popular in academic research and industry applications due to their ability to provide rapid feedback and scale efficiently. This paper introduces SummScore, a novel scoring method that employs cross-encoders to assess summary excellence. We demonstrate that SummScore achieves performance comparable to, or superior to, state-of-the-art scoring systems across multiple datasets. Furthermore, our experiments on a real-world scenario highlight the superior performance of SummScore, establishing it as a valuable resource for both researchers and practitioners. Fusing data from cameras and LiDARs is essential for the training and inference of autonomous driving systems. However, effectively combining these inputs remains difficult due to their distinct perceptual characteristics and the need for precise calibration and projection. This paper introduces a straightforward BEV fusion module that is easily embeddable for both training and inference. Unlike current methods, our approach requires no complex parameter tuning and is resilient to misalignment between LiDAR and camera data. By directly projecting camera features into the BEV space using LiDAR-beamed information and applying a straightforward fusion strategy, we achieve competitive results on the nuScade and Waymo Open datasets while maintaining high efficiency. Additionally, we provide implementation details to facilitate the easy integration of our codebase. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/charlesw2019/BEVFusion. This study examines liquid turbulence at high Reynolds numbers, focusing on the kinetic energy cascade and the influence of high-speed fluctuations on energy transfer. The analysis reveals that turbulent velocity gradients significantly impact the cascade process, while the interaction between fluctuating velocity and density remains negligible. Consequently, distinct similarity ranges emerge in liquid turbulence, differing from those in gas turbulence. Furthermore, liquid turbulence exhibits greater dissipation, extending its range and modifying the structure of the inertial range. Finally, the paper explores the impact of thermal disturbances on the turbulence state and examines the coupling mechanism between liquid turbulence and thermal transfer. These findings offer a more precise theoretical framework for analyzing liquid turbulence and its interaction with heat transfer. The research is grounded in the generalized Boussinesq approximation and utilizes a comprehensive set of similarity theories. Ultimately, the proposed theoretical framework serves as a valuable resource for analyzing liquid turbulence and heat transfer. A comprehensive comparison between the theoretical results and existing experimental data will be presented in future publications. Additionally, further validation of these theoretical conclusions is required through both experimental and numerical investigations. The numerical studies referenced here are derived from [1] and conducted using the Lattice Boltzmann Method. Finally, the comprehensive comparison will be utilized as a foundation for developing numerical validation methods. Gas turbulence, in contrast, is characterized by an interaction range where similarity theory applies. Furthermore, gas turbulence is governed by the condition that the Prandtl number exceeds unity. Finally, when thermal disturbance is absent, liquid turbulence reverts to the state of gas turbulence. Therefore, gas turbulence can be regarded as a specific instance of liquid turbulence. Theoretically, this conclusion is supported by the universality of similarity theory. Experimentally, this conclusion is validated by the applicability of the generalized Boussinesq approximation. Numerically, this conclusion is confirmed by the broad applicability of the Lattice Boltzmann Method. Collectively, these factors demonstrate the universality of the proposed theoretical framework. Additionally, gas turbulence is influenced by the coupling mechanism between turbulence and thermal transfer. Furthermore, liquid turbulence is affected by the coupling mechanism between turbulence and thermal transfer. Thus, both conclusions are grounded in the principles of similarity theory. Finally, the theoretical, numerical, and experimental universality of this conclusion is comprehensively validated. This study addresses the limitation of existing models, which typically assume a uniform thermal profile in liquids at the moment of laser exposure, to accurately explain complex diffraction patterns. We propose an enhanced analytical method incorporating a Gaussian thermal profile derived from laser-liquid interaction dynamics, which significantly improves the fit to experimental data regarding the relationship between spot size and periodicity. Furthermore, numerical simulations of heat conduction confirm that the laser's power density is insufficient to alter the thickeness of the thermal profile. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that liquid thermal profiles cannot be universally modeled; rather, the specific profile arises from the characteristics of laser-liquid interaction. Our findings offer a comprehensive numerical characterization of laser-generated thermal profiles in liquids to aid the design of future liquid lens-based optical systems. Additionally, we present an advanced analytical model that facilitates a deeper understanding of the physics governing laser-induced heating in liquids. Finally, our methodology enables the calculation of thermal profile parameters from a single experimental data point, streamlining the design of liquid lens optical devices. This approach is demonstrated through its successful application in a liquid lens optical system featuring a beam expander. By employing our model, users can readily design liquid lens systems that meet specific requirements, such as achieving a desired beam expansion ratio. Ultimately, this research facilitates the creation of user-friendly tools for the design and analysis of liquid lens optical systems. Design conversation extraction stands as a key challenge in design mining, yet it is frequently compromised by poor performance due to the instability of machine learning models when handling natural language inputs. This issue stems from arbitrary changes in linguistic expressions caused by semantic shifts. To address this, we introduce a conclusion stability function grounded in logical reasoning, which measures the consistency of learned natural language labels relative to their original forms. This function is optimized alongside the learning objective using a min-max loss strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms baseline methods on the DiC 2.0 dataset. Additionally, validation using language expression generators confirms that the proposed solution effectively enhances conclusion stability. Finally, we apply the function to analyze natural language expressions in DiC 2.0, revealing insights into how conclusions are formulated within design conversations. Overall, this work not only tackles the challenge of natural language expression learning but also deepens the understanding of design conversation structures through logical reasoning. Designers can leverage these insights to better articulate design concepts. Furthermore, by improving statement learning accuracy, design mining systems utilizing this approach achieve higher performance. This paper serves as a companion to [1]. Recent advancements in open-source big data frameworks have fueled the proliferation of analytics pipelines, driven by the need to process and analyze vast volumes of data. However, existing solutions often fail to address the specific operational and functional requirements of many business processes. This paper introduces H-STREAM, a novel framework designed to handle large data streams. We examine the limitations of current frameworks and propose solutions by developing specific operational and functional components that integrate into analytics pipelines using H-STREAM. Additionally, we outline a potential application within business process monitoring to demonstrate these pipelines in action. Finally, we validate the proposed solutions through a series of experiments. Our findings indicate that H-STREAM effectively enables analytics pipelines to meet the operational and functional requirements of various business processes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these pipelines can significantly enhance query performance by reducing execution time. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/bernd-p/storm-hstream. This work is based on our recent research published in the 2019 IEEE 16th International Conference on Services Computing (ServiceComputing).

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has recently been extended to handle Knowledge Base (KB) information, enabling the translation of sentences while incorporating additional knowledge from a KB tailored to the specific source and target languages. However, many NMT models fail to accurately replicate the structure and content of a provided KB during training. This paper introduces a content-based replication mechanism for structural components within a KB to enhance accuracy and improve the model's fidelity to the input knowledge. Additionally, we propose a method for identifying and clustering similar KB components based on their textual features. Experimental results on a multi-domain dataset demonstrate that our approach boosts performance by 1.2 F1 points compared to a baseline structural NMT model. Furthermore, results from a knowledge-intensive NMT task at the TexT-2021 Challenge on the SUBJ2Subt dataset confirm that replication mechanisms significantly improve NMT system output when knowledge is provided. The code for this work is accessible at \url{https://github.com/rafal-mazur/replication-mechanism-KB-NMT}. Consequently, this work represents a critical step toward automating knowledge replication to ensure greater model accuracy and better alignment with user-provided knowledge. The paper concludes with a discussion on the advantages and potential applications of knowledge-enhanced NMT systems. Finally, the paper addresses ethical considerations regarding the use of such systems. Keywords: Knowledge-enhanced Neural Machine Translation, Knowledge Base, KB Replication Mechanism, KB Similarity Clustering.

The fields of science and academia are heavily influenced by various metrics, which often shape researchers' daily decisions regarding publication timing, venue selection, and topic initiation. These citational standards are increasingly problematic, particularly for early-career scholars, and may foster an environment of stress, imposter syndrome, and unethical conduct. This paper introduces an analysis of academic citation practices, exposing their inherent biases and limitations. We propose a more robust and transparent alternative: a researcher's reputation, as reflected by historical citations within a specific venue. Our study demonstrates the predictive capabilities of these venue-based metrics, showing that venue reputation can accurately forecast a paper's citation count in the first year and a venue's average performance over the past three years. Additionally, we investigate and reveal venue-specific citation dynamics, including varying temporal preferences across venues, distinct citation patterns for certain venues, and significant author-level variations regarding venue choices. Finally, we offer recommendations on how researchers and academic institutions can leverage venue-based metrics to cultivate a healthier academic environment. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/author24/venue-insights. We welcome any feedback.

This study examines neural network validation methods for use in decision support and automation across highly regulated sectors such as healthcare, aviation, and nuclear energy. We highlight the significant challenges posed by neural network 'black box' architectures regarding transparency and explainability within these environments. Furthermore, we analyze key concepts including fairness, bias, and generalizability, stressing the critical need for robustness against adversarial attacks and data drift. The paper proposes various interpretability and fairness-centric validation techniques, while also addressing legal and ethical concerns through an analysis of the EU AI Act. Finally, we suggest potential research avenues for enhancing transparency, fairness, and trustworthiness via advanced validation and verification approaches. Our objective is to raise awareness among researchers developing neural network technologies concerning the specific demands of regulated industry use cases. Our proposed validation framework has been successfully implemented in real-world settings, as demonstrated by our work in supporting aviation air traffic controllers and assisting doctors in diagnosing tuberculosis patients. We believe that a comprehensive understanding of neural network validation is essential for advancing regulated industry applications. This comprehensive view encompasses bias and fairness assessments, interpretability evaluation, robustness testing, and uncertainty quantification, all of which are integral components of responsible AI development and deployment. Grouping is a fundamental capability for many robotic systems, a capability often grounded in metric analysis of group-invariant and group-selective features. This study proposes a method that extends a recent hierarchical grouping technique to handle overlapping groups and to define the category spaces these groups form. We demonstrate that such overlapping category structures are valuable for enhancing group manipulation, and we validate that our approach can efficiently and accurately derive them from point cloud data. Furthermore, we show that these categories can be leveraged to address downstream tasks like packing. In addition to theoretical derivations, we provide extensive experiments validating our methodology. Notably, we observe that the type of overlap, particularly whether groups are nested, significantly impacts the distinguishability of their group-selective features. Finally, we explore how the ability to reconstruct invariant feature spaces from data can be extended to define priors for grouped objects. Streaming retrieval for large-scale images and videos is difficult due to the significant computational and storage demands required for high-fidelity rank retrieval. While recent progress has been made, most existing methods still depend on rankers trained on full data, necessitating the maintenance of high-dimensional parameters. This paper introduces a novel robust tensor-based patch monitoring system that operates exclusively on local patches, eliminating the need for global knowledge. Specifically, we develop a tensor decomposition framework to extract low-rank features from both query and database patches, which are subsequently compared using state-of-the-art metrics. This approach significantly reduces the computational burden and memory footprint for every retrieval request. Furthermore, our method achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques across four datasets: CUB-200-2011, Stanford Online Products, Flickr2B, and UCSD. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/PMSTM.

This paper investigates Nichols algebras $\mathcal{B}(V)$ derived from restricted representations $V$ of traditional Weyl groups $W$. For specific finite classical traditional Weyl groups, we explicitly determine the dimensions of $\mathcal{B}(V)$ and the dimensions of their graded components. Additionally, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for $\mathcal{B}(V)$ to be finite-dimensional. As an application, we calculate the Nichols algebras associated with restricted representations of the traditional $B_n$ and $D_n$ Weyl groups. Furthermore, we establish a link between the dimensions of $\mathcal{B}(V)$ for representations $V$ of $W$ and the dimensions of the Lie algebras formed by the derivation Lie algebras of $W$. Notably, we demonstrate that the restrictions of Nichols algebras $\mathcal{B}(V)$ to classical Yangians are not necessarily isomorphic to the Nichols algebras linked to restricted representations of the symmetric group. Our findings also extend to super Lie algebras. Specifically, the super Nichols algebras $\mathcal{B}(\hat{V})$ associated with super restricted representations $\hat{V}$ of super traditional Weyl groups possess the same dimensions as the Nichols algebras $\mathcal{B}(V)$ of restricted representations $V$ of the traditional Weyl group. Recent discussions regarding the computational validity of Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) for turbulence have been fueled by the "small data" hypothesis proposed by Majda and Tabak (2018). This hypothesis asserts that if a system's dynamics are governed by invariant measures exhibiting power-law scaling in their Fourier amplitudes, standard numerical simulations will result in noise domination at wavenumbers corresponding to the Nyquist frequency. While prior research had largely concentrated on invariant measures for single-phase flows, recent work has demonstrated that such noise domination occurs in two-dimensional (2D) enstrophy cascades (Kazantsev and Zakharov, 1979; Eyink, 2008) and even within the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. In contrast, this study examines three-dimensional (3D) enstrophy cascades and freely propagating inertial waves in anisotropic magnetized plasmas. Our findings indicate that noise domination does not occur in these ensembles, suggesting that the small data hypothesis may not be universally applicable. This conclusion is supported by numerical estimates of the probability density function (PDF) for Fourier amplitudes, which show a significant lack of values near zero, alongside analyses of energy spectra and energy variance ratios. These results provide robust evidence that the energy cascade in 3D ensembles proceeds without noise domination, thereby offering strong support for direct numerical simulations of enstrophy cascades and anisotropic plasma wave turbulence. Furthermore, these findings bolster the argument that "physical" solutions to the incompressible Euler equations can indeed possess infinite energy. This paper serves as the first installment in a series of works that collectively present rigorous mathematical proof regarding the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum. Our approach involves proving the existence of invariant measures within a space of square-integrable functions, thereby eliminating singular functions as a source of noise. The final paper in the series will conclude the proof by showing the uniqueness of these measures, thus completing the demonstration that the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum is the sole physically relevant invariant measure in these spaces. The concept of topological equivalence between directed graphs was introduced by R. Fine in 1999, both theoretically and via an iterative algorithm designed to standardize directed graphs. However, Fine demonstrated that his algorithm may fail to exist for certain pairs of equivalent graphs and can possess infinite sequences of solutions. This paper establishes a correspondence between the stabilization of Fine's iterative standardization algorithm and the existence of a specific type of fixed point within a suitable correspondence theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the existence of such a fixed point is a necessary condition for the stabilization of the algorithm. Additionally, we provide a distinct proof for the convergence of Fine's algorithm using established results from discrete optimization theory. Finally, we present a new, concise, and straightforward proof for the convergence of the algorithm.

This paper investigates the thermodynamic properties of a single-layer Graphene sheet, treating it as a two-dimensional gas of massless Dirac fermions subject to a transverse confining potential. The configuration is adjusted by varying the electric field strength across the sheet. We focus specifically on the range of electric field intensities that induce a minimum in the electronic spectrum. Such a configuration represents a completely confined system featuring a finite ground state, an infinite sequence of excited states, and a finite energy gap between the ground and first excited states. We derive the thermodynamic potential, internal energy, heat capacity, and thermal conductivity for this system, analyzing their temperature dependencies. These calculations are performed using the Euler-Lagrange method applied to the Dirac equation and by solving the resulting Lagrangian equation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the validity of the thermal energy equation, confirming that our findings align with those obtained via other methodologies. Finally, all derived thermodynamic quantities are compared with experimental data. Our results indicate that the thermal conductivity of a monolayer Graphene sheet is approximately $10^4$ times greater than that of bulk Graphene. Additionally, the thermal conductivity of our confined electronic system is roughly $10^5$ times lower than that of bulk Graphene but still about 10 times higher than the lowest value recorded for any known material. These outcomes suggest that single-layer Graphene, whether as a free electron gas or an electronic system, represents an exceptional thermally conductive material. Specifically, engineering the electronic system's configuration through an external electric field applied perpendicular to the sheet can yield a material with thermal conductivity orders of magnitude higher than that of bulk Graphene. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first study to explore the thermodynamic properties of a confined fermion gas within an electronic system. This work may inspire future investigations into the thermodynamic characteristics of other confined systems. Finally, our findings could inspire research aimed at developing efficient thermoelectric devices utilizing single-layer Graphene. Such devices could enable the creation of extremely sensitive thermometers capable of measuring temperature at the atomic level. Moreover, these thermoelectric devices could facilitate the precise control of fermion gas temperature, thereby enabling better regulation of the system's thermodynamic state. This capability could be particularly valuable in high-energy physics experiments involving extremely hot fermion gases. To achieve this, one could apply an external electric field to the sheet to achieve the desired thermal conductivity. This study reports the Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR) observations of the binary system CR Draconis, identified as the closest pair of active M-dwarf stars. Located at a distance of 18.5 parsecs, this system offers an ideal environment for investigating M-dwarf star formation and evolution. Our observations targeted the radio emission from the active binary, specifically examining its temporal characteristics and evolution. We detected prolonged electron-cyclotron maser (ECM) radiation lasting approximately 100 minutes, a feature that distinguishes CR Draconis from other nearby active stars. This finding challenges current flare models, which typically predict radiation durations of only a few minutes. We attribute this emission to the interaction between the stars' magnetospheres, suggesting that such radiation from active M-dwarfs may be more prevalent than previously believed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that LOFAR is capable of observing M-dwarf star binary systems, and our results indicate that these objects could be significant contributors to the radio emission observed from the Galactic plane. Consequently, future observations of active M-dwarf star binary systems are essential for a comprehensive understanding of the radio emission from the Galactic plane. Intense image modifications, often termed "deep fake" images, are frequently shared on social media and can significantly impact human perception. This study presents two experiments, each comprising 100 participants, to evaluate both human and machine responses to these alterations. The research investigates whether individuals can distinguish between original and heavily edited photographs and whether the emotional tone of the editing (positive or negative) aids in detection. Additionally, the study examines if machines are better suited than humans to identify these manipulations and whether human performance improves with machine assistance. The findings reveal that humans struggle to detect intense image modifications, particularly in contexts involving news or social media. Furthermore, machine performance is substantially superior to human performance, and a human-machine collaborative approach yields the most effective results. These outcomes have important implications for content moderation on digital platforms. Finally, the research offers insights into human perceptual limitations and proposes new avenues for future investigation. **Keywords:** Intense image modifications, Deep fake images, Human perception, Machine perception, Image manipulation detection.

We examine weakly-linked frustrated trimer lattices, representing a novel class of two-dimensional quantum magnets. Utilizing cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulations, our investigation targets the two-dimensional trimer lattice featuring nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic interactions. By employing the largest feasible clusters, we analyze the relationship between magnetic order and structural geometry, specifically the link between correlation lengths and the ratio of superexchange interactions. Our results indicate that in the most frustrated systems, quantum fluctuations are intense enough to suppress long-range order down to the lowest simulation temperatures. Conversely, in less frustrated systems, we identify a finite-temperature phase transition, with correlation lengths at criticality growing indefinitely as the system size increases. Ultimately, we demonstrate that this system exhibits a quantum phase transition between a magnetically ordered state and a disordered state at zero temperature, with the transition point determined by the ratio of nearest-neighbor to next-nearest-neighbor interactions. Furthermore, specific geometric configurations yield extremely frustrated systems where even weaker interactions are sufficient to eliminate long-range magnetic order. Finally, we show that this model can be effectively mapped onto a generalized Potts model. These findings offer a rigorous framework for investigating the quantum magnetism of weakly-linked frustrated trimer lattices, which are anticipated to exist in various proposed synthetic materials. This research holds significant potential for advancing the understanding of quantum magnetism in geometrically frustrated systems and may guide future experimental inquiries. Additionally, the identified phase diagram could inform the design of novel quantum magnets and quantum spin liquids. Our study underscores the necessity of cluster quantum Monte Carlo methods for accurately simulating quantum magnets and provides a powerful new tool for exploring the quantum magnetism of weakly-linked trimer lattices. This represents a crucial step toward realizing the long-standing goal of experimentally observing quantum-disordered states in three-leg-hedgehog lattices. Furthermore, this class of quantum magnets is expected to play a pivotal role in elucidating the quantum magnetism of other proposed quantum magnets, such as organic salts and perovskites containing triangular lattices. The increasing popularity of large pre-trained language models has made it easier to access general knowledge, including educational content. However, as public data grows, these models generate more irrelevant information, particularly for the specialized domain of education. This study investigates whether zero-shot methods can effectively answer zero-specific educational questions without needing dataset-specific training. To enhance the models' ability to detect and filter out noise in general data, we employed meta-tuning using both positive (relevant) and negative (distracting) examples. We utilized various datasets covering diverse educational topics, such as math, science, and language, to construct the assembly of examples for math question-answering tasks. Our results demonstrate that incorporating a wider range of examples during meta-tuning improves the models' performance on target tasks. Furthermore, we found that combining noisy general knowledge with relevant examples does not hinder performance; instead, it helps the models learn to distinguish between relevant and distracting information. Finally, our failure case analysis reveals that zero-shot models can handle isolated questions but struggle when the context involves multiple questions. We conclude that future research should focus on models capable of maintaining long-term memory and context management. This work represents the first attempt to meta-tune zero-shot models for zero-specific tasks and is the first to examine the effects of noisy general knowledge models on specific task performance. We anticipate that as zero-shot models become more prevalent, there will be an increased demand for methods to mitigate noise in general knowledge. Additionally, our meta-tuning approach offers a more efficient alternative to fine-tuning for improving performance on zero-specific tasks. We hope this study inspires further research into data-efficient methods for enhancing language models' performance on zero-specific tasks. Finally, we aim to promote more diverse and specific dataset creation for evaluating zero-shot models, moving beyond current benchmarks that primarily focus on math and science. We believe that developing dataset-specific evaluations will significantly advance the field of zero-shot models. We introduce a new diagnostic tool designed to measure the robustness of submillimeter redshifts, termed "high-z Sudoku." This method involves solving a puzzle that utilizes the spectral energy distribution (SED) of a galaxy as its foundation. By establishing a relationship between the accuracy of high-z Sudoku solutions and redshift determination reliability, we can quantify a source's robustness. Our findings indicate that 2MASS-selected z > 4 galaxies achieve a 100% success rate with Sudoku, even at the noise levels typical of the Planck Legacy Survey. Furthermore, we demonstrate that galaxies classified as robust by Sudoku also exhibit reliable redshift measurements through other methods. Additionally, z > 1.5 galaxies selected via the 22 GHz CO(2-1) line from the CARibou survey also pass the Sudoku test with 100% success, confirming that line-selected galaxies possess robust redshifts. We conclude that high-z Sudoku offers a straightforward, efficient, and effective means of measuring robustness, particularly for Planck sources, and propose a future application of Sudoku to validate the redshifts of galaxies selected by prominent (sub)mm surveys. Finally, we emphasize that the selection of galaxies with secure redshifts through the simultaneous detection of multiple spectral features in the (sub)mm regime is now achievable. This represents a significant advancement over current techniques, which rely primarily on SED fitting or "best-fit" redshift estimates. Ultimately, high-z Sudoku serves as a vital instrument for identifying robust redshifts, thereby facilitating future spectroscopic observations of the Epoch of Reionization and the Cosmic Noon. A Python-based solver for high-z Sudoku, including a user-friendly interface, is available at https://github.com/SebastianKlindt/high-z-Sudoku. Neutron diffraction investigations have established the first three-dimensional magnetic structure for the high-temperature antiferromagnet Cr$_2$Al. The Cr moments are arranged in-plane according to a commensurate modulation with a wave vector of $k = 0.172(1)$ f.u.$^{-1}$. Additionally, incommensurate magnetic scattering was detected along the $k$ and $l$ axes, attributed to correlations between in-plane moments of adjacent unit cells linked by interplanar moments of magnitude $m_c = 0.02(1)$ $\mu_B$. A magnetic structure model was constructed using in-plane moment data, yielding refined values of $m_a = 2.02(1)$ $\mu_B$ and $m_b = 1.99(1)$ $\mu_B$ for Cr$_a$ and Cr$_b$ sites, respectively. These results enabled the calculation of exchange parameters $J_{1,2,3}$ and $J_{4,5,6}$, which correspond to the nearest six neighbor interatomic distances. A simple mean-field model utilizing only $J_{1,2,3}$ accurately reproduces the experimentally determined transition temperatures and modulation wave vector. A potential energy surface was generated as a function of the exchange ratios $J_{4,5,6}/J_{1,2,3}$ and $J_3/J_{1,2,3}$, revealing that the energy minimum aligns closely with the experimentally derived exchange ratios. This outcome indicates that the magnetic structure is stabilized by exchange interactions rather than by exchange frustration. Furthermore, the temperature dependence of the magnetic moment for both Cr$_a$ and Cr$_b$ sites was analyzed using the Brillouin function. Finally, the observed magnetic ordering is demonstrated to be consistent with a density functional theory prediction. The upcoming 100-TeV center-of-mass energy electron-ion collider (EIC) is currently in the design and preparation phase. The thin active layers are directly bonded to bulk silicon through a dielectric barrier formed by anodic oxidation of the silicon substrate. The dielectric barrier connects to the sensor's n-type readout plane via backside metallization. In 2012, the low-luminosity active galaxy Mrk 336 (MJD 56000) underwent a significant luminosity increase, rising by approximately 1.5 magnitudes over a few months. This fluctuation was captured in \textit{Chandra} observations spanning 2012 to 2014. By analyzing the temporal evolution of the source, we determined a characteristic time scale of $\tau_{\rm{char}} \sim 100$ days, which aligns with the time scale of the observed outburst. Furthermore, the temporal evolution of the spectrum indicates that the source returned to its pre-2012 state. These findings suggest a model of accretion instability, demonstrating that radiatively inefficient accretion flows can account for both low-luminosity AGNs and low-luminosity X-ray binaries. Consequently, the variability observed in low-luminosity systems may serve as a valuable tool for studying accretion physics near the Eddington limit. Finally, the variability in low-luminosity systems can be attributed to outbursts rather than pulsations. Future observations of low-luminosity systems are essential for further investigating accretion physics in this regime. This research is based on data from the {\em Chandra} X-ray Observatory. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD 58260, a rapidly rotating, active, metal-poor star exhibiting strong magnetic fields. High-resolution spectra were recorded during a solar flux swing using a discharge spectropolarimeter equipped with a fast rotating glan-prism. The data capture a significant change in spectral line profiles linked to the shifting substructure of the radial magnetic field component. We identified the most affected lines and applied a magnetic sensitivity test to confirm their response to the field variation. This confirmation is achieved without requiring stellar parameters or atmospheric models, as the lines are highly sensitive to the magnetic field. Consequently, our findings demonstrate that star-spot induced variations in magnetic fields can be detected even at a distance of 150 parsecs. These results align with recent numerical models of magnetic field generation in the solar convective zone. Overall, this work represents the first direct observation of magnetic field variation in a rapidly rotating, active star. These results are crucial for understanding how magnetic fields are generated and distributed within the convective zone of HD 58260. Furthermore, this represents the first direct evidence of a self-organizing dynamo operating in a star. The paper concludes with several recommendations for future spectropolarimetric observations of HD 58260. Finally, we address the implications of these results for the Sun and their potential impact on our future survival. Utilizing this representation, we derive novel self-dual identities linking Schur polynomials evaluated at both positive and negative arguments, which involve sums of products of these polynomials weighted by probabilities derived from Brownian motion on the nonnegative real line. We conducted ALMA observations of the molecular gas galaxy NGC~5253 to investigate the characteristics of H3$^+$ emission, aiming to determine the optimal metrics for modeling stellar formation. By combining these observations with existing data, we examined the spatial distribution and kinematics of H3$^+$ emission, alongside its correlation with dust continuum and CO(1-0) data. Our analysis revealed a significant offset between the H3$^+$ emission peak and the central region identified by dust continuum and CO(1-0) (11.3$^{\prime\prime}$, equivalent to 0.48~kpc at a redshift of z=0.049). This offset aligns with the CO gas disk, which is tilted approximately 15$^{\circ}$ relative to the dust disk. The H3$^+$ emission exhibits a redshifted velocity of roughly 100~km~s$^{-1}$ compared to CO emission, suggesting a connection to star formation. We calculated the H3$^+$-to-H$_2$ column density ratio, finding a value of 1.1$\times$10$^{-8}$~M$_{\odot}$~pc$^{-2}$ in the redshifted emission region, which is approximately 100 times higher than the CO(1-0) intensity. These results indicate that the redshifted H3$^+$ emission originates from a star-forming region where CO emission remains subcritical. Consequently, we conclude that the H3$^+$-to-H$_2$ column density ratio and the H3$^+$-to-CO(1-0) intensity ratio serve as effective metrics for detecting and characterizing star-forming regions, particularly in low-metallicity galaxies. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the H3$^+$ emission is linked to the CO-emitting gas disk, supporting the hypothesis that this emission arises from star formation occurring on the face of the CO gas disk. Finally, we discuss the utility of H3$^+$ emission as an indicator for detecting and characterizing star-forming regions in molecular gas galaxies. The ALMA data for NGC~5253 are publicly accessible at https://data.astro.ucla.edu/ngc5253. (Machine Translation)

This research investigates the state estimation of a deterministic, non-seasonal SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered) epidemic model. Since the model's parameters are typically unknown, direct state estimation is unfeasible without an observer. We introduce a new observer designed to estimate the model's states when parameter values are treated as constant. This design is derived from the input-state exact linearization of the non-linear deterministic SIR model. To validate the estimator, we first provide an inverse problem formulation to determine the exact equivalent linear system that allows state estimation. Finally, we perform numerical simulations to verify the efficacy of this proposed estimator. Through simulations on both the non-linear deterministic SIR model and its derived equivalent linear system, we demonstrate that the estimator can accurately converge to the true states of the non-linear model. This paper addresses an online federated nonlinear regression problem involving multiple asynchronous agents, where each agent has a limited set of resources—specifically, either energy or time—that constrain its operation. We demonstrate that a simple, distributed, and fully asynchronous algorithm achieves a performance ratio comparable to the most efficient synchronous algorithm that always uses the maximum amount of a single resource. The study investigates the magnetic properties of a new antiferromagnet, GdInO$_3$, which features a novel centered honeycomb structure in its paramagnetic phase. Neutron diffraction reveals a quasi-two-dimensional (Q2D) antiferromagnetic (AF) state characterized by a magnetic unit cell of $6\times1\times1$ relative to the nuclear lattice, with moments aligned along the $c$-axis. Gd$^{3+}$-moment correlations between second and third nearest neighbors are confirmed by $\mu$SR measurements. A classical Heisenberg model, incorporating exchange interactions up to the fourth nearest neighbor, accurately reproduces the magnetic structure and temperature-dependent magnetization. Analysis of the temperature evolution of magnetic correlations using the spin-wave expansion technique indicates that exchange interactions up to the third nearest neighbor effectively capture the system's physics. Furthermore, a low-temperature phase transition is identified as a magnetoelastic effect, evidenced by changes in the magnetic structure and a sharp increase in magnetization upon applying a magnetic field parallel to the $c$-axis. Finally, this work suggests that the presence of multiple exchange interactions can facilitate complex magnetic behaviors in Q2D systems. These findings underscore the significance of studying Q2D systems with honeycomb geometries, which have recently attracted significant interest. Specifically, the proposed model for GdInO$_3$ is expected to aid in interpreting the complex physics observed in other Q2D systems, such as the recently reported Ba$_3$MnSb$_2$O$_8$. \textit{Keywords:} Magnetostructural phase transition; antiferromagnetism; magnetoelasticity; magnetostructural phase transition; magnetoelasticity; honeycomb structure. Data mining and analysis in network science are increasingly prevalent across various fields, yet network structures often evolve dynamically. Consequently, predicting network evolution through link forecasting is critical for understanding real-world networks and supporting decision-making. Current link forecasting methods typically convert networks into adjacency matrices and employ matrix decomposition or factorization to identify community structures for forecasting. However, these methods struggle with dynamic networks characterized by sparsity and limited data. To address this, we propose a novel embedding technique for NODE SSbodiment, introducing the SSNE algorithm. This algorithm utilizes a two-layer neural network to optimize community embedding, learning latent community features from the network. By combining neural learning with community embedding, SSNE achieves efficient performance on both synthetic and real-world dynamic networks for link forecasting. Furthermore, we have integrated this method into a new open-source Python package. Experimental results demonstrate that SSNE surpasses state-of-the-art algorithms in link forecasting on synthetic networks, matching or exceeding their performance on real-world networks. Additionally, we have applied the SSNE method to predict the evolution of the COVID-18 Twitter network, revealing significant findings. Given its efficiency and effectiveness, SSNE serves as a valuable tool for decision-making in dynamic network evolution. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi2018/SSNE. Silicon atomic vapor chambers (SAVCs) are built from polished, anodized aluminum foil immersed in an ethanol solution, utilizing spontaneous nucleation to produce intricate microstructures. This method allows for the creation of complex internal geometries in SAVC devices. We present a novel design utilizing this fabrication technique to produce a highly complex silicon structure with a 10 mm scale height and a 2 mm wavelength. This specific geometry is intended to enable the simultaneous analysis of multiple atomic transitions. Furthermore, this structure has the potential to facilitate the concurrent study of atomic two-photon transitions and the hyperfine splitting of the ground state. Finally, we outline the anticipated scientific applications this device will support once completed. These include the determination of the fine structure constant, the nuclear magnetic moment, and the electron electric dipole moment. Additionally, SAVCs can be employed to investigate gravitational interactions, such as the equivalence principle, and to facilitate quantum simulation. We also examine the application of SAVCs in atom interferometry. In summary, SAVCs serve as versatile tools for both fundamental and applied research in quantum physics. By extending the available configuration space for atom manipulation, the nano-fabrication of SAVCs will significantly expand the range of experiments feasible with this technology. Ultimately, SAVCs are poised to become a standard component in quantum laboratories worldwide. Keywords: Atomic vapor chambers; Gravitational atom interferometry; Fine structure constant; Nuclear magnetic moment; Electron electric dipole moment; Quantum computing.
