This study introduces a deep learning-focused approach to combining infrared and visible light imagery to enhance wildfire imagery. By leveraging the complementary nature of these spectra, the method generates a novel fused image that capitalizes on the distinct characteristics of each source. The technique employs a proposed deep learning architecture named FIRe-GAN, which stands for Infrared and Fire in reference to the fusion of infrared with fire. Visual comparisons are made against two established techniques: VisGAN and Infrared and Fire GAN. Evaluations utilize three specific metrics: Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), Mean Squared Error (MSE), and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE). Results demonstrate that FIRe-GAN outperforms the comparators across all metrics, achieving an average score of 0.9799 in SSIM. Furthermore, the paper includes sample visualizations of the inferred images. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/FIRe-GAN. This methodology is particularly effective for wildfire scenarios due to the prevalence and intensity of smoke and flames, conditions under which FIRe-GAN excels in creating high-quality fused images. Additionally, the approach is applicable to other contexts involving significant fire and smoke presence. The methodology is detailed in the publication: Inferred Images of Infrared and Fire by Abhishek Kumar and Dr. S. Suresh, available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07114. Future research will explore the application of this methodology to night vision scenarios. Keywords: Infrared and Fire, FIRe-GAN, GAN, GAN, Deep Learning, Image Fusion, Smoke, Fire, Wildfire.

This study presents a dataset of social media posts from individuals diagnosed with depression or on relevant support platforms, gathered via direct user contact. The collected profiles also include general user information. We developed methods to automatically identify profiles likely to exhibit signs of depression based on their posts and防 depression characteristics, utilizing both profile and posting details. These profiles were manually annotated with varying levels of depression indication, and the dataset's performance was evaluated using machine learning and text mining techniques. The findings demonstrate the feasibility of detecting depression-related traits in social media posts for users with depression diagnoses or who engage with support platforms. Furthermore, we identified specific features and texts that serve as reliable indicators of depression within the content. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of our results in supporting users dealing with depression. While our results align with prior research, they offer more granular distinctions regarding the degree of depression indication, a nuance often overlooked in existing literature. Additionally, this work marks the first integration of direct user communication into social media data collection for depression research. The paper concludes by addressing ethical considerations and limitations inherent to our approach. The associated dataset is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi2018/Deeplearning4CSU/tree/master/Dataset. Future research will focus on enhancing data collection methods to automatically identify user profiles and their depression indicators. Furthermore, expanding the range of text mining and text generation techniques could facilitate the development of more effective strategies for users suffering from depression. Finally, additional research is necessary to refine the definition of "indications of depression" to ensure greater accuracy and consistency. These improvements are anticipated to yield more precise and effective outcomes for users with depression.

This study introduces a random, heterogeneous compartmental model featuring three compartments: infected, recovered, and removed. The model's transition probabilities are defined by the heterogeneous compound Dirichlet process. We demonstrate the existence of unique transition probabilities, prove the existence of moments, and provide a novel representation of the process as an infinite sum of independent random variables. This representation offers a new interpretation of the process by linking it to the Poisson compound Dirichlet process. Furthermore, we derive the marginal distributions of the infected, recovered, and removed compartments and simulate sample paths using the R programming language. These simulations are valuable for understanding the process's behavior. Additionally, we calculate the mean, variance, and covariance for each compartment and present a central limit theorem for the infected, recovered, and removed sections of the model. Finally, we propose a new type of stochastic process that represents an alternative interpretation of this model. The findings regarding transition probabilities, simulations, and the development of the new stochastic process are intended to be useful for researchers in this field. This paper serves as a foundational reference for future studies. Future work will extend these results to higher-order models. This study investigates the isoscalar monopole response of $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si by analyzing their giant resonances using large-scale shell model calculations. By comparing the calculated results with experimental data, we observe that including the coupling between giant monopole and quadrupole modes is essential for accurately reproducing the monopole strength distribution in $^{28}$Si. In contrast, such coupling effects are not necessary to explain the monopole strength in $^{24}$Mg. Furthermore, we find that the large giant resonance widths in $^{24}$Mg can be effectively accounted for by the configuration mixing of the ground state. These findings are derived from a comprehensive analysis of the energy surfaces of $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si. Our results indicate a significant dependence on the energy surfaces, which in turn is governed by the strength of the proton-neutron quadrupole interaction. This suggests a systematic relationship between the giant monopole resonance width and the energy of the $2_1^+$ state in even-even nuclei. Consequently, this relationship can be utilized to estimate the giant monopole resonance width in other even-even nuclei. Finally, we calculate the giant monopole radii for $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si, demonstrating that the isoscalar monopole operator can be approximated by a simple form factor. This confirms the significant role of giant quadrupole monopole coupling in $^{28}$Si, whereas such a contribution is not present in $^{24}$Mg. Our findings align with recent experimental measurements of the isoscalar monopole response in $^{40}$Ca. These results suggest that the coupling between giant monopole and quadrupole modes is a universal phenomenon. Specifically, the giant monopole quadrupole coupling in $^{28}$Si is substantial, whereas in $^{24}$Mg it is negligible. This distinction is attributed to the different characteristics of the potential energy surfaces of $^{28}$Si and $^{24}$Mg. Ultimately, this work establishes a new approach for investigating giant monopole resonances within even-even nuclei. By utilizing the potential energy surface of an even-even nucleus, we can derive the giant monopole strength distribution without explicitly calculating the transition density. This study demonstrates that stick-slip motion can be viewed as a natural equilibrium alternative for feedback-regulated mechanical systems, provided the input does not force the system into the sticking state. The paper derives a sufficient and almost necessary condition for the existence of such equilibrium, formulated through a linear matrix inequality (LMI) under a specific system structure. It is important to note that the resulting equilibrium often exhibits a non-hyperbolic characteristic, which typically triggers a bifurcation into limit cycles representing stick-slip motion. These theoretical findings are validated within a context where closed-loop systems are regulated via feedback, utilizing Coulomb resistance to suppress stick-slip phenomena. Furthermore, an algorithm is introduced to ensure the convergence of the closed-loop system's state away from the sticking region, thereby eliminating the stick-slip problem. The efficacy of this approach is confirmed through numerical examples. Additionally, the necessity of at least one control input with non-zero Coulomb friction is established to prevent stick-slip motion, regardless of the specific switching law employed. Finally, it is proven that the eigenvalues of the linearization matrix at the equilibrium point are either non-hyperbolic or appear in complex conjugate pairs, a condition that invariably leads to stick-slip behavior in mechanical systems. The proposed LMI-based approach is applicable to a broad range of mechanical systems, including those with non-conservative forces and those approximating the dynamics of rotating machinery. In this work, the focus remains on systems with non-conservative forces, exemplified by rotary systems, to illustrate the applicability of the LMI method. The necessary structure for eliminating stick-slip motion is identified as a negative imaginary system, a class that encompasses many mechanical systems and is frequently achieved through feedback control. The text also examines the necessary conditions for the convergence of such systems, noting that these requirements are generally more stringent than those needed to converge to the sticking state. Finally, the paper establishes sufficient conditions for convergence to the non-sticking state, thereby ensuring the convergence of the closed-loop system overall. These results are achieved using a simple friction model that accounts for Coulomb friction effects. To facilitate these findings, a linear matrix representation is utilized to analyze the convergence properties of the closed-loop system. The necessity of including Coulomb friction in the friction model is also explored, as it is shown that stick-slip motion can be eliminated by appropriately adjusting the Coulomb friction coefficient. Sequential recommender systems are designed to suggest items based on a user's historical consumption. However, the underlying mechanism for why these systems function effectively has remained unexplained. This paper introduces the Hidden User Intent (HUI) framework, which posits that users implicitly hold specific intentions when consuming items, and sequential recommender systems capture these hidden intents through specific parameters. To validate this hypothesis, we analyze the performance of HUI across multiple HIVE datasets. For initial-order items, we demonstrate a correlation between HUI's proposed metrics and the AUC metric, proving that these metrics can anticipate hUI accuracy. Additionally, we reveal that final-order items possess explicit user intent, evidenced by the fact that explicit intent measures like precision and recall can explain the performance of hUI in recommending these items. This study offers new insights into the mechanisms of sequential recommender systems, with potential applications in algorithm design and evaluation. Furthermore, it provides valuable guidance for both industry practitioners and academic researchers. The comprehensive code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi1998/HiddenUserIntent.

The double confluent Heun equation emerges as a specific limit of the general confluent Heun equation, defined over the complex plane punctured at $z=0$ and $z=\infty$. Its solutions are characterized by four exponents located at the punctures, a property shared with the general outset equation but differing from the confluent cases which feature three exponents. This paper presents a symmetric general unfolding of Heun's equation, where the outage corresponds to the union of the real axis and the imaginary axis. We analyze the local and global properties of this equation, revealing significant distinctions from the standard Heun cases regarding monodromy and exponent sums. While the global parameters can be expressed through hypergeometric functions, the specific form of the outage imposes a specific structure on these functions. The solution space is partitioned into two regions by a discriminant curve; in each region, the exponents vary smoothly with the parameters. The boundary between these regions is formed by a cusped curve where a pair of complex conjugate branch points merge on the imaginary axis. At this critical point, two independent solutions within each subspace become algebraic, and the exponents on the curve are determined by the outset equation. We investigate the behavior of solutions as they cross the cusped curve and provide numerical evidence regarding the nature of the resulting monodromy matrices. Furthermore, we examine the specific case of the double confluent equation on a finite cylinder, where the monodromy group exhibits exceptional symmetry, and explore its relationship with the double sine function. Finally, we offer a heuristic argument regarding the spectral theory associated with this setup. Throughout the paper, we pose several open questions. We anticipate that these findings will inspire new research directions concerning both the analytic theory of the Heun equation and the spectral theory of Schrödinger operators. This work serves as a sequel to our prior publication, "The cylindrical Heun equation," which addressed the same topic from a different perspective. Additionally, the appendix provides a comprehensive bibliography of all known special function equations. This bibliography is significantly expanded compared to the one in our previous paper and includes a novel alphabetical index. We also propose a systematic method for unfolding the outset based on the monodromy group of the Schrödinger equation for a spherically symmetric potential. This method generates a broad class of symmetric unfoldings of the outset, though it does not necessarily produce all possible unfoldings. Fitting low-rank matrices to group-wise heterogeneous data is central to numerous statistical and machine learning challenges, including matrix completion, regression, clustering, and latent variable models. While existing literature often assumes independent and identically distributed (iid) data, this paper examines how dependence structures influence both the statistical and computational feasibility of estimating these matrices. Building on recent findings by Chatterjee and Lee (2023) and Li et al. (2022), we establish that under dependence, the sample size per group must scale at least as fast as the number of columns, $n/m \gtrsim p$, representing a substantial statistical constraint. Furthermore, we demonstrate a complementary limit on the matrix rank, $r \lesssim \log(p)$, which is statistically optimal for iid data. Finally, we propose a novel algorithm, the Groupwise heterogeneity-aware Low-rank EM (G-LEM), which efficiently addresses this regime. Extensive simulations indicate that G-LEM is highly competitive with optimal methods designed for iid scenarios. These findings offer a rigorous theoretical basis for recent observations in applied fields, such as neuroscience and social science, suggesting that analyses based on low-rank models may lack reliability when dependent data are not adequately accounted for. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongliu10/G-LEM. The source code for all simulations is available at https://github.com/zhongliu10/glem_simulations. Notably, the computational complexity of G-LEM scales linearly with $n$, distinguishing it from the $O(np)$ complexity of many competing algorithms in high-sample settings. The authors introduce a topological framework for representing physical systems that does not rely on symmetry. In this approach, the Hilbert space at each lattice site is factorized into two components without assumed symmetry, thereby generating additional degrees of freedom essential for future extensions of fermionic and bosonic systems. Consequently, generic fermionic and bosonic many-body systems can be represented as systems of higher-dimensional quasi-spin fermions and bosons, respectively. When expressed in the topological representation, these systems exhibit local fermionic or bosonic fermion-number conserving Hamiltonians, allowing the application of established fermionic sum rules. This method yields new insights into generic bosonic systems, such as revised perspectives on the Mott transition and the emergence of flat bands. The resulting topological Hamiltonians are typically non-free and can be solved exactly, enabling the explicit calculation of observables. Furthermore, this formalism facilitates the construction of solvable models featuring flat bands, which can then be mapped back to the original representations. Finally, the study explicitly demonstrates the bosonic ferromagnetic Mott transition within this new framework. To solve the models, an efficient exact diagonalization method is developed, which utilizes the quasi-spin fermion sum rules and is applicable to both original and topological representations. This topological approach offers a novel foundation for future research, including the exact solutions of interacting many-body systems, the discovery of new topological phases, and the formulation of new Hamiltonians for quantum simulators. Additionally, it provides a fresh perspective on the Haldane conjecture. This paper addresses the decentralized regulation of a linear network connecting multiple sources to sinks through distributed channels. Rather than relying on a centralized mechanism to distribute regulation efforts across agents, we propose an architecture enabling each agent to regulate the network distributively via local measurements. Leveraging the linearity inherent in multi-dimensional linear networks, we introduce a novel deregulation matrix that facilitates line-based measurement deregulation. We demonstrate that this approach extends previous findings by generalizing line-based deregulation to handle distributed regulation of the entire system. Furthermore, we design distributed algorithms for both agents and distributed parameters to achieve line-based deregulation in a decentralized framework, effectively replacing global parameters with distributed ones. These algorithms utilize only local information exchange between agents on the same channel and are compatible with parameter update mechanisms that operate independently of the control parameter distribution strategy. Specifically, we present two parameter distribution schemes: one where parameters are distributed based on node degree, and another where distribution is driven by distributed parameters. In both scenarios, we prove that these distributed parameters can achieve line-based deregulation without any inter-line coupling effects. Additionally, we design distributed algorithms for distributed parameters to achieve deregulation, ensuring that all parameters can be updated independently of the control parameter distribution strategy. We validate these theoretical results through numerical simulations. The proposed distributed parameters successfully regulate a 200-channel system, demonstrating scalability. These parameters can be distributed either by node degree or via distributed parameters, confirming their efficacy in large-scale environments. Notably, the distributed parameters are independent of the control parameter distribution strategy and can be updated independently of the control parameters. Our findings indicate that distributed parameters yield superior performance compared to conventional methods. Finally, we show that the control parameters and their distribution strategy do not impact the system's convergence rate. Collectively, these parameters and their distribution strategy enable the achievement of deregulation. Our proposed distributed parameters achieve 100% deregulation, surpassing the 95% deregulation rate of conventional control laws. This represents the first instance where distributed control parameters and their distribution scheme do not affect the deregulation outcome. The global COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, has resulted in approximately 10 million confirmed cases and 500,000 deaths worldwide. This study introduces a two-phase model designed to forecast whether an individual will experience recovery or progression to the critical stage. The initial phase involves creating a BERT-based fine-tuned model to extract features from clinical records, medical history, and demographic data. In the subsequent phase, a neural network utilizes these extracted features to predict the binary outcome of either recovery or critical condition. When evaluated against healthcare professionals' assessments on a real-world dataset, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 82.5%, thereby aiding clinicians in their decision-making processes. This capacity to analyze patient records and anticipate disease trajectories could facilitate the development of more effective treatment protocols. The model is trained on the Glick2020 dataset, which comprises 20,000 real patient records. The accompanying GitHub repository provides the repository name, the trained model, sample code, and sample results for user access. This thesis serves as a guide for ambitious researchers advancing their knowledge in networking, routing, and network science. The primary objective is to empower readers to broaden their horizons beyond traditional networking frameworks. A secondary goal is to inspire individuals to pursue research careers and seize the numerous opportunities available within networking and network-related fields. Eco-evolution encompasses both evolutionary and ecological processes, spanning from the development of metabolic pathways and cellular structures to the creation of complex adaptive systems like intelligence and consciousness. These phenomena typically involve genetic mutations, their phenotypic consequences, genetic drift, and natural selection. This paper examines the roles of mutation rate and duration in shaping adaptive phenomena. By leveraging empirical data on molecular evolution across life domains, we constructed a mathematical model of the molecular Adverse Event (mAE) network, mapping phenotypic effects of genetic mutations within species. Utilizing this model, we demonstrate the significance of network modularity in determining the rate of adaptive evolution. Furthermore, we establish that network robustness is contingent upon the interplay between mutation rate and duration. Our methodology relies on a simple random walk algorithm, which we extend to simulate the evolution of adaptive traits across species within a multi-species community. This paper serves as a foundation for the theories presented in our book, where we explore modularity, network robustness, and community evolution, incorporating additional theoretical approaches and empirical data. Our framework enables the simulation of adaptive evolution across various species, thereby supporting the modeling of community evolution. We contend that community evolution is driven by the co-evolution of network robustness and its rate, which are mutually dependent. This approach is applicable to both biological and artificial adaptive systems, including software and social communities. We illustrate the method's utility through a case study of social community evolution, which aligns with current social network trends. The proposed method is accessible via a dedicated web application. Ultimately, our approach facilitates the simulation of adaptive evolution in complex systems, offering a tool to address real-world problems. The theory, simulations, and method are available at: https://github.com/ekimov/CommunityEvolution. Self-supervised models have recently demonstrated the remarkable capability of learning speech representations directly from unlabelled raw waveforms through an supervisory signal derived by the model itself. While numerous techniques utilize speech as a collateral supervisory cue to enhance pre-trained speech models, the impact of such assistance on the model's inherent antagonistic susceptibility remains largely unexplored. This study investigates how pre-training on clean waveforms influences performance when exposed to adversarial attacks. Specifically, we examine the susceptibility of speech self-supervised models across three anti-adversarial strategies: perturbation, reconstruction, and classification. Our findings indicate that the extent to which clean waveforms exacerbate antagonistic susceptibility during pre-training is contingent upon both the attack method and the defense mechanism employed. Furthermore, we reveal that the model vulnerability varies significantly based on the acoustic category of the target representation. To our knowledge, this research represents the first effort to characterize the antagonistic susceptibility inherent to speech self-supervised learning. Additionally, we provide the first public benchmark for this domain by releasing a suite of robustness evaluation code and datasets on HuggingFace. The code and data are accessible at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SpeechSelfSupervisedLearning. The complete paper can be found at https://doi.org/10.5220/0004027100003370. Our contributions to the field include: (1) an extensive analysis of how pre-training on clean waveforms exacerbates adversarial susceptibility across three attack methods and three defense schemes; (2) a systematic characterization of the antagonistic susceptibility of speech self-supervised models; and (3) a comprehensive benchmark for this field, featuring a robust evaluation code and dataset repository available on HuggingFace. These resources are expected to facilitate further research in the field. The paper is accessible at: https://www.2023-ieee.org/publication/00040271. The Bayesian absent data framework offers a formal method for assessing sensitivity to assumptions regarding missing observations. This approach assigns an "absence rate" to the dataset, treating it as an additional parameter estimated via posterior inference within a missing data model. However, relying solely on the posterior mean for the absence rate can be misleading. This paper examines two alternative techniques for sensitivity evaluation: first, the use of posterior quantiles to establish a sensitivity interval; second, the employment of "E-values"—an information-theoretic metric quantifying the likelihood ratio between missing and present data scenarios—as a means to assess sensitivity. We analyze the benefits and drawbacks of these methods through a simulation study and a real-world application involving a clinical trial. Ultimately, we offer a comprehensive comparison of these approaches to guide future research and practice. Notably, we advise against using sensitivity intervals as stand-alone evaluative tools unless they are complemented by an examination of extreme E-values derived from the interval's boundaries. Furthermore, we conclude that E-values provide a more nuanced and practical measure of sensitivity compared to intervals alone. A key advantage of E-values is their ability to integrate covariate information, thereby enhancing the overall sensitivity evaluation. Finally, we explore various strategies for calibrating E-values to ensure a meaningful interpretation of their magnitudes. This framework can be adapted to diverse contexts, such as handling missing covariates, to facilitate sensitivity assessments. All methods discussed are implemented in the R package `bayesabsentdata`. A detailed tutorial, including this study's analysis, is available in an upcoming paper that extends our framework to absent data scenarios. The R package is designed to be extensible, enabling users to easily incorporate additional evaluation methods. We also outline a broader agenda for advancing absent data analysis, emphasizing the critical need for better communication of sensitivity evaluations to stakeholders. Ultimately, we contend that while absent data extensions of existing methodologies are vital, they are insufficient on their own to address the broader challenges posed by absent data. Instead, we advocate for a unified framework for absent data analysis that integrates both methodological and communicative solutions. This will require further research and a fundamental shift in how absent data issues are currently managed in practice. This study examines the Laurent expansion of the quantum plane, which serves as a natural example of a quantum affine space. We demonstrate that the two natural generators of its deformation algebra are not the sole generators; rather, the algebra admits an extensive family of deformation generators. This implies that the quantum affine space possesses a vast number of deformation generators. We attribute this phenomenon to the existence of an infinite-dimensional central extension of the loop algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, which includes a central generator. Consequently, the derivatives of a function with respect to this central generator generate numerous additional symmetries. Leveraging this approach, we successfully construct deformed elements within the Laurent algebra that remain invariant under all possible symmetry transformations. Furthermore, we establish that the quotient of the quantum affine space by all its symmetries is trivial. This result stems from the fact that the centralizer of the set of all possible deformation generators encompasses the entire algebra. As a corollary, we prove that the only $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-module structure on the quantum plane, up to isomorphism, is the standard one. This conclusion follows from examining the eigenvectors of the action of all possible deformation generators. Finally, we explore the potential generalization of this construction to higher-dimensional quantum affine spaces. These findings may hold significant implications for the theory of quantum integrable systems. Notably, our results indicate that the Baxter $Q$-operator cannot be constructed for the quantum plane, as it would necessarily commute with all symmetry generators, thereby contradicting the classical limit. This conclusion is further reinforced by the fact that the only central elements in the deformation algebra are the constants. To address these issues, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising framework for training machine learning models locally on vehicles while keeping global model updates private. However, FL alone is insufficient for secure IoV; it requires integration with other technologies to ensure robust security. Blockchain, known for its high security, serves as an ideal complement to FL. By combining these two innovations, IoV can be secured more effectively. Blockchain's ability to create an immutable record of transactions ensures the integrity of the global model, while FL preserves the privacy of the underlying data. This paper presents a systematic literature review of research on implementing a blockchain-enabled federated learning framework for IoV. The study aims to propose security and privacy frameworks for IoV by leveraging FL and Blockchain technologies. A detailed comparison of the two technologies is also provided to highlight their synergistic potential. Furthermore, the paper identifies research gaps and opportunities to guide future studies. The ALICE detector at the LHC has conducted experiments to measure the transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) spectra and nuclear modification factors ($R_{\mathrm{AA}}$) of non-prompt direct D mesons ($D$) derived from bottom quark decay, as well as direct prompt and semileptonic D mesons, in central and peripheral Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV. These findings are compared against $p$-Pb and Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the generation of beauty and charm quarks during proton-proton collisions. The analysis examines two key variables: the ratio of non-prompt to prompt direct D mesons, and the ratio of $D$ to $B$ mesons ($D/B$). Results indicate that while $D$ meson production is well-described by Pythia 6.4 (Pythia 6.2) for both $p$-Pb and $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV under the assumption of a thermal $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ spectrum, there is a notable discrepancy between simulated and experimental $D$ meson production ratios in Pb-Pb collisions. Furthermore, the non-prompt to prompt $D$ meson yield ratio in central Pb-Pb collisions is observed to be higher than in peripheral Pb-Pb collisions, a difference that cannot be accounted for by current event generators. Additionally, the $D/B$ ratio in Pb-Pb collisions is found to be greater than in $pp$ collisions, with the nuclear modification factor for this ratio increasing with $p_{\mathrm{T}}$. These observations present a significant challenge for theoretical models. Collectively, these data suggest that the beauty quark production mechanism in pp collisions may differ from both the conventional thermal model and the predictions of state-of-the-art event generators. These findings may also imply a violation of the common assumption that the $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ spectra of heavy quarks in heavy-ion collisions are purely thermal. This implies the necessity of developing a new theoretical framework to describe heavy quark production in pp collisions, which could also enhance the understanding of the initial quark composition of the quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ion collisions. This study underscores the critical role of high-precision heavy-flavour measurements in high-energy $pp$ collisions for advancing our understanding of heavy quark generation in the quark-gluon plasma. This study introduces NuSPAN, a novel class of proximal mean networks (PMN) tailored for nonuniform sparse modeling, with specific focus on seismic reflectivity recovery. We establish the theoretical underpinnings of SpuSPAN, a specific instance of NuSPAN designed for handling sparsity-uncertainty. Building on this framework, we develop NuSPAN as a general PMN component capable of modeling a broad spectrum of learning tasks, utilizing its proximal operator to facilitate training via any compatible proximal operator. Furthermore, we propose a reparameterization method that enhances the scalability of these models. The efficacy of NuSPAN is validated through numerical experiments on both synthesized and actual 3D seismic datasets, demonstrating its superiority over existing sparse modeling techniques. Additionally, we successfully apply NuSPAN to infer geological uncertainty within fault structures. To address the substantial memory requirements for large-scale data, we also introduce a distributed training approach based on parameter averaging, enabling parallel processing across GPUs. Finally, we demonstrate the method's effectiveness in recovering reflectivity from noisy, undersampled, and fault-disrupted seismic data using real-world 3D seismic datasets. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/NuSPAN.

We introduce a numerical framework for amalgamating operator distributions by analyzing their "wavefunctions" within the operator transfer matrix formalism. This approach is demonstrated on the critical Ising model, where the method achieves optimal accuracy and effectively suppresses both finite-size and finite-length (finite separation) artifacts. Universal corrections arising from finite length can significantly enhance the numerical precision of inner functions within operator amalgamated series. Furthermore, we successfully apply this technique to a c=7/16 Di Vito-Pakvasa model exhibiting non-local operator amalgamation. By employing inner operator amalgamation corrections, we determine the complete set of universal amplitudes for both operator correlation and amalgation series, thereby enabling high-precision extrapolations of the operator spectrum and their corresponding scaling dimensions. Additionally, we establish a direct numerical method to calculate the scaling dimensions of non-local operators, achieving an accuracy of delta h = 10^{-4} for the Haagerup model's non-local operator, despite the challenge of finite-length corrections. Finally, we demonstrate that operator amalgation corrections can be derived without prior knowledge of the operator product expansion algebra. These findings underscore the efficacy of inner operator amalgation and the universal nature of its corrections, suggesting that this approach holds broad generality and can be readily extended to other models, including those with non-integer central charges. Our technique is particularly valuable for accelerating convergence in operator amalgation series, which is essential for achieving the high-precision necessary to extract reliable conformal data, such as operator scaling dimensions. Furthermore, our work provides a robust numerical foundation for studying non-local operator scaling dimensions, a crucial element in reconstructing non-perturbative data, including formfactors, for non-local operators. These advancements are expected to significantly advance the study of two-dimensional quantum criticality. All code required to reproduce our results is publicly accessible. Historical documents present significant challenges for automatic grammatical labeling due to evolving vocabulary, shifted word meanings, and linguistic changes caused by historical events. To address this, we introduce a new method that enhances the reliability of part-of-speech tagging by utilizing a forecast of meaning shifts. This approach, implemented via a non-decreasing set-valued neural network, achieves results comparable to standard deterministic tagging systems, such as those produced by GATE's Annotator2. Additionally, the method demonstrates a substantial improvement in segmenting words that have undergone semantic transformation. The system is fully automated, requiring no manual intervention, and includes a detailed methodology for assessing performance through novel metrics designed for meaning representations. Furthermore, a large test dataset was created by applying two distinct pos-tagging systems to 19th-century Hans Reuter newspaper articles. To our knowledge, this represents the first time meaning-based post-editing systems have been evaluated on historical corpora in a fully automated manner. The source code and data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/koenbostoen/pos-shift-forecasting. Our method is anticipated to be a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners engaged in historical text analysis. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 outlines the historical labeling task and defines relevant concepts; Section 4 presents the proposed methodology; Section 5 details the experiments conducted; and Section 6 concludes with a discussion of the method's implications. The successful delivery of Software as a Service (SaaS) systems relies heavily on effectively managing requirements. This paper introduces a technique designed to support the development of requirements-driven SaaS by converting user expectations written in Natural Business Language (NBL) into formal specifications. This approach holds significant promise for SaaS development because it addresses user expectations rather than traditional requirements, thereby lowering entry barriers for non-expert stakeholders and fostering user involvement. The method was successfully applied to two real-world SaaS cases, System4 and Anyware, which handle software licensing and usage monitoring, respectively. Conventional two-qubit logic errors in quantum circuits, primarily leakage and entanglement failures, are typically mitigated using quantum error correction, which demands substantial resources. Here, we introduce a straightforward and efficient strategy to lower these logic error rates without the overhead of error correction. By employing a unitary transformation that conceals leakage states within the computational subspace during gate operations, we achieve this reduction through a method we term the concealed inverse protocol. This approach effectively suppresses leakage and enhances entanglement fidelity by an order of magnitude. Our analysis and experimental results, conducted on superconducting quantum circuits, demonstrate that the concealed inverse protocol is both feasible and scalable. This technique can be integrated into quantum apparatuses to directly improve gate performance and is applicable to various error-prone platforms. Furthermore, when combined with quantum error correction, the protocol can decrease the threshold for error correction. Consequently, it serves as a vital component for advancing towards fault-tolerant quantum computing. This paper extends the well-known Cartesian closed depiction of preorders to the setting of regular categories. Specifically, a preorder $\mathcal{P}$ is said to cocartesianly depict a regular category $\mathcal{E}$ via a functor $G \colon \mathcal{P} \to \mathcal{E}$ if $\mathcal{P}$ is a preordered set, $ob(G)$ is the identity on the underlying set of objects, and $G$ exhibits Cartesian closed structure relative to $\mathcal{E}$, meaning it preserves equivalence connections while mapping non-equivalent morphisms to isomorphisms. We demonstrate that such a cocartesian depiction exists if and only if $\mathcal{P}$ is a total preorder. Furthermore, we prove that two preorders $ \mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ are cocartesianly equivalent—meaning there exist totally preordered preorders and equivalence connections $F \colon \mathcal{P} \to \mathcal{Q}$ and $G \colon \mathcal{Q} \to \mathcal{P}$ such that $G \circ F$ and $F \circ G$ are identities—if and only if the associated categories $\mathcal{E}$ and $\mathcal{F}$ are equivalent. Finally, we examine preorders that admit cocartesian depictions and characterize those that are cocartesianly complete within the category of preordered sets. These findings represent a significant generalization of several classical results originally due to Lawvere. Additionally, the construction of cocartesian depictions provides a novel method for generating preordered sets, which we utilize to establish that every preorder possesses a cogroupoid reflection. We characterize this reflector and characterize preordered sets that are the images of such reflections. We also characterize depictions and preorders that yield equivalent categories under these reflections, and characterize depictions that commute with the reflection along with the necessary conditions on preorders and equivalence connections. Finally, we characterize depictions and preorders for which the functor mapping morphisms to their transitive closures commute with the cogroupoid reflector. Throughout this study, we have consistently linked concepts, results, and terminology within category theory to those within preordered set theory. This creates a parallel between our work and existing literature, where preorders are viewed either categorically or via their associated posets. A key challenge in analyzing multivariate data is modeling the dependencies among components, which is critical for predicting and assessing future risks. This study addresses extreme risks in the marine sector, specifically when environmental conditions like wind speed and water temperature are known. We introduce a new model for multivariate spatial extremes, termed the multivariate spatial conditional peak (MSCP) model. By representing the data through a copula and decomposing it into latent standard marginal components, we develop non-stationary Gaussian stochastic processes to capture these latent structures. We provide statistical tools for model estimation, including a closed-form expression for the joint density of the observations and a maximum likelihood parameter estimation method. Furthermore, we calculate the copula parameters and construct copula-based confidence sets. The spatial structures of the latent variables are modeled using Gaussian stochastic processes, with their parameters estimated via restricted maximum likelihood. Finally, we validate the utility of the MSCP model by assessing extreme risks in marine weather fields, such as sea surface wind speed and temperature, given specific environmental conditions. Our results demonstrate that the MSCP model effectively models multivariate spatial conditional peaks and accurately predicts extreme risks in the marine field under specified environmental states. This approach holds significant promise for supporting decisions in marine industries, including shipping and offshore wind power generation. Finally, an R package named MSCP, which implements the proposed model, is made available for users. This package features user-friendly functions for estimation, inference, and prediction, complete with default settings and illustrative examples. It can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenchenLi/MSCP. The package documentation and source code are also accessible at https://chenli.github.io/MSCP/. Current vision-language models (VLMs) are typically trained using input data comprised of images, images rendered from 3D data structures, and images paired with descriptive images. However, these existing models fail to fully leverage the strong complementary relationship between visual and linguistic information. This paper introduces a novel training strategy aimed at enhancing VLMs by incorporating training data that includes images paired with sentences specifically focused on visual details. We term this approach Visual-directed Text-guided Contrastive Language Image Pre-training (VT-CLIP). Our method utilizes two new datasets, MIMO-INST and MIMO-Visual, which offer image-text pairs where the text is directed toward visual content. Specifically, we employ a global contrastive loss to ensure the image encoders for standard and visual-directed text inputs share a consistent latent space, alongside a new loss function designed to minimize the description distance between images and text. We demonstrate that VT-CLIP yields significant performance improvements on standard image-text retrieval benchmarks, instar, object recognition tasks (ImageNet, CIFAR-100), and image-text generation tasks (COCO, MS-COCO Captions). Furthermore, our model exhibits a substantial reduction in hallucination rates on the MIMO-Visual dataset. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/1000x1000/VT-CLIP. Our results confirm that visual-directed text serves as an effective complement to free-text descriptions, thereby improving VLM performance and reducing hallucinations. Additionally, our findings indicate that VT-CLIP training models can generalize to free-text descriptions, achieving performance comparable to that of standard CLIP models. The implementation details of VT-CLIP, including data preparation and training procedures, can be found in our supplementary materials. Implementing matrix product state (MPS) algorithms on current noisy quantum hardware remains difficult because existing qubit-based architectures lack the native multi-qubit and single-qubit gates required for these simulations. This study presents a universal algorithm that maps matrix product operator (MPO) systems onto a restricted set of two-qubit and single-qubit operations, enabling execution on standard hardware. The method relies on a compact MPS representation of the operator graph, which facilitates the optimization of parameters for a short sequence of entangling gates. This sequence is managed by an adaptive loop that applies a limited set of multi-qubit and single-qubit operations to iteratively refine the MPO. The resulting algorithm is universal, applicable to any qubit system defined by an MPO. We demonstrate the approach using two key examples: first, a universal universal non-universal quantum algorithm for any qubit system defined by an MPO, and second, a universal quantum algorithm for any qubit system defined by an MPO, specifically the Heisenberg model. These instances validate the method's effectiveness in simulating qubit systems on existing hardware. Furthermore, the paper explores extensions to higher-dimensional models and potential adaptations for near-term quantum hardware. This research paves the way for universal quantum algorithms that are robust against hardware limitations and errors. Furthermore, we establish that the segments of the truncated suspension spectrum of the complex Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectrum are not generally Quinn modules, even when restricted to dimensions up to $2n-1$. Our findings are achieved through a systematic approach that refines the relative Adams spectral sequence featuring complex $K$-theory as the source for Ext groups. This method explicitly tracks the action of the commutative $K$-algebra $A$ on the spectral sequence. Additionally, we outline a strategy for proving that this technique extends to the truncation of the suspension spectrum of the product of a commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and a commutative $k$-algebra spectrum $X$. Numerous studies in radiology and histopathology now integrate deep learning models to enhance clinical decision-making. However, these efforts face two significant hurdles: a lack of standardization and insufficient reproducibility. The first challenge stems from the diverse and heterogeneous nature of input data in this rapidly evolving field, encompassing various image types, patient demographics, annotations, and performance metrics. While DICOM (Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine) is the established standard for medical imaging, it does not adequately cover non-image data or the specific results of deep learning models. To address this, we introduce Highdicom, a Python framework designed to provide a standardized encoding scheme that complements DICOM by utilizing extended tag sets and the HL7 FHIR (Health Level Seven International Financial Healthcare) information exchange standard. Highdicom facilitates data harmonization and ensures compatibility with DICOM and DICOMweb, thereby supporting the seamless integration of image data and deep learning outcomes into existing clinical workflows. We demonstrate the framework's utility through two representative deep learning applications in radiology and histopathology. Additionally, the companion paper by Demirciog et al. details the model implementation and evaluation using Highdicom-standardized data. We anticipate that our approach will significantly contribute to data harmonization and improve the reproducibility of clinical studies in radiology and histopathology. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/AI-Berlin/highdicom. This work is the companion paper to: Zeyad Demirciog, Alexander Maier, Alexander Enzinger, Alexander Langs, and Björn Menze. This paper introduces a new method for calculating entropy from the Einstein-Hilbert action at the horizon. By partitioning the spacetime manifold into two regions along the horizon and applying Noether charge, we derive the total entropy of black holes and degenerate horizons. The calculation involves integrating the surface expression of the Einstein-Hilbert action over spatial and temporal dimensions within the horizon's symmetry group. Instead of selecting an arbitrary integration path in time, we employ the Hamiltonian associated with the symmetry generator to represent this dimension. This approach successfully recovers the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy for both static and rotating black holes. Furthermore, when applied to a Schwarzschild black hole in 2+1 dimensions, the resulting entropy satisfies the first law of thermodynamics and commutes with the Virasoro algebra on the horizon, thereby confirming the validity of the proposed formula. Additionally, this method avoids the need to introduce a gauge field at the horizon, a step typically required in other frameworks. The research was conducted in the context of the "Black Hole Thermodynamics" course taught by Prof. Ted Jacobson at the University of Maryland. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly enhanced various bioinformatics applications, such as gene function prediction and sequence variation classification. Nevertheless, most of these approaches rely on hand-crafted features or deep models trained through extensive cross-validation. This paper introduces an unsupervised embedding of DNA sequences, generated via a deep neural network that learns sequence representations without requiring annotated training data. Specifically, we adapt a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) pre-trained on natural language to process nucleotide sequences. Utilizing a self-supervised pre-training approach fosters an LLM that inherently understands nucleotides and learns sequence representations from vast unlabeled datasets. We demonstrate that these unsupervised embeddings can be directly applied to downstream tasks involving single nucleotide polymorphisms and gene functions. Furthermore, we show that incorporating structural information, such as secondary structures, allows the model to predict representations for single nucleotide variations. Our results indicate that the LLM generates embeddings that capture single nucleotide differences and the resulting variations in nucleic acid sequences. Finally, we demonstrate that these unsupervised embeddings achieve competitive performance in downstream tasks relative to state-of-the-art methods. To our knowledge, this study represents the first application of LLMs to DNA sequence representation learning. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/DeepMind/alphafold_dna. Specifically, the MIT induces a surface modification that shifts the epitaxial alignment from (1102)-(0001) to (1040)-(1000). This study investigates the influence of such surface modifications on the MIT in V$_2$O$_3$ films by fabricating a heterostructure consisting of a single-crystal Al$_2$O$_3$ buffer layer, an amorphous AlO$_x$ interfacial layer, and a polycrystalline V$_2$O$_3$ top layer. X-ray diffraction analysis confirms that this heterostructure design eliminates surface-induced alignment effects, thereby enabling a MIT that closely resembles that of bulk V$_2$O$_3$. These findings underscore the critical role of interface and surface modifications in governing the MIT of epitaxial V$_2$O$_3$ films. Furthermore, the ability to engineer these interfaces in epitaxial heterostructures offers a pathway to control and manipulate the material's physical properties. Consequently, polycrystalline V$_2$O$_3$ films on amorphous AlO$_x$ and single-crystal Al$_2$O$_3$ buffers hold promise for nanoscale spintronic and neuromorphic device applications. This conclusion is supported by comprehensive characterization techniques, including X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and transport measurements. The resulting heterostructures present a novel platform for investigating the physics of the MIT in epitaxial V$_2$O$_3$ films. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that precise control over surface and interfacial properties is essential for manipulating the MIT in epitaxial V$_2$O$_3$ films. We introduce a thorough investigation of 2018 sub-prime-field exoplanets identified by the KMTNet Planetary Anomaly Investigation team, detailing the methodologies and outcomes of the project's most exhaustive analysis to date. Our study encompasses 118 microlensing events, from which we selected 20 planets exhibiting significant deviations from the anticipated planet fraction ($f_p \sim 10\%$) derived from statistical models. Utilizing the KMTTel telescope, we conducted follow-up observations of these anomalies to determine planetary host stars and refine planetary parameters. We present the final results for all 20 events, classifying them as planetary, stellar, or unconstrained based on our findings. Among the confirmed planetary candidates, 11 are hosted by M-dwarfs, with eight falling within the habitable zone; notably, four are the most massive planets found around M-dwarfs to date. The remaining candidates include two with low impact parameters ($b \sim 0.1$), one with a low mass host star ($M_* \sim 0.15 M_{\odot}$), and one potentially hosted by a brown dwarf. We also identified two events likely to be stellar, featuring high impact parameters ($b \sim 0.3-0.4$) and masses exceeding the stellar limit ($M_* \gtrsim 0.08 M_{\odot}$). Finally, we discuss the broader implications of this anomalous sample, suggesting that the KMTParallax survey may be uncovering a previously unexplored region of the planet fraction parameter space. The distribution of these anomalies indicates that either the planet fraction model underestimates the occurrence of high-planet fraction systems, or the true planet fraction is high but remains undetected due to the rarity of favorable anomalies in the dataset. This work demonstrates the efficacy of the Anomalous Sample Investigation approach for mitigating sample bias in statistical analyses. The full dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.0q08256. Our codebase can be accessed at https://github.com/KMTNet/planetary_anomaly_investigation. A primary focus is the development of spatially exact solution managers that stabilize specific modes within solution spaces, whether finite or infinite. Additionally, solution managers are constructed to address errors arising from numerical integration. The stability and accuracy of these algorithms are evaluated through various problem benchmarks, with an emphasis on the compatibility between modal bases and solution managers. Finally, the study explores the relationship between solution managers and adjoint methods, demonstrating how solution manifold reduction techniques can be enhanced by utilizing the compression properties inherent in these managers. This study evaluates the performance of 21 machine learning algorithms using 11 performance metrics across 120 distinct data configurations derived from 18 datasets. These configurations vary by 4 features: Network, Amount, Payee, and Transaction Duration. Feature significance was evaluated using 12 different methods. Key findings include: (1) Linear models (Ridge, Lasso, KNN Regressor) and Random Forests demonstrate the strongest predictive capability, with Random Forests yielding the most interpretable results; (2) Transaction duration is the most significant feature for 50% of the metrics, followed by network for 25%, though no single feature dominates across all metrics; (3) Feature interactions prove critical for Random Forest classification but are less dominant in other methods. This comprehensive analysis of algorithms, features, and interactions offers valuable insights for credit risk modeling and fraud detection systems. The study's feature-level results are particularly beneficial for feature engineering, while its algorithmic evaluations support the selection of methods for new ML models. Additionally, the analysis identifies limitations of both traditional and deep learning approaches, with all code and data accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2001/ML-Algorithms-Assessment-and-Feature-Significance-Analysis. We anticipate this evaluation will serve as a foundational step for future research in financial machine learning.

This paper introduces a family of colorful Dyck paths derived from standard Dyck path theory, reinterpreting it within the framework of q-rook theory. By substituting non-attacking rooks with "colorful" rooks, we develop colorful symmetric functions that encode the statistics of both colorful Dyck paths and colorful q-rook tables. We investigate the structure and combinatorial properties of these functions and establish a connection between colorful and standard Dyck paths via a bijection that preserves specific statistics. Notably, this approach extends previous findings by proving that the poset of colorful Dyck paths is isomorphic to the poset of standard Dyck paths under the weak order relation, while simultaneously preserving Majumdar's statistics. Finally, we provide explicit combinatorial interpretations for certain special cases, such as Shu-Otsuka's functions. As an application, we demonstrate that for any two colorful symmetric functions $f$ and $g$, if $g$ is Schur-positive with respect to $f$, then $f$ and $g$ are both Schur-positive with respect to one another. Furthermore, we show that the transition matrix between two colorful symmetric functions $f$ and $g$ is invertible if and only if $f$ is Schur-positive with respect to $g$. These findings generalize results by Chen et al. regarding classical symmetric functions. Finally, we offer initial numerical evidence suggesting that for any colorful symmetric function $f$, the coefficients of $f$ are unimodal. Additional details regarding the proof of our main theorem can be found in our full paper. Interested readers are encouraged to consult our arXiv version for the complete details.

This paper introduces an architecture designed to address orientation invariance within convolutional neural networks (CNNs). We propose that a network achieves invariance to a specific feature transformation if the representation remaining after applying the transformation is merely a reordering of the original, indicating that the transformation leaves the set of coefficients invariant. We provide a detailed examination of these invariant sets and their corresponding transformed features. Subsequently, we define a family of convolutional architectures built upon these invariant sets, which we contend offers distinct advantages over traditional CNNs. Specifically, we demonstrate that certain architectures in this family exhibit invariance to a broader range of feature transformations than conventional CNNs. Finally, we present experimental results comparing our proposed architecture against a standard CNN on the MNIST dataset, showing that our approach not only achieves higher accuracy but also does so with reduced computational cost. Furthermore, we observe that a conventional CNN requires numerous layers to detect global symmetries, whereas our proposed architecture accomplishes this with significantly fewer layers. All code and datasets required to replicate the experiments are publicly accessible.

Let $G$ be a graph and $S \subseteq V(G)$. A list assignment $L$ on $G$ is termed an $S$-list assignment if $|L(v)| = |S|$ for every $v \in S$ and $|L(v)| = |S| - 1$ for $v \in V(G) \setminus S$. An $L$-coloring is defined as a proper vertex coloring using colors from the lists specified by $L$. In 2011, Borodin et al. demonstrated that if $G$ is a $k$-regular graph with a minimum degree $\delta(G) \ge k-1$ and a cycle $C$ exists such that $V(C) \subseteq S$, then an $L$-coloring always exists for any concave $k$-list assignment $L$ on $G$. This paper enhances this result by proving the following: Let $G$ be a $(k, d)$-nearly regular graph where $S \subseteq V(G)$ and $C$ is a cycle satisfying $V(C) \subseteq S$. Then, an $S$-list assignment $L$ admitting a $C$-coloring necessarily allows for an $L$-coloring, provided that every list $L(v)$ is a subset of a list $L'(v)$ of size $d+1$ for all $v \in S$. Furthermore, the theorem is complemented by a series of examples illustrating scenarios where the hypotheses cannot be relaxed. Finally, the paper concludes with an open question. The escalating global threat of infectious diseases has created an urgent need for highly efficient, highly accurate, and robust automated detection systems. Deep neural networks have emerged as a leading solution for this automation. However, deep learning models typically require extensive, well-labeled datasets for training, which are often unavailable in practical scenarios. Consequently, recent approaches have increasingly focused on high-capability networks that function effectively with minimal data. This study introduces a two-stage time-distributed capsule network that achieves state-of-the-art performance in classifying COVID-19, viral pneumonia, and normal cases from low-dose chest Computed Tomography (CT) scans without relying on any external auxiliary information. Specifically, the method first uses a time-distributed capsule network to extract features across various time steps, followed by a secondary network to synthesize these features and make the final prediction. The proposed framework was evaluated on low-dose CT images, and experimental results demonstrate its superior performance. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhongtao1214/TDCN.

This study introduces a two-stage approach for generating coarse quadrilateral meshes on CAD models with superior quality. The initial stage involves identifying an optimal set of vertices through a global linear optimization process constrained by whole numbers. The second stage refines these vertices using the Z2 quadrilateral algorithm to produce the final coarse mesh. Compared to quadrilateral meshes created by commercial software, the quadrilaterons resulting from this method exhibit greater regularity in angle distribution, element size, and quadrilateral orientation. Additionally, the method demonstrates robustness and efficiency when applied to CAD models of varying sizes and complexities. The proposed algorithm has been implemented in a open-source system, Qhull, which is accessible at http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~chrysan/. In this implementation, the input CAD model is represented as a watertight boundary complex, which can be converted from file formats such as STL, AMF, or XTF. The algorithm is executed by inputting the STL file name and the desired count of vertices for the initial coarse triangulation. Users can access the STL file at http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~chrysan/cadmodels/, where they may select any model, modify it, or submit a new one. Upon running the system, the system automatically generates and displays the quadrilateron file. Furthermore, commercial meshing software is also utilized to generate quadrilaterons, and the resulting files are compared. Ultimately, the high quality of the quadrilaterons and the method's applicability to diverse CAD models suggest its potential as a tool for finite element analysis. Future work will extend the system's capabilities to handle CAD models with internal structures. Keywords: CAD model, coarse mesh, quadrilateral algorithm, finite element analysis, quadrilateron. This paper derives analytical formulas for the sample moments of the sample correlation across all possible data arrangements. Using a systematic approach, we generalize existing formulas for the first moment, which were primarily limited to sets containing only odd or only even integers. Our derivation is based on the distribution of data arrangements, where each distribution is defined by the count of individual data arrangements. The resulting expressions for the $k$th moment of the sample data arrangement are polynomials of degree $k-1$ in the degree of the leading polynomial for the $k$th moment of the sample data arrangement. Furthermore, we provide expressions for the means, variances, skewness, and kurtosis of the sample data. Numerical examples are included to validate the analytical formulas for these moments. Additionally, we present expressions for the first four cumulants of the sample data, which can be derived from the cumulants of the sample data. Finally, numerical examples are provided to illustrate these expressions for the first four cumulants. We conclude that our formulas are applicable to any integer set, whether finite or infinite. Our approach offers an efficient method for estimating the moments of the sample correlation coefficient, a task that typically requires extensive numerical simulations. This method is particularly valuable for determining the moments of the Pearson's sample correlation coefficient, given its dominance over other sample correlation measures, such as Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, in the literature. Our technique is effective for calculating moments up to at least the eighth order. The efficiency gained by deriving analytical formulas for the moments of the sample correlation coefficient over data arrangements stems from the ability to express these moments as polynomials, thereby simplifying the computational burden. We have made the computer code used for these derivations publicly available. We anticipate that our approach will serve as a foundation for future research. Specifically, our formulas can be adapted to calculate the moments of the asymptotic distribution of the sample correlation coefficient, which is crucial for statistical inference. Additionally, our approach can be extended to estimate the moments of the rank correlation coefficient, which remains under-researched compared to the well-studied moments of the Pearson's sample correlation coefficient. Finally, our formulas can be utilized to derive the moments of the permutation distribution of the sample correlation coefficient, which is essential for conducting permutation tests. This study addresses the uniform stabilization of 3D Navier-Stokes equations, originally formulated by Foias, Jones, and Li, through finite-dimensional localized feedback controls. The control region is located within a bounded domain $\Omega$, and the feedback mechanism utilizes low-frequency components of the velocity field. By applying the Foias-Jones-Li framework alongside the Foias-Temam methodology, the authors achieve uniform stabilization across $H^1$ norms defined in critical $L^p$ spaces. This approach extends uniformly to a broader class of smooth Besov spaces designated as "critical." These critical spaces align with those identified by Koch and Smith for optimal regularity in the Cauchy problem for the Navier-Stokes equations. Furthermore, the stabilization remains uniform even when initial data are drawn from these critical spaces, a result that also applies to certain turbulent scenarios. Notably, the control region $\Omega_c$ can be positioned within an arbitrarily small subdomain, demonstrating that this small region contains essential information sufficient to stabilize the entire domain $\bar{\Omega}$. These findings serve as a rigorous foundation for the hypothesis that observing and controlling the flow within a vanishingly small region is sufficient to stabilize the entire fluid domain. Additionally, several related problems are addressed by the methods employed. Finally, these results provide a substantial contribution to the ongoing investigation into whether a finite-dimensional observer located in a small region can monitor the entire domain $\bar{\Omega}$. We introduce LitMind Lexicon, a web-based dictionary designed to support writers in selecting appropriate vocabulary. This free, open-source platform enables users to define neologisms and share them, making these new terms instantly searchable and visible to the community. The system integrates natural language processing techniques to suggest existing words based on context and definition input, and it allows for the generation of personalized word suggestions tailored to each user's submitted contexts. Writers can input contextual sentences along with definitions to explore the dictionary, revealing terms that are either searchable or to be added by the community. The platform's functionality is driven by a web application built with Python and Django, which implements the described algorithms. Furthermore, to enhance the user experience, the team has developed the Lexicon API, which provides the backend services directly in the browser. Recent studies have explored using local surrogates to interpret black-box function predictions. However, the statistical nature of these methods causes them to overestimate uncertainty in individual predictions and to violate compliance and stability within their explanations. Compliance refers to consistency across multiple queries for the same input, while stability denotes small variations in output across a neighborhood of similar inputs. This work investigates these properties within the LIME-RS recommender interpretation framework. We first outline a theoretical uncertainty quantification approach for local surrogates, proving that LIME-RS violates this framework by being both compliant and stable. We demonstrate that these issues stem from the sampling distribution LIME-RS employs for local analogs and that they can be mitigated by utilizing a weighted, non-uniform sampling distribution. Our theoretical findings are supported by computational experiments on standard recommendation benchmark datasets. These results offer both a theoretical and practical foundation for enhancing the reliability of LIME-RS interpretations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of these improvements by facilitating more effective recommendation lists and enabling greater trust in LIME-RS explanations. Finally, we propose several potential research directions for improving the reliability of other local surrogate frameworks. To support this research, we have made our code and uncertainty quantification implementation available on GitHub. This repository also includes an extended version of the paper's experimental code and results for the proposed research directions. Specifically, the included results show that the proposed improvements enable more effective recommendation lists and generate more trustworthy LIME-RS explanations. In semiconductor quantum wells (SQWs) incorporating heavy doping, near-surface ultra-doped InAs SQWs (UDSQWs) represent a promising avenue for enhancing device performance. The ultra-doped layer functions as an effective metallic back gate, enabling precise tuning of the Fermi level and facilitating TCO-free fabrication. This letter demonstrates the fabrication of near-surface InAs UDSQWs on InP substrates and the growth of GaSb barriers on top. We experimentally investigate how varying barrier thicknesses influence the fixation of the Fermi level within the conduction band of these structures. Our findings confirm that increasing the barrier thickness in growth-directionally stacked SQWs shifts the Fermi level deeper into the conduction band, as indicated by an increase in photoluminescence intensity. Furthermore, our results indicate that the UDQSW architecture maintains a high two-dimensional carrier concentration even after growth, with a minimal impact on planar quality. These UDSQW-based heterostructures are considered promising candidates for future spintronic applications. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for the fabrication of high-performance spintronic devices. To achieve high-performance spin qubits, it is essential to maintain a high concentration of two-dimensional (2D) carriers within the quantum dot. Although regional correspondence loss has proven effective in improving the structural integrity of generated images, particularly in complex scenarios like object occlusion, its efficacy in the regional learning framework of GAN distillation remains uncertain. This paper investigates the resilience of the generator and discriminator against adversarial attacks during joint training to determine when applying this loss is advantageous. Our findings indicate that while regional correspondence loss significantly enhances the resilience of both networks in standard training, it offers no improvement in resilient learning environments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying this loss to the discriminator within regional learning framework GAN distillation can actually degrade the performance of both generators. To address these challenges, we propose an algorithm that adaptively regulates the correspondence loss to align regional features and mitigate noise. This method boosts performance in both standard and resilient scenarios, achieving a 4.4% increase in region similarity score and a 10.5% boost in Frechet Inception Score (FID) on CIFAR-10, with corresponding gains of 12.2% and 22.6% on CelebA. Additionally, empirical evidence confirms that our method consistently improves the performance of both single and multiple distilled generators across both standard and resilient settings. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/1229chen/ResRegional.

This study derives Rapid Sinkhorn, a novel and highly efficient algorithm for approximating optimal transport among $N$ distributions, each defined by a kernel matrix of size $M \times M$. By leveraging a specific structure identified by Carlier et al., where $M$ follows a growth pattern known as a "collinear triangular array," the method achieves a per-iteration cost that is nearly linear in $N$—specifically $O(N \log N)$—while maintaining quadratic cost under the "conditional growth" structure, a slightly more rigorous definition of collinearity. This collinear triangular array structure holds significant interest across diverse fields, ranging from image processing to scientific data involving particle distributions.

The approach also enables the construction of a highly accurate set of optimal maps in $O(N \log N)$ time, ensuring an arbitrary precision $\varepsilon$ without imposing an inverse-linear constraint on $\varepsilon$ that typically hinders scalability. This capability is realized through "Rapid Sinkhorn II," a refined version of the original method that delivers these results with high probability. The paper further establishes a hierarchy of structures that facilitates the precise computation of optimal transport, introducing "parental" and "grandparental" structures as intermediate steps between the collinear triangular array and the "pyramidal" structure. Finally, the work provides a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's performance, including a detailed study of its "Pyramidal Growth" pattern, which results in a linear-time optimal map construction. The study includes extensive numerical experiments and real-world applications, demonstrating the method's practical performance.
