An exact weak-coupling expansion for the static density response function of a Bose fluid yields insights into collective excitations and structural properties. Utilizing this method, we construct the spin response function to identify a signature of Pauli blocking within weakly interacting Bose fluids composed of composite particles, such as molecules or dimers. This serves as an indicator of emergent Pauli obstruction. We demonstrate that this phenomenon arises from the virtual creation of Pauli-blocked composite particles within the response function. Our analysis reveals that while the Pauli obstruction effect is exponentially weak at low temperatures in the leading order, it becomes algebraically significant in higher orders. We present the exact leading-order result and survey multiple higher orders, showing that they constructively contribute in specific low-temperature regimes. Consequently, we establish the existence of a crossover temperature that marks the onset of the algebraically dominated regime. Furthermore, we illustrate how higher-order effects influence the structural properties of the fluid. We provide weak-coupling series for the static structure factor and correlation length of bosonic excitations for a selection of molecules, along with the first derivative of the compressibility with respect to the interaction strength. Finally, we outline the necessary conditions for performing weak-coupling expansions on general response functions. Specifically, we show that an appropriate high-momentum asymptotic behavior of the interaction potential and the presence of a mass gap in the single-particle excitation spectrum are essential for achieving convergence in the perturbation series. These insights are broadly applicable to composite bosonic fluids in both three and two dimensions. Software testing is a labor-intensive and intricate endeavor. Over time, the industry has developed various testing strategies and practices to mitigate these challenges. However, despite this progress, there remains a lack of understanding regarding how software developers perceive testing processes and the extent to which they regard them as healthy or problematic. This study empirically investigates developers' viewpoints on the severity of these issues, along with their attitudes toward common testing practices. Specifically, we examined how developers assess the severity of three specific "testing odors": (1) test cases lacking defect detection capability, ( (2) test cases that are difficult to construct, and (3) developers lacking confidence in their ability to create effective tests. Our analysis involved a survey of 102 developers from eight software organizations. The findings reveal that the severity of these three odors is considered high by 41% to 62% of developers. Additionally, we analyzed the relationship between the odors and the participants' adherence to standard testing practices. The results indicate that the severity of testing odors varies depending on the testing practices employed by the developers. Consequently, this research offers valuable insights for addressing testing process challenges and enhancing the overall quality of testing procedures. It also aids in identifying specific areas where testing processes require improvement. Ultimately, this study underscores the necessity of adopting practices that minimize the impact of testing odors. By utilizing the identified practices, testing processes can be refined to reduce the severity of these issues. Our work also establishes a foundation for future research to develop techniques for detecting the presence of these odors within testing processes. This will enable the adoption of effective practices to eliminate or significantly reduce their severity. Our study addresses the limited empirical research on the impact of "testing odors" and their influence on the effectiveness of testing practices. This gap was identified through a systematic literature review conducted as part of this research. This work is particularly relevant for organizations aiming to improve their testing processes and increase their defect detection capacity. By implementing the suggested practices, organizations can achieve these goals. Furthermore, our research offers insights into the practices that developers consider most effective for eliminating or minimizing the severity of these odors. This enables the identification of practices that yield the greatest benefits for both developers and end-users. Finally, our research highlights the need for further empirical studies to investigate the impact of specific practices on the severity of these odors. Such studies would provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of various practices in addressing testing process challenges. Additionally, our research supports the growing body of work on the effectiveness of addressing testing odors

We introduce KKMCee, a Monte Carlo event generator designed for electron-positron annihilation into lepton and quark pairs, incorporating the effects of hadronization and initial- and final-state radiation. Built upon the exact tree-level $e^+e^- \to q\bar{q}$ and $e^+e^- \to \mu^+\mu^-$ matrix elements, theee (ee) module calculates and resums soft and hard multi-photon radiation to $\mathcal{O}( \alpha^2 )$. It further includes soft and hard photon radiation from final-state leptons, as well as soft photon radiation from initial-state leptons, all of which are collectively resummed to all orders in the fine structure constant. Initial- and final-state beamstrahlung, along with beam polarization, are incorporated to all orders in $\alpha_{em}$. Additionally, the quark and lepton masses are included to all orders, as are beam energy spread, beam crossing angle, and a parton-shower module for final-state leptons and quarks. Calculating a tensor's singular value decomposition (SVD) is a fundamental task in various fields, including quantum physics, machine learning, and data mining. However, current efficient algorithms struggle with large-scale tensors, often requiring multiple passes over the data. This passage constraint restricts their use to scenarios where the entire dataset fits into main memory. This limitation motivates the need for more efficient algorithms capable of unrestricted passes over large-scale data, such as those residing on hard drives or distributed systems. This limitation also hinders the practical evaluation of existing algorithms, which are typically tested only on small-scale tensors. This paper introduces a novel stochastic algorithm for tensor SVD that operates without restrictions on pass count, applicable to large-scale tensors stored on disk systems. The method is straightforward, enabling parallel implementation with minimal communication overhead. Additionally, extensive numerical experiments are conducted on large-scale tensors stored in disk systems to validate the algorithm's performance. Furthermore, the study includes a practical analysis of data distribution and an assessment of the algorithm's scalability within high-performance computing environments. Finally, examples from quantum physics and machine learning illustrate the algorithm's practical utility. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/kyuhyunlee/TensorSVD}. Our findings suggest that stochastic algorithms, including the one proposed here, require only a few passes over data to achieve sufficient accuracy for practical applications, and these passes can be distributed in parallel across high-performance computing systems. Consequently, stochastic algorithms may prove more practical for large-scale data than deterministic ones, which often demand excessive computational resources. Furthermore, a practical examination of large-scale data reveals that data compression is frequently necessary to manage the input size. Therefore, this paper also explores tensor SVD applications alongside tensor compression. The results indicate that stochastic algorithms for tensor SVD and compression can significantly reduce data volume in large-scale datasets. Overall, our research demonstrates that stochastic algorithms, such as the proposed method for tensor SVD, serve as a highly effective tool for large-scale data analysis. Finally, the authors aim to extend and refine these methods for broader data analysis applications. To achieve this, this paper also introduces a tensor-based data analysis system. While numerous methods exist for static graph node embedding, developing node embeddings on evolving graphs presents unique challenges due to the need to manage both temporal signals and the evolution of edges. This paper reviews various approaches for embedding evolving graphs, highlighting their key differences and the specific challenges they address. Additionally, we present a summary table comparing these techniques across multiple criteria and discuss emerging challenges and opportunities in evolving graph embedding. We conclude that future research should address, among other issues, the lack of comprehensive benchmarks, which would facilitate more effective comparisons among evolving graph embedding methods. Furthermore, evolving graphs often exhibit functional relationships between nodes, suggesting a need for functional embedding. We also highlight several functional embedding techniques, which differ from standard evolving graph embeddings in several ways. Given their distinct characteristics and the distinct problems they solve, functional embeddings on evolving graphs should be regarded as a separate category. Finally, we identify current functional embedding techniques and propose that functional embeddings on dynamic-attributed graphs represent a promising future research direction. To the best of our knowledge, this survey is the first of its kind. We anticipate it will assist researchers in understanding evolving graph embeddings and functional embeddings, as well as guide future research efforts. We present findings from an analysis of the unbound nature of the $^7$H nucleus, utilizing a model where the $^7$H ground state functions as a resonance built upon the core configuration of a $^3$H nucleus paired with four neutrons. The $^7$H bound-state problem is formulated using the four-nucleon cluster model, while the $^3$H+4n resonant state is defined by its formation width, derived through a variant of the Dirac delta interaction method. This resonant state exhibits strong coupling among the four-nucleon clusters, with dominant two-nucleon interactions that are not suppressed by spin-orbit effects. The study calculates the energy spectrum, wave functions, and binding energies for the $^7$H system, comparing these results with experimental data. This paper examines the Nirenberg problem on the half-sphere $S^{n}_{+}$. Specifically, it establishes the Nirenberg problem as solvable for even dimensions $n \in \{4,6,\ldots \}$ under mild conditions, and imposes no additional constraints for dimension $n=3$. The proof relies fundamentally on a non-trivial blow-up analysis. The nontangentiality of the blow-ups is derived from a novel Carleman-type estimate featuring a weighted normal derivative. This estimate represents the primary contribution of the work and holds independent significance. The result extends the findings of del Pino-Kowalczyk-Vázquez (Annals of Mathematics 174, 2011) from the sphere to the half-sphere. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate the existence of a nontrivial solution to a related linearized problem on the half-sphere, which serves as the starting point for the blow-up analysis. The paper begins with an exposition of the Penfield-Gidas-Spruck (J. Differential Geometry 19, 1984) non-existence theorem on the sphere, followed by an exposition of the Li-Sterbenz (Adv. Math. 226, 2011) theorem regarding the solvability of the Nirenberg problem on half-spheres. The exposition of the Penfield-Gidas-Spruck theorem is tailored to facilitate the subsequent proof of the Li-Sterbenz theorem. The exposition of the Li-Sterbenz theorem is designed to provide the reader with a clear understanding of how to prove the nontangentiality of the blow-ups. The blow-up analysis is conducted using the tools introduced in the exposition, followed by a blow-up argument. Finally, the blow-up analysis is completed by addressing the remaining gaps. The entire argument is presented in a self-contained manner, with the exposition forming the basis of the paper's contribution. The results are expected to be applicable to various geometric problems. The paper concludes with several open questions and conjectures. Some of these were subsequently resolved in the author's thesis, while others remain unresolved. The exposition is also intended to serve as a resource for researchers working on the nontangentiality of the blow-ups. The Carleman-type estimate is presented in a self-contained manner. The paper concludes with the author's final remarks. The reader is expected to gain a deeper understanding of the topic and to be inspired to pursue further research in the area. The author

The efficacy of deep learning models is heavily reliant on the quality of their learned representations. Although various existing techniques have attempted to optimize these representations directly via similarity metrics—such as Maximize Information Necessity (MAXIM)—they often fail to fully leverage model capacity, resulting in overly loose lower bounds. This study introduces a novel representation learning framework that establishes functional similarity through an iterative, coupled training of two models: a feature learner and a score maximizer. By calculating the Sinkhorn distance between feature sets, we construct an entropy-based objective that optimizes the feature learner's representations. We demonstrate the model's effectiveness across representative datasets, showing that our approach outperforms prior methods in both qualitative and quantitative aspects, such as classification transfer and clustering. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYuan1997/R3.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, contact tracing was implemented to curb the transmission of SARS-CoV-2. However, its effectiveness is often constrained by the limited reach of public health agencies and public fatigue. To address this, governments have increasingly adopted open data strategies, enabling third parties to contribute to tracing efforts. This study evaluates how the integration of regional open data and information sharing among tracing components affects overall performance. Using a computational model, we simulated various open data interventions in England, incorporating realistic data collection rates and inter-agency sharing mechanisms. Our results indicate that England's current open data policy could potentially double the impact of contact tracing. Nevertheless, the success of such initiatives depends on effective public engagement, which poses additional challenges. This research was conducted in close collaboration with the UK National Infection Services. Given the dynamic nature of the pandemic, this work also aims to provide a framework for future evaluations of similar interventions. Consequently, we plan to make the code and models public to facilitate their application to other diseases and contexts. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this work, including the analysis of different network types, tracing strategies, and interventions. These model-based insights could guide public health policy decisions regarding open data initiatives in the future. Other code and materials referenced in this paper are available at https://github.com/epi-team/interconnected-epi. Specifically, the code used to generate the results presented here can be found at: https://github.com/epi-team/interconnected-epi/tree/main/interconnected-epi-england-results. This repository also includes a Jupyter notebook detailing the extensions discussed in this paper, along with a tutorial on how to utilize these tools to analyze other networks, diseases, and tracing interventions. Additional requests should be directed to https://github.com/epi-team. Additional materials related to this paper are hosted at: https://github.com/epi-team/interconnected-epi/tree/main/interconnected-epi-tutorials. These resources offer examples of various interventions, including those analyzed in this paper, as well as a variety of networks and diseases. We also provide multiple tracing strategies, ranging from those analyzed in this study to others, such as "test and trace" interventions. Finally, we have developed a web application to visualize the outcomes of these analyses: https://epi-team.github.io/interconnected-epi/. This platform allows users to explore different interventions, networks, and diseases, select specific open data policies, and observe the resulting changes in performance. Users

Determining the physical characteristics of open clusters is essential for comprehending stellar evolution and the formation of stellar systems. This study analyzes the kinematic properties of Melotte 72 (M72) by analyzing the two most populous cluster regions within the new Gaia DR2 catalog. Utilizing proper motions and parallaxes, we identify 18 probable cluster members. Our analysis yields an age of $1.0 \pm 0.1$ Gyr, a distance of $1.05 \pm 0.05$ kpc, and a line-of-sight velocity of $-10.0 \pm 0.1$ km/s. Additionally, we determine the cluster's distance modulus as $(m-M)_0 = 13.97 \pm 0.03$, with a line-of-sight velocity dispersion of $\sigma_{los} = 1.1 \pm 0.1$ km/s. These findings are compared against existing literature values, and the resulting heliocentric coordinates and other cluster parameters are presented. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for future studies. The data, including catalogs of members and non-members, are accessible at https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.10000.20000. We establish bounds on the average Betti numbers for complex Gaussian journeys within the sparse domain. A journey refers to a sublevel set formed by a function linked to a Hermitian matrix, encompassing both diagonal and off-diagonal elements; this model integrates the random matrix model for isolated nodes with that for independent edge lengths. In this context, a journey's Betti number corresponds to a homology group of the resulting sublevel set. Our approach unifies techniques from prior research regarding isolated nodes and off-diagonal terms, yielding a more streamlined proof of the former and a new, initial bound on the latter. Specifically, we demonstrate that the average Betti number is bounded by $O(n^{\alpha+b+\epsilon})$, where $n$ represents the matrix dimension, $\alpha$ is the off-diagonal bound, $b$ is the diagonal bound, and $\epsilon$ is an arbitrarily small constant. This result holds for functions comprising monomials of degree $b$ and $\alpha$. Furthermore, when off-diagonal terms are absent, this finding refines the bound previously established by Lov\'asz. These results are applicable to graphs exhibiting the "no short cycles" property. Finally, we outline an open question concerning the extension of these bounds to scenarios involving higher-order interactions. This inquiry holds significance for network dynamics, as it addresses the likelihood of clustering and synchronization. The proof relies on techniques from probabilistic combinatorics, sparse random matrix theory, and persistent homology. Additionally, our methodology introduces a novel bound on resolvent traces in the sparse domain, which demonstrates its robustness and distinctiveness. We also discuss an alternative approach to our resolution, which leverages findings from both probabilistic combinatorics and persistent homology. Achieving accurate object localization in unstructured environments necessitates a disparity between the object's coordinate system and the camera's system. While numerous research efforts have attempted to teach robots to interpret the scene captured by their eye-in-hand camera to derive meaningful insights, most studies rely on calibrated camera parameters and known camera positions to interpret this scene. However, calibrating eye-in-hand cameras presents significant challenges due to its dynamic nature. To overcome this dependency on calibration, we introduce a unique method for estimating camera position using only a single image. This approach utilizes the camera's internal structure and the known 3D coordinates of at least three objects within the viewed scene. Our core hypothesis is that a single image contains sufficient information for reliable position estimation, a claim we validate through extensive simulations and real-world experiments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this single-image method surpasses traditional calibration techniques by eliminating the need for a calibration pattern. Finally, we illustrate the method's practical utility by enabling a robot to manipulate an object solely based on a single image of that object. To our knowledge, this represents the first formulation of a camera adjustment problem centered around a solitary image. The proposed algorithm is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKlapp/SingleImageCameraAdjustment. Additionally, we have released a simulation environment for reproducing our experiments, available at https://github.com/SebastianKlapp/SingleImageCameraAdjustment-Replication. Our code and replication materials can be found at https://github.com/SebastianKlapp/SingleImageCameraAdjustment-Replication. Our team consists of Sebastian Klapp, Lukas Schaefer, and Lukas Schaefer. Our objective is to facilitate autonomous object manipulation using a single image, thereby simplifying the interpretation process and removing the requirement for calibration. Our approach is grounded in a robust algorithm that accurately predicts camera position from a single image, supported by a comprehensive evaluation involving over 100 simulations and 10 physical experiments. We have tested our method on two distinct manipulators: a UR5 equipped with a JACO2 joint and a UR10 with a Schunk FG500 gripper. The following sections detail the method, its evaluation, and its application to the described manipulation tasks. We hope readers find our method valuable for their own research endeavors. Our method is robust and effective, as demonstrated by its success in enabling accurate object localization without calibration using only a single image. We believe this method will be highly valuable to the research community. Our method is effective and efficient

This paper introduces a novel vertex divider designed to enhance the performance of several treewidth-based algorithms, including exact solutions, CEGMR, and approximation methods. These techniques partition the vertex set $V$ of a graph $G$ into four V-shaped minor models, ensuring that any V-shaped query involving specific vertex subsets can be resolved by querying the vertex bags of an elimination scheme. We demonstrate that our divider yields superior performance compared to existing dividers for these algorithms. Furthermore, we apply our four-way divider to a treewidth-based approach for the Steiner Tree problem, producing high-quality solutions for diverse instances, particularly when the Steiner ratio is close to 1. Additionally, we successfully solve instances that were previously intractable for the CEGMR algorithm. Finally, we examine the relationship between our four-way divider and the existing $k$-way dividers utilized in hierarchical elimination schemes. We examine the modeling of network data, specifically focusing on group effects and power-law degree distributions. Our analysis reveals that standard dyadic-level covariates are insufficient for explaining group-level attributes, such as why certain groups are more densely interconnected than others. To address this, we propose augmenting the network vector with a new group influence vector, under the assumption that each group's connection propensity toward other groups is governed by a logit model. Furthermore, we examine scenarios involving sparsely sampled networks within groups and varying sample sizes across groups and across networks. We assess these models using synthetic data and, where applicable, public data, while also comparing our approach against methods found in the literature. Finally, we conclude by discussing the advantages and limitations of group influence alongside other critical considerations when working with network data grouped by common attributes. **Keywords:** Heterogeneous networks, inferred networks, network data, modeling, group effects, power laws, sparsity, public data. **Acknowledgments:** We thank the anonymous reviewers for their insightful comments, which significantly improved the manuscript. This paper introduces a method for evaluating and mitigating errors in solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). The approach relies on the fundamental principle that any solution satisfying the governing equations will yield zero when substituted into the residual expression. By reformulating the target problem as an initial-value system, we develop a technique to assess and control errors in PINN solutions. This method enables an estimation of the error magnitude at every point within the solution domain, thereby facilitating a more precise understanding of the accuracy achieved by PINNs. Additionally, we propose a strategy to enhance solution accuracy by adjusting the training data selection process. Our approach is validated using an initial-value problem involving the one-dimensional advection equation. Results demonstrate that our method achieves an order-of-magnitude improvement in solution accuracy compared to PINNs applied without these modifications. Finally, we conclude that this technique is applicable to any well-posed initial-value problem, regardless of whether it is linear or non-linear, conservative or non-conservative. However, for inverse problems characterized by ill-posed initial conditions, PINNs inherently rely on the data itself to resolve the issue, rendering our proposed modifications ineffective for such scenarios. Consequently, this study focuses exclusively on mistake analysis for initial-value problems to establish a foundation for future work aimed at extending these methods to inverse problems. Future research will explore leveraging this capability to evaluate and improve the effectiveness of various regularization strategies employed in PINNs for inverse problems. Keywords: physics-informed neural networks, mistake analysis, mistake assessment, mistake mitigation. AMS classification: 65L12, 65L20, 65L70, 65N30, 65N35.

Atmospheric contamination significantly influences human health, making its study essential for advancing disease prevention and control. This atmosphere, influenced by geographical, environmental, and socio-economic factors, is not uniform; instead, pollutants disperse in complex patterns, creating spatial heterogeneity in health risks. Consequently, researchers must identify locations with elevated risks to inform public health strategies. Geostatistics and machine learning are pivotal tools for analyzing spatial data, yet they often struggle to incorporate real-time atmospheric data. This thesis addresses this limitation by developing novel contamination models that integrate spatial-temporal artificial intelligence with traditional geostatistical frameworks. Validated against spatial datasets, these new models enable the rapid generation of spatial risk maps, facilitating informed decision-making. Their efficacy was demonstrated through two case studies: the first focused on the 2019 COVID-19 outbreak in Wuhan, China, while the second examined occupational lung diseases in Santiago, Chile. The spatial-temporal AI models were trained on historical atmospheric pollution records and validated using disease-related data. Ultimately, these findings provide innovative methodologies and frameworks that can be extended to other regions and diseases, thereby enhancing disease prevention and control efforts. Key words: Atmospheric contamination, Artificial intelligence, Geostatistics, Epidemiology, Spatial-temporal.

We suggest a robust approach for distinguishing Majorana modes from conventional superconducting Andreev bound states by employing tunneling electrodes subjected to ohmic dissipation. Our findings indicate that while ordinary superconducting Andreev bound state peaks are suppressed due to ohmic dissipation, peaks associated with Andreev bound states trapped in zero modes remain intact. This dissipation effect is incorporated into a tunneling model that includes a zero mode, utilizing parameters for electron temperature and ohmic dissipation strength that are experimentally feasible. Furthermore, we offer a practical strategy for analyzing tunneling data by adjusting these two parameters. We conclude that simultaneously fitting multiple peaks and accounting for ohmic dissipation is more dependable than merely searching for negative-differential-conductance peaks to confirm the existence of Majorana modes. Consequently, the simultaneous verification of Majorana and ordinary Andreev bound states is essential to definitively establish the presence of Majorana modes. Finally, we emphasize the critical role of the tunnel electrode in tunneling spectroscopy and propose a specific design that enables the observation of ohmic dissipation effects. This design involves inserting a thin metal film into the tunneling electrode to achieve the necessary resistance for inducing dissipation. We anticipate that these proposed designs and analytical methods will significantly aid in correctly identifying and verifying Majorana modes. Specifically, we have already utilized a similar tunneling electrode configuration to successfully observe the effects of ohmic dissipation. Additionally, we have successfully detected Majorana peaks in samples featuring both proximal and intrinsic superconductivity, providing strong evidence that ohmic dissipation does not destroy Majorana modes. These results offer compelling proof that superconducting zero modes can persist under conditions of ohmic dissipation. Ultimately, we believe that rigorously differentiating between ordinary and proximal superconducting Andreev bound states is crucial for the definitive confirmation of Majorana modes. Therefore, we strongly recommend that all future experiments regarding Majorana modes incorporate a mechanism to induce ohmic dissipation. Finally, we propose a specific technique for observing the dissipation effect on tunneling peaks by utilizing resistive electrodes, such as the thin metal film configuration mentioned above. We firmly believe that integrating ohmic dissipation into tunneling electrode structures is essential for accurately identifying Majorana modes. Furthermore, we have observed the dissipation effect on tunneling peaks using a tunneling electrode with a thin metal film. Linear contextual bandits have become a cornerstone of online decision-making systems. Although most current research assumes a common action space where all agents share the same features, real-world applications often involve distinct action spaces, such as different online ads possessing unique feature structures. This paper demonstrates that standard methods relying on a common space lead to significantly inflated false positive rates in scientific inference. We then examine several bandit formulations with divergent action spaces, analyzing their implications for inference. Our primary focus is on two distinct setups: one featuring overlapping action spaces and another where spaces are completely separate. To address the issue of false positives, we propose a novel linear bandits inference framework capable of handling both common and divergent action spaces. Extensive simulations indicate that our method achieves superior statistical power compared to existing approaches while maintaining a controlled false positive rate. Finally, we apply our method to a real-world linear budget allocation problem, highlighting the critical need for robust inference techniques in practical contexts. This study demonstrates that the orbital Hall effect (OHE) serves as a substitute for the valley Hall effect (VH) in Landau-boosted graphene, which remains massless even under strong static strain fields. While boosting generally induces a nontrivial valley curvature in spin-orbit-coupled gapped graphene—enabling a boost-induced OHE (BOHE) without—this curvature vanishes in specific static strain configurations even at high velocities. In these scenarios, the system exhibits a unique property where both charge and valley currents disappear, leaving only the OHE as the remaining nontrivial response. This orbital current is attributed to the boost-induced change in band ordering, which generates a nontrivial curvature even when external static strain opens a valley-independent gap. Furthermore, the orbital Hall conductivity is not confined to integer multiples of the elementary charge; it can reach the quantum limit under particular strain conditions. These findings expand the understanding of nontrivial Hall responses in boosted chiral systems and suggest potential applications in field-free spin-orbitronics. Additionally, the proposed orbital Hall effect is expected to be observable in various two-dimensional materials, including graphene, graphene nanoribbons, graphene nanomeshes, silicene, and stanene. Finally, these results may be leveraged to investigate fundamental boost physics and boost symmetry breaking in relativistic field theories. Graph Neural Architectures (GNA) have recently demonstrated superior performance in classifying data contaminated by independent and identically distributed (I.I.D.) malware, which is randomly selected from large sets. However, their effectiveness diminishes significantly when malware is chosen adversarially, as the GNA must also generalize to threats unseen during training. This study investigates reinforcement learning (RL) within a graph-based neural architecture designed to detect intrusions in contaminated traffic. Specifically, we employ an off-policy RL algorithm to train the neural architecture, enabling the system to identify significantly greater volumes of advanced malware compared to standard models trained solely on selected features. Furthermore, utilizing RL to optimize weight parameters in a Q-learning context further enhances detection capabilities. Our results indicate that this approach not only avoids overfitting to extensive sets of I.I.D. malware but also effectively identifies sneakier, adaptive malware variants that learn to bypass traditional network security mechanisms. This research holds practical value for network operators, as it demonstrates the ability to detect highly sophisticated malware in production environments. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of detection rates regarding both true positives and false positives. We evaluate our proposed Q-learning algorithm against established models and baseline methods, demonstrating that our approach significantly surpasses existing solutions in classifying new, advanced malware samples. This enables network operators to mitigate risks from emerging malware in production settings without compromising the ability to detect previously identified malware families. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of reinforcement learning for data contamination detection within graph-based neural architectures. Our contributions include: (i) an in-depth analysis of the impact of graph features on the detection of intrusive malware samples; (ii) a comparison of graph-based neural architectures against established models and baselines for malware classification; and (iii) the application of reinforcement learning to enhance the detection of intrusive malware samples. Catalogue alignment serves as a critical preprocessing stage in large-scale spectroscopic surveys, yet it presents significant challenges due to systematic errors from optical distortions and non-linear detector responses. These issues complicate the identification of sources across multiple images, making it difficult to match objects between different catalogues. To address this, we introduce a novel method that leverages external photometric data to model source positions, thereby improving the construction of source lists. By utilizing data from the Gaia Data Release 2, we demonstrate that modeling sources with external photometry significantly enhances accuracy. Specifically, this approach reduces the number of spurious matches by a factor of 1,000 and 20, respectively, when alignging QSOs and galaxies between the 2MASS and Gaia catalogues. Furthermore, the integration of external photometry facilitates the modeling of distorted source locations, enabling the detection of rare sources that traditional methods miss. Consequently, this technique is particularly valuable for rare source searches, as it allows for the discovery of distorted objects that can be precisely aligned with rare sources in other catalogues. Overall, our findings indicate that augmenting source position models with external photometric data is essential for catalogue alignment in current and future spectroscopic surveys. This method is now publicly accessible through our GitHub repository. Additionally, we have developed a new QSO catalogue by aligning the 2MASS and WISE all-sky infrared surveys with Gaia DR2, which can be downloaded from the same repository. This catalogue features improved completeness and accuracy in matching QSOs between the infrared surveys and Gaia, offering better source matching, more accurate source modeling, and superior source recovery compared to existing QSO catalogues. We anticipate that this new QSO catalogue will prove beneficial for both scientific research and future studies. Our work also underscores the necessity of incorporating external photometric data for source position modeling in future surveys, which could facilitate catalogues that exploit external photometric information. In this context, we propose the Catalogue Alignment by Enhancing QSOs (CAEQ) project, which employs our proposed method to create QSO catalogues. This initiative aims to advance QSO research by providing high-quality QSO catalogues for future surveys. The code for this project is available on our GitHub repository. Furthermore, we have identified a new population of QSOs in the 2MASS-Gaia-WISE catalogues that exhibit unique properties, such as faintness and low completeness, distinguishing them from other QSO catalogs. Ontologies serve as formal frameworks for knowledge, typically visualized through hierarchical graphs that display class memberships and relationships. While hierarchical structures are effective for browsing and searching, they often obscure the rich, non-hierarchical aspects of class relationships. Current ontology visualization tools struggle to clearly and concisely represent these complexities. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new system designed to enable the clear visualization of class relationships within large ontologies containing thousands of classes. OntoPlot achieves a concise representation of class memberships by leveraging display space and implementing novel techniques to handle non-hierarchical relationships, including multiple relationships, cyclic structures, and relationships among unnamed entities. The effectiveness of OntoPlot is validated through a case study of the Gene Ontology and discussions with domain experts. The results demonstrate that OntoPlot significantly enhances the ability to identify concepts and their relationships, and that users can efficiently browse and explore large ontologies using this approach. We introduce a method to improve semi-supervised end-to-end speech transcription by incorporating a style-transfer based unsupervised domain adaptation strategy. In this framework we adapt the source language model which is trained on speech data from one domain (e.g., clear speech data) to the target domain (e.g., noisi speech data) using an unsupervised domain adaptation technique CycleGAN. We show that our model outperforms the baseline end-to-end speech to speech text recognition system on the wild domain by 1.7 WER. In addition we show that our model is able to generate an synthetic domain that is very close to the wild domain in terms of Mel Spectrogram distribution using Fréchet Inception Distance metric. Finally, we show that our technique is scalable to different amounts of speech data in different domains. On the other hand, we show that our technique is not able to help the end-to-end speech to text generation task as it generates sentences that are far from grammatical correct. This is due to the fact that grammaticality is not a property inherent to noisy speech data. We believe that future work should focus on modeling the penality for non-grammatical sentences using an external language model which is trained on large amount of text data. We believe that our work can help other areas of NLP and speech to automate the process of domain transfer and adaptation. This can help reduce the training and inference time and storage requirements of language models which are trained on large amount of clean data. This can be very helpful in deploying end-to-end speech to text systems in real world applications. This can also help other areas of computer vision and signal processing to automatically adapt to different domains without the need for manual labeling. Our code can be found at https://github.com/ashishkumar1234567/CycleGAN_Speech_to_Text.
Keywords: unsupervised domain adaptation, end-to-end speech to text, semi-supervised, CykleGAN, distributed training.

Navigating unexplored environments demands the ability to deduce and utilize environmental models for discovery and survival. This paper presents the first comprehensive experimental evaluation of a cell-probability map-based navigation framework, originally proposed by Kirk et al. (2019), designed for self-governing robot navigation. We analyze the algorithm's core components—environment discovery, deduced behavior, algorithmic initialization, and the discovery loop—by implementing them in Python and assessing their impact on navigation performance. Using Python's extensive library ecosystem, we achieve a 1000-fold speedup compared to a C++ implementation of the same algorithm. Our implementation faithfully represents the authors' original publication while also exploring further algorithmic extensions. These findings offer valuable insights for developing an autonomous navigation system capable of self-governed operation. Specifically, our analysis demonstrates that modifying the algorithm's original discovery loop can significantly enhance performance. We illustrate this with a discovery loop inspired by frontier-based exploration, which improves execution time by 300% and reduces executed code by 60% relative to the original implementation. Furthermore, we provide Python code for a novel adaptive initialization method that boosts execution speed by 300% and decreases executed code volume by 60% compared to the original approach. Finally, we offer open-source Python code for both the original and new algorithms, enabling researchers to easily evaluate, compare, and extend them. Additionally, we detail a custom, extensible evaluation framework designed to facilitate easy and direct assessment of similar algorithms. To our knowledge, this represents the first comprehensive analysis of this algorithmic family and offers the first Python implementations, significantly lowering the barrier to entry for researchers. We anticipate that our implementation and evaluation code will serve as a valuable resource for advancing self-governing robot navigation. Through both experimental and numerical means, we investigate how internal flexibility in soft molecules influences the Soret effect. Our findings indicate that the internal structure of these molecules significantly impacts the thermal diffusion coefficient, with the observed experimental increase in $s_T$ aligning with simulations that included internal flexibility. Additionally, we demonstrate that the mechanism driving the Soret effect in this context remains the same as in rigid systems: random thermal fluctuations induce local density variations, which are subsequently amplified by the preferential interaction between solute and solvent. Finally, we outline that the distinct internal structures of molecules can result in either an enhanced or diminished Soret coefficient. These insights deepen our comprehension of the complex behavior of flexible molecules in thermal gradients, offering valuable insights for the targeted delivery of flexible molecules across biological membranes. Specifically, our results suggest that the difficulty in experimentally determining a universal relationship between a molecule's internal flexibility/structure and its $s_T$ value stems from the fact that both the sign and magnitude of the Soret coefficient are influenced by the specific chemical nature of the solute and solvent. By explicitly separating solute-solute, solvent-solvent, and solute-solvent interactions, we show that our approach can be extended to various molecular models, including both rigid and flexible systems. This represents a significant advancement over prior studies, which were limited to analyzing interactions within a single, specific system. Our work paves the way for systematically investigating the impact of internal structure on thermal diffusion using both experimental and computational methods. Finally, we propose a general framework for understanding the influence of internal structure on $s_T$ that integrates our simulations with the framework established by Alim and co-workers for the diffusion coefficient. This approach offers a unified understanding of the mechanisms driving thermal fractionation of soft molecules under thermal gradients. Furthermore, it enables the prediction of the effect of internal flexibility on $s_T$ without requiring explicit knowledge of chemical interactions, thereby advancing our understanding of the intrinsic complexity of internal flexibility's influence on thermal diffusion. This capability offers a promising avenue for the targeted delivery of flexible molecules through biological membranes. Automated Composition Evaluation (ACE) involves automatically assessing student essays by comparing them to model answers. While current research primarily focuses on developing new network architectures, this study examines a different variable: the effectiveness of transformer-based language models. We tested 14 distinct pre-trained transformer language models using the same computational architecture and training data within a uniform evaluation pipeline. Our findings indicate that the choice of pre-trained model significantly impacts essay scoring performance, with BERT and CamemBERT outperforming other baselines for Chinese and French compositions, respectively. This work represents the first investigation into the effects of pre-trained language models for ACE, offering a new perspective that may help guide future research directions. Neural pedestrian networks frequently generate false positives during detection and identification due to limited domain adaptation and insufficient generalization. To address this, we introduce Box Reordering, an unsupervised method for filtering false positives in pedestrian identification networks through order inference. Our approach posits that non-matching instances can be identified by analyzing the relative positions of matching ones. Specifically, we frame box reordering as an order inference task that adapts a pretrained domain-invariant pedestrian network, leveraging its features and attribute predictions. By combining an energy function for order inference with an energy function for sequence identification, we derive an optimal dynamic programming-based inference algorithm. Experiments on a real-world dataset show that this method reduces false positives by 40% without significantly impacting true positives or true matches, while also enhancing pedestrian identification performance in terms of mean average precision and mAP. Notably, our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in crowded scenes and when visual similarity exists. The entire method is fully unsupervised, requiring no additional training or manual annotation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/chenchen1992/BoxReordering. Furthermore, we have released the first real-world benchmark dataset for box reordering under domain adaptation and unsupervised conditions. We anticipate this will advance future research on box reordering for pedestrian identification and offer a foundation for developing novel domain adaptation and unsupervised learning techniques for pedestrian attribution. The dataset can be downloaded here: https://github.com/chenchen1992/BoxReorderingAttribution. Additionally, we have made pedestrian attribution models accessible at https://github.com/chenchen1992/Pytorch-APAP. The corresponding paper titled "Pedestrian Attribution Learning: Unsupervised Pedestrian Identification with Box Reordering" is available at https://github.com/chenchen1992/Pytorch-APAP. Finally, we have released an attribution module for pedestrian identification featuring advanced box reordering techniques: https://github.com/chenchen1992/Pytorch-APAP. This paper introduces a novel approach to single-source audio super-resolution and enhancement by integrating images with vocoding. Specifically, we frame the enhancement of mono music recordings as a multi-scale representation learning challenge focused on audio spectrograms. To address this, we propose a network named the Audio Auto-Encoder with Multi-Scale Context (A2MC-NET), which captures audio features at various scales using an pyramid structure. These learned multi-scale features are then integrated and transformed into high-resolution spectrograms through an image transformation technique adapted from single-image super-resolution. Finally, an enhanced audio signal is reconstructed from the high-quality spectrogram via vocoding. Experiments demonstrate that our method surpasses existing methods in enhancing single-source music recordings, achieving top performance among top-ranked algorithms in the DARPA Speech Enhancement Challenge 2019 for music super-resolution and enhancement. Additionally, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art multi-source separation methods on the Slakh dataset. In both scenarios, the model requires minimal computational resources, making it suitable for deployment on edge devices. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/1000010000100001/MusicEnhancement. Furthermore, both our system and the top 10 methods from the DARPA SE C2 task are available at https://github.com/1000010000100001/DARPA_SE_C2. Researchers can utilize these resources to develop novel music enhancement algorithms and potentially achieve new state-of-the-art results in the competition. Human throwing is a complex skill vital for daily activities and professional sports. However, the specific factors influencing performance and their relative significance remain unclear. This study aimed to identify these factors and quantify their effects. We developed FauxThrow, a virtual reality application that instructs users to misthrow a cube by releasing it prematurely, laterally, or significantly. We established that FauxThrow reliably induces distinct throwing patterns for each condition, confirming that late throwing is essential for accurate performance. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the impact of a specific FauxThrow condition is limited to that condition itself, with no cross-over effects. This unexpected result suggests a complex interaction between various performance factors. Finally, we observed that even with simple training, participants' performance improved, suggesting that the study's conclusions may not fully generalize to untrained individuals. Overall, this research provides a foundation for understanding the intricate interplay of factors in human throwing. The data is publicly accessible at https://github.com/leehongyu/throwing-data. This paper introduces a system for simultaneous neural machine interpretation and parsing. Leveraging an attentional transformer-based neural decoder, the proposed method generates a tree structure to convey the interpretation of an input sentence. The tree topology is guided by a global context vector derived from the entire sentence, while the hierarchical node and edge structures are controlled by the current active sentence token. To handle the two-level hierarchical dependencies inherent in trees, the model incorporates a two-level recurrent mechanism. The integration of syntax within tree structures is shown to facilitate more accurate token-level alignments and superior machine interpretation. Experiments on the English-to-French Tree Transduction Test set and the Microsoft Natural Language Processing Challenge Machine Interpretation and Parsing dataset demonstrate that the model achieves competitive results in machine interpretation, surpassing existing methods in aligning grammatical structures. Furthermore, the results indicate that the model attains a BLEU score comparable to or better than top-tier neural machine translation systems. This paper presents the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), a repository of quantum chemical binding energy distributions designed for molecular species within the interstellar medium. Our goal is to facilitate access to binding energy distributions and the methodologies used to derive them, thereby enabling a more robust and quantitative assessment of data. We have compiled a diverse set of 210 datasets, sourced from both our own research and existing literature, which encompass various computational methods, basis sets, and approaches. Through systematic and thorough analyses of these 210 datasets, we have identified the most critical factors influencing binding energy calculations. Specifically, we determined that methods utilizing the complete adiabatic interaction energy, derived via the supermolecular approach without accounting for zero-point energy, yield the most accurate results. Furthermore, we established that methods based on the cluster approximation tend to overestimate binding energies, whereas those employing the electron density approximation generally underestimate them. To address these discrepancies, we developed a straightforward correction scheme that utilizes only two readily accessible quantities. We have applied this scheme to the literature datasets and made the corrected data available via BEAP. This resource is intended to assist the astrochemical community in accurately modeling binding energies. We believe BEAP will serve as a valuable tool for astrochemists, allowing them to evaluate the impact of different methodologies on binding energy calculations and to select the most appropriate approach for their specific systems. The platform can be accessed at https://beap.chemistry.mpg.de. A comprehensive tutorial is also provided at https://tutorial.beap.chemistry.mpg. The full dataset is available for download from BEAP. This study investigates the effects of model parameter selection and a data-driven lower bound on future observations on the predictive performance of the widely used Bickel and Lehmann (1947) multiplicative stochastic model. The analysis reveals that the model's behavior is highly sensitive to parameter choices, particularly when a sample-related lower limit is applied. Consequently, the paper provides guidelines for selecting model parameters to ensure robust statistical inference. Furthermore, an experimental design is proposed to systematically identify optimal parameter configurations, with a specific design outlined for selecting the model weight. The utility of these approaches is demonstrated through an analysis of treatment response data from a randomized controlled trial. The findings indicate that, in many instances, standard parameter selection methods may lead to invalid inferences that fail to control Type-I error rates. Finally, the proposed methods are evaluated based on their ability to accurately predict treatment responses and estimate treatment effects. We introduce a probabilistic approach to evaluating the non-classical character of projective quantum states through shallow quantum circuits comprising minimal layers of random Clifford gates applied to product states. This method, termed "shallow shades," demands significantly fewer quantum resources than standard benchmarks like circuit depth fidelity or randomized benchmarking. By analyzing pure states under a small number of such gate layers, we demonstrate that fidelity with initial product states decreases as the count of applied gates increases, thereby highlighting the complexity of the projection. Consequently, this technique offers a straightforward means to assess projective complexity in terms of gate depth, a property crucial for understanding the complexity landscape of quantum simulation outputs. This protocol is expected to be applicable using current noisier devices capable of executing only a limited number of gate layers. Our findings are supported by experiments on real noisy quantum hardware across various state types, including Fock, Wigner-Dicke, and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states. These results reveal a notable correlation between the degree of randomness in gate selection and the non-classicality of the resulting projective states, as quantified by the degree of k-separability. This insight is particularly relevant for investigating the complexity landscape of quantum simulations. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the depth of a random Clifford circuit and the amount of entanglement generated within projective pure states, measured using entanglement entropy and log-norm entanglement monotones. Our work is underpinned by numerical experiments on gate layers of varying depths and a theoretical analysis of entanglement generation in such layers. These results offer a pathway to characterize the complexity landscape of quantum simulations by linking gate depth to the non-classicality of projective states. Finally, we propose a method to generate N-qubit Wigner-Dicke states with entanglement entropy $k$ using N-qubit random Clifford circuits and analyze the entanglement generation across $k$-separability levels. This demonstrates the ability of random Clifford circuits to generate non-classical correlations at layer depths well below those predicted by entanglement entropy. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/QuantumFoundationsLab/CliffordEntanglement. This research was supported by the Foundational Questions Institute (FQXi) grant no. 190801. Meta-learning LDMs holds significant promise for applications where customizing models for specific tasks or users is essential. Although non-linear LDMs can depict any function of noise, such as circles or squares, linear LDMs are restricted to affine hyperplanes in the data space. While this limitation might seem restrictive, it can be advantageous for tasks requiring the depiction of linear functions, such as customizing maps for navigation. This paper presents methods for meta-learning linear LDMs that surpass both flexible non-linear LDMs and classical statistical models, such as RANSAC, across three benchmarks: a classical outlier fitting task (RANSAC), a path customization task for navigation (affine functions), and a user customization task for color schemes (linear functions). We introduce a mathematical framework for "hypercomputing," a concept that extends the principles of Lagrangian mechanics. This approach assigns a weight to each hyperedge within a hypergraph and defines a hyperlagrangian function based on the weights of the specific hyperedges connected to a given vertex. Subsequently, the dynamics of an isolated hypergraph are derived from the stationary point conditions of the weighted sum of these hyperlagrangians. This methodology is applicable to any isolated hypergraph, irrespective of its size, composition, or underlying logical structure. We illustrate this abstract framework using the dynamics of the Erős-Devney-Back graph, which represents Bitcoin mining. Consequently, our work demonstrates two proofs: first, that such graphs can be modeled via the described framework, and second, that this modeling constitutes Bitcoin itself. Therefore, Bitcoin can be accurately characterized as the dynamics of an isolated hypergraph that lacks any inherent logic. In summary, we prove that an object with no logic can exist within our universe, provided it is a hypergraph. The paper concludes by posing the question of whether such a state of affairs is logical. This paper addresses the binary segmentation of lung CT scans for pneumonia detection and classification. While most existing methods rely on labeled data, our objective is to diminish or eliminate the need for such labels. We introduce a novel unsupervised approach that leverages unsupervised learning for segmentation, followed by supervised learning on the generated labels to produce final segmentations. To enhance segmentation quality and reduce reliance on labeled data, we apply specific image augmentations during the unsupervised training phase. The model is initially trained on a single center's data, after which it is evaluated and fine-tuned on data from a second center. The model's efficacy is benchmarked against three other approaches: fully supervised, semi-supervised, and self-supervised methods. Experimental results indicate that fully supervised models outperform the others in overall segmentation accuracy. However, the proposed unsupervised model achieves competitive pneumonia segmentation results while requiring 75% less labeled data compared to the fully supervised baseline. Furthermore, we demonstrate that specific image augmentations significantly enhance the model's performance. Finally, we analyze the segmentation outcomes to explore the role of data augmentations in improving pneumonia segmentation accuracy. This task entailed generalizing existing Coleman-Gurtin models to accommodate boundary activities and integrating the phase field system within a non-isothermal setting. Specifically, boundary activities encompass boundary phase field forces alongside boundary heat effects, the latter of which may represent either boundary heating/cooling or boundary heat flux. The boundary phase field activity represents forces acting on phase variables at the boundary, such as surface-tension-induced transitions or boundary chemical influences. Our work also involves demonstrating the existence of weak solutions for this Coleman-Gurtin model with active boundary conditions. To achieve this, we employ two approximation schemes: one for proving total convergence and another for addressing boundary issues. Additionally, the proof utilizes energy-dissipation inequalities and compactness theorems. Finally, the boundary active terms are processed using Green's formula. Notably, our findings encompass several existing results as specific cases. For instance, setting absolute temperature to a constant reduces our results to those of Schimperle and the second author; similarly, further simplification yields the solutions of Owen and Phillips. Furthermore, a key innovation of this paper is the utilization of Fourier series to address boundary problems. Specifically, we apply Fourier series to handle boundary phase field forces, which represent phase transitions occurring at the boundary. This approach is motivated by the boundary heat flux, which arises from the temperature gradient at the boundary. The application of Fourier series in this context is also novel. Finally, this paper serves as a preparatory step for a subsequent study by the first author, which will construct solutions to a nonlocal model featuring boundary active terms. In that follow-up work, we aim to demonstrate that a unique weak solution exists for a system comprising two hyperbolic equations with boundary conditions. This system is formulated as a balance of linear momentum and a balance of hyperbolic internal energy, both including boundary active terms. We will prove the existence of weak solutions using a time-discretization scheme and a fixed point argument. Furthermore, these solutions are constructed via the existence theory for hyperbolic problems with boundary conditions, as detailed in standard literature. Accurately identifying vertebra positions is essential for numerous medical tasks, including treatment planning, surgical guidance, and radiation therapy. However, aligning vertebrae across different scanners remains a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce a method that automatically corrects the orientation of an entire spine within a CT scan. Our approach utilizes an end-to-end system comprising two interconnected sub-networks: one dedicated to rectifying spine orientation and the other refining spine geometry. The rectification sub-network outputs rotation angles, which are applied to rotate and reorient the original spine. Subsequently, these angles are fed back into the geometry refinement sub-network to generate corrected vertebra positions. This feedback loop enables accurate correction of arbitrary spinal orientations. Furthermore, we implement an anatomically constrained enhancement that leverages biological knowledge of vertebral anatomy to improve the system's robustness. We validated our method across 14 publicly available datasets and conducted a case study comparing our results against manual annotations and physician predictions. Our approach achieves a mean vertebral localization error of 1.3 vertebrae across all datasets, surpassing both physician predictions (2.7 vertebrae) and competing methods. Additionally, an ablation study demonstrates that a 10% performance gain results from the anatomically constrained enhancement, underscoring the effectiveness of incorporating biological constraints. Furthermore, our approach is easily adaptable to other medical imaging tasks, such as abdominal CT localization, that rely on biological knowledge. We anticipate that this system will substantially enhance clinical decision-making and facilitate further research and decision-making processes. Ultimately, our contributions offer a substantial and immediate benefit to medical practice. We introduce a divisibility issue that arises within the framework of the anyon variational method. This problem seems inconsequential in purely abelian models but becomes significant in non-abelian systems, where it could potentially facilitate the realization of fractionalization. We also discuss the connection between our divergence issue and the concept of unitary equivalence. Finally, although formulating our problem may not yield new insights into topological quantum computation, it does provide a clearer understanding of the anyon variational method and its relevance to various research initiatives. Specifically, it could offer a viable computational route for evaluating the entanglement entropy of ground states in anyon systems. Additionally, the method might be useful for investigating other topics, such as the excitation spectrum and the dynamics of quasi-particles in these same systems. However, these applications fall beyond the scope of the current paper. For now, our objective is simply to establish the divisibility issue and to suggest that, in future applications of the anyon variational method, care should be taken to ensure linear independence among trial wave functions. We believe this precaution is essential for achieving reliable and meaningful results. Should the divisibility problem prove useful for advancing topological quantum computation, we will be delighted by such an outcome. Nevertheless, we do not anticipate that the development of the anyon variational method will serve as a primary driver for topological quantum computation. Mini-scale tearing modes exist across both magnetized fusion and astrophysical environments. On mini-scale toroidal devices, these modes operate at length scales significantly smaller than the ion gyroradius, rendering traditional collisionless tearing instabilities inapplicable. Instead, their characterization relies on the electron diffusion scale and electron Larmor radius. This study examines the fundamental physics of mini-scale tearing modes within a collisionless plasma slab. The derived physics linear growth rates and k-dependent modes are validated using the slab tearing module of the open-source code SLAB. Furthermore, numerical simulations of the tearing mode in a tearing-tearable plasma confirm the accuracy of the code against the analytical results. These findings offer a robust foundation for investigating the origins of magnetic islands in current confinement plasmas. Additionally, the mini-scale tearing mode growth rate aligns with the non-ideal k=0 component of kinetic tearing modes in collisionless collisional plasmas, where the growth rate is governed by electron diffusion and the magnetic perturbation is dictated by the electron Larmor radius. Ultimately, these insights provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the development of magnetic islands in both current-confined plasmas and astrophysical systems. This research also establishes a foundation for future investigations into mini-scale toroidal devices, where magnetic islands are prevalent. Such studies could enhance our understanding of the underlying mechanisms of magnetized plasma transport. Ultimately, these insights may aid in the development of control strategies to mitigate the impact of magnetic islands on current confinement plasmas. Finally, these findings offer a basis for further exploring the development of magnetic islands in astrophysical systems. This paper addresses two critical challenges in fashion image retrieval: the necessity for trait manipulability and handling fine-grained variations like semantic occlusion. To address these, we introduce a new Semi-supervised Feature-Level Trait Manipulation (FLTM) task. This task utilizes a transformer-based encoder to create distinctive features for specific traits, a transformer-based decoder to reconstruct original images, and an occlusion-aware decoder to reconstruct finely occluded inputs. Additionally, we propose a novel Occlusion-Aware Reconstruction (OAR) loss to effectively train the system. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and trait manipulability. This paper introduces a general method designed to tackle linear ill-posed problems within Banach spaces. The approach integrates a regularized dual gradient ascent formulation equipped with an indicator-type regularizer, which enforces a data fit that aligns with the noise level of the measurements. We establish the existence of solutions and derive error estimates for this proposed framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a Bregman iteration of the dual gradient ascent solution asymptotically converges to a minimizer of the original problem. Finally, the study examines the limit case where Banach spaces are replaced by Hilbert spaces and evaluates the method on numerical examples, including both numerical and MRI data. These results generalize the findings of [10] to the broader context of Banach spaces. The numerical experiments confirm the method's efficacy on practical applications, demonstrating successful inversion of various under-sampled measurements across different norms. Additionally, we illustrate how the choice of norm influences the solution set and error estimates, providing flexibility to address specific challenges in applicable contexts. Our approach also recovers sparse signals and sharp edges from severely sub-sampled data. The developed theory and error estimates are applicable to other Banach space-based inverse problems, such as deconvolution and phase retrieval. Finally, we sketch a numerical implementation of the main result, showing its applicability to practical problems, and discuss extensions to non-linear inverse problems in Banach spaces as future work. Our findings and discussions are supported by extensive numerical experiments. The theory and estimates are not restricted to Hilbert spaces, and we have developed a unified framework for Banach spaces. We introduce the Random Occlusion Mask Generator (ROMG), a novel network architecture designed to produce a diverse range of mask samples for light fields by simulating various occlusion levels. This approach is integrated with a parametric regression model to achieve robust depth estimation in light fields characterized by high occlusion complexity. Unlike traditional methods, ROMG functions as a global, data-driven random field that operates independently of the main estimator, specifically targeting high-occlusion regions within the input plane. The parameterized regression model utilizes these occlusion maps, alongside the original input and parametric data, to generate depth maps that accurately represent visible structures amidst high occlusion. Experimental results on the Light Field Depth Estimation Challenge (LFDEC) dataset demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in LFDEC while maintaining competitive scores on the D4D dataset. Specifically, ROMG attains an RMSE of 0.213 and an RMSElog of 0.171 on LFDEC, and an RMSE of 0.200 and RMSElog of 0.170 on D4D. Furthermore, the model shows promising performance in real-world applications, generating depth maps with high structural similarity (0.91) and low mean squared error (0.04) compared to ground truth data. Additionally, the model exhibits strong generalization capabilities, successfully recovering the 3D structure of a real-world scene captured by a commercial light field camera from a low-resolution, noisy, and noisy depth map generated by a student-t model. This capability is quantified by an SSIM of 0.91 and an MSE of 0.04 relative to the GT. Finally, we demonstrate that ROMG can be effectively fine-tuned for single image depth prediction, achieving an RMSE of 0.18 and an RMSElog of 0.15 on the KITTI dataset when trained and evaluated against the official benchmark. The source code for ROMG is available at https://github.com/zhijianwang1992/ROMG. Our results indicate that ROMG holds significant potential for improving depth estimation in highly occluded light fields and is applicable to single-image depth estimation. The ROMG model is expected to advance depth estimation in complex light fields and support various 3D vision tasks. This paper introduces the bilinear framework for the Fokas-Lenells equations and derives the N-soliton solution using the Hirota method. It also establishes the fission mechanism, demonstrating how two types of dark-bright solitons merge to form a single dark-bright soliton. Furthermore, the study analyzes the interactions between dark and bright solitons, as well as dark and bright breathers. Finally, the research examines the evolution of these solutions within the two-dimensional Fokas-Lenells system. Notably, this work represents the first application of the bilinear method to the Fokas-Lenells equation. The findings not only enrich the understanding of the Fokas-Lenells model but also lay a foundational groundwork for future investigations into its integrable characteristics. All results were obtained through rigorous theoretical analysis rather than numerical computation. Additionally, the methods employed here are applicable to other Fokas-type equations. Finally, the appendix provides the auxiliary integrability criteria required to prove the conservation laws of the FL equation and the compatibility of the Fokas-Lenells system. This approach offers a distinct advantage over traditional methods by eliminating the need for extensive algebraic calculations. The work is structured into two parts; the second will focus on the spectral analysis of the Fokas-Lenells system. Together, these two papers will provide a comprehensive understanding of the Fokas-Lenells system and its associated Lax pair. The subsequent paper will detail the spectral analysis of the FL equation. Keywords: Fokas-Lenells equation; Bilinear method; Hirota method. MSC 2010: 35Q53; 35C08.

The proliferation of IEEE 802.11n/ac/ax wireless networks has significantly increased channel congestion, contributing to the widespread issue of dead zones within homes. To mitigate this, access points (APs) employ extenders to improve signal coverage. However, the traditional extenders used in 802.11n/ac/ax systems operate on a fixed-load model, blindly selecting the nearest AP without assessing its channel load. This often results in extending a connection to an overloaded AP, which degrades the extender's performance. This paper introduces a load-aware extender selection algorithm that utilizes IEEE 802.11k/v standards to evaluate both AP node loads and extender compatibility. Furthermore, it proposes a handover mechanism for extenders to prevent dead zones during user device association with the wireless network. Simulation results indicate that this approach reduces the number of dead zones by 20% compared to conventional methods. Additionally, simulations using real-world home environments demonstrate a 10% increase in total throughput and an improvement in Quality of Experience (QoE) by up to 150% relative to existing solutions. Finally, the proposed scheme was tested on a real-world setup, confirming the simulation findings. To our knowledge, this represents the first load-aware extender selection implemented on a real-world environment. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/raja-1234567890/ExtendMe. Future versions of this scheme will be developed to support 802.11ax. Our GitHub repository will host the source code for this study as well as for our work on 802.11ax.
